Returns byte[] AES-GCM encrypted token bytes. GenerateAndEncryptToken(ConnectionEncryptionData, string, long, long, int, byte[], AccessLevel, out byte[]?, string?) Builds, signs, and encrypts an auth token for transmission to the client over an AES-GCM encrypted channel. Used by login servers after successful SRP authentication. public static byte[]? GenerateAndEncryptToken(ConnectionEncryptionData encryptionData, string username, long loginServerId, long signingKeyId, int tokenExpirationMinutes, byte[] signingKey, AccessLevel accessLevel, out byte[]? rawTokenForHashing, string? realIp = null) Parameters encryptionData ConnectionEncryptionData Connection encryption state (keys, nonces, version). username string Account name to embed in the token. loginServerId long ID of the issuing login server. signingKeyId long Database ID of the signing key used for this token. tokenExpirationMinutes int Token validity duration in minutes. signingKey byte[] HMAC-SHA256 signing key. accessLevel AccessLevel Account access level to embed. rawTokenForHashing byte[] Raw token bytes (caller must hash for DB storage, then zero). realIp string Returns byte[] Encrypted token bytes for transmission, or null if generation failed. HashToken(byte[]) Computes the SHA-256 hex hash of a raw token for revocation tracking. public static string HashToken(byte[] rawToken) Parameters rawToken byte[] Raw token bytes to hash. Returns string Lowercase hex-encoded SHA-256 hash string. TryDecryptAndPartialParse(byte[], ConnectionEncryptionData, uint, out byte[]?, out long, out long) Decrypts a token from an AES-GCM encrypted payload and performs partial parsing to extract the login server ID for signing key lookup. Does NOT verify the HMAC. Call VerifyToken(byte[], byte[], bool, long, long) after obtaining the signing key. public static bool TryDecryptAndPartialParse(byte[] encryptedToken, ConnectionEncryptionData encryptionData, uint seq, out byte[]? rawToken, out long loginServerId, out long signingKeyId) Parameters encryptedToken byte[] AES-GCM encrypted token bytes from client. encryptionData ConnectionEncryptionData Connection encryption state. seq uint Broadcast sequence number. rawToken byte[] Decrypted raw token bytes (caller must zero after use). loginServerId long Extracted login server ID for signing key ownership checks. signingKeyId long Extracted signing-key ID for signing key lookup. Returns bool true if decryption and partial parse succeeded. Remarks Pre-decryption size gate: No explicit ciphertext length check is performed here because DecryptAES(byte[], byte[], byte[], byte[]) enforces a hard cap of MaxAesCiphertextSize (64 KiB) and a minimum of AesGcmTagLengthBytes (16 B). Since GCM decryption is authenticated, oversized or malformed payloads are rejected before any plaintext is exposed, making an additional pre-check redundant. Cross-checked against the HMAC-verified value. preParseSigningKeyId long Signing-key ID from partial parse. Cross-checked against the HMAC-verified value. Returns TokenService.TokenVerifyResult Verification result with parsed token fields.

api/auth/FishMMO.Auth.Implementation.Tot.title: Class TotpMasterKek | FishMMO Documentation
api/auth/FishMMO.Auth.Implementation.Tot.summary: Class TotpMasterKek Namespace FishMMO.Auth.Implementation Assembly FishMMO-AuthShared.dll The deployment-shared 32-byte master KEK that wraps every account's TOTP secret at rest (see EncryptTotpSecret(byte[], string, byte[], int)). public static class TotpMasterKek Inheritance object TotpMasterKek Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why this exists. The TOTP master KEK used to be derived from the LoginServer's HMAC token-signing key via LocalDeriveKmsProvider.DeriveKey("fishmmo-totp-master-key-v1"). That signing key is generated fresh with CryptoHelper.GenerateKey on every process start and then upserted over the stored row, and it is never read back. The consequences were: Every account's TOTP secret became undecryptable the moment the LoginServer restarted — and 2FA enrolment is mandatory at account creation, so this locked players out of their own authenticators. A second LoginServer derived a different key, so an account enrolled on one could not complete 2FA on another. Signing-key rotation orphaned every existing secret. Nothing outside the enrolling LoginServer process — the Control Panel included — could ever verify a code. The KEK is therefore a deployment secret, provisioned once and shared, exactly as signing_key_kek already is. It is stored in the deployment_secrets table under DatabaseKey as Base64 of 32 random bytes, and it must never be rotated without re-wrapping every stored envelope, because rotation invalidates them all. This type deliberately performs no I/O and has no database dependency, so the Unity server and the ASP.NET Control Panel can each fetch the row through their own service layer and share one validation and one set of rules. Fields DatabaseKey Row key in the deployment_secrets table. public const string DatabaseKey = "totp_master_kek" Field Value string KeyLength Required length in bytes. AES-256, matching EncryptTotpSecret's contract. public const int KeyLength = 32 Field Value int Methods Generate() Generates a fresh KEK as a Base64 string, for provisioning tools. public static string Generate() Returns string Remarks Generating a second one for a deployment that already has accounts enrolled makes every stored TOTP secret undecryptable. Provisioning must be create-if-absent, never overwrite. TryDecode(string?, out byte[]?, out string?) Validates and decodes a Base64 KEK fetched from deployment_secrets. public static bool TryDecode(string? base64Value, out byte[]? key, out string? error) Parameters base64Value string The stored value, or null/empty when the row is absent. key byte[] The decoded 32-byte key on success; otherwise null. error string A human-readable reason on failure; otherwise null. Returns bool true when a valid key was decoded.

api/auth/FishMMO.Auth.Implementation.htm.title: Namespace FishMMO.Auth.Implementation | FishMMO Documentation
api/auth/FishMMO.Auth.Implementation.htm.summary: Namespace FishMMO.Auth.Implementation Classes AccountData Holds account-related data for a server session, including authentication state, access level, and optional SRP authentication data. AccountManager<TConnection> Thread-safe base manager for account and connection data, including encryption state and the unified AuthState machine. All public methods are synchronized via a shared lock to support concurrent access from network broadcast handlers and async worker threads. Subclass SrpAccountManager<TConnection> or TokenAccountManager<TConnection> for authentication-method-specific behaviour. BaseAuthenticatorCore<TConnection> Abstract engine-independent base for all server authenticators. Provides X25519 ECDH handshake logic, stale-auth TTL sweeps, per-IP and global handshake rate limiting, and connection auth-state tracking — with no dependency on Unity, FishNet, or any game-engine type. Concrete implementations supply transport-specific callbacks (broadcast, disconnect, IP resolution) by implementing the abstract members, then call OnHandshakeReceived(TConnection, byte[], byte[], string, ushort, ushort, string) from their transport layer. ClientAuthenticatorCore Engine-independent client-side authenticator state machine. Implements the full SRP-6a + X25519 ECDH client auth flow, including cookie challenge echo, key agreement, token auth (World/Scene), SRP verify/proof, TOTP, and key material cleanup. Concrete implementations (e.g., FishNet ClientLoginAuthenticator) implement abstract callbacks for broadcasting messages and notifying the application layer. ClientSrpData Holds SRP (Secure Remote Password) authentication data and logic for a client-side session. ConnectionEncryptionData Holds per-connection encryption state including directional AES keys, nonce contexts, and negotiated protocol version. Keys are established via X25519 ECDH key agreement during the handshake phase. Thread-safety: nonce contexts use Interlocked internally for counter operations. CryptoHelper Static class providing cryptographic helper methods for X25519 ECDH key agreement, AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption, HKDF-SHA256 key derivation, HMAC-SHA256 signing, and authentication token management. BouncyCastle is used for cross-platform support on all Unity targets. CryptoHelper.GcmNonceContext CryptoHelper.TwoFactor TOTP two-factor authentication helpers. Uses OtpNet for TOTP generation/verification, AES-256-GCM for encrypting TOTP secrets at rest, and PBKDF2-SHA256 for hashing recovery codes. CryptoHelper.X25519EphemeralKeyPair Disposable container for an ephemeral X25519 keypair that enforces private-key zeroization via API ownership. The private key is never exposed to callers. HandshakeService Transport-agnostic service for X25519 ECDH handshake operations and stateless cookie challenge management. Provides both server-side and client-side key agreement, IP normalisation, and HMAC-SHA256 cookie computation/verification. KeyEnvelope AEAD envelope (AES-256-GCM) for wrapping symmetric key material at rest. LocalDeriveKmsProvider Local fallback IKmsProvider implementation that derives keys via HMAC-SHA256 from a long-lived root key. This is the legacy behaviour and is exposed here for parity; production deployments should swap in a hardware-backed implementation. ProcessHardening OS-level hardening hooks invoked early during server startup to reduce the risk that sensitive in-memory key material (TOTP KEK, signing keys, SRP verifier) leaks via process core dumps or ptrace from unprivileged peers. ServerSrpData Holds SRP (Secure Remote Password) authentication data and logic for a server-side session. SrpAccountManager<TConnection> SRP-specific account manager for LoginServer authentication. Extends AccountManager<TConnection> with SRP data population, connection account creation, and periodic sweep of stale unauthenticated connections. Auth state machine methods (TryAdvanceAuthState, HasAuthState) are inherited from the base AccountManager<TConnection>. SrpAuthenticatorCore<TConnection> Engine-independent SRP-6a authenticator core for LoginServer use. Extends BaseAuthenticatorCore<TConnection> with bounded-channel SRP verify/proof workers, TOTP two-factor authentication, kick-request tracking, and per-IP/per-account rate limiting — with no dependency on Unity, FishNet, or any game-engine type. Subclasses provide transport-specific callbacks for broadcasting auth results, disconnecting connections, resolving IP addresses, and performing database operations. SrpIdentity What SRP hashes as an account's identity, and how a sign-in identifier is written on the wire. SrpService Transport-agnostic SRP-6a authentication service. Provides server-side and client-side SRP field decryption/encryption, fake SRP salt derivation for anti-enumeration, and SRP session helpers. TokenAccountManager<TConnection> Token-specific account manager for World and Scene server authentication. Extends AccountManager<TConnection> with a simplified connection account creation method that does not require SRP state. TokenAuthenticatorCore<TConnection> Engine-independent token-based authenticator core for World/Scene servers. Extends BaseAuthenticatorCore<TConnection> with a bounded-channel token auth worker that decrypts, verifies, and revocation-checks client-supplied auth tokens issued by the LoginServer. Subclasses supply transport-specific callbacks (broadcast, database validation). TokenService Transport-agnostic service for authentication token operations. Provides token generation, encryption, decryption, and verification for both server-side issuance and client/server token authentication. TotpMasterKek The deployment-shared 32-byte master KEK that wraps every account's TOTP secret at rest (see EncryptTotpSecret(byte[], string, byte[], int)). Structs CryptoHelper.SessionKeys Container for derived session keys and prefixes. HandshakeService.ClientKeyAgreementResult Result of a client-side X25519 key agreement operation. HandshakeService.ServerKeyAgreementResult Result of a server-side X25519 key agreement operation. SrpAuthenticatorCore<TConnection>.SrpAccountLookupResult Result of an account fetch for SRP login. SrpProofRequest<TConnection> Immutable request data for async SRP proof processing. Contains encrypted proof and pre-validated account data to avoid blocking the network thread. Generic over connection type to maintain engine independence. SrpVerifyRequest<TConnection> Immutable request data for async SRP verification processing. Contains ENCRYPTED credentials to avoid blocking the network thread with decryption. Generic over connection type to maintain engine independence. TokenService.TokenVerifyResult Result of a token decryption and verification operation. Interfaces IKmsProvider Abstraction over a Key Management Service. Allows operators to plug in AWS KMS, Vault, PKCS#11/HSM, or other backends in place of the local-derive default. Enums CryptoHelper.AuthMessageType Message type identifiers for AAD binding. Values are fixed and must be used by both client and server. CryptoHelper.NonceSide Disposable container that owns a GCM session prefix and provides thread-safe nonce generation. Zeroes the prefix on dispose to prevent accidental reuse across sessions. SrpAuthenticatorCore<TConnection>.TwoFactorVerifyOutcome The result of checking a two-factor code. See VerifyTotpCodeAsync(string, string, byte[]).

api/database/FishMMO.Database.BulkWriteR.title: Struct BulkWriteResult | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.BulkWriteR.summary: Struct BulkWriteResult Namespace FishMMO.Database Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll What a bulk write actually did, as distinct from whether it errored. public readonly struct BulkWriteResult Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks A batched, version-gated write has a richer outcome than success or failure, and collapsing it to a boolean loses the part callers need. Rows go missing between the caller's list and the database for two entirely different reasons, and only one of them is benign: Filtered — the service refused to attempt the row at all: the character is deleted, the template is unresolvable, or two rows in the batch collided on the same key. The caller asked for something that could not be done, and nothing about the database's state explains it. This is worth surfacing. Superseded — the row was attempted and lost the version race, because the database already holds a version at least as new. Nothing is lost: the stored value is the more recent of the two. Routine under concurrency, and not a failure. The distinction matters because the caller cannot recover it on its own. The service deduplicates and filters before writing, so comparing Applied against the length of the list the caller passed in would attribute both causes to whichever the caller happened to assume. Unowned is the part of Filtered an ownership-gated write refused because the writer no longer holds that character's session claim (see CharacterWriteGate). It is counted inside Filtered on purpose: a refused row never reached the database, so every caller that clears its dirty marks only when nothing was filtered keeps them without having to know the gate exists. It is broken out only so the log can say why. Constructors BulkWriteResult(int, int, int) Initializes a new instance of the BulkWriteResult struct. public BulkWriteResult(int supplied, int attempted, int applied) Parameters supplied int Rows the caller handed over. attempted int Rows the statement tried. applied int Rows written. BulkWriteResult(int, int, int, int) Initializes a new instance of the BulkWriteResult struct. public BulkWriteResult(int supplied, int attempted, int applied, int unowned) Parameters supplied int Rows the caller handed over. attempted int Rows the statement tried. applied int Rows written. unowned int Rows refused because the writer does not hold their character's claim; part of the filtered count. Properties Applied Rows inserted or updated. public int Applied { get; } Property Value int Attempted Rows the statement actually tried, after the service dropped duplicates and anything belonging to a character or template it could not resolve. public int Attempted { get; } Property Value int Empty An outcome with nothing to do — an empty or fully filtered batch. public static BulkWriteResult Empty { get; } Property Value BulkWriteResult Filtered Rows the service declined to attempt. Non-zero means the caller's batch contained something it could not act on — see the remarks on BulkWriteResult. public int Filtered { get; } Property Value int IsComplete True when every supplied row was written. public bool IsComplete { get; } Property Value bool Superseded Rows attempted but not written, because the database already held a version at least as new. Benign. public int Superseded { get; } Property Value int Supplied Rows the caller handed to the service. public int Supplied { get; } Property Value int Unowned Of the Filtered rows, those refused because the writer does not hold the session claim of the character they belong to. Never attempted, like every filtered row. public int Unowned { get; } Property Value int Methods ToString() Returns a short description of the outcome, suitable for a log line. public override string ToString() Returns string Formatted counts. Operators operator +(BulkWriteResult, BulkWriteResult) Adds two outcomes, for a service that writes its batch in more than one statement. public static BulkWriteResult operator +(BulkWriteResult left, BulkWriteResult right) Parameters left BulkWriteResult First outcome. right BulkWriteResult Second outcome. Returns BulkWriteResult The combined outcome.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Accou.title: Class AccountAdminData | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Accou.summary: Class AccountAdminData Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll An account as an operator needs to see it. public sealed class AccountAdminData Inheritance object AccountAdminData Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This type must never carry Salt, Verifier, TotpSecret, VerifyCode or DiscordLinkCode. AccountData carries all of them because the login path is the one caller that needs them: SRP cannot verify a password without the salt and the verifier, and the TOTP check cannot run without the secret. An operator view that carried the same fields would put every account's password material — and every account's second factor — behind nothing but an access-level check, on a surface that is read by a panel, serialized to JSON, and logged. The whole point of SRP is that the verifier never leaves the authentication path; a stolen verifier is an offline dictionary attack against that account with no further access needed, and a stolen TOTP secret makes the second factor forgeable forever. That is precisely why this is a separate type and not a projection, a subset view, or a nullable-ed copy of AccountData. A projection is one careless MapEntityToDto edit away from leaking, and the leak would be invisible at the call site. A type that has no such field cannot leak it, and a future field added to AccountData does not silently appear here. TotpEnabled and TotpVerifiedAt are safe and are deliberately kept: an operator answering "why can this person not sign in" needs to know whether a second factor is in the way, and neither field helps forge a code. Properties AccessLevel Account access level. Zero is AccessLevel.Banned, so this doubles as the ban flag — there is no separate banned column. public byte AccessLevel { get; set; } Property Value byte Address Postal address, as they gave it. public string? Address { get; set; } Property Value string Remarks Personal data, like RealName. BanReason { get; set; } Property Value string BannedBy Operator account that applied the ban, when recorded. public string? BannedBy { get; set; } Property Value string BannedUntil When a temporary ban lifts (UTC); null for a permanent ban, or for no ban. public DateTime? BannedUntil { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? CharacterCount How many non-deleted characters the account owns. public int CharacterCount { get; set; } Property Value int Remarks Soft-deleted characters are excluded because the count exists to answer "is this a real, played account", and a row an operator already deleted is not evidence of that. Country Country or region, as they gave it. public string? Country { get; set; } Property Value string Created When the account was created (UTC). public DateTime Created { get; set; } Property Value DateTime DiscordDmClaimedAt When the bot took the DM to send it, or null. Set with no sent time means it never confirmed. public DateTime? DiscordDmClaimedAt { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? DiscordDmLastError Why the DM has not gone out yet, as the bot last recorded it, or null. public string? DiscordDmLastError { get; set; } Property Value string DiscordDmSentAt When the one verification DM was delivered, or null. public DateTime? DiscordDmSentAt { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? DiscordUserId The Discord user the account is linked to, or null. public long? DiscordUserId { get; set; } Property Value long? DiscordUsername The Discord username the player gave, lowercase, or null. public string? DiscordUsername { get; set; } Property Value string DiscordVerified Whether the Discord channel has been proven. public bool DiscordVerified { get; set; } Property Value bool Email Contact email, or null when the account has none. public string? LoginLockedUntilUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? MuteReason The reason recorded with the mute. public string? MuteReason { get; set; } Property Value string Muted Whether an account-wide chat mute is set. Name Account name, as the row stores it. This is the account's primary key. public string Name { get; set; } Property Value string Phone Phone number in E.164 form, or null. public string? Remarks Null with TotpEnabled true means setup was started and never finished, which is the state an operator is usually looking at when a player reports being locked out. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Accou.summary: Class AccountProfileRules Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll The rules for the optional contact and identity details on an account. public static class AccountProfileRules Inheritance object AccountProfileRules Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks One copy, here, because three surfaces accept these fields — the game's account creation, the Control Panel's registration, and the panel's self-service — and the database is the one layer all three write through. Fields InvalidDiscordUsernameError The one refusal for a Discord username that is not one. public const string InvalidDiscordUsernameError = "Enter your Discord username as it appears on your profile, for example fishfan or FishFan#1234." Field Value string MaxAddressLength Longest postal address accepted. public const int MaxAddressLength = 512 Field Value int MaxCountryLength Longest country or region accepted. public const int MaxCountryLength = 64 Field Value int MaxDiscordTagLength Longest stored Discord name: a username, #, and a four-digit discriminator. public const int MaxDiscordTagLength = 37 Field Value int MaxDiscordUsernameLength Longest Discord username Discord allows, not counting a discriminator. public const int MaxDiscordUsernameLength = 32 Field Value int MaxRealNameLength Longest real name accepted. public const int MaxRealNameLength = 128 Field Value int MinDiscordUsernameLength Shortest Discord username Discord allows. public const int MinDiscordUsernameLength = 2 Field Value int Methods NormalizeDiscordUsername(string?) Normalises a Discord username in either form Discord uses: a unique username (fishfan), or a name with its four-digit discriminator (FishFan#1234). public static string? NormalizeDiscordUsername(string? input) Parameters input string Returns string The normalised username, or null when it is not one. Remarks Trimmed, a leading @ dropped, and lowercased, because Discord matches both forms without regard to case. A unique username is 2 to 32 lowercase letters, digits, underscores and periods, never two periods together. A name with a discriminator is the older form, whose names were freer — capitals, spaces, most of Unicode — so its name part is held only to its length and to what Discord never allowed in one: @, #, :, a code fence, control characters. The discriminator is exactly four digits. Anything in neither form is refused rather than guessed at: the bot looks the name up exactly, and a DM sent to the wrong person is a verification code in a stranger's hands. NormalizePhone(string?) Normalises a phone number to E.164: a leading + and 8 to 15 digits. public static string? NormalizePhone(string? input) Parameters input string Returns string The normalised number, or null when it is not one. Remarks Spaces, hyphens, dots and parentheses are dropped, because that is how people write numbers. A leading 00 becomes +. A number without a country code is refused rather than guessed at: an SMS sent to the wrong country's number is a verification code in a stranger's hands. TryValidate(AccountProfileData, out AccountProfileData, out string) Validates and normalises a profile. Blank optional fields become null. public static bool TryValidate(AccountProfileData input, out AccountProfileData clean, out string error) Parameters input AccountProfileData What was submitted. clean AccountProfileData The profile to store. error string Why it was refused, written for the person who filled the form in. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Accou.summary: Class AccountVerificationRules Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Which verification codes an account is sent and asked for. One copy, shared by the game's login server and the Control Panel, so the two can never disagree about whether an account is let in. public static class AccountVerificationRules Inheritance object AccountVerificationRules Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Any one channel verifies the account. A player may choose email, SMS and a Discord DM together; a code goes out on each, and whichever is entered first sets verified. Verification is required when the server switches at least one channel on. A channel the player chose is asked for only when it is switched on and the account can receive it — SMS needs a phone number, Discord a username. When none of the player's choices qualifies, the account falls back to the first channel that does, in the order email, SMS, Discord: every account has an email address, so a player who picked a switched-off channel is still asked for a code rather than let in without one. Only an account that can receive no enabled channel at all is verified without a code, because no code could ever reach it. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Arena.title: Class ArenaMatchComposer | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Arena.summary: Class ArenaMatchComposer Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Decides which waiters fill which team of an arena match. Pure, so it is testable without a database and so the transaction that applies it has nothing to decide. public static class ArenaMatchComposer Inheritance object ArenaMatchComposer Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Pre-made groups are kept together and only ever fill a team of their own size or larger. A group of three queued for 3v3 is one team; a group of three queued for 4v4 is three of a team's four seats and one solo player takes the fourth. A group larger than a team can never be seated and is skipped — it should have been refused at queue time, and the composer does not paper over that by splitting it. First come, first served. Candidates arrive in queue order. Teams are filled in that order with a first-fit packing: each unit (a group, or a solo) goes on the lowest-numbered team it fits on. Two groups that could complete a match but were behind a solo who fits anywhere still get seated, because the solo takes one seat and leaves the rest. This is not an optimal bin packing and does not try to be; the queue is expected to be short and fairness by wait time matters more than squeezing one extra match out of an unlucky arrangement. Banding and balancing are opt-in through ArenaComposeOptions. A rating band keeps the match within reach of whoever has waited longest — the caller widens it as they wait, so a lonely high rating eventually finds a game. Balancing assigns units, largest and highest-rated first, to whichever team currently has the lower total rating and room, which keeps the two sides' averages close without abandoning the fairness of first-come eligibility: who plays is still decided by the queue, only which side they play on moves. A match is composed only when every team is exactly full. Nothing partial is ever returned, because a match with uneven teams is not a match. Methods TryCompose(IReadOnlyList<ArenaCandidate>, int, int, ArenaComposeOptions, out List<ArenaSeat>) Tries to fill teamCount teams of teamSize from the candidates, in order, within a rating band and balanced when asked. public static bool TryCompose(IReadOnlyList<ArenaCandidate> candidates, int teamCount, int teamSize, ArenaComposeOptions options, out List<ArenaSeat> seats) Parameters candidates IReadOnlyList<ArenaCandidate> teamCount int teamSize int options ArenaComposeOptions seats List<ArenaSeat> Returns bool TryCompose(IReadOnlyList<ArenaCandidate>, int, int, out List<ArenaSeat>) Tries to fill teamCount teams of teamSize from the candidates, in order. public static bool TryCompose(IReadOnlyList<ArenaCandidate> candidates, int teamCount, int teamSize, out List<ArenaSeat> seats) Parameters candidates IReadOnlyList<ArenaCandidate> Eligible waiters in queue order (oldest first). Members of one group must all be present; a group missing members is treated as the members present. teamCount int Teams to fill. At least 2. teamSize int Seats per team. At least 1. seats List<ArenaSeat> Receives one seat per player when a match was composed. Returns bool True when every team is exactly full.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.BetaC.title: Class BetaCodeFormat | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.BetaC.summary: Class BetaCodeFormat Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll The shape of a beta code, and of the program name a batch of codes is minted under. public static class BetaCodeFormat Inheritance object BetaCodeFormat Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Twelve characters from a 32-symbol alphabet with 0/O and 1/I removed, displayed as three groups of four. A code is read off an email or a forum post and typed by hand, and those are the pairs a player cannot tell apart in most fonts: a code that is valid but untypeable is a support ticket. 32^12 is 2^60, so guessing one is not a strategy even before the login server's rate limits. The stored form is the displayed form, hyphens included. Every path that accepts a code from outside runs it through Normalize(string?) first, so abcd efgh jkmn and ABCD-EFGH-JKMN are one code and the unique index on beta_codes.code is over one spelling of it. Fields Alphabet The symbols a code is drawn from: A–Z and 2–9 without O and I. public const string Alphabet = "ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ23456789" Field Value string CodeLength Significant characters in a code, hyphens excluded. public const int CodeLength = 12 Field Value int DisplayLength Length of the displayed and stored form, XXXX-XXXX-XXXX. public const int DisplayLength = 14 Field Value int GroupSize Characters per displayed group. public const int GroupSize = 4 Field Value int InvalidProgramError The message for a program name that fails IsValidProgram(string?). public const string InvalidProgramError = "A program name is 1 to 32 characters of lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores." Field Value string ProgramMaxLength Longest program name. public const int ProgramMaxLength = 32 Field Value int Methods Generate() Generates a new code in display form from a cryptographic random source. public static string Generate() Returns string Remarks Rejection sampling rather than byte % 32: a byte that falls in the incomplete top range is thrown away, so every symbol is exactly equally likely. With a 32-symbol alphabet 256 divides evenly and nothing is ever rejected, but the loop stays correct if the alphabet is ever changed to a size that does not — which is exactly when a modulo would quietly start favouring the first few letters. RandomNumberGenerator.GetInt32 would do this for us, but it is .NET 6 and this assembly targets netstandard2.1. IsValidProgram(string?) Whether a program name is 1–32 characters of [a-z0-9_-]. public static bool IsValidProgram(string? program) Parameters program string Returns bool Remarks Tests the name as given; callers normalise with NormalizeProgram(string?) first. The name is an identifier the login server's configuration lists, so it is kept to characters that survive a config file, an environment variable and a URL without quoting. Normalize(string?) Canonicalises a code typed or pasted by a person. public static string? Normalize(string? code) Parameters code string The code as entered. Returns string The code as XXXX-XXXX-XXXX, or null when it is not a well-formed code. Remarks Uppercases, drops hyphens and whitespace wherever they appear, and requires exactly twelve alphabet characters. Anything else — including a 0 or O the player believed they saw — is null rather than a best guess: silently mapping a mistyped symbol onto a valid one would turn a typo into somebody else's code. NormalizeProgram(string?) Trims and lowercases a program name. Null becomes the empty string, which is not valid. public static string NormalizeProgram(string? program) Parameters program string Returns string Remarks Lowercased so "Closed-Beta" in a config file and "closed-beta" typed into the panel are one program: a mismatch here would lock every tester out while the codes looked fine.

That type is the game's transfer shape and carries neither the soft-delete columns nor the session lease, because the game never loads a deleted character and a server already knows whether it holds the lease itself. An operator needs exactly those two things: whether the row is deleted, and whether somebody is holding it. It carries no sub-entity data. Value IReadOnlyList<CharacterBuffData> Remarks Null and empty are different instructions. A save that carries a set — including an empty one — makes the stored buffs exactly that set: rows it does not name are deleted, in the same transaction as the character row and under the same version and ownership checks, so a set is written only when the row it was captured with is. Null leaves the stored buffs untouched, which is what every snapshot that did not come from a live character means: a fetched row, the world server's flag edits, a character being created. Why the set rides the row instead of its own table write. Buffs used to be upserted on their own and never deleted, so a buff that expired or was dismissed after it was first saved came back at the next login. Deleting what the set no longer names needs an ordering that survives two saves landing out of order — an older save must never re-add a row a newer one dropped — and per-buff versions cannot give one: a buff re-applied after it ended is a new instance whose counter starts again, and a set that became empty leaves no row to carry a version at all. The character row's own version is the per-character ordering that already exists, and writing the set under it is what makes the set as ordered as the row. Never populated by a fetch; buffs are read through ICharacterBuffService. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Chara.summary: Struct CharacterDialogueChoiceData Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One character's persisted "already chosen" bitmask for a single dialogue template. public struct CharacterDialogueChoiceData Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Why a bitmask and not a row per choice. A dialogue template can track at most DialogueTemplate.MaxTrackedChoices (16) choices, and both the server session and the wire format (DialogueStartBroadcast.CachedChoices) already carry that state as a single short. A row-per-choice table would store the same 16 bits as up to 16 rows of roughly 40 bytes each — a ~300x expansion of a value that is read and written whole, never queried by individual bit — and every read would have to fold the rows back into the mask the caller actually wants. The mask is stored as it is used. Volume. One row per character per caching template, so the table is bounded by (characters x templates with CacheDialogueChoices enabled) — not by the number of conversations held, which is what an event-log shape would have grown with. Rows are only ever created for templates that opt in. When dialogue assets change. The bit index comes from DialogueTemplate.GetChoiceBitIndex, which counts choices positionally in authoring order. Appending a node or a choice at the end is safe: existing bits keep their meaning. Inserting or deleting a choice in the middle, or reordering nodes, shifts every later bit, so a stored mask would then describe different choices than the ones the player made — the failure mode is a one-time reward appearing already-taken, or an exhausted one becoming available again. That is an authoring-time hazard, not something the store can detect, so the service exposes ResetTemplateAsync for content to be re-cut deliberately. When a template is removed. Its rows are left in place. A template ID that does not resolve on this process is not evidence the asset was deleted — scene servers load different content sets, and a load failure looks identical — so deleting on a lookup miss would quietly destroy live players' one-time-choice history during a partial content rollout. An orphaned row costs two bytes and is invisible; that is the cheaper mistake. Constructors CharacterDialogueChoiceData(long, int, short) Initializes a dialogue choice mask. public CharacterDialogueChoiceData(long characterID, int templateID, short choices) Parameters characterID long Character that made the choices. templateID int Dialogue template ID. choices short Bitmask of choices already taken. Fields CharacterID Character that made the choices. public readonly long CharacterID Field Value long Choices Bitmask of choices already taken in this template. Bit N corresponds to the Nth choice in authoring order, as computed by DialogueTemplate.GetChoiceBitIndex. public readonly short Choices Field Value short TemplateID Dialogue template ID (a CachedScriptableObject ID). public readonly int TemplateID Field Value int

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Chara.summary: Struct CharacterItemData Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One item belonging to a character, in whichever container currently holds it. public struct CharacterItemData : IVersioned<CharacterItemData> Implements IVersioned<CharacterItemData> Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Extension Methods VersionExtensions.WithIncrementedVersion<T>(T) Remarks Replaces CharacterInventoryData, CharacterEquipmentData and CharacterBankData, which were three copies of one shape distinguished only by the table they were written to. Container is what that distinction became. ID identifies the ITEM, not the slot. That is the whole point of the merge. Under the previous schema a row was keyed (character_id, slot), so moving an item between two slots produced two different rows with two different ids and passing two items through one slot gave them the same id. Here the row is keyed by ID and Container and Slot are ordinary mutable columns, so an item keeps its number from the moment it is first written until it is destroyed — across slot moves, across container moves, and across sessions. An ID of zero means "not yet written": the database assigns one on first insert and returns it, and the caller writes it back onto the runtime item. See ICharacterItemService.PersistAsync. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Chara.summary: Enum CharacterPersistOutcome Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll What became of one row of a batched character save. public enum CharacterPersistOutcome : byte Fields Invalid = 5 The row was malformed (no id, no version, a claim for a different character) and was not attempted. NotFound = 2 The character does not exist or has been deleted. OwnershipLost = 4 The caller supplied a claim and no longer holds it. Another server is authoritative for the character, and the caller must stop simulating it rather than retry. Replayed = 1 The row already holds exactly this version under this caller's claim: a replay of a write that landed, typically a transaction retried after its commit reply was lost. Nothing is missing, so callers treat it as Saved. Saved = 0 The row was written. Stale = 3 A newer version is already stored. Nothing is lost: the stored row is the newer of the two. Remarks The same distinctions the single-row save reports as error codes, per row, because one statement now speaks for many characters and each needs its own answer: a lost claim means the caller must stop simulating that character, a stale row means a newer write is already stored, and neither says anything about the rows around it.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Chara.title: Struct CharacterWaypointData | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Chara.summary: Struct CharacterWaypointData Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One page of a character's discovered waypoints in one scene: a 64-bit mask where bit N is waypoint page * 64 + N. public struct CharacterWaypointData Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Why a mask. A waypoint is a bit — discovered or not — and a scene has tens of them, all read together on login and written together on save. A row per waypoint would spend roughly forty bytes on each bit and have the load path fold them back into the set the game actually wants. The mask stores the set as it is used, exactly as CharacterDialogueChoiceData does for dialogue choices; pages keep it unbounded rather than capped at 64 per scene. Merge, not replace. Bits are only ever set, so the write is mask | EXCLUDED.mask: idempotent under retries, and two scene servers writing during a transfer converge on the union rather than one discarding the other's discoveries. That is also why there is no version column — there is no stale write to reject. When scenes change. The bit index is the waypoint's authored index, which is stable by contract (see Waypoint.WaypointIndex). A renamed scene orphans its rows; they cost eight bytes each and are never read. A removed waypoint leaves a bit nothing consults. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.ChatA.summary: Class ChatAdminData Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One persisted chat message as an operator needs to see it. public sealed class ChatAdminData Inheritance object ChatAdminData Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Deliberately not ChatData. That type is the game's transfer shape: the scene servers fetch it to re-broadcast a message, so it is built for delivery and its fields are the ones delivery needs. This one is built for reading a report, which is a different job — it keeps both timestamps rather than treating them as interchangeable, because the question an operator is answering ("when did they say it") and the question the chat pump is answering ("what is new since my cursor") are not the same question. It carries no Version. The chat table is append-only in practice — nothing updates a message after it is written — so the concurrency token tells an operator nothing, and a column on an operator screen that is always 1 trains people to ignore columns. Every string here is player-supplied. Message is whatever somebody typed into the chat box, and CharacterName reaches this table denormalized, without passing back through the character row's validation. Anything rendering these has to escape them; this is the one screen in an operator panel whose content is written by the person being investigated. Properties AccountName The sender's account name, as recorded when the message was written. public string AccountName { get; set; } Property Value string Channel The channel, as the raw ChatChannel value. public byte Channel { get; set; } Property Value byte Remarks Kept as the byte rather than the enum so a row written by a newer server, carrying a channel this build has no name for, still reads back instead of throwing. Whatever presents this is responsible for naming it: "channel 5" is not an answer to a report. CharacterID The character that sent the message. public long CharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks The character row may no longer exist: chat outlives deletion by design, which is the whole reason the names below are denormalized onto it. A panel linking to the character has to tolerate the link leading nowhere. CharacterName The sender's character name, as recorded when the message was written. public string CharacterName { get; set; } Property Value string Remarks A snapshot, not a lookup. If the character has since been renamed this shows the name they were using at the time, which is what a report about that name needs. ID Primary key. Also the tie-break that orders messages inside one clock tick. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long Message The message body, exactly as the player typed it. public string Message { get; set; } Property Value string SceneServerID The scene server the message originated on. public long SceneServerID { get; set; } Property Value long ServerReceivedTime When the server received the message (UTC). public DateTime ServerReceivedTime { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks This is the legal-audit instant: it is stamped by the scene server that took the message from the player, so it survives the message sitting in a persistence batch. TimeCreated When the row was written (UTC). public DateTime TimeCreated { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks The row's own clock, and the column every index and every ordering here uses. It can trail ServerReceivedTime by the width of a persistence batch, so the two are shown separately rather than one standing in for the other. WorldServerID The world server the message originated on. public long WorldServerID { get; set; } Property Value long

Fields DefaultPageSize The page size used when a caller asks for none. public const int DefaultPageSize = 50 Field Value int Remarks Fifty, rather than the twenty-five an account search uses: a conversation is read in sequence, and a page that ends mid-exchange makes an operator page back and forth to reconstruct it. AccountName { get; set; } Property Value string Remarks The account filter is what catches somebody using a second character to continue the same harassment, which is why it is separate from CharacterName rather than one combined "who" box. Channel Exact ChatChannel value to match, or null for every channel. public byte? Channel { get; set; } Property Value byte? Remarks A byte rather than the enum so an unrecognised channel can still be searched for, and so a caller parsing a query string does not have to know the enum to pass one through. CharacterName Exact character name to match, or null for any sender. public string? CharacterName { get; set; } Property Value string Remarks Exact, not a prefix, and there is no index behind it — see the search implementation. An operator handling a report has the name in front of them, copied from the report, so matching it exactly costs them nothing and keeps the scan it forces as narrow as it can be. FromUtc Inclusive lower bound on TimeCreated, or null. public DateTime? FromUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Remarks This is the bound that actually narrows a search: it is the one an index on time_created can start a range scan from. ToUtc alone cannot. HasNarrowingFilter Whether this query narrows the search by something other than the message text. public bool HasNarrowingFilter { get; } Property Value bool Remarks Deliberately does not count ToUtc or Channel. An upper time bound with no lower bound spans the whole history up to that instant, and a channel filter divides the table by a ten-valued column where the common values hold most of the rows — neither one turns a scan into anything smaller. Counting them would make the guard below feel satisfied while changing nothing about what the database does. Page 1-based page number. public int Page { get; set; } Property Value int PageSize Rows per page. Clamped by the service, whatever is asked for. public int PageSize { get; set; } Property Value int Text Substring the message must contain, or null for no text filter. public string? Text { get; set; } Property Value string Remarks A substring, unlike Query, which is a prefix precisely to stay index-serviceable. There is no prefix version of this filter that answers the question: a report says "they called me <slur>", and the slur is in the middle of the sentence. So this one accepts the leading wildcard it needs. What it does not accept is being the ONLY filter. Supplied alone, it is refused with a validation error rather than silently bounded; see the search implementation for why refusing beats defaulting. Remarks Exclusive so that two adjacent windows tile without a row appearing in both, matching the convention AdminAuditService.SearchAsync already set.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.ChatR.summary: Class ChatReadWindow Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Where a reader of the chat table has got to, and which rows it has already handled, on the database clock. Pure bookkeeping: no database, no network, one thread at a time. public sealed class ChatReadWindow Inheritance object ChatReadWindow Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why a window and not a cursor. A chat row is stamped by the database clock when its INSERT runs, and becomes visible only when its transaction commits. Two writers can commit in the opposite order to their stamps — and to their IDs, which are also taken at the INSERT. A reader that pages by "everything after the last row I saw", by ID or by (time, id), moves past a row that has not committed yet and never sees it (hot-path audit H5). So the reader reads from Watermark, held CommitWindow behind what it has settled, and skips by ID what it has already handled (SnapshotSeenIds() for the query, Admit(long, DateTime) for the rows it returns). A row is read exactly once as long as it commits within the window of its stamp; ChatService.PumpCommitWindowSeconds is that window, shared with the writers. Why a floor. Nothing stamped before the reader's first read is ever read. The first read starts at the database's own "now" and later reads reach back a window from their start, so without the floor the second read would replay the window before the reader started: a restarted reader would republish what it had already published. The scene servers' pump (ChatPumpCursor, in the game's server code) keeps the same window and adds per-recipient relevance on top; this is the window alone, for a reader that takes every row, such as the Discord relay. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Daemo.summary: Class DaemonCommandExpiry Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Whether a claimed daemon command may still be executed, judged without the daemon's wall clock. public static class DaemonCommandExpiry Inheritance object DaemonCommandExpiry Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A command is stamped, claimed and completed by the database clock. A daemon that compared the command's deadline with its own UtcNow measured the skew between its host and the database along with the time left: one running five minutes fast refused every command it was given (five minutes is the lifetime), and one running slow executed commands after the operator had stopped waiting for them. So the claim returns the seconds left, measured by the database in the statement that claimed the row (ExpiresInSeconds), and the daemon counts them down on a monotonic clock, which no wall-clock step, correction or time-zone change can move. The daemon anchors that count when it SENDS the claim, not when the reply arrives: the database measured somewhere in between, so an early anchor can only overstate the time elapsed. Every error is therefore toward refusing, because a restart carried out after its requester stopped waiting is the failure this check exists to prevent. Returns bool Remarks Exactly zero left is expired: the claim takes a row only while expires_utc > now, so this is the same boundary seen from the daemon. Remarks The kind exists because the sender does something after a successful delivery that only makes sense for one of them. A verification mail ends the new account's grace period: once verification_email_sent_at is stamped, an unverified account can no longer sign in to the game or the panel until it verifies. A password reset mail must leave that stamp alone — stamping it would lock an unverified player out of everything at the exact moment they finished recovering their password. This is a column and not a look at the subject line. Five separate subject literals already exist across the LoginServer, the panel's registration, email-change and reset paths; deciding a lockout from one of them would mean a reworded subject silently changes who can log in, with nothing anywhere saying so. Verification is 0 so that the column's NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 gives every row written before this existed — and every row still written by a caller that does not name a kind — the meaning it already had.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Email.title: Class EmailQueuePage | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Email.summary: Class EmailQueuePage Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One page of the email queue, with the numbers that say whether it is moving. public sealed class EmailQueuePage Inheritance object EmailQueuePage Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks OldestPendingCreatedAt is the number this whole read exists for. Account verification reaches a player through this table and nothing else. When no login server is claiming rows — the process is down, SMTP is refusing, the credentials expired — registration stops working for every new account, and there is no other symptom: the website accepts the registration, the row is written, and the player simply never gets their mail. A depth count does not show it either, because a healthy queue and a dead one both read as a small number on a quiet shard. The age of the oldest unclaimed row is what separates them, and it is the one value on this page an operator should be alarmed by. Both ages are supplied because they answer different questions. OldestPendingCreatedAt asks whether anything is draining the queue. OldestUnsentCreatedAt asks how long the longest-waiting account has been waiting, which includes rows a login server claimed and then stopped reporting on — those are stuck too, and a pending-only number would show zero while they sat there forever. Properties Counts How many rows are in each state, over the whole table. public EmailQueueCounts Counts { get; set; } Property Value EmailQueueCounts Items The rows on this page. public IReadOnlyList<EmailQueueAdminData> Items { get; set; } Property Value IReadOnlyList<EmailQueueAdminData> OldestPendingCreatedAt When the oldest Pending row was enqueued (UTC), or null when nothing is waiting to be claimed. public DateTime? OldestPendingCreatedAt { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? OldestUnsentCreatedAt When the oldest row that has not been delivered was enqueued (UTC), or null when everything has gone out. Includes claimed and failed rows. public DateTime? OldestUnsentCreatedAt { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Page 1-based page number. public int Page { get; set; } Property Value int PageSize Rows per page, after clamping. public int PageSize { get; set; } Property Value int ReadAtUtc When the read was taken (UTC), by the database clock. public DateTime ReadAtUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks The ages above are differences against this instant, computed by the caller rather than stored. It is the database's time because the database stamps created_at (a column default), so both sides of every age come from one clock and a panel clock that disagrees with the database's cannot turn a young queue into an alarm or an old one into silence. It used to be the panel's own DateTime.UtcNow, and the alarm moved with the panel host's clock. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Email.title: Enum EmailQueueState | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Email.summary: Enum EmailQueueState Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Where an email queue row is in its life. public enum EmailQueueState Fields Claimed = 1 Claimed by a login server, which has not yet said whether it went out. Failed = 2 Claimed, and the last delivery attempt recorded an error. Pending = 0 Queued and unclaimed. Waiting for a login server to pick it up. Sent = 3 Delivered. Remarks There is no state column. email_queue models delivery with three nullable columns — sent_at, claimed_at and last_error — and the state is the combination of them. This enum is that combination named, decided in one place so the filter, the counts and the badge in the browser cannot disagree about what "failed" means. The order of the tests matters and is part of the definition: sent_at set — Sent. Delivered; nothing else about the row matters. claimed_at null — Pending. In line, waiting for a login server to take it. This is the state the queue drains from, and the state that piles up when no login server is running. last_error set — Failed. A login server took it and the delivery attempt errored. otherwise — Claimed. A login server holds it and has not reported an outcome. Pending is tested before the error so that a retried row reads as pending again: retrying releases the claim but deliberately keeps last_error, because the text of the failure is the only evidence of why it failed and an operator retrying a second time needs it. Were the order reversed, a row put back in line would still read as failed.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.title: Enum DaemonAppStatus | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.summary: Enum DaemonAppStatus Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll What a daemon last reported about one supervised application. public enum DaemonAppStatus Fields Exhausted = 4 Not running and the daemon has given up restarting it. Distinct from Stopped on purpose: a process the daemon is still trying to revive needs patience, and one it has abandoned needs a person. Healthy = 1 Running and passing its health checks. Starting = 2 Running, but still inside its initial check delay. Stopped = 3 Not running. StoppedByOperator = 5 Deliberately stopped by an operator, and not to be restarted. Unknown = 0 The daemon has not determined a state yet. Remarks Reported, not inferred. The panel must not decide a process is down because a row looks old — a stale row means the daemon stopped talking, which is a different fault with a different fix, and conflating them sends an operator to the wrong machine.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.title: Enum DaemonCommandVerb | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.summary: Enum DaemonCommandVerb Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll What a daemon may be asked to do. public enum DaemonCommandVerb Fields Restart = 2 Stop and launch again. Start = 0 Launch a supervised application that is not running. Stop = 1 Stop a supervised application and leave it stopped. Remarks A closed enumeration, and it must stay closed. A command queue that can start processes on other machines is the most dangerous thing in this system, well past banning an account — and the property that contains it is that a command row selects from a fixed list of verbs against an application the daemon already knows, rather than carrying anything the daemon executes. There is no path here, no arguments, no environment and no shell. Those live in the daemon's own configuration file on disk, so changing what a name actually runs requires filesystem access to that host, not a database insert. Anyone who reaches the database can restart a FishMMO process; they cannot make the daemon run something new. If a verb is ever added that takes free text, that containment is gone.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.title: Enum GroupFinderQueueStatus | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.summary: Enum GroupFinderQueueStatus Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Where a group finder queue row is in its life. public enum GroupFinderQueueStatus Fields Matched = 1 Matched. party_id and instance_id are set, and the scene server hosting the character will move them on its next pump. Waiting = 0 Waiting for enough players, or for a run with room. Remarks Two states, deliberately. Forming a group — claiming the waiters, creating their party, opening their instance and marking them matched — is one database transaction, so there is no window in which a row is "being matched" for anything to observe, and therefore no state for it. A row is either still waiting or it names the party and instance it is bound for.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.title: Enum LeaderboardSourceKind | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.summary: Enum LeaderboardSourceKind Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Which stored number a leaderboard ranks characters by. public enum LeaderboardSourceKind : byte Fields ArenaSeasonRating = 1 arena_rating.rating in the active season. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.title: Enum MaintenanceStatus | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.summary: Enum MaintenanceStatus Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Where a maintenance operation, or one of its targets, has got to. public enum MaintenanceStatus Fields Cancelled = 3 The shutdown was called off. The servers are still locked. Cancelling clears shutdown_at_utc and nothing else: the locked column that scheduling set in the same statement stays set, because halting a shutdown and reopening a world to players are separate decisions. A cancelled operation therefore leaves every target closed to new arrivals until somebody unlocks it, and every surface that reports this status has to say so. Completed = 2 The target's rows now read the way a stopped server's rows read. A world server deletes its registration as it exits, so a missing row is the completion signal there. A scene server keeps its row and instead clears its own consumed deadline and lock on teardown, so that is the completion signal for a scene target. The two tiers genuinely differ; see the service for the rules. Draining = 0 Locked, with a shutdown deadline written, and the deadline has not arrived. Players already on the servers are still playing; that is the point of the drain. Nobody new is admitted above Player, because scheduling the shutdown locked every target in the same statement. Failed = 4 It did not happen, and the record says why rather than pretending otherwise. The cases are: the row could not be written at all; the deadline passed and the server is still pulsing; or the target was not pulsing when the operation was planned and has not pulsed since, so nothing ever read the row that was written for it. ShuttingDown = 1 The deadline has passed and the target has not yet been observed to stop. A short state in a healthy shutdown — the server acts on the deadline within a pulse — and a state that turns into Failed rather than lingering, so a server that ignored its deadline is not displayed as "shutting down" indefinitely. Remarks One enumeration for both the operation and its targets, because they are the same five answers and an operator reading a target row asks the same question they ask of the operation. The operation's value is derived from its targets on every read — see IMaintenanceService.AdvanceAsync — and is never a claim made independently of them. None of these values mean "the panel did something to a process". A maintenance operation writes the locked and shutdown_at_utc columns on each target's own row, and the servers adopt those on their next pulse. So Draining means the rows are written and the deadline has not arrived; Completed means the server rows now look the way a stopped server's rows look. Both are observations, which is the strongest thing a database can honestly say about a machine it cannot address.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums.summary: Enum SupportTicketStatus Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data.Enums Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Where a support ticket has got to. public enum SupportTicketStatus Fields AwaitingPlayer = 2 Staff have asked the player something and are waiting for an answer. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Group.title: Struct GroupFinderPulseData | FishMMO Documentation

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Guild.summary: Class GuildAdminData Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One guild, as a support agent needs to see it in a list. public sealed class GuildAdminData Inheritance object GuildAdminData Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Deliberately not GuildData. That type is the game's transfer shape: it carries the three advertisement strings a client renders and nothing about who is in the guild, because a client that is in a guild already has its roster. A support agent has neither, and the first two questions asked of any guild in a ticket are how many members it has and who leads it. There is no leader column, and LeaderName is a derivation, not a fact. A guild's ladder is the set of guild_rank rows it owns and a membership row stores a rank_order; the leader's seat is the highest rung the ladder defines, and a member leads by reaching it — the same test the game server applies. Nothing stops two members reaching it, so when several do, the earliest to join is named and LeaderIsAmbiguous is set rather than picking one silently. A guild with no ranks has no seat, and so no leader to name. Zero is an ordinary answer, not a missing read. public int MemberCount { get; set; } Property Value int Name Display name. Player-supplied text. public string Name { get; set; } Property Value string RankCount Rungs on the guild's rank ladder. public int RankCount { get; set; } Property Value int Tags Comma-separated recruitment tags, as the guild wrote them. public string Tags { get; set; } Property Value string TimeCreated When the guild was founded. public DateTime TimeCreated { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Version Row version, which every write moves. public long Version { get; set; } Property Value long

Actor: officer. Target: applicant. ApplicationDeclined = 15 An application was declined. Actor: officer. Target: applicant. Created = 1 The guild was created. Actor: founder. Demoted = 6 A member was demoted. Actor: demoter. Target: demoted. Joined = 2 A member joined. Actor: the member. Kicked = 4 A member was removed. Actor: remover. Target: removed. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.KickR.summary: Class KickRequestReadWindow Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Where a game server's poll of the kick requests has got to, and which requests it has already handled, on the database clock. Pure bookkeeping: no database, no network, one poll at a time. public sealed class KickRequestReadWindow Inheritance object KickRequestReadWindow Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why the database clock. A request is stamped by the database when it is written. The poller's cursor used to be seeded from its own host clock and compared with those stamps: a host running ahead of the database skipped every kick stamped inside the lead, for good. Every instant here comes from the database, through KickRequestPage, and the one local measurement — how long ago the reader started — only ever reaches the database as a duration (FirstReadLookbackSeconds). Why a window and not a cursor. A request becomes visible when its transaction commits, some time after its stamp: a ban writes its kick inside a longer transaction, stamped at that transaction's start. Two writers can therefore commit in the opposite order to their stamps, and a strict (time, id) cursor that has moved past a stamp before its row committed never sees the row. So the poll reads from Watermark, held CommitWindow behind what it has settled, and skips what it has already handled (SnapshotHandled(out long[], out DateTime[])), as the chat pump does (ChatReadWindow). A kick is acted on exactly once as long as it commits within the window of its stamp. Why handled is (id, stamp). Requests are upserted per account: kicking an account that already has a row keeps the row's ID and moves its stamp. Keyed on the ID alone, that second kick would be skipped as already handled. Why a floor. Nothing before the reader's first read is re-read by the window's reach back; the first read itself starts at the moment the reader began watching. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.PlotT.summary: Enum PlotTaxChargeOutcome Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll How one offline tax charge ended. public enum PlotTaxChargeOutcome : byte Fields OwnedElsewhere = 2 A server holds the owner's session. Nothing was charged; the plot is not retried until the deferral passes. OwnerGone = 4 The period was won but the owner's character is deleted or gone, so it cannot pay. Treated exactly as Unpaid: the mark is set and the grace period runs. Paid = 0 The bill was won and the owner paid all of it; any earlier missed-payment mark came off in the same commit. Skipped = 3 Not attempted this time: the plot or its owner was locked by another transaction, or the period had already moved on. Nothing changed; the next sweep sees it again if it is still due. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Serve.summary: Class ServerAdminData Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One server process, as an operator needs to see it. public sealed class ServerAdminData Inheritance object ServerAdminData Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks One type for all three tiers rather than three near-identical ones. A login server has no character count and no control columns, so those are simply zero and null for it — which is honest, because the reason they are absent is that a login server has no players on it and cannot be locked, not that the panel failed to read them. Staleness is not stored and is not decided here. Only LastPulse is a fact; whether that counts as dead depends on the pulse interval the deployment runs, so the caller is given the age and the threshold and makes the call. A boolean baked into the row would be a judgement frozen at read time. The ages are measured by the database, never by the reader. PulseAgeSeconds and ShutdownInSeconds are computed inside the statement that read the row, against the clock that stamped LastPulse. The panel used to subtract the stamps from its own DateTime.UtcNow, so a panel host running a minute fast marked every healthy server stale and one running slow hid a dead one, which is the only thing the board's staleness exists to show. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.Serve.summary: Struct ServerControlState Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll The operator-controlled lifecycle state of a world or scene server. public readonly struct ServerControlState Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks The database row is the authority for both fields, not the process. A server writes them only when an operator asks it to; on every pulse it reads them back and adopts whatever it finds. That inversion is what makes the controls usable at all — the previous arrangement had each server write its own in-memory locked flag on every pulse, so anything that set the column out of band was overwritten within five seconds, and nothing in the process ever set the flag either. It also means any tool that can write the row (the Discord bot, the Control Panel, psql) controls the servers, exactly as the kick-request table already does for accounts. Constructors ServerControlState(bool, DateTime?, double?) Creates a control state. public ServerControlState(bool locked, DateTime? shutdownAtUtc, double? shutdownInSeconds) Parameters locked bool Whether the server is closed to new arrivals. shutdownAtUtc DateTime? Scheduled stop time, or null. shutdownInSeconds double? Seconds until shutdownAtUtc as the database measured them when it read the row. Ignored, and stored as null, when no shutdown is scheduled. Fields Locked Whether the server is closed to new arrivals. public readonly bool Locked Field Value bool Remarks A drain, not an eviction: players already on the server keep playing. Elevated accounts are admitted anyway, so locking a world does not lock out the operator who has to go in and look at it. ShutdownAtUtc When this server stops, or null when no shutdown is scheduled. public readonly DateTime? ShutdownAtUtc Field Value DateTime? Remarks An absolute UTC instant on the row, so every process that reads it agrees on which shutdown is scheduled. It is the schedule's identity (a changed value is a rescheduled shutdown) and what the logs print. It is NOT what a reader counts down against: that would compare the database's clock with the reader's, see ShutdownInSeconds. ShutdownInSeconds Seconds from the moment the database read this row until ShutdownAtUtc, measured by the database clock; zero or negative once the deadline has passed. null exactly when no shutdown is scheduled. public readonly double? ShutdownInSeconds Field Value double? Remarks The deadline is stamped by whoever scheduled it and read by every server the shutdown concerns, so no reader's own clock is a fair judge of how far away it is. Each server used to subtract DateTime.UtcNow from the instant: a world host running a minute fast stopped a minute early, one stepped forward by NTP stopped at once, and every process serving one world counted down to a different moment. The database measures the remaining time inside the statement that reads the row, and a reader anchors that on its own monotonic clock the moment the reply arrives. Properties HasShutdown Whether a shutdown is scheduled at all. public bool HasShutdown { get; } Property Value bool

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Data.World.summary: Class WorldClockText Namespace FishMMO.Database.Data Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll The written forms of world time, shared by every surface that reads or writes the world clock (the Control Panel, and available to the in-game /admin time commands) so the two can never disagree about what a typed value means. public static class WorldClockText Inheritance object WorldClockText Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A WORLD TIMESTAMP is the calendar epoch (Unix seconds) plus the world milliseconds, written yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff in the invariant culture with no zone: it is UTC-style arithmetic on a calendar, not anybody's local time. The index is the portal's authored, per-scene stable index (PortalActivation.PortalIndex). Merge, not replace. Permanent ORs and ActiveUntilUtc takes the later of the stored and written moments, so the write is idempotent and two servers opening the same portal at once end with the longer opening.
