api/database/FishMMO.Database.Database.h.summary: Class Database Namespace FishMMO.Database Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Main orchestrator and facade for the FishMMO database layer. Provides centralized access to database services, health monitoring, and metrics. This class initializes the database context factory, discovers and registers concrete service implementations, and exposes monitoring points to the host application. public sealed class Database : IDatabase, IAsyncDisposable Inheritance object Database Implements IDatabase IAsyncDisposable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Constructors Database(IConfiguration, bool, int?, int, int) Initializes a new instance of the Database class with a pre-built IConfiguration. Creates the DbContext factory, discovers and registers all services, and sets up monitoring. public Database(IConfiguration configuration, bool enableLogging = false, int? commandTimeout = null, int healthCheckWarningMs = 100, int healthCheckCriticalMs = 500) Parameters configuration IConfiguration Application configuration containing an Npgsql section. Cannot be null. enableLogging bool Enable sensitive data logging for development (default: false). commandTimeout int? Optional database command timeout override in seconds. healthCheckWarningMs int Health check warning threshold in milliseconds (default: 100). healthCheckCriticalMs int Health check critical threshold in milliseconds (default: 500). Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown when configuration is null. DatabaseException Thrown when initialization fails due to configuration or registration issues. Properties DbContextFactory Gets the database context factory. Exposed for direct access when needed (e.g., custom queries, migrations, raw SQL). In most cases, prefer using services from ServiceRegistry. public INpgsqlDbContextFactory DbContextFactory { get; } Property Value INpgsqlDbContextFactory Remarks Exposes the configured INpgsqlDbContextFactory used to create short-lived NpgsqlDbContext instances. Prefer service interfaces from ServiceRegistry for application operations. HealthMonitor Gets the database health monitor for connectivity and performance checks. Use this to verify database availability and response times. public DatabaseHealthMonitor HealthMonitor { get; } Property Value DatabaseHealthMonitor Remarks The DatabaseHealthMonitor performs lightweight connectivity and response-time checks against the underlying database using INpgsqlDbContextFactory. MetricsTracker Gets the database metrics tracker for operation statistics. Provides insights into query performance and connection pool usage. public DatabaseMetricsTracker MetricsTracker { get; } Property Value DatabaseMetricsTracker ServiceRegistry Gets the service registry for accessing database services. Provides type-safe access to all registered database service interfaces. public IDatabaseServiceRegistry ServiceRegistry { get; } Property Value IDatabaseServiceRegistry Remarks The service registry is populated during construction by discovering implementations in the FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Services assembly. Consumers should call TryGet<TService>(out TService) to obtain services. Methods DisposeAsync() Disposes the database orchestrator asynchronously. Delegates to ShutdownAsync(CancellationToken) for graceful cleanup. public ValueTask DisposeAsync() Returns ValueTask Remarks NOTE: GC.SuppressFinalize is intentionally omitted because this class does not have a finalizer. Calling SuppressFinalize on a non-finalizable object is a no-op but adds unnecessary metadata. If a finalizer is ever added in the future, add GC.SuppressFinalize(this) back. Shutdown() Shuts down the database orchestrator. Unity-friendly synchronous shutdown (safe to call from main thread). After shutdown, new DbContext creation should be rejected. public void Shutdown() ShutdownAsync(CancellationToken) Asynchronously shuts down the database orchestrator. A refusal a service decided — a validation failure, a stale write, a missing row, a unique or check violation — carries the service's own words, and a caller may show them. Remarks Identifier Safety: The schema and table name are resolved from EF Core metadata (not user input). However, SQL identifiers cannot be passed as parameters. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class AccountBetaCodeEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll The permanent record that an account redeemed a beta code. public class AccountBetaCodeEntity Inheritance object AccountBetaCodeEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A row is written once, in the same transaction that takes a use from the code, and is never updated or deleted. Whether the account still has access is decided at read time from the code it points at: a revoked code ends it, an expired one does not. No foreign keys, deliberately. The link is evidence of who was admitted to which program, and it has to outlive anything that might happen to either side. Codes are revoked, never deleted, and accounts are never deleted in this system, so a cascade could never fire in normal operation — its only possible effect would be to erase the evidence when somebody removed a row by hand, which is precisely the case the record exists for. Code and Program are copied from the code at redemption. Neither ever changes after a code is minted, so the copies cannot drift, and a staff lookup of "who is in closed beta" reads one table. Access checks still join to the code, because revocation lives there. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class AdminAuditEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One operator action, recorded permanently. public class AdminAuditEntity Inheritance object AdminAuditEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Append-only by construction. There is no update path and no delete path on IAdminAuditService, and no property here that an action could sensibly revise: a row describes a thing that happened, and what happened does not change afterwards. That is also why it carries no xmin concurrency token, unlike every other entity in this assembly — a concurrency token exists to mediate competing writers of one row, and this row has exactly one writer, once. The actor is a plain string with no foreign key, deliberately, and this is the single most important decision in the table. A cascade from accounts would mean that deleting an operator erases the record of everything that operator did, which is precisely the case the log exists for. The name is copied in, not referenced. Refusals are recorded as well as successes. An operator repeatedly failing to reach something is more interesting than one who succeeds, and a log that holds only successes cannot tell the difference between "never attempted" and "attempted and stopped". Properties Action What was done, as a stable dotted identifier such as character.rename. Stable because queries and retention rules are written against it; the human wording belongs in the interface, not in the data. public string Action { get; set; } Property Value string ActorAccessLevel The actor's access level at the moment of the action, not now. A later demotion must not rewrite what the record says they were allowed to do at the time. public byte ActorAccessLevel { get; set; } Property Value byte ActorName The account that acted, copied from accounts.name without a foreign key so the record survives the account. public string ActorName { get; set; } Property Value string ActorSessionID The panel session the action came from, or null. Lets a run of actions be tied together as one sitting even when the session row is long gone. public long? ActorSessionID { get; set; } Property Value long? Details What actually changed, as compact JSON, or null. Free-form because the shape differs per action; it is for a human reading one row, never for querying. public string Details { get; set; } Property Value string ID Surrogate key. Ascending, so it also orders ties within a timestamp. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long IpAddress The address the request came from, as the panel resolved it. public string IpAddress { get; set; } Property Value string OccurredUtc When the action was attempted, UTC. public DateTime OccurredUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Outcome Why it was not, when it was not. public string Outcome { get; set; } Property Value string Reason The reason the operator gave. The point of the whole exercise. public string Reason { get; set; } Property Value string RequestKey The writer's once-per-request identity: a retry after a lost reply finds the row its first attempt wrote instead of writing a second one. Null for rows written without one. public Guid? RequestKey { get; set; } Property Value Guid? Source Where the action was taken: panel or game. public string Source { get; set; } Property Value string Remarks Both write to this one table deliberately. An operator who cannot do something in the panel and then does it from a chat command should not thereby leave a gap in the record, and "show me everything this person did" must not require two queries against two logs with two different shapes. Succeeded Whether the action was carried out. public bool Succeeded { get; set; } Property Value bool TargetID The target's identifier, as text, because targets are keyed by number in some tables and by name in others and one column has to hold both. public string TargetID { get; set; } Property Value string TargetName The target's name as it read at the time. Denormalised on purpose: a character renamed later must not make this row describe the wrong thing. public string TargetName { get; set; } Property Value string TargetType What kind of thing was acted on: character, account, and so on. public string TargetType { get; set; } Property Value string

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class BetaCodeEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll A beta code: one admission ticket, possibly multi-use, to a named test program. public class BetaCodeEntity Inheritance object BetaCodeEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Codes are minted in batches under a program (alpha, closed-beta, a private test). While beta mode is on, only an account linked to a live code of an active program may register or sign in; see AccountBetaCodeEntity for the link. Codes are revoked, never deleted. A code row is what every account link points at, and deleting one would leave links recording an admission to a program nobody can look up. Revocation keeps the row and ends the access it granted. Redemption does not rely on the xmin token. It is one conditional UPDATE — use_count < max_uses, not revoked, not expired — whose WHERE clause is the concurrency control, so two accounts racing for the last use cannot both get it. The token is there for staff edits made through EF, which would otherwise overwrite a redemption that landed between their read and their save. Properties Code The code in XXXX-XXXX-XXXX form. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class CharacterDialogueChoiceEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Database entity holding one character's "already chosen" bitmask for one dialogue template. public class CharacterDialogueChoiceEntity Inheritance object CharacterDialogueChoiceEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Deliberately carries no Version column, unlike the character tables beside it. The optimistic-concurrency machinery exists to decide which of two competing writes to the same row wins, and for this row the answer is always "both": the mask only ever gains bits, so the write merges with choices | EXCLUDED.choices rather than overwriting. That is idempotent under the execution strategy's retries and safe when a character's old and new scene servers overlap during a transfer — and, critically, it can never lose a bit, which is the only direction that matters: a lost bit is a one-time dialogue reward the player can take again. Also carries no soft-delete columns. There is nothing to tombstone — a mask is either there or the character has taken no tracked choice in that template, which reads the same. Clearing one is an authoring operation (see ResetTemplateAsync) and is a real delete. Properties Character Navigation to the owning character. public CharacterEntity Character { get; set; } Property Value CharacterEntity CharacterID Foreign key to the owning character. Part of the composite primary key. public long CharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long Choices Bitmask of choices already taken in this template, at most DialogueTemplate.MaxTrackedChoices (16) bits wide. public short Choices { get; set; } Property Value short TemplateID Dialogue template identifier. Part of the composite primary key. public int TemplateID { get; set; } Property Value int TimeCreated Row creation timestamp (UTC). public DateTime TimeCreated { get; set; } Property Value DateTime TimeUpdated Timestamp of the most recent merge into this row (UTC). public DateTime TimeUpdated { get; set; } Property Value DateTime

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.title: Class DaemonAppEventEntity | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class DaemonAppEventEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One observed change in a supervised application, appended when a heartbeat differs from what was already stored. public class DaemonAppEventEntity Inheritance object DaemonAppEventEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This table exists because DaemonAppEntity has no memory. That row is overwritten on every heartbeat, so it says only what is true now. A game server that restart-looped at three in the morning and came back before anybody looked leaves no trace anywhere: the status reads Healthy, the restart counter has been reset, and the event is gone. This is the record of what the supervisor saw while nobody was watching. It is not process output, and the daemon writes none of it. Every column is either a value from a closed enumeration, an integer, or a name the daemon already reported on its own row — there is no free-text column, and nothing here is a string the daemon chose. The rows are derived server-side by comparing an incoming report against the stored one, which is what keeps a compromised daemon from putting attacker-chosen text on an operator screen. A description of the transition is composed from these values at read time; it is never stored and never supplied. Adding a column the daemon fills with text would undo that in one commit. Append-only, and free of foreign keys, for the reasons that govern admin_audit_log: nothing updates or deletes a row, there is no xmin token because there is no second writer to mediate, and the host and application are copied as text so that decommissioning a host does not take the history of what it did with it. A cascade here would delete the evidence exactly when a machine is removed for having misbehaved. Properties AppName The supervised application, by the name the daemon knows it as. public string AppName { get; set; } Property Value string HostName The host that reported it, copied as text with no foreign key. public string HostName { get; set; } Property Value string ID Surrogate key. Also the tie-break for rows inside one timestamp. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long ObservedUtc When the heartbeat carrying this observation was recorded. public DateTime ObservedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks The moment the database saw it, not a clock reading from the reporting host. A timestamp chosen by the daemon would let a host with a wrong clock — or a lying one — reorder the history of every other machine on the page. PreviousProcessID The process id before, when there was one. public int? PreviousProcessID { get; set; } Property Value int? Remarks The whole story on its own in one case: a status that reads Healthy on both sides with a different process id is a crash and a relaunch that finished inside one poll interval. Without this column that beat is indistinguishable from nothing happening. PreviousRestartAttempts The restart count before, or null on a first sighting. public int? PreviousRestartAttempts { get; set; } Property Value int? Remarks Not in the original sketch for this table, and added because a decrease is meaningful: the daemon zeroes its counter the moment an application checks out healthy again, so a fall from three to zero is the recovery. A row that carried only the new value would show a zero indistinguishable from an application that never failed. PreviousStatus What was stored before this observation, or null when this is the first sighting. public DaemonAppStatus? PreviousStatus { get; set; } Property Value DaemonAppStatus? Remarks Null is a fact rather than a gap: it means no row existed for this application, which is what a newly configured application — or one the panel has never seen a heartbeat for — looks like. ProcessID The process id now, when it is running. public int? ProcessID { get; set; } Property Value int? RestartAttempts Restarts in the current failure cycle, as reported. public int RestartAttempts { get; set; } Property Value int Status What the daemon observed this time. public DaemonAppStatus Status { get; set; } Property Value DaemonAppStatus

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class DaemonCommandEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One instruction for a daemon: start, stop or restart a named application. public class DaemonCommandEntity Inheritance object DaemonCommandEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The security of the whole control plane is the shape of this row. It carries a verb from a closed enumeration and the name of an application the daemon already supervises. It carries no path, no arguments, no shell and nothing else the daemon executes. Somebody who can write to this table can restart a FishMMO process; they cannot make a game host run something new. Adding a column that changes that would turn a database password into remote code execution. Claimed before it is executed. A daemon takes a command atomically and stamps itself on it, so two daemons cannot both act on one row, and a daemon that dies mid-command leaves a claimed row that can be seen rather than one that is silently done twice. And it expires. A command nobody collected is abandoned rather than executed late: restarting a world server twenty minutes after an operator asked, once they have moved on and players are back on it, is worse than never doing it at all. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class GroupFinderQueueEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One character waiting in the dungeon group finder, or matched by it and about to be moved. public class GroupFinderQueueEntity Inheritance object GroupFinderQueueEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The queue lives in the database rather than in any one process because the players in it are spread across scene servers. Whoever presses Find Group first may be standing on a different scene server from the four people who complete their group, and the only thing all of those servers share is this table. A row is created when a character asks to find a group and deleted when they leave the queue, log out, or are moved into the run the finder built for them. A character has at most one row — the queue is not a wishlist — which is what character_id's unique index enforces. LastPulse is a heartbeat written by the scene server the character is connected to. A row whose heartbeat has gone quiet belongs to a server that died or a character that vanished without the disconnect path running, and it is excluded from matching and eventually reaped rather than being handed a party it cannot join. Dungeons never set it — the finder fills a party's dungeon through the open run instead. Decides who has waited longest. public DateTime TimeCreated { get; set; } Property Value DateTime TimeMatched When the row was matched (UTC), or null while waiting. public DateTime? api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class MaintenanceOperationEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One planned maintenance window across a set of servers. public class MaintenanceOperationEntity Inheritance object MaintenanceOperationEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This row is the plan, and the plan is the whole point. Taking a shard down is a sequence — lock so nobody new joins, wait for players to drain, then stop — and done by hand across a dozen servers somebody misses one. Writing it down means the operator can close their laptop: the drain does not live in a browser tab. It carries no steps to execute. Everything that acts on a server is written the moment the operation starts, into the servers' own locked and shutdown_at_utc columns, which each server reads back on its next pulse and adopts. The deadline is absolute, so the drain counts down inside every server process whether or not anything else is running — no panel, no scheduler, no tab. What is left here afterwards is a record and an observation, which is why Status is derived from the target rows rather than advanced by anybody. No foreign key from StartedBy to accounts, for the audit log's reason: who took a shard down must outlive the account that did it. Properties CancelReason Why it was cancelled. public string CancelReason { get; set; } Property Value string CancelledBy The operator account that cancelled it. public string CancelledBy { get; set; } Property Value string CancelledUtc When it was cancelled. public DateTime? CancelledUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? CompletedUtc When every target reached a terminal state. public DateTime? CompletedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? DeadlineUtc The absolute instant every target is due to stop. public DateTime DeadlineUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks Stored on the operation as well as on each target so a cancelled or half-written window still says what it was going to do, and so the drain's end can be read without loading every target row. DrainSeconds How long players were given, in seconds. public int DrainSeconds { get; set; } Property Value int ID Surrogate key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long Name What the operator called this window. public string Name { get; set; } Property Value string Outcome What happened in the end, in words. public string Outcome { get; set; } Property Value string Reason Why. Mandatory at the API, and recorded in the audit log as well. public string Reason { get; set; } Property Value string RequestKey The writer's once-per-request identity: a retry after a lost reply finds the row its first attempt wrote instead of writing a second one. Null for rows written without one. public Guid? RequestKey { get; set; } Property Value Guid? Remarks Here a second write would not even be written: the retry found its own window's targets live and refused itself with "already in maintenance window N", so the operator was told a window they had just started had failed. StartedBy The operator account that planned it. Copied, with no foreign key. public string StartedBy { get; set; } Property Value string StartedUtc When the plan was written, which is when the servers were locked. public DateTime StartedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Status Where the window has got to. Derived from the targets; see the remarks. public MaintenanceStatus Status { get; set; } Property Value MaintenanceStatus Targets The servers in this window. public ICollection<MaintenanceTargetEntity> Targets { get; set; } Property Value ICollection<MaintenanceTargetEntity>

A world server deletes its registration as it exits — that deletion is precisely how this row knows the shutdown worked — so a foreign key would either block the server from stopping or cascade away the record of the window that stopped it. The server id and the name are copied for the same reason. The columns split into two groups, and keeping them apart is what makes this row readable: *_written_utc is what this operation did, and observed_* is what the server's row said the last time anybody looked. A disagreement between them is not a bug, it is the interesting case — somebody rescheduled the shutdown by hand, or the server never read it. Note What was concluded, and why, in words. public string Note { get; set; } Property Value string ObservedCharacterCount Players on it at that moment. ObservedLastPulseUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Characters are global — the same character can be played on any world server, deliberately, so that friends can play together wherever they are — but a party spans scene servers by being replicated through the database, and that replication is scoped to a world server. So this is the column that lets a character's party membership be dropped when they arrive on a different world server, rather than being carried into one where it cannot work.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class PasswordResetTokenEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll A single outstanding "forgot my password" token. public class PasswordResetTokenEntity Inheritance object PasswordResetTokenEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Only the SHA-256 of the emailed token is stored, exactly as WebSessionEntity stores only the hash of a session identifier: a database read must not yield working reset tokens. A plain hash is correct here rather than a slow KDF because the token is 32 bytes of RandomNumberGenerator output and therefore not guessable — the hash exists to stop a leaked table being replayed, not to resist a dictionary. Possession of a token proves control of the mailbox and nothing else. Redeeming one replaces the SRP credentials and must never touch totp_enabled, totp_secret, totp_verified_at or the recovery codes: if an emailed link could also clear the second factor, a compromised mailbox would be a complete account takeover and the second factor would protect nothing. There is deliberately no foreign key to accounts, which is where this table differs from AuthTokenEntity and WebSessionEntity. Accounts are never deleted in this system, so the cascade those tables buy can never fire; and a row is only ever written after an account has already been read, so the constraint could never reject a row this code would otherwise create. The cost is that a row could outlive an account removed by hand — harmless, because redemption re-reads the account and refuses when it is missing or banned. There is no xmin concurrency token either. Redemption is one conditional UPDATE (used_utc IS NULL AND expires_utc > now) whose WHERE clause is the concurrency control: two simultaneous redemptions of the same token cannot both affect a row. Properties AccountName Account the token was issued for, matching accounts.name. public string AccountName { get; set; } Property Value string CreatedUtc When the token was issued. Drives the per-account resend cooldown. public DateTime CreatedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime ExpiresUtc When the token stops being redeemable. public DateTime ExpiresUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime ID Surrogate key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long RequestedIp Client address that asked for the reset, for abuse investigation. public string? RequestedIp { get; set; } Property Value string TokenHash Lowercase hex SHA-256 of the emailed token. The token itself is never stored. public string TokenHash { get; set; } Property Value string UsedUtc When the token was redeemed, or null while it is still outstanding. Redeeming one token also stamps this on every other outstanding token for the account. public DateTime? UsedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime?

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class PlotAccessEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One player's standing permission on somebody else's plot. public class PlotAccessEntity : IVersionedEntity Inheritance object PlotAccessEntity Implements IVersionedEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The owner never appears here. Ownership is not a grant: it cannot be revoked by deleting a row, and a house whose owner's key lived in the same table as their friends' would be one bad delete away from being a house its owner could not enter. Who owns a plot is on the plot row; this table is only about the people they have let in. Rows are per plot, not per owner. A player who loses a plot and buys another does not bring their old guest list with them — the grants were made about a particular house, and carrying them over would silently re-admit people to somewhere they were never invited. Properties CharacterID The character being granted access. public long CharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long GrantedByCharacterID Who granted it. public long GrantedByCharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks Kept for the owner's benefit rather than the system's: a plot with InviteFriends handed out is a plot whose guest list the owner did not write all of, and "who let this person in" is the first thing they will ask. ID Primary key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long Permissions What they may do, as a FishMMO.Shared.PlotPermission bitmask. public int Permissions { get; set; } Property Value int Remarks An integer rather than a set of boolean columns, because permissions are read as a unit — every question asked of this table is "what may this person do here", never "who may place items" — and because adding one should not be a migration. Unknown bits are meaningless and are masked off on read by PlotAccess.Sanitize. A permission retired in a later version therefore stops meaning anything rather than quietly becoming whichever permission is given its bit next. PlotID The plot this grant is about. public long PlotID { get; set; } Property Value long TimeGranted When the grant was made or last changed (UTC). public DateTime TimeGranted { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Version Application-level concurrency token. Incremented on every write to detect stale updates. public long Version { get; set; } Property Value long

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.title: Class PlotEntity | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class PlotEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Ownership of one authored plot of land. public class PlotEntity : IVersionedEntity Inheritance object PlotEntity Implements IVersionedEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The row records who owns a foundation area, not where or how big it is. The geometry is part of the scene asset a designer authored it in, so it needs no storage and no synchronisation; what the cluster has to agree on is the answer to "who has claimed this", which is the only thing here that changes at runtime. Identified by SceneName and PlotKey together, deliberately not by any scene instance. Channels are several live copies of one scene, and a plot is meant to look the same in every one of them. Properties ID Primary key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long OwnerCharacterID The owning character, or zero when no character owns it. public long OwnerCharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks No foreign key, because zero is a real stored value and would have nothing to point at. Characters are soft-deleted in any case, so the row a key would protect never actually goes away; a guild does get hard-deleted, and releasing its plots is the housing system's job rather than the schema's. At most one of this and OwnerGuildID is ever set. Nothing in the schema enforces that — the invariant lives in FishMMO.Shared.PlotOwner, which cannot represent both and refuses to read a row that holds both. OwnerGuildID The owning guild, or zero when no guild owns it. public long OwnerGuildID { get; set; } Property Value long PlotKey The designer-authored key identifying this foundation within its scene. public string PlotKey { get; set; } Property Value string Remarks Stored already canonicalised, lower-cased and trimmed, by FishMMO.Shared.PlotIdentity. One stored form means a designer cannot create two plots that differ only in casing and read as the same one everywhere they are displayed. SceneName The Unity scene the plot's foundation is authored in. public string SceneName { get; set; } Property Value string State Where the plot is in its lifecycle. public int State { get; set; } Property Value int Remarks Stored rather than derived from the owner columns, because they cannot tell the two unowned states apart. Land that has never been claimed and land somebody stopped paying for both read as owner zero, and they are not the same place: one is a bare lot, the other is a house standing empty with its contents in a vault. A channel loading the scene renders them differently and a player walking up to one is told a different thing. The values are FishMMO.Shared.PlotState, stored as its underlying integer — this assembly cannot reference the Unity shared assembly, so the mapping is a cast. PlotStateParityTests pins the pairing; do not renumber either side. TaxDelinquentSinceUtc When the owner first failed to pay, or null while they are up to date. public DateTime? TaxDelinquentSinceUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Remarks Stored rather than derived, and the reason is the pin above. TaxDueUtc has to advance on every billing attempt — that is what stops two servers charging the same period — so it advances whether or not the money was actually collected. A plot that never pays would therefore keep a due date marching into the future and never look overdue by more than one period, which is to say it would never be reclaimed at all. This is the date the grace period is measured from: set on the first missed payment, left alone on later ones so the clock does not restart, and cleared the moment a payment succeeds. TaxDueUtc When the next tax payment falls due, or null while the plot is unowned. public DateTime? TaxDueUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Remarks The only tax state stored. Everything else is derived from it: the plot is delinquent once this is in the past, and reclaimable once it is further in the past than the grace period. A stored "is delinquent" flag would be a second source of truth that could disagree with the date beside it. Also the concurrency pin. Charging advances this date and requires it to still hold its old value, so several scene servers sweeping the same world produce exactly one charge per period rather than one per server. TaxNextAttemptUtc The earliest moment a sweep may try this plot's due period again, or null when it may be tried as soon as it is due. public DateTime? TaxNextAttemptUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Remarks Set when a sweep found the owner held by another server, and only then. Such an owner is billed by the server holding them (their balance lives in that server's memory, so nobody else may take it), and until that happens the plot stays due. Without this column it also stayed at the head of the sweep's ORDER BY tax_due_utc page: a page's worth of owners playing somewhere else and every sweep on every server re-read the same plots and billed nobody behind them. Not a second due date. TaxDueUtc is still the only thing that says what is owed, and still the pin; this only says when to look again. Every write that moves TaxDueUtc — an advance, a restore, a claim, a release — clears it, because it only ever describes the period currently due. TimeClaimed When the current owner claimed the plot, or null while it is unclaimed. public DateTime? TimeClaimed { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Remarks Cleared on release rather than kept, so it always describes the ownership recorded alongside it instead of some previous owner's tenancy. TimeCreated Row creation timestamp (UTC). public DateTime TimeCreated { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Version Application-level concurrency token. Incremented on every write to detect stale updates. public long Version { get; set; } Property Value long WorldServerID The world server this land belongs to. public long WorldServerID { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks Part of the plot's identity, not a detail of it. Several world servers run the same scenes from the same build, so a plot keyed only by scene and key would be one row shared between them — and a player who bought a house on one world would find it already owned on every other. Each world has its own land. Not the scene server: those come and go, and several may host copies of one world's scene at once. Not a scene instance either — channels are several live copies of one scene and a plot looks the same in all of them.

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class PlotVaultEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One thing held in a character's house vault after their land was taken back. public class PlotVaultEntity : IVersionedEntity Inheritance object PlotVaultEntity Implements IVersionedEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Reclaiming a plot destroys a house somebody built and paid for, and doing that with no way back would make a missed tax payment the most punishing event in the game. The vault is the answer: what stood on the plot is moved here rather than deleted, and the owner may buy it back or let it go. Keyed by character, not by plot. The plot is about to belong to somebody else — that is the whole reason these rows exist — so anything hanging off it would be cleared out from under them by the next owner's first change. OriginalPlotID is kept as a label, deliberately without a foreign key, so the row survives the plot being reused. Properties Amount How many of it are held. public int Amount { get; set; } Property Value int Remarks Stacked, so a house with forty identical fence panels is one row rather than forty. The retrieval fee is charged per row, which makes the stack the unit a player buys back. BaseFee The fee charged the moment it was stored, before any time had passed. public long BaseFee { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks Frozen onto the row rather than recomputed from the template's price. A server that rebalances what a structure costs must not thereby change what a player owes on something already sitting in their vault — they were quoted a figure when it went in. CharacterID The character whose vault this is. public long CharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long FeeRatePerDay How much of BaseFee is added per day stored. public float FeeRatePerDay { get; set; } Property Value float Remarks Frozen for the same reason as the base fee. Together they make the row self-describing: what it costs to get back is answerable from the row and the clock, with nothing else loaded. ID Primary key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long OriginalPlotID The plot it came off, kept as a label rather than a relation. public long OriginalPlotID { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks No foreign key on purpose. The plot is being handed to somebody else and may be claimed, built on and reclaimed again many times over; a cascading key would delete the previous owner's belongings the moment the new one's house was cleared. StoredAtUtc When it went into the vault (UTC). The instant the retrieval fee is measured from. public DateTime StoredAtUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime TemplateID The structure template that was stored. public int TemplateID { get; set; } Property Value int Remarks A template rather than a structure row. The structure itself is deleted with the plot it stood on, and its position was relative to a foundation that is no longer the owner's, so there is nothing about the placement worth keeping. What the player is owed back is the thing, not where it used to stand. Version Application-level concurrency token. Incremented on every write to detect stale updates. public long Version { get; set; } Property Value long

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class SceneEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Scene instance entity representing a currently loaded scene on a scene server. public class SceneEntity : IVersionedEntity Inheritance object SceneEntity Implements IVersionedEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Properties CharacterCount Number of characters currently in this scene. public int CharacterCount { get; set; } Property Value int CharacterID Character ID of the player than opened this scene if it's instanced. public long CharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long Difficulty Difficulty this instance was opened at, as an index into the dungeon's own difficulty list. 0 is the first entry a dungeon declares. public int Difficulty { get; set; } Property Value int Remarks Stored per instance rather than per dungeon because the same dungeon runs at several difficulties at once, and the ruleset has to survive the round trip through the queue: the scene server that eventually loads this row is not the one that enqueued it and has nothing else to read the choice from. Every dungeon declares its own list, so this is meaningful only alongside SceneName. ID Primary key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long IsPrivate True when the owning party has hidden this instance from the dungeon finder's list. public bool IsPrivate { get; set; } Property Value bool Remarks A lock on the front door, not on the instance: a private instance is still enterable by the party that owns it, it simply stops being offered to everyone else. Public by default, because a finder whose list is empty by default is not a finder. PartyID Party that owns this instance, or 0 when it was opened by an ungrouped character. public long PartyID { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks The durable answer to "whose dungeon is this". CharacterID records only who happened to open it, and that character can leave the party, log out, or be dropped from it — after which the remaining members could no longer resolve their own instance and would silently open a second one, splitting the group. Membership is looked up through this column so the instance survives any change to who created it. RequestKey The writer's once-per-request identity: a retry after a lost reply finds the row its first attempt wrote instead of writing a second one. Null for rows written without one. public Guid? RequestKey { get; set; } Property Value Guid? SceneHandle The hosting scene server's own scene-manager handle for this instance. public long SceneHandle { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks Diagnostic only. A scene-manager handle is assigned by the process that loaded the scene, so it is meaningful solely inside that process — two scene servers running the same build routinely produce the same value for different scenes. Anything that needs to identify a scene instance from outside its host uses ID. A Unity scene handle is 64 bits (SceneHandle.GetRawData(), an entity ID whose top bits are its version). It is stored bit for bit, so a real handle can read as a negative bigint. Before the row is Ready there is no handle, and the column has one other use: 0 while Pending, and while Loading the claim token of the dequeue that took the row, which is how a retried dequeue finds its own claim. SetReadyAsync replaces the token with the real handle. A token and a handle are told apart by the row's status, never by the value. See ISceneService.DequeueAsync. SceneName Scene name (e.g. the Unity scene asset name). public string SceneName { get; set; } Property Value string SceneServerID Scene server that hosts this scene: the one that claimed it from the queue while it is Loading, and the one that made it Ready after. 0 while Pending. public long SceneServerID { get; set; } Property Value long SceneStatus Current status of the scene (e.g. loading, running, unloading). public int SceneStatus { get; set; } Property Value int SceneType Scene type (over-world vs instanced). public int SceneType { get; set; } Property Value int TimeCreated Row creation timestamp (UTC). public DateTime TimeCreated { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Version Concurrency version for optimistic locking. public long Version { get; set; } Property Value long WorldServerID World server ID this scene belongs to. public long WorldServerID { get; set; } Property Value long

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class ServerBandwidthHourEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll One server's traffic in one UTC hour, rolled up from ServerBandwidthMinuteEntity. Table server_bandwidth_hour. public class ServerBandwidthHourEntity Inheritance object ServerBandwidthHourEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A pure function of the minute rows. Every column is recomputed from the minutes of its hour by the Control Panel's rollup job and written with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col, so running the rollup twice, from two panels, or after a minute row was rewritten, always leaves the same row. Nothing is ever added to a stored value. Summed over process instances: a server that restarted inside the hour has one row here, and Instances says it restarted. Kept 13 months, so a year-on-year egress comparison is always possible. No foreign key and no xmin, for the reasons on the minute table. Properties AppRecvBytes FishNet bytes delivered by the transport. Measured. public long AppRecvBytes { get; set; } Property Value long AppSentBytes FishNet bytes handed to the transport. Measured. public long AppSentBytes { get; set; } Property Value long BucketStart The UTC hour this row covers (database clock, as the minutes it came from). public DateTime BucketStart { get; set; } Property Value DateTime ConnectionsRefused Connections refused before becoming a session in the hour. public long ConnectionsRefused { get; set; } Property Value long HandshakeFailures Connections that failed their handshake in the hour. public long HandshakeFailures { get; set; } Property Value long Instances How many process instances wrote those minutes. More than one means a restart. public long Instances { get; set; } Property Value long IntervalMs The counted intervals summed, in milliseconds: about 3 600 000 for a server that ran the whole hour, less for one that started or stopped inside it. public long IntervalMs { get; set; } Property Value long MinutesSampled How many minute rows the hour was rolled from. public long MinutesSampled { get; set; } Property Value long ServerKind Which tier: 1 login, 2 world, 3 scene. public int ServerKind { get; set; } Property Value int ServerName The server's configured name, copied as text. public string ServerName { get; set; } Property Value string SessionsActiveMax The highest minute's session gauge in the hour. public long SessionsActiveMax { get; set; } Property Value long SessionsActiveSum The minutes' session gauges summed. Measured; an upper bound under bursts (see the minute table). public long UdpSentDatagrams { get; set; } Property Value long

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.title: Class ServerBandwidthMinuteEntity | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class ServerBandwidthMinuteEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll What one server process sent and received in one minute, as its own transport counted it. Table server_bandwidth_minute. public class ServerBandwidthMinuteEntity Inheritance object ServerBandwidthMinuteEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Written by the process it describes, once a minute, as a set. Each login, world and scene server samples its transport's cumulative counters on a 60 second timer and writes the difference since the minute began (ServerBandwidthLedger in the Unity project). The write is INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col, never an addition: a retry after a lost commit reply rewrites the same numbers, and a second sample that lands in the same minute rewrites the minute's running total. An additive upsert would count a retried write twice, which is the failure the idempotency work of 2026-09-25 exists to prevent. Keyed by InstanceID as well as the server's name. A restart starts its counters from zero in a new process; the instance id keeps the two processes' rows apart, so a restart inside one minute neither overwrites the old process's last minute nor mixes the new one's first minute into it. Summing over instances is the reader's job. Measured values only. Every counter here was counted by the process: the application bytes by the managed WebTransport socket, the UDP payload bytes and datagram counts by msquic. The bytes on the wire (payload plus 28 bytes of IPv4 and UDP header per datagram) are an estimate and are computed when read, never stored, so a change to the estimate never leaves history wrong. See ServerBandwidthMath. No foreign key to login_servers, world_servers or scene_servers, and the name is copied as text. Those rows are deleted when a server deregisters; the bandwidth it used must outlive it, or a month's egress total would shrink every time a server was retired. Append-mostly (a minute's row is rewritten only by its own process), so there is no xmin token either, as with admin_audit_log. Kept 14 days, then rolled into ServerBandwidthHourEntity and deleted, one whole hour at a time, by the Control Panel's rollup job. Properties AppRecvBytes FishNet bytes the transport delivered, both channels. Measured. public long AppRecvBytes { get; set; } Property Value long AppSentBytes FishNet bytes handed to the transport, both channels. Measured. public long AppSentBytes { get; set; } Property Value long BucketStart The UTC minute this row covers, from the DATABASE clock: the minute the process's sample was taken in, read from the database and truncated before the write. public DateTime BucketStart { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks Not the process's own clock. Rows from every host are compared and summed per minute, and a host whose clock ran a minute fast would file its traffic under the wrong minute. The traffic is the interval that ENDED in this minute; IntervalMs says how long that interval was. ConnectionsRefused Connections refused before becoming a session in the interval: by the transport's own listener limits, by msquic under load, or for no matching ALPN. public long ConnectionsRefused { get; set; } Property Value long HandshakeFailures Connections that started and failed their handshake in the interval. public long HandshakeFailures { get; set; } Property Value long InstanceID A random id the process took when it started. See the remarks on the class. public Guid InstanceID { get; set; } Property Value Guid IntervalMs How long the counted interval was, in milliseconds on the process's monotonic clock. public long IntervalMs { get; set; } Property Value long Remarks About 60 000. More when a sample was deferred (the database was unreachable, so the counters kept accumulating and the next sample carried the whole stretch), and about double when two samples landed in one minute. A rate is always bytes / interval, never bytes / 60. ServerKind Which tier: 1 login, 2 world, 3 scene (ServerBandwidthKind). public int ServerKind { get; set; } Property Value int ServerName The server's configured ServerName, copied as text. With ServerKind it identifies the server across restarts. public string ServerName { get; set; } Property Value string SessionsActive WebTransport sessions open when the minute was sampled (a gauge, not a total); the higher reading when two samples landed in the minute. public long SessionsActive { get; set; } Property Value long SessionsOpened Sessions accepted in the interval. public long SessionsOpened { get; set; } Property Value long UdpRecvBytes UDP payload bytes received. Measured by msquic, process-wide. public long UdpRecvBytes { get; set; } Property Value long UdpRecvDatagrams UDP datagrams received. Measured, exact. public long UdpRecvDatagrams { get; set; } Property Value long UdpSentBytes UDP payload bytes sent: QUIC headers, AEAD tags, padding, ACKs, retransmissions and the handshake included. Measured by msquic, process-wide. public long UdpSentBytes { get; set; } Property Value long UdpSentDatagrams UDP datagrams sent. Measured by msquic, which over-counts a flush sent in several batches (handshakes, bursts), so the header estimate built from it is an upper bound. public long UdpSentDatagrams { get; set; } Property Value long

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class SupportTicketEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll A support ticket: something a player asked staff to deal with. public class SupportTicketEntity Inheritance object SupportTicketEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Filed from in-game and worked from the Control Panel. The player can follow it and reply; staff can reply, take notes the player never sees, and act. No foreign keys on any of the account or character names here. The same reasoning as the audit log: a ticket describes something that happened, and deleting an account must not erase the report somebody filed about it — which is exactly the account most likely to be deleted. The names are copied in, and the character id is kept beside the name so the panel can still link to a character that has since been renamed. Properties AssignedTo The staff account working it, or null if nobody has taken it. public string AssignedTo { get; set; } Property Value string Body What the player wrote when they filed it. public string Body { get; set; } Property Value string Category What it is about. public SupportTicketCategory Category { get; set; } Property Value SupportTicketCategory ClosedBy The staff account that finished it. public string ClosedBy { get; set; } Property Value string ClosedUtc When it was resolved or closed. public DateTime? ClosedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? CreatedUtc When it was filed. public DateTime CreatedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime EscalatedBy The staff account that last moved the ticket to another tier. public string EscalatedBy { get; set; } Property Value string EscalatedUtc When the ticket last moved to another tier. public DateTime? EscalatedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? ID Surrogate key, and the reference a player quotes. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long LastActivityUtc When anything last happened on it: a reply, a note, a status change. public DateTime LastActivityUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks Denormalised so the queue can sort by it without joining the messages. A queue that cannot cheaply answer "what has been waiting longest" is a queue nobody works from. Messages The conversation, oldest first. public ICollection<SupportTicketMessageEntity> Messages { get; set; } Property Value ICollection<SupportTicketMessageEntity> Priority Staff-set priority, higher is more urgent. public int Priority { get; set; } Property Value int Remarks Set by staff, never by the player. A reporter-set priority is a field where every ticket is urgent. ReporterAccount The account that filed it. public string ReporterAccount { get; set; } Property Value string ReporterCharacterID That character's id, so a later rename does not break the link. public long ReporterCharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long ReporterCharacterName The character they were playing, if any. public string ReporterCharacterName { get; set; } Property Value string RequiredAccessLevel The lowest access level that may see and work this ticket: its support tier. public byte RequiredAccessLevel { get; set; } Property Value byte Remarks Tiers are access levels, not a parallel ladder: GameMaster (2) is the first tier and Admin (3) the second. A separate tier number would be one more thing for an operator to keep in step with the access level that actually decides what they can do, and a ticket escalated to "tier 2" that a tier-2 game master can still act on is a promotion that promotes nothing. Stored as the byte value of AccessLevel, like accounts.access_level. Resolution What staff decided, written when it is resolved or closed. public string Resolution { get; set; } Property Value string SceneName Where it happened, for context and for searching the chat log around it. public string SceneName { get; set; } Property Value string Status Where it has got to. public SupportTicketStatus Status { get; set; } Property Value SupportTicketStatus Subject One-line summary, shown in the queue. public string Subject { get; set; } Property Value string TargetAccount The accused account, for a player report. public string TargetAccount { get; set; } Property Value string TargetCharacterID The accused character's id. public long TargetCharacterID { get; set; } Property Value long TargetCharacterName The accused character, for a player report. public string TargetCharacterName { get; set; } Property Value string Version Concurrency token. Two staff working one ticket is the normal case. public uint Version { get; set; } Property Value uint

Staff need somewhere to say "this is the third report this week, I am inclined to ban" without the reporter reading it, and without that they will say it somewhere the ticket cannot remember. Leaking an internal note is the classic failure of a support system, so the flag is a column enforced by the read projection on the server, never by whether a view remembered to hide it. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class TwoFactorResetRequestEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll A request to remove an account's second factor after a waiting period, for a player who has lost both their authenticator and their recovery codes. public class TwoFactorResetRequestEntity Inheritance object TwoFactorResetRequestEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The delay is the security. Whoever asks has, at most, the password; if asking removed the second factor straight away, the second factor would protect against nothing a stolen password does not already give. The waiting period is the window in which the real owner — who still has their authenticator — signs in normally, and a normal sign-in cancels the request. Staff may shorten the wait once they have verified the player some other way. Completing a request never satisfies two-factor. It removes the old factor so the account can enrol a new one; the session that completes it has proved the password and nothing more, and must be sent to enrolment, not treated as having passed a second factor. At most one request per account is pending, enforced by a partial unique index on account_name WHERE status = 0. Asking again returns the existing request unchanged, so repeating the request can neither restart the clock on the owner nor shorten it for an attacker. No foreign key to accounts, for the reasons given on PasswordResetTokenEntity: accounts are never deleted, and every write here follows a read of the account. Properties AccountName The account, matching accounts.name, stored lowercase. public string AccountName { get; set; } Property Value string EffectiveUtc When it may be completed. public DateTime EffectiveUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime Remarks Only ever moved earlier, and only by staff. Pushing it later is a cancel followed by a new request, so the longer wait starts from a request the history can show. ID Surrogate key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long RequestedIp Client address that asked, for abuse investigation. public string? RequestedIp { get; set; } Property Value string RequestedUtc When it was asked for. public DateTime RequestedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime ResolvedBy Who cancelled or completed it: a staff account, or the account itself. public string? ResolvedBy { get; set; } Property Value string ResolvedUtc When it was cancelled or completed. public DateTime? ResolvedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? ShortenedBy The staff account that last brought it forward. public string? ShortenedBy { get; set; } Property Value string ShortenedUtc When staff last brought the effective time forward. public DateTime? ShortenedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? StaffReason Why staff last shortened or cancelled it. public string? StaffReason { get; set; } Property Value string Status Where the request has got to. public TwoFactorResetStatus Status { get; set; } Property Value TwoFactorResetStatus Version PostgreSQL xmin concurrency token. Staff shortening a request while the player signs in and cancels it is two writers on one row. public uint Version { get; set; } Property Value uint

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class WebSessionEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll A browser session for the Control Panel. public class WebSessionEntity Inheritance object WebSessionEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Deliberately separate from AuthTokenEntity. That table's rows are game tokens issued by a LoginServer and carry a foreign key to login_servers; the Control Panel is not a login server, has no row to point at, and its sessions must not be accepted by a World or Scene server that validates game tokens. Only the SHA-256 of the session identifier is stored, so a database read does not yield usable sessions. Properties AccessLevelAtIssue The account's access level when the session was issued. Compared against the account's current level on every request so a demotion takes effect immediately rather than at the session's next renewal. public byte AccessLevelAtIssue { get; set; } Property Value byte AccountName Account this session authenticates, matching accounts.name. public string AccountName { get; set; } Property Value string CreatedUtc When the session was created. public DateTime CreatedUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime ExpiresUtc Absolute expiry, independent of activity. public DateTime ExpiresUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime ID Surrogate key. public long ID { get; set; } Property Value long IpAddress Client address the session was issued to, for the operator's own session list. public string IpAddress { get; set; } Property Value string LastSeenUtc Last request on this session; drives the idle timeout. public DateTime LastSeenUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime LastStepUpUtc When the operator last re-proved possession of their authenticator, or null if never. Drives the step-up window on destructive actions. public DateTime? LastStepUpUtc { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? Revoked Whether the session has been explicitly revoked. public bool Revoked { get; set; } Property Value bool SessionHash Lowercase hex SHA-256 of the opaque session identifier held by the browser cookie. The identifier itself is never stored. public string SessionHash { get; set; } Property Value string TwoFactorSatisfied Whether two-factor has been satisfied. A session that has authenticated by password but not yet by code exists in this table with the flag clear and can do nothing else. public bool TwoFactorSatisfied { get; set; } Property Value bool UserAgent Truncated user agent, for the operator's own session list. public string UserAgent { get; set; } Property Value string Version PostgreSQL xmin exposed as an EF concurrency token, matching every other versioned entity in this schema. public uint Version { get; set; } Property Value uint

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ent.summary: Class WorldClockControlEntity Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Entities Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll The one world clock: a single row (ID = 1) that every scene server adopts on its next pulse and that admins write, in game (/admin time) or from the Control Panel. public class WorldClockControlEntity Inheritance object WorldClockControlEntity Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks World time is "world milliseconds since the calendar epoch", and it is never stored as a running value. The row is an anchor: at database time BaseReferenceMs the world read BaseWorldMs, and it has advanced at Rate world seconds per real second since. World ms now = base_world_ms + rate × (db_now_ms − base_reference_ms), computed in SQL against the database clock, so every reader agrees on it whatever its own clock says. See WorldClockControlService. Every write re-anchors at the moment it is made and bumps Revision. A scene server that reads a new revision treats it as an instant jump rather than smoothing towards it — that is what an admin setting the time asked for. No xmin token: every write is one raw UPDATE … RETURNING that computes from the row it locks, so there is no read-modify-write for a token to protect. Properties BaseReferenceMs The DATABASE clock, in Unix milliseconds, when BaseWorldMs was written. public long BaseReferenceMs { get; set; } Property Value long BaseWorldMs World milliseconds since the calendar epoch at BaseReferenceMs. public long BaseWorldMs { get; set; } Property Value long EpochUnixSeconds The calendar epoch the scene servers use, in Unix seconds. Stored so a reader without the Unity calendar asset (the Control Panel) can write and read world timestamps. public long EpochUnixSeconds { get; set; } Property Value long ID Always 1. A check constraint keeps it the only row. public int ID { get; set; } Property Value int Rate World seconds per real second: 0 held, 1 real time, above 1 raced. public double Rate { get; set; } Property Value double RequestKey The idempotency key of the last write. A retried write whose first attempt committed but lost its reply finds its own key here and is not applied twice — which matters for a relative shift, where a second application would move the world twice as far. public Guid? RequestKey { get; set; } Property Value Guid? ResumeRate The pace a resume returns to. Always above zero. public double ResumeRate { get; set; } Property Value double Revision Incremented on every write. public long Revision { get; set; } Property Value long UpdatedAt UTC time of the last write, by the database clock. public DateTime? UpdatedAt { get; set; } Property Value DateTime? UpdatedBy Account that made the last write, or null for the seed. public string? UpdatedBy { get; set; } Property Value string

api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Npg.summary: Class NpgsqlDbConfiguration Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll Encapsulates validated Npgsql database configuration. Responsibility is limited to binding and validating a provided IConfiguration instance. public sealed class NpgsqlDbConfiguration Inheritance object NpgsqlDbConfiguration Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks WARNING — NoResetOnClose = true. This configuration sets NoResetOnClose = true on the Npgsql connection string, which skips DISCARD ALL / RESET ALL when returning connections to the pool. This is a deliberate performance optimization, but it means the following session-level state will NOT be automatically reset: SET LOCAL / SET SESSION / SET ROLE Temporary tables created with CREATE TEMP TABLE Prepared statements via PREPARE / DEALLOCATE Advisory locks acquired at session scope LISTEN / UNLISTEN subscriptions search_path changes via SET search_path If any future code introduces session-level state, it MUST manually reset that state before returning the connection to the pool, or change NoResetOnClose to false. See the comment on the NoResetOnClose = true line in BuildConnectionString(NpgsqlSettings, string, string) for details on the performance trade-off. Constructors NpgsqlDbConfiguration(IConfiguration, bool, int?) Initializes configuration from a pre-built IConfiguration instance. public NpgsqlDbConfiguration(IConfiguration configuration, bool enableLogging = false, int? commandTimeoutOverride = null) Parameters configuration IConfiguration Configuration root containing an Npgsql section. enableLogging bool Whether to enable sensitive data logging support in dependent components. commandTimeoutOverride int? Optional command timeout override in seconds. Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown when configuration is null. DatabaseException Thrown when required identifiers or numeric settings are invalid. Deliberately a report rather than a thrown exception: whether a schema mismatch should stop a server or merely warn depends on the server, and that call belongs to the caller. This reports pending migrations only. It does not detect model drift — an entity changed with no migration generated for it. That check existed here and never worked: EF builds ModelSnapshot.Model with an empty convention set, so the relational model the differ needs is never attached and the comparison threw on every single startup. EF Core 5 exposes no supported way to rebuild it (SnapshotModelProcessor is design-time only; IModelRuntimeInitializer and HasPendingModelChanges both postdate it), so the check was removed rather than left reporting a failure forever. See issue #162. Drift is caught by scaffolding a migration and asserting it is empty, which belongs in CI where the design-time package is available. Methods BanAsync(string, DateTime?, string?, string?, CancellationToken) Bans an account: drops it to AccessLevel.Banned, revokes its auth tokens and Control Panel sessions, queues a kick so the game servers disconnect it, and records who banned it, why, and when the ban lifts. public Task<DatabaseResult> BanAsync(string accountName, DateTime? bannedUntilUtc, string? bannedBy, string? reason, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters accountName string Account to ban. Matched case-insensitively. bannedUntilUtc DateTime? When the ban lifts, or null for a permanent ban. bannedBy string Operator account applying the ban, or null when not recorded. reason string The reason, or null when not recorded. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancellation token. Returns Task<DatabaseResult> Success, or DB_NOT_FOUND when no such account exists. Remarks All four writes land together or none of them do. A half-applied ban leaves the account playing: the access level is the login gate and nothing else, so lowering it alone stops the next sign-in and does nothing to the session already connected, while revoking tokens alone lets the player sign straight back in. The failure this atomicity exists to prevent is exactly that — an operator who is told the ban succeeded, watching the banned account keep playing. This layer does no policy checking. Who may ban whom is the caller's decision, and every caller must record the ban in the audit log. A null bannedUntilUtc is a permanent ban. A temporary one is lifted by FetchForLoginAsync(string, bool, CancellationToken) at the first sign-in attempt after the instant passes, which restores Player. The only ban. A one-argument overload that recorded neither actor nor reason was removed (issue #267): an account page showing "banned by: —, reason: —" is a ban nobody can explain or appeal, and every real caller already passed both. api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ser.title: Enum BaseService<TEntity>.BulkVersionConflictPolicy | FishMMO Documentation
api/database/FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Ser.summary: Enum BaseService<TEntity>.BulkVersionConflictPolicy Namespace FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Services Assembly FishMMO-DB.dll How a bulk versioned write should treat rows that lose the version race. protected enum BaseService<TEntity>.BulkVersionConflictPolicy Fields Fail = 0 The batch is one indivisible statement and a skipped row invalidates the rows around it, so the whole write is rolled back. Correct for slot-addressed layouts — inventory, bank, equipment, hotkeys — where a row's key is a position that its contents move between. Applying "the item is now in slot 5" without "slot 3 is now empty" leaves one item occupying two slots, which is item duplication, and applying the reverse loses it outright. The batch is a layout; half a layout is not a smaller layout, it is a wrong one. SkipStaleRows = 1 Rows are independent facts. A row that loses to a newer write is correctly left alone and the rest of the batch stands. Correct for template-addressed state — attributes, buffs, abilities, factions, quests, pets — where a row's key is its identity and never migrates. Two such rows have no bearing on one another, so there is nothing for a skipped row to corrupt. Remarks Every bulk upsert in this layer is gated EXCLUDED.version > table.version, so a row whose incoming version is not newer than what is already stored is simply not applied. Whether that is a failure depends entirely on what the batch means, and the two meanings need opposite handling.

Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This base type provides three primary execution paths: ExecuteTransactionAsync(Func<Task>, CancellationToken) and ExecuteTransactionAsync<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>>,string,CancellationToken) create a fresh NpgsqlDbContext, begin an explicit transaction, execute the delegate, then call SaveChangesAsync(CancellationToken) and commit. ExecuteWriteAsync(Func<Task>,string,CancellationToken) and ExecuteWriteAsync<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>>,string,CancellationToken) create a fresh NpgsqlDbContext, execute the delegate, then call SaveChangesAsync(CancellationToken) without starting an explicit transaction. ExecuteReadAsync(Func<Task>,string,CancellationToken) and ExecuteReadAsync<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>>,string,CancellationToken) create a fresh NpgsqlDbContext but do not start an explicit transaction and do not call SaveChanges. Standalone Execution (no ambient scope): A new context is created per attempt to avoid EF change-tracker state leaking across retries. Transient database failures are retried with exponential backoff. Optimistic concurrency conflicts (Version-based authority) and StaleStateException are never retried; they are returned as non-transient failures so the caller can re-read and decide how to proceed. Ambient Scope Execution (inside an existing Unit of Work): When an operation detects an active FishMMO.Database.Npgsql.Services.DatabaseExecutionScope, it reuses the ambient NpgsqlDbContext and does NOT retry on transient failures. This is by design for the following reasons: Transaction State Corruption: PostgreSQL aborts the entire transaction on most transient failures. The connection and transaction become unusable, making retry with the same context impossible. Context State Pollution: The DbContext's change tracker accumulates state. Retrying with a polluted change tracker can cause duplicate key violations or incorrect updates. Semantic Correctness: If operation A succeeded and operation B failed transiently, retrying B alone without re-evaluating A's preconditions could violate business invariants. When a transient failure occurs inside an ambient scope, the failure is returned immediately so the caller can restart the entire unit of work with fresh state. Savepoints are used for nested atomicity but cannot recover from connection-level failures. Constructors BaseService(INpgsqlDbContextFactory) Initializes the service and caches the table name for TEntity. protected BaseService(INpgsqlDbContextFactory contextFactory) Parameters contextFactory INpgsqlDbContextFactory Factory used to create new EF Core contexts. Exceptions ArgumentNullException contextFactory is null. Fields DatabaseUtcClockSql The database's UTC wall time as a statement runs: clock_timestamp(), as a UTC timestamp without time zone like every stamp this layer writes. protected const string DatabaseUtcClockSql = "(clock_timestamp() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')" Field Value string Remarks clock_timestamp() rather than now(): now() is the start of the transaction, and a caller that reads the clock after its row locks were granted means the instant it was granted them. A read that wants one instant for several statements in one snapshot uses now() itself, as the server board does.
