api/installer/FishMMO.Installer.AdminAcc.title: Class AdminAccountInstaller | FishMMO Documentation
api/installer/FishMMO.Installer.AdminAcc.summary: Class AdminAccountInstaller Namespace FishMMO.Installer Assembly FishMMO-Installer.dll Creates an Administrator account from the console: Database ▸ Create Admin Account. public static class AdminAccountInstaller Inheritance object AdminAccountInstaller Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A fresh deployment has nobody who can sign in to the Control Panel, and with the beta gate on nobody can register either, because registration needs a beta code that only an administrator can mint. This is the way in. The account must be indistinguishable from one the game or the Control Panel registered, so the steps are theirs (AccountRegistrationService.RegisterAsync and SelfServiceService.EnrolAsync), through the same database services: an SRP salt and verifier from the fixed identity and the game client's parameters, the profile with email as its channel, verified without a code (an operator at the server's console needs none), and two-factor enrolled: a TOTP secret encrypted under the deployment master key, enabled, and the hashed recovery codes. The Control Panel's Operator policies require Admin AND two-factor, so an administrator without it could sign in but not mint a beta code. Unlike a registration, the writes are one transaction, so a failure leaves no half-made administrator behind. The level change is recorded in the audit log, as every caller of PersistAccessLevelAsync must. The connection is the servers' own (the installer's appsettings.json Npgsql section with the credentials from FISHMMO_DB_USERNAME / FISHMMO_DB_PASSWORD or the secrets file), not a superuser: creating an account is an application write. Fields AuditAction Audit log action for an administrator created here. public const string AuditAction = "account.create-admin" Field Value string AuditSource Audit log source for rows this step writes (the column holds 16 characters). public const string AuditSource = "installer" Field Value string Methods CreateAdminAccountAsync() Database ▸ Create Admin Account. public static Task CreateAdminAccountAsync() Returns Task

api/installer/FishMMO.Installer.SecretsE.title: Class SecretsEnvironmentInstaller | FishMMO Documentation
api/installer/FishMMO.Installer.SecretsE.summary: Class SecretsEnvironmentInstaller Namespace FishMMO.Installer Assembly FishMMO-Installer.dll The one place FishMMO's secrets and environment variables are configured. public static class SecretsEnvironmentInstaller Inheritance object SecretsEnvironmentInstaller Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks One screen, one writer, one copy. Every FISHMMO_* variable the servers actually read lands in a single file — /etc/fishmmo/db-secrets.env on Linux, %ProgramData%\FishMMO\db-secrets.env on Windows — which every systemd unit loads with EnvironmentFile=-/etc/fishmmo/db-secrets.env. Splitting that file between several wizards is how it used to lose data: each one rewrote the whole file and emitted only the keys it knew about, so configuring the database silently deleted the mail credentials. There is now exactly one editor, it loads every key before it writes any, and a full rewrite is therefore safe. The file is the only thing this screen reads. It never seeds itself from the process environment. A shell that still exports an old FISHMMO_DB_PASSWORD from some earlier session would otherwise show that stale value as "current", and saving would copy it back over the real one — which is how a secrets file and an exported snippet ended up holding two different passwords written half a minute apart. What the environment does get is a comparison: DescribeEnvironmentMismatches(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>, Func<string, string?>?) names every variable whose value in this shell differs from the file's, without printing either one. That warning matters because the runtime precedence is the opposite. DatabaseSecrets resolves the environment first and the file second, so a process started by hand from a polluted shell uses the shell's value no matter what this screen writes. That order is deliberate — an operator must be able to override a deployment for one run — so the fix is to say so plainly, not to reorder the runtime. Keys it does not know are still preserved. An operator will have added something — a proxy variable, a feature flag, a note to themselves. Unrecognised assignments, comments, blank lines and anything this parser cannot make sense of are carried through verbatim. There is no export. This screen used to be able to write the same values out again as a fish/PowerShell/CMD snippet or a stray .env. Every one of those was a second copy of a live credential, and the fish one landed in conf.d, where every new shell sourced it and re-exported the database password into itself and into every process it launched. The services never needed it: systemd hands them the secrets file. Only the creation is gone — FishMMO.Installer.SecretsEnvironmentInstaller.ExportedSnippetPaths() still lists those paths so the uninstall can offer to delete the copies an earlier version already made. What is deliberately not here: FISHMMO_PG_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD — prompted per run by design. Persisting the PostgreSQL superuser password to disk is a worse trade than persisting the application user's, because it is the credential that can drop the cluster. FISHMMO_SIGNING_KEY_KEK_BASE64 and FISHMMO_CLIENT_GATE_SECRET — owned by SecurityKeyInstaller, which provisions them into the deployment_secrets table. Writing them here as well would give the deployment two sources of truth for the same key, and the wrong one would win silently. FISHMMO_CONNECTION_STRING / ConnectionStrings__NpgsqlConnection — an alternative spelling of the FISHMMO_DB_* set below. Offering both invites a deployment where the two disagree. Tooling-only variables (FISHMMO_UNITY_EXE, FISHMMO_INSTALL_ROOT, FISHMMO_TRADE_RENDER_DIR, FISHMMO_ALLOW_COREDUMPS, FISHMMO_PG_LISTEN_ADDRESSES) — they steer a developer's machine, not a server. Mail is the one setting with a second destination. The Control Panel is the process that drains the outbound email queue and sends (the LoginServer still creates accounts and enqueues, but its own Smtp:DrainQueue is off), and it resolves each SMTP setting from the environment first and its configuration second. The non-secret values are therefore mirrored into FishMMO-Setup/<environment>/appsettings.ControlPanel.json so a deployment that does not use the secrets file still works — but the password is written to the secrets file only. That JSON ships in the repository, and a live sending credential must never be committed. Methods ComposeSecretsFile(string?, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>) Produces the full text of the secrets file: every known key set to the value given, and everything else in the existing file left exactly as it was. public static string ComposeSecretsFile(string? existingContent, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> values) Parameters existingContent string Current file content, or null when there is no file yet. values IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> The known keys and their values. A key absent from this map (or present with an empty value) is removed from the file; the servers treat an empty variable as unset anyway, and an empty assignment is noise. Returns string Remarks Known keys are rewritten where they already stand, so the comment above a key stays with it. Keys that are not in the file yet are appended. Duplicate assignments to a key being written are collapsed to one: both systemd and DatabaseSecrets take the last assignment, so a leftover duplicate further down would quietly beat the new value. Values are written raw, never quoted. DatabaseSecrets takes everything after the first = literally — it does not strip quotes — so quoting here would deliver the quote characters to the server as part of the password. Quotes an operator wrote by hand around a key we are not writing survive untouched, because those lines are preserved rather than re-emitted. Public only so it can be tested directly; it is the one function here whose failure would destroy an operator's credentials. Configure() Runs the interactive editor until the operator goes back. public static Task Configure() Returns Task Remarks Four guided steps rather than seventeen numbered settings and five letter actions. The flat list showed every variable at once and made the operator assemble a database connection out of six separate menu entries; each step now prompts its fields in the order they belong together, with the current value as the default so Enter keeps it. B goes back, not 0: a lone zero in a column of letters reads as the letter O, and was asked about as one. 0 and Escape are still accepted, silently. DescribeDatabase(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>) The database connection in one line. Never includes the password. public static string DescribeDatabase(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> values) Parameters values IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> Returns string DescribeEnvironmentMismatches(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>, Func<string, string?>?) Names every variable whose value in the launching shell differs from the file's. public static IReadOnlyList<string> DescribeEnvironmentMismatches(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> fileValues, Func<string, string?>? readEnvironment = null) Parameters fileValues IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> What the secrets file holds — the values this screen edits. readEnvironment Func<string, string> How to read a variable; defaults to this process's environment. Injectable so the comparison can be tested without touching the real environment, and so the screen can ask ReadInherited(string) instead of the live process. Returns IReadOnlyList<string> Remarks This is the diagnostic the screen could not previously give. An operator whose shell still exported an old password had no way to see that the shell and the file disagreed, and the disagreement is what decides which password a hand-started server actually uses: DatabaseSecrets takes the environment first and the file second. Neither value is returned, formatted or logged — only the key name and the fact that the two differ. An empty variable is not a disagreement, because the runtime treats an empty variable as unset and falls through to the file; the shell's value is compared trimmed, because trimming is what the runtime does to it before use, so trailing whitespace is not reported as a difference that would not exist in practice. api/installer/FishMMO.Installer.Uninstal.title: Class UninstallInstaller | FishMMO Documentation
api/installer/FishMMO.Installer.Uninstal.summary: Class UninstallInstaller Namespace FishMMO.Installer Assembly FishMMO-Installer.dll The Uninstall screens: removing PostgreSQL, and deleting the secrets file. public static class UninstallInstaller Inheritance object UninstallInstaller Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Nothing here is undoable. Removing PostgreSQL deletes the cluster data directory, and that directory is every account, character, guild, item and audit row the deployment has ever had. There is no recycle bin and no second copy. The confirmation flow is therefore the feature, not the packaging around it: Resolve the real commands and the real paths for this machine and show them. Say which services are running that will break the moment the database is gone. Offer a dump first, and stop dead if the dump is asked for and fails. Require a typed phrase nobody types by reflex — not a keypress. Run the steps in order, stop at the first real failure, and report every outcome, so a half-done uninstall is visible rather than silent. The command and path resolution lives in UninstallPlanner, which touches nothing and can be asserted on its own. This file is the part that talks to the operator and runs what the planner decided. Methods DeleteSecretsFile() Deletes the secrets and environment file that every FishMMO process reads its database credentials from. public static Task DeleteSecretsFile() Returns Task Remarks The key names are listed because knowing what has to be re-entered is useful. The values are never printed: a password or an API key on a terminal ends up in scrollback, in a screen recording, and in whatever the terminal logs. UninstallPostgreSQL() Removes PostgreSQL and its cluster data, after showing exactly what will run and taking a typed confirmation. public static Task UninstallPostgreSQL() Returns Task

api/installer/FishMMO.Installer.Uninstal.summary: Class UninstallPlanner Namespace FishMMO.Installer Assembly FishMMO-Installer.dll Builds the uninstall plan for PostgreSQL. Pure: it reads nothing, runs nothing, and deletes nothing. public static class UninstallPlanner Inheritance object UninstallPlanner Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The planning is separated from the doing on purpose. Every command and every path this installer would run rm -rf or an unattended uninstaller over is decided here, by functions that can be called and asserted without a PostgreSQL anywhere near them — and the same list is what the operator is shown before being asked to confirm. A plan that is shown and a plan that is run cannot drift apart, because they are the same object. The two platforms never mix. A Linux plan contains no uninstaller executable and a Windows plan contains no sudo, systemctl or rm -rf. Distribution layouts differ too: /etc/postgresql/ is the Debian layout and does not exist on Arch, where the configuration lives inside the data directory, so it appears only in the apt-get plan. Fields LinuxServiceName PostgreSQL's own systemd unit name on every supported distribution. public const string LinuxServiceName = "postgresql" Field Value string WindowsDefaultInstallRoot Where EnterpriseDB's one-click installer puts PostgreSQL by default. public const string WindowsDefaultInstallRoot = "C:\\Program Files\\PostgreSQL" Field Value string Remarks The install path (InstallPostgreSQLWindows) accepts the installer's default prefix, which is this directory with a version-numbered subdirectory under it. WindowsUninstallerFileName The uninstaller EnterpriseDB leaves in each version directory. public const string WindowsUninstallerFileName = "uninstall-postgresql.exe" Field Value string Methods BuildLinuxPlan(PackageManagerKind, IReadOnlyList<string>?) Builds the Linux uninstall: stop, disable, remove the packages, then remove the data and configuration directories — in that order, because each step depends on the one before it. public static PostgreSQLUninstallPlan BuildLinuxPlan(PackageManagerKind kind, IReadOnlyList<string>? dependantUnitsToStop = null) Parameters kind PackageManagerKind The detected package manager. dependantUnitsToStop IReadOnlyList<string> FishMMO and pooler units to stop first. Only units observed to be running should be listed; their failure does not abort the run. Returns PostgreSQLUninstallPlan BuildWindowsPlan(string, string, string?, IReadOnlyList<string>?) Builds the Windows uninstall around EnterpriseDB's own uninstaller, which is the supported way to undo the one-click installer the install path runs. public static PostgreSQLUninstallPlan BuildWindowsPlan(string installRoot, string version, string? serviceName = null, IReadOnlyList<string>? dependantServicesToStop = null) Parameters installRoot string The directory holding the version subdirectories, normally WindowsDefaultInstallRoot. version string The installed version directory name, for example 16. serviceName string The Windows service name, when it was discovered. Defaults to EnterpriseDB's postgresql-x64-<version>. dependantServicesToStop IReadOnlyList<string> FishMMO services observed running, stopped first. Returns PostgreSQLUninstallPlan Remarks Deleting the program files by hand would leave the registry entries and the service behind. The uninstaller removes both; what it routinely leaves is the data directory, which is why that is a separate, separately confirmed step. Exceptions ArgumentException If the version or install root is empty or malformed. An empty version is the accident this throws for: it would aim the leftover-data step at the whole PostgreSQL directory. DataAndConfigDirectories(PackageManagerKind) The directories PostgreSQL's data and configuration live in for the given manager, in removal order. public static IReadOnlyList<(string Path, string What)> DataAndConfigDirectories(PackageManagerKind kind) Parameters kind PackageManagerKind Returns IReadOnlyList<(string Path, string What)> Remarks Only Debian keeps configuration in /etc/postgresql/. On Arch and on RHEL the configuration files live inside the data directory, so naming /etc/postgresql there would be a recursive delete aimed at a directory the distribution never created. IsRemovablePath(string?, UninstallPlatform, out string) Decides whether a path may be handed to a recursive delete. public static bool IsRemovablePath(string? path, UninstallPlatform platform, out string refusal) Parameters path string Candidate directory. platform UninstallPlatform Which layout rules apply. refusal string Why it was refused, when this returns false. Returns bool True when the path is specific enough to delete. Remarks The accident this exists to prevent is an unset or empty value interpolated into a delete: an empty version turning C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL<version>\data into C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL, or an empty path turning rm -rf $DIR into rm -rf with whatever the shell puts next. Nothing is deleted without passing here first, and this refuses on the safe side. LinuxDirectoryRemovalCommand(string) The Linux command that removes one directory, with its own existence test built in. public static string LinuxDirectoryRemovalCommand(string path) Parameters path string Directory to remove. Must have passed IsRemovablePath(string?, UninstallPlatform, out string). Returns string Remarks The if test -d is not redundant with the caller's existence check. The caller often cannot see inside /var/lib/postgres (mode 700, owned by postgres) without root, so its answer can be "unknown"; this form deletes only what is actually there and exits 0 either way, so an absent directory reads as "nothing to remove" rather than a failure that aborts the run. PackageRemovalCommand(PackageManagerKind) The command that removes the PostgreSQL packages for the given manager. public static string PackageRemovalCommand(PackageManagerKind kind) Parameters kind PackageManagerKind Returns string PostgreSQLPackageNames() The package names the install path installs, keyed by manager. Passed to DetectAsync(Dictionary<string, string>) so detection here picks the same manager the install picked. public static Dictionary<string, string> PostgreSQLPackageNames() Returns Dictionary<string, string> TryResolvePackageManagerKind(string?, out PackageManagerKind) Maps the human-readable name DetectAsync(Dictionary<string, string>) reports onto the kind the plan is built from. public static bool TryResolvePackageManagerKind(string? managerName, out PackageManagerKind kind) Parameters managerName string For example "pacman (Arch/CachyOS)". kind PackageManagerKind The matching kind when this returns true. Returns bool True when the name is recognised. WindowsDirectoryRemovalCommand(string) The Windows command that removes one leftover directory. public static string WindowsDirectoryRemovalCommand(string path) Parameters path string Returns string

internalLogCallback = null, IEnumerable<Type> extraLoggerConfigTypes = null) Parameters configPath string The path to the JSON configuration file. consoleFormatter IConsoleFormatter The formatter to If null, defaults to Console.WriteLine. extraLoggerConfigTypes IEnumerable<Type> Optional: Any additional ILoggerConfig types to register with the JSON converter. Returns Task IsEnabled(LogLevel) Returns true when at least one sink — the console formatter or any enabled ILogger — would accept a message at level. public static bool IsEnabled(LogLevel level) Parameters level LogLevel The level a caller is considering logging at. Returns bool True when the message would reach at least one sink. Remarks Intended for hot call sites that build their message with string interpolation. The early-out inside Write(LogLevel, string, string, Exception, Dictionary<string, object>) cannot prevent that string from being built, because the interpolation is evaluated by the caller before Write(LogLevel, string, string, Exception, Dictionary<string, object>) is entered; only a test at the call site can: if (Log.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug)) { Log.Debug("HasGuildCondition", $"{character.Name} has no guild."); } This is a cheap read of already-loaded state (a set lookup plus a walk of the logger dictionary) and performs no allocation. It answers by exactly the same rule Write(LogLevel, string, string, Exception, Dictionary<string, object>) dispatches by, so a false here can never drop a message some sink would have taken. It returns false when the manager is not initialized or has been shut down. In that state Write(LogLevel, string, string, Exception, Dictionary<string, object>) does still emit an [INTERNAL] CRITICAL line through OnInternalLogMessage, so guarding an uninitialized-manager diagnostic on IsEnabled would suppress it. That is the intended trade: the guard exists for per-frame gameplay logging, not for startup diagnostics, and a hot path must not pay for a not-initialized notice tens of times per cast. api/patcher/FishMMO.Patcher.PathContainm.title: Class PathContainment | FishMMO Documentation
api/patcher/FishMMO.Patcher.PathContainm.summary: Class PathContainment Namespace FishMMO.Patcher Assembly Updater.dll Resolves a manifest-supplied relative path against the install root and proves the result stays inside it. public static class PathContainment Inheritance object PathContainment Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This is the fix for the archive-extraction traversal ("zip slip") class of bug. Every path in a patch manifest is attacker-controlled the moment the patch host is spoofed or compromised, and Combine(string, string) is not a security boundary: it happily returns the second argument outright when that argument is rooted, and it does not collapse .. at all. So Path.Combine(installRoot, "../../.bashrc") and Path.Combine(installRoot, "/etc/cron.d/x") both escape, and the updater writes, overwrites, or DELETES whatever they name — with whatever privileges the player's install runs under. The delete path matters as much as the write path. An unchecked delete is arbitrary file deletion, which needs no code execution to be destructive, so every site that turns a manifest string into a filesystem path goes through here — new files, patched files, deletions, and the directory pre-creation pass that runs ahead of all three. The checks are deliberately layered and deliberately strict. Each one alone has a known bypass: a textual .. scan misses C:\, a prefix comparison against the resolved path misses a symlinked subdirectory, and rejecting rooted paths misses ..\ on a manifest authored on Windows and applied on Linux (where \ is a legal filename character rather than a separator, so Path would not split on it at all). Together they leave no gap, and the cost is a few string operations per manifest entry. Methods ResolveOrThrow(string, string) TryResolve(string, string, out string, out string), throwing PathContainmentException on refusal. public static string ResolveOrThrow(string rootDirectory, string relativePath) Parameters rootDirectory string relativePath string Returns string Remarks The throwing form is what the patch phases use: it fails the whole patch and triggers the existing rollback, rather than skipping the offending entry and committing a partially-applied update the manifest author chose the shape of. TryResolve(string, string, out string, out string) Resolves relativePath under rootDirectory. public static bool TryResolve(string rootDirectory, string relativePath, out string fullPath, out string rejectionReason) Parameters rootDirectory string The install root. Must be an existing, rooted directory. relativePath string The manifest-supplied path, which is untrusted. fullPath string The resolved absolute path when the call returns true. rejectionReason string Why the path was refused, when the call returns false. Returns bool True when the path is safe to act on.

Type Parameters T The type of the value. Remarks Every value is formatted with InvariantCulture, and that is not a nicety. This used to call value.ToString(), which formats with the current culture, while every reader below parses with the invariant one. On any machine whose locale writes a comma as the decimal separator — most of Europe — a float written here came back as a different number entirely: 0.75f was stored as "0,75" and read back by TryGetFloat(string, out float, float), which accepted the comma as a digit-group separator, as 75. Interface scale, brightness, every audio volume and every window position round-tripped to roughly a hundred times their value and were then clamped to whatever bound the reader enforced. The setting looked like it had not been saved; in fact it had been saved and misread. float and double take the round-trip ("R") format, so a stored value parses back to the identical bits. Everything else that knows how to format itself is asked to do so invariantly, which also keeps enum names, dates and negative signs stable across locales. api/sharedutility/FishMMO.Shared.ZstdDel.summary: Class ZstdDelta Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO-SharedUtility.dll Binary deltas between two versions of a file, as Zstandard frames that use the old file as a reference prefix (what zstd --patch-from does). public static class ZstdDelta Inheritance object ZstdDelta Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Used by the native client patches: the patch generator stores each changed file as a delta against the version the player already has, and the Updater rebuilds the new file from the old one plus the delta. Unlike a same-offset chunk diff, a zstd match can point anywhere in the old file, so inserted or removed bytes do not invalidate everything after them; and a file Addressables renamed because a dependency's name inside it changed costs a few kilobytes instead of its whole size. The reference file is memory-mapped and handed to zstd as a prefix, so neither side copies it into managed memory. A frame is a single zstd frame with the content size and a checksum, readable by the stock zstd tool (zstd -d --patch-from=old delta). The window is sized from the larger of the two files, capped at MaxWindowLog (1 GiB), the largest window every decoder, 32-bit included, accepts. A file larger than MaxReferenceBytes cannot be referenced in full; callers ship such files whole (see CanReference(long, long)). Fields DefaultLevel Default level: the smallest output, since patches are encoded once and downloaded many times. public const int DefaultLevel = 22 Field Value int MaxLevel Highest compression level zstd offers. Slow to encode, no slower to decode. public const int MaxLevel = 22 Field Value int MaxReferenceBytes Largest file (either side) a delta can fully reference. public const long MaxReferenceBytes = 1073741824 Field Value long MaxWindowLog Largest window log used or accepted (1 GiB). public const int MaxWindowLog = 30 Field Value int Methods CanReference(long, long) True when a delta between files of these sizes can reference the whole of the old one. public static bool CanReference(long referenceLength, long newLength) Parameters referenceLength long newLength long Returns bool Decode(string?, Stream, Stream, long) Rebuilds a file from referencePath (the old version, or null for a delta written without one) and a delta written by Encode(string?, string, Stream, int). public static long Decode(string? referencePath, Stream delta, Stream output, long expectedLength) Parameters referencePath string The exact file the delta was made against, or null. delta Stream The delta stream; read to its end. output Stream Receives the rebuilt file. expectedLength long The rebuilt file's size; anything else is an error, and output beyond it is never written. Returns long The number of bytes written. Exceptions InvalidDataException The delta is corrupt, truncated, does not match the reference, or has trailing data. Encode(string?, string, Stream, int) Writes a delta that turns referencePath into newPath. A null referencePath writes plain zstd compression of the new file. public static long Encode(string? referencePath, string newPath, Stream output, int level = 22) Parameters referencePath string newPath string output Stream level int Returns long The number of bytes written to output. Exceptions InvalidOperationException Either file is larger than MaxReferenceBytes, or zstd reported an error. WindowLogFor(long, long) The window log for a delta between files of these sizes. public static int WindowLogFor(long referenceLength, long newLength) Parameters referenceLength long newLength long Returns int

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.AdditionalLight.summary: Class AdditionalLightTable Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll WebGPU: URP's per-light arrays (additional lights, their shadow parameters and slices, their cookies, and the Forward+ reflection probes) gathered once per camera into one storage buffer the lit passes read (FishLightTable.hlsl), so they are no longer members of every lit program's $Globals. public static class AdditionalLightTable Inheritance object AdditionalLightTable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks On WebGPU URP's lighting cbuffers are plain globals (FishShadowVariants.hlsl: the pipelines must stay within the device's 10 dynamic uniform buffers), which put ~14 KB of arrays into each lit program's $Globals; Unity copies a program's whole $Globals on every pass application, and that copy was the largest engine cost left in the browser (measured 2026-11-03). The table is not a second account of URP's light setup. A compute kernel (FishLightTableGather, in the profile's terrain-instancing compute, as the depth pyramid's kernels are) declares URP's arrays by URP's names and sizes, so its constants are filled from the very globals URP has just set, and copies them bit for bit. It runs after the shadow passes, when the last of them (the additional lights' shadow parameters and slices) has been set, and before anything is lit; every camera runs its own, so each camera's draws read its own lights. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.CachedMainLight.summary: Class CachedMainLightShadows Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Cached static casters for the main light's cascaded shadows: the GPU-driven props' static casters (structures, rocks, cliffs — TerrainGpuRenderer.ShadowCache.cs) are drawn into a persistent copy of URP's cascade atlas only when a cascade changes, and that copy is merged, depth-tested, into URP's own shadow map every frame after URP has drawn the rest. public static class CachedMainLightShadows Inheritance object CachedMainLightShadows Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why a merge, not a replacement. URP keeps its cascade slices and its shadow pass to itself, and every receiver (props, vegetation, GPU terrain, grass, scatter, water, the clouds' shadow reads) samples URP's map with URP's matrices. So URP still draws the shadow map — every live caster: trees and plants (their sway stays), characters, ships, scatter, grass, terrain — and only the batch group's static casters move out of it (TerrainGpuRenderer.Brg.cs leaves them out of the main light's culling while this serves the camera). After URP's pass the cache is merged into the same map with the depth test, so each texel keeps the nearer of the live and the cached depth: exactly what drawing them together gives. Nothing a receiver reads changes. Windows, not URP's slices (2026-11-03). URP re-fits each cascade to the camera every frame, snapped to its texels. Caching URP's slice itself meant a moving camera redrew every cascade nearly every frame (natively ~1,240 static draws a frame, +2 ms CPU, no saving). Each cascade is now cached over a window: URP's slice at the refresh with its orthographic projection widened by MarginDivisor of its texels on each side (and a quarter of its depth range at each end), at URP's own texel size and rotation. URP's slice in a later frame is the same orthographic grid moved by whole texels (stable cascades), so it maps into the window as a whole-texel shift and a depth offset (TryMap(in Window, in CascadeKey, int, int, out Mapping)), and the merge copies from there. A cascade is redrawn only when URP's slice leaves its window (its tile or its depth range), the slice's rotation, texel size, resolution or bias changes (a sun step, a setting), the atlas changes, or the static casters themselves change (a layout or an instance upload: the camera no longer counts). A redraw culls the casters itself for the whole window, from the camera's position then (TerrainGpuRenderer.RecordShadowCacheCull): its levels chosen there and drawn whole (no crossfade dither, which would freeze mid-fade), so a cached shadow can hold an instance's level from up to a margin away until its window moves on. While caching, the sky lights' directions step on a fixed azimuth/elevation lattice (SunStepDegrees): the sun's direction is a pure function of the shared clock and the lattice is a pure function of the direction, so every client steps at the same world time; between steps the windows hold. Limits. A sun step redraws every cascade that frame. A redraw costs what every frame cost before (one indirect draw per static command; Unity pays a SetPass for each, whatever their order). Only the props' batch-group casters are cached; MeshRenderers, scatter and the GPU terrain stay live. Needs the instance index to carry the run's start (Vulkan; WebGPU with indirect-first-instance); elsewhere it does nothing. Fields CachePass The cache pass (before URP's shadows) and the merge pass (after them); enqueued by FishCloudsFeature. public static readonly ScriptableRenderPass CachePass Field Value ScriptableRenderPass DebugClearDepth Diagnostic: a raw depth the cache's tiles clear to instead of the far plane (negative: the far plane). With DebugOverwrite a mid value shades every cascade, which shows the merge reads the cache. public static float DebugClearDepth Field Value float DebugDrawNothing Diagnosis (harness shadowCacheDrawNothing): the cache's passes run and set their state, but draw no casters, and the batch group keeps the static casters in URP's map: what the cache's passes do to a frame besides its casters. public static bool DebugDrawNothing Field Value bool DebugForceExact Diagnostic: every frame drawn over exact windows (the refused frame's path), to test that path alone. public static bool DebugForceExact Field Value bool DebugLiveCull Diagnosis (harness shadowCacheLiveCull): the cache draws the camera's own culling of the static casters, not its own. public static bool DebugLiveCull Field Value bool DebugMergeNoDraw Diagnosis (harness shadowCacheMergeNoDraw, shadowCacheMergeNoState): the merge pass without its draws, or without its depth bias and viewport. public static bool DebugMergeNoDraw Field Value bool DebugMergeNoState Diagnosis (harness shadowCacheMergeNoDraw, shadowCacheMergeNoState): the merge pass without its draws, or without its depth bias and viewport. public static bool DebugMergeNoState Field Value bool DebugOverwrite Diagnostic: the merge overwrites URP's map with the cache (depth test off), showing only the cached casters. public static bool DebugOverwrite Field Value bool DebugSkipCull Diagnosis (harness shadowCacheSkipPass, shadowCacheSkipCull, shadowCacheSkipMerge): one of the cache's passes left out. public static bool DebugSkipCull Field Value bool DebugSkipMerge Diagnosis (harness shadowCacheSkipPass, shadowCacheSkipCull, shadowCacheSkipMerge): one of the cache's passes left out. public static bool DebugSkipMerge Field Value bool DebugSkipPass Diagnosis (harness shadowCacheSkipPass, shadowCacheSkipCull, shadowCacheSkipMerge): one of the cache's passes left out. public static bool DebugSkipPass Field Value bool DefaultOn Whether the cache starts on. The owner chose on in browser players and off natively (2026-11-03); it stays off everywhere until its merge is right. 2026-11-06: with URP's three cascades in the browser, the cache's image has dark areas the live map has nowhere (the live map with one cascade has none either), and the merge alone, with nothing cached (harness shadowCacheDrawNothing), still changed ~8% of the close view's pixels: on WebGPU the merge writes depth that no caster put there. The editor (Vulkan) merge wrote nothing in the same state (RenderDoc; measured 2026-11-05). public const bool DefaultOn = false Field Value bool Enabled The switch (harness setting cachedShadows), on by default in browser players only (DefaultOn). api/unity/FishMMO.Client.CancelKey.html.summary: Class CancelKey Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll The keys that cancel, close and back out: Escape, and ~ (the backquote key) everywhere except a text field. public static class CancelKey Inheritance object CancelKey Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks ~ exists because of the browser. A web build cannot have Escape: it always releases the pointer lock and leaves fullscreen, no page can cancel that, and the browser often does not deliver the key at all. Escape is kept beside it for the desktop client and for the times a browser does pass it through. While the player is typing, only Escape counts. ~ and ` are characters, and a field that ate them could not hold a password containing one, or a chat line. Typing also means the cursor is already free, which is when a browser lets Escape through. The same pair is bound in the input asset to Player/Cancel and Player/CloseLastUI, whose handlers apply the same rule through InputControlHasFocus(UITKControl); see PlayerInputController. Fields BackquoteControlPath Input System control path of the ~ key, as bound in PlayerControls.inputactions. public const string BackquoteControlPath = "<Keyboard>/backquote" Field Value string EscapeControlPath Input System control path of Escape. public const string EscapeControlPath = "<Keyboard>/escape" Field Value string Methods IsInTextField(VisualElement) True when element is a text input or sits inside one. public static bool IsInTextField(VisualElement element) Parameters element VisualElement Returns bool Remarks A TextField delegates focus to its inner text element, so a key event targets that child; walking up catches both. Matched by USS class rather than type so every field type (TextField, IntegerField, ...) is covered, and Buttons and Labels — which are TextElements too — are not. Matches(KeyDownEvent) True when a key press should cancel: Escape always, ~ unless it was pressed inside a text field. public static bool Matches(KeyDownEvent evt) Parameters evt KeyDownEvent The key-down event a panel received. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.Cartography.htm.summary: Class Cartography Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll The one place the map subsystem asks how good the player's maps are. public static class Cartography Inheritance object Cartography Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why a seam rather than a number. Cartography is going to scale half a dozen unrelated things — how far the fog lifts as you walk, how much of the world map you can see at once, whether region names and coordinates are shown, how many notes you may keep. Each of those is a different formula in a different file, and hard-coding today's constants into them means finding all six again later. Every one of them reads a property here instead, so wiring up the real skill is a single registration. Why the default is the maximum. The skill does not exist, so there is nothing for a player to level and no way to earn a better map. Shipping a crippled map that unlocks against a system nobody can interact with would be a bug, not a preview. When the profession arrives, the starting tier becomes whatever it grants a new character, and that change belongs in the provider — not here. Where the skill must be earned. Not from the fog file. See FogOfWarStore: exploration progress is on the player's disk and is forgeable, so Cartography experience has to be awarded by the server from the positions it already receives. The fog file decides what the map looks like and nothing else. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.CharacterSheetV.summary: Class CharacterSheetView Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Binds UICharacterSheet.uxml to one subject: the ten sockets, the character preview and the HP / MP / Stamina chips. public sealed class CharacterSheetView Inheritance object CharacterSheetView Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This is the half of the character sheet that is the same whoever is looking at it. The player's own equipment panel and the inspect window mount the same markup and show the same three regions; what differs is only what they are allowed to reveal, which is CharacterSheetOptions, and what they do with a click, which is not this class's business at all. Deliberately not a UITKSlotPanelBase. That class is not a set of drawing helpers, it is an operation tracker: its OwnContainer, IsSlotBlocked and ApplySlotLockVisual all bottom out in Character — which UIManager fills with the LOCAL player for every UITKCharacterControl it enrols, with no way to opt out. An inspect window holding a subject who is somebody else, deriving from that base, would silently inherit the local player's containers and in-flight equip state. So the sharing here is composition, the way UITKItemIcon and EquipmentPreviewRenderer are shared, and the slot PAINTING is UITKSlotPainter's. It resolves the sockets and hands them out. SlotElementNames is the contract with ItemSlot — one authored element per enum value, in enum order — and it lives here, once, because both panels need it. Each panel still does its own marking and wiring on the elements it takes: the equipment panel registers the interactive handlers, the inspect window registers none. That is the rule UITKSlotPanelBase already states about slot creation, kept intact. Constructors CharacterSheetView(VisualElement, CharacterSheetOptions) Resolves the sheet's elements and hides the regions this viewer may not see. public CharacterSheetView(VisualElement root, CharacterSheetOptions options) Parameters root VisualElement The mounted sheet's root element. options CharacterSheetOptions What this viewer is allowed to see. Fields SlotElementNames UXML element name for every ItemSlot, indexed by its enum value. public static readonly string[] SlotElementNames Field Value string[] Remarks THIS ARRAY IS A CONTRACT, NOT A CONVENIENCE. EquipmentController sizes its container from Enum.GetNames(typeof(ItemSlot)).Length, so slot i of the container is (ItemSlot)i and must be drawn by SlotElementNames[i]. Every enum value needs an entry, in order, and every entry needs an element of that name in UICharacterSheet.uxml. The comment that used to sit on a copy of this array claimed it listed "only slots that exist in both the enum and the UXML", which was untrue in both directions: it named slot-accessory, which the UXML did not define, while the UXML defined slot-neck and slot-ring, which are not ItemSlot values and which this array did not name. The result was an Accessory slot that could never render — Q returned null and the per-slot guard quietly skipped it — and two dead elements the player could click to no effect. Both halves are fixed; the markup now declares exactly these ten names, and there is one array rather than one per panel. TITLE_NAME Name of the label showing the subject's name. public const string TITLE_NAME = "header-title" Field Value string Properties PanelRoot The window itself — the authored panel-root, not the document's container. public VisualElement PanelRoot { get; } Property Value VisualElement Remarks A UIDocument hands out a container element that the UXML tree is cloned INTO, so the tree's own root is a CHILD of the element a panel is tempted to treat as "the root". A class added to the container is therefore matched by nothing in the stylesheet, and its position is not the position of anything on screen. Everything that places this window belongs on this element, and so does anything that considers where the window is: UITKControl drags the nearest fish-panel ancestor of the header, which is exactly this one. A placement override written to the container would not move the box the player drags, and the first drag would then have to fight it. ShowAttributes Whether this viewer may see the attribute list. public bool ShowAttributes { get; } Property Value bool SlotRoots The ten sockets, indexed by ItemSlot, null where the markup lacks one. public IReadOnlyList<VisualElement> SlotRoots { get; } Property Value IReadOnlyList<VisualElement> Subject The subject this sheet is showing, or null. public IPlayerCharacter Subject { get; } Property Value IPlayerCharacter TitleLabel The label a panel may set to name the subject. public Label TitleLabel { get; } Property Value Label Remarks Exposed rather than set here, because the two windows disagree about it: the player's own sheet always says EQUIPMENT, and an inspect window names the character it is showing. Methods ClearSockets() Paints every socket empty. public void ClearSockets() Dispose() Releases everything this sheet owns for the rest of the session. public void Dispose() Remarks Disposes rather than dropping the reference: the camera belongs to the character and would otherwise stay enabled — rendering the character into a texture nobody draws, every frame, for the rest of the session. EnableSocketHover() Wires the read-only item tooltip onto the sockets. public void EnableSocketHover() Remarks Opt-in, and it has to be. The player's own sheet gets this behaviour from OnSlotPointerEnter(int, VisualElement), which looks the item up in the container that panel is bound to; a viewer that may not act on a socket has no such container and asks the sheet for the behaviour instead. Wiring both would open the same tooltip twice. A tooltip is not an interaction. Inspecting a character is how a player judges their gear, and an item's name and stats live in its tooltip — reading one changes nothing about the character being read. InvalidatePreviewFraming() Marks the preview framing as stale. public void InvalidatePreviewFraming() Remarks Equipment changes the silhouette: a two-handed weapon reaches further than a dagger, and a frame sized before it existed crops it. Re-framing on the next frame rather than this one is deliberate — the mesh is attached by the visual controller in the same call chain, and measuring before it lands would measure the old silhouette again. PaintSockets() Paints the ten sockets read-only from this sheet's subject. public void PaintSockets() Remarks Every socket is painted, empty ones included, so a sheet pointed at a second character cannot leave the first one's gear on screen. A sheet with no subject paints every socket empty for the same reason. The painting itself is UITKSlotPainter's, and it is the same call the player's own sheet makes. What this method deliberately never does is register a handler on what it paints: the equipment panel's sockets get their press, drag and drop behaviour from UITKSlotPanelBase, and a second set registered here would double it. Refresh() Re-reads everything the sheet shows from its subject, without rebuilding the tree. public void Refresh() Remarks The preview is rebuilt on every open, not just the first: the camera and texture belong to the character and are handed back when the sheet closes, so the opening after that starts from nothing. RefreshPreview() Adopts the subject's preview camera and renders it into the viewport. public void RefreshPreview() Remarks Safe to call every frame: it returns immediately until the UI layout engine has measured the viewport, and once the preview is framed it is one small orthographic render into a texture already sized for the element. The camera is taken from the character rather than injected by whoever opened the sheet. It used to be handed over by the equipment hotkey, which meant the preview depended on how the panel was opened and not on what it was showing. For an inspected character this photographs their race model and nothing else: no equipment geometry is ever built for a character you do not own. See the panel's remarks. ReleasePreview() Hands the preview camera and texture back. public void ReleasePreview() Remarks Called when the sheet goes off screen, when its subject changes and when it is destroyed. The camera is handed back rather than simply left enabled because the preview's cost is paid every frame whether or not anyone is looking at it. SetSubject(IPlayerCharacter) Points the sheet at a character, replacing whatever it was showing. public void SetSubject(IPlayerCharacter subject) Parameters subject IPlayerCharacter The character to show, or null to show nothing. Remarks The outgoing character's subscriptions and preview camera are released BEFORE the reference moves. Doing it the other way round is the bug this class inherits from the panel it came from: detaching afterwards looked up the attributes of the INCOMING character and left the outgoing one wired to this sheet forever, while its camera stayed enabled and rendered into a texture nothing was drawing.

on the render rate, before the display's own limit is applied. public const int MaximumTargetFrameRate = 500 Field Value int Remarks 500 is also FishNet's own NetworkManager.MAXIMUM_FRAMERATE, which ClientManager.SetFrameRate clamps to. Matching it means the two never disagree about what was requested. The effective ceiling is normally lower — see ResolveMaximumFrameRate(). MinimumTargetFrameRate Lowest render rate a client may be capped to. public const int MinimumTargetFrameRate = 30 Field Value int Remarks The floor exists because of the tick, not because of visual quality. FishNet derives ticks from the update loop, so a frame rate below the tick rate cannot deliver them on time: ticks bunch up several to a frame and the client falls behind the server's timeline. 30 matches the project's tick rate, and ResolveMinimumFrameRate() raises it automatically if the tick rate is ever increased. NetworkManager Reference to the FishNet NetworkManager singleton used by all client networking. public static NetworkManager NetworkManager Field Value NetworkManager Properties AudioListener AudioListener component used by the client for 3D audio positioning. public AudioListener AudioListener { get; } Property Value AudioListener CanRejoinWorldQueue Whether RejoinWorldQueue() can run now: the connection the world server closed has finished closing. public bool CanRejoinWorldQueue { get; } Property Value bool Remarks Reconnecting while that close is still in flight lets it land on the new attempt's teardown flag and abort the attempt without a word, so the button that calls it waits for this instead. ClientPostbootSystem Optional post-boot system for client-side initialization after scene load. public ClientPostbootSystem ClientPostbootSystem { get; } Property Value ClientPostbootSystem Connection Manages the client's connection lifecycle (connect, disconnect, reconnect). public ClientConnectionManager Connection { get; } Property Value ClientConnectionManager CurrentConnectionType The current server connection type (None, Login, World, or Scene). public ServerConnectionType CurrentConnectionType { get; } Property Value ServerConnectionType LoadingSuppressed Called when the local character starts. Sets up input controller and UI. public static bool LoadingSuppressed { get; } Property Value bool Remarks This deliberately does not suppress genuine scene transitions. The overlay has two independent drivers: AddressableLoadProcessor.OnProgressUpdate, which fires for any background asset work and would otherwise flash the overlay over live gameplay, and FishNet's SceneManager load events, which are real zone changes the player must see a loading screen for. Gating both on this flag meant that once it latched — which happened at the network handshake, before the first scene had even loaded — no loading screen could ever appear again for the rest of the session, including zone-to-zone teleports. The flag is now checked only on the Addressable path. LoginAuthenticator Authenticator used for login and world server authentication. public ClientLoginAuthenticator LoginAuthenticator { get; } Property Value ClientLoginAuthenticator LoginServerPorts Cached list of login server addresses discovered via API host probing. public List<ushort> LoginServerPorts { get; } Property Value List<ushort> LoginServerRequestTimeoutSeconds Timeout in seconds for each login server probe request. public int LoginServerRequestTimeoutSeconds { get; } Property Value int WorldPreloadScenes List of addressable scenes to preload when entering the game world. public List<AddressableSceneLoadData> WorldPreloadScenes { get; } Property Value List<AddressableSceneLoadData> Methods ApplyTargetFrameRate(int) Caps how fast the client renders. public static void ApplyTargetFrameRate(int framesPerSecond) Parameters framesPerSecond int Target frames per second, normally the user's saved frame-rate preference. Clamped between ResolveMinimumFrameRate() and ResolveMaximumFrameRate() — that is, no slower than the tick rate and no faster than the display can present. Remarks Render rate and tick rate are independent. This sets only how often the client draws. Simulation runs on the FishNet TimeManager tick — a fixed 30 Hz, set per-scene and identical on client and server — and every authoritative system rides it: prediction, reconciliation, cooldowns, ability activation and NPC brains. A player at 500 FPS and one at 30 FPS send the same number of packets, simulate the same number of physics steps, and reconcile against the same ticks. The only things a higher frame rate buys are smoother interpolation between ticks and slightly fresher input sampling within one. The single point where the two touch is the floor above: the frame rate must clear the tick rate for ticks to be delivered on schedule. That is a one-way dependency — the tick rate is never derived from the render rate. Clamped rather than rejected. The previous version returned without doing anything for an out-of-range value, so a monitor reporting an unusual refresh rate left the cap at whatever it happened to be — silently ignoring the user's setting instead of honouring it as closely as it can. Setting UnityEngine.Application.targetFrameRate alone is not reliably enough. FishNet's NetworkManager.UpdateFramerate writes targetFrameRate from ClientManager.FrameRate every time the connection state changes, so a value set here can be discarded at the next connect or server hop. The client scene now ships with ChangeFrameRate disabled so FishNet leaves the render rate alone entirely, but the matching ClientManager.SetFrameRate call below is kept: it costs nothing, and it keeps the preference intact if the flag is ever re-enabled or the client runs as a host, where FishNet takes the higher of the client and server rates. Applying the screen refresh rate via Screen.SetResolution changes the display mode only; with vSync off it does not limit the render loop. Broadcast<T>(T, Channel) Sends a network broadcast to the server on the specified channel. public static void Broadcast<T>(T broadcast, Channel channel = Channel.Reliable) where T : struct, IBroadcast Parameters broadcast T The broadcast message to send. channel Channel The network channel to use (default Reliable). Type Parameters T The broadcast message type. ConnectToServer(ushort, bool) Connects the client to a game server at the specified port. Hostname is always GameHost. With WebTransport, the port is a QUIC connection parameter, not a URL path. public void ConnectToServer(ushort port, bool isWorldServer = false) Parameters port ushort The server port. isWorldServer bool If true, marks this as a world server connection. DismissLoadingScreen(bool, bool) Hides the loading overlay and optionally suppresses future incidental re-shows. Called on local character start, when the player actually exists in the world. public static void DismissLoadingScreen(bool suppress, bool waitForSceneContent = false) Parameters suppress bool True to stop background asset loads from re-showing the overlay. Genuine scene transitions are unaffected — see LoadingSuppressed. waitForSceneContent bool World entry: keep the overlay up until the scene's own content loads have finished (FinishWorldEntry()). False tears it down now. ForceDisconnect() Forces an immediate disconnection from the current server. public void ForceDisconnect() GetLoginServerList(Action<string>, Action<List<ushort>, string>) Probes API host candidates for a login server address list and the connection token that must accompany the next handshake. Always performs a fresh probe. public IEnumerator GetLoginServerList(Action<string> onFail, Action<List<ushort>, string> onDone) Parameters onFail Action<string> Callback invoked with an error message if all probes fail. onDone Action<List<ushort>, string> Callback invoked with the list of discovered server addresses. Returns IEnumerator Coroutine enumerator. Remarks This deliberately does not cache. IPFetch returns the port list and the connection token in one response, the token is single-use, and every connect needs one — so a cache hit could never skip the round trip it would have to make anyway to mint a fresh token. A TTL-based port cache used to sit here; it was unreachable, because its guard required an unspent FishMMO.Client.Client.cachedConnectionToken and FishMMO.Client.Client.TakeConnectionToken() clears that on the same synchronous path that sets it. Serving a stale list with a spent or expired token would present as a silent login failure that only a client restart clears, so re-probing is also the safe behaviour, not merely the simpler one. Initialize() Initializes NetworkManager, authenticator, transport, audio, UI, and event handlers. This starts the primary client behaviour. public void Initialize() IsConnectionReady(LocalConnectionState, bool) Checks whether the client connection is in the specified state and ready. Backward-compatible overload accepting LocalConnectionState. public bool IsConnectionReady(LocalConnectionState state, bool requireAuth = false) Parameters state LocalConnectionState The connection state to check for. requireAuth bool If true, the connection must be authenticated to be considered ready. Returns bool True if the connection is in the specified state and ready; otherwise, false. IsConnectionReady(bool) Checks whether the client connection is ready (authenticated by default). public bool IsConnectionReady(bool requireAuth = true) Parameters requireAuth bool If true, the connection must be authenticated to be considered ready. Returns bool True if the connection is ready; otherwise, false. LeaveWorldQueue() Leaves the world server's scene-routing queue on purpose and returns to the login screen, giving up the place in line. public void LeaveWorldQueue() Remarks The world server holds a queued account's place for a short grace window when its wait ends without the player's say (a dropped connection, a purge), so that coming back resumes it. A deliberate leave looks exactly like a drop from the server's side, so it is announced with a WorldSceneQueueLeaveBroadcast first. The broadcast is written before QuitToLogin(bool), whose disconnect waits for the outgoing bundle to flush precisely so that what was written on the way out is sent. Quit() Exits the application (play mode in editor, Application.Quit in builds, or WebGL key-hijack path). public void Quit() QuitToLogin(bool) Disconnects from the game world and returns to the login screen. public void QuitToLogin(bool forceDisconnect = true) Parameters forceDisconnect bool If true, forces an immediate disconnection. ReconnectCancel() Cancels any active reconnection attempt. public void ReconnectCancel() RejoinWorldQueue() Connects to the world server this client was last routed through again, to queue for a place after the previous wait ended without one. public bool RejoinWorldQueue() Returns bool False when the old connection has not finished closing; nothing was started. Remarks The session is still held — the token was not revoked when the wait ended — so this is the ordinary world reconnect, with the reconnect display and the loading overlay showing it. It keeps the place in line: the world server holds an account's place for a grace window after a wait it ended (about a minute by default), and the same account rejoining the same scene's queue inside it resumes the place. Later than that, it queues from the back. A client with no world server to return to ends up on the login screen, through the reconnect loop's own failure path. RequestHopTokenThenConnect(ushort, bool) Asks the currently connected server for a connection token, then connects to port once it arrives (or the wait times out). public void RequestHopTokenThenConnect(ushort port, bool isWorldServer) Parameters port ushort isWorldServer bool Remarks Used for both server hops — Login → World and World → Scene. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientAudioSett.summary: Class ClientAudioSettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll The client's audio volumes: one level per AudioChannel, persisted to configuration, applied at boot, and readable by anything that plays a sound. public static class ClientAudioSettings Inheritance object ClientAudioSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Only Master is offered today. See PlayableChannels: the other five levels are stored and applied correctly but nothing in the client plays through them yet, so the options panel does not show sliders that cannot be heard. Why this is not an AudioMixer. A mixer would be the natural home for per-channel levels, but it has to exist as an asset with a matching exposed parameter per group, and a mixer parameter set before the mixer has been loaded is silently dropped. This keeps the levels as plain data that any caller can read synchronously and that survives having no audio asset loaded at all — which is the state the client boots in. Master is the one level with somewhere to go on its own: UnityEngine.AudioListener.volume scales everything the scene plays, whether or not the caller knew about channels. Levels are stored, and applied, as a perceptual curve. Loudness is not linear in amplitude: a slider at half travel that halves the amplitude sounds far quieter than half. ToAmplitude(float) squares the slider value, which is the cheap approximation everything from game options to mixing desks uses, so the middle of the slider lands near the middle of the perceived range. The stored value is always the slider position, so the curve can be changed later without invalidating anybody's settings. Muting when unfocused is a volume decision, not a pause: the client keeps simulating, and a player who alt-tabs to a browser should not have to hear it. It is applied on top of Master rather than by writing zero into it, so the saved level is not destroyed by switching windows. Fields ChannelLabels Player-facing label for each channel, indexed by AudioChannel. public static readonly string[] ChannelLabels Field Value string[] PlayableChannels The channels the client currently routes audio through, and therefore the only ones the options panel offers. public static readonly AudioChannel[] PlayableChannels Field Value AudioChannel[] Remarks Master alone, because Master is the only one that reaches anything. It is applied to UnityEngine.AudioListener.volume, which scales every sound the scene plays whether or not the caller knew about channels. The other five have no consumer: nothing in the client owns an AudioSource yet, so a Music or Effects slider would save its value perfectly and change nothing a player could hear. A control that does nothing is worse than a missing one — it teaches the player that the settings screen lies. The rest of this class deliberately stays whole. Every channel keeps its key, its default, its stored level and its change event, so wiring up the audio system later is adding entries to this one array rather than rebuilding the model — and a level saved by a build that offered more channels is still read back correctly by one that offers fewer. Properties MuteWhenUnfocused Mute the client while its window is not focused. public static bool MuteWhenUnfocused { get; set; } Property Value bool Methods ApplySaved() Reads every channel from configuration and applies the result. public static void ApplySaved() DefaultVolume(AudioChannel) The default level for a channel. public static float DefaultVolume(AudioChannel channel) Parameters channel AudioChannel Returns float EffectiveVolume(AudioChannel) The amplitude a sound on this channel should actually be played at. public static float EffectiveVolume(AudioChannel channel) Parameters channel AudioChannel The channel the sound belongs to. Returns float A multiplier in the range 0..1, ready to assign to AudioSource.volume. Remarks Master is not folded in here. It is already applied to the UnityEngine.AudioListener, and applying it twice would square it — a master at 0.5 would play everything at a quarter. Callers therefore pass their own channel and get only that channel's contribution. GetVolume(AudioChannel) The slider position saved for a channel, in the range 0..1. public static float GetVolume(AudioChannel channel) Parameters channel AudioChannel Returns float KeyFor(AudioChannel) The configuration key a channel's level is stored under. public static string KeyFor(AudioChannel channel) Parameters channel AudioChannel Returns string LabelFor(AudioChannel) The player-facing label for a channel. public static string LabelFor(AudioChannel channel) Parameters channel AudioChannel Returns string ResetToDefaults() Restores the offered channels to their defaults and persists the result. public static void ResetToDefaults() Remarks Scoped to PlayableChannels, which is what the button the player pressed actually offers. That is now every channel, but the scoping stays: it is the reason a channel retired from the list stops being written to Configuration.cfg rather than lingering there as a setting nobody is shown. A channel with no stored key already resolves to DefaultVolume(AudioChannel), so there is nothing to put back for one left out. SetVolume(AudioChannel, float) Sets a channel's level, persists it, and applies it. public static void SetVolume(AudioChannel channel, float value) Parameters channel AudioChannel The channel to change. value float Slider position in the range 0..1. Clamped. ToAmplitude(float) Converts a slider position into an amplitude multiplier. public static float ToAmplitude(float sliderValue) Parameters sliderValue float Returns float Remarks Squared, so the slider's travel maps roughly onto perceived loudness rather than onto raw amplitude. Zero stays exactly zero, which matters — a channel dragged to the bottom must be silent, not merely quiet. Events OnVolumeChanged Raised whenever any channel's level changes. public static event Action<AudioChannel> OnVolumeChanged Event Type Action<AudioChannel> Remarks Playback that has already started cannot be rescaled by reading a number later, so a looping source — music, an ambient bed — has to be told. One-shots do not need to subscribe; they read the level as they are fired.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientBoundaryW.summary: Class ClientBoundaryWarning Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Shows the scene boundary as a glass barrier that breaks where the local player pushes into it, so the edge of the playable area is never a surprise. Driven from Client.Update. public sealed class ClientBoundaryWarning Inheritance object ClientBoundaryWarning Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The same boxes the server enforces. The scene server checks SceneBoundaryDetails.ContainsPoint: axis-aligned boxes, inside any one of them is inside. This reads the scene's SceneBoundary components — what that cache is built from — and measures the same boxes, so the glass stands exactly where the server will stop the player. A face shared with a neighbouring box is not an edge, and shows nothing. One break, set entirely by distance. Each frame the shader is told where on the face the player's chest is, how hard they are pressing (from how close they are), and how much of the invisible force a metre or two short of the boundary is on. The fracture pattern itself is fixed to the face, so walking closer breaks it further, backing off eases it back, and walking along the wall carries the break through the pattern. Nothing is timed, so nothing restarts. The look is FishMMO/Boundary Glass; see RequestSceneTextures(bool) for what its refraction costs and when. Every face, the ceiling included. A flier meets the top of the box the same way a walker meets a side, and sees the same glass overhead. Whose glass it is. Initialize() follows the local player's character as it starts and stops; Initialize(Transform) follows one transform for as long as its owner keeps it, which is how the world test bed shows the glass round its walker, with no player and no client. Either way the owner calls Tick() once a frame and Shutdown() when done, which takes the panes down and gives the camera back. Presentation only: it never moves the player or blocks anything. Client-only by assembly: FishMMO.Client is not compiled into the server. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientCameraSet.summary: Enum ClientCameraSettings.AntialiasingOption Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Edge smoothing modes offered to the player, in the order the dropdown shows them. public enum ClientCameraSettings.AntialiasingOption Fields Balanced = 2 Subpixel morphological. Sharper than FXAA for a modest cost. Fast = 1 Fast approximate. Very cheap, softens the whole image somewhat. Off = 0 No edge smoothing. Cheapest, and what the camera currently ships with. Temporal = 3 Temporal. Best on still edges, and the only one that can ghost in motion. Remarks Deliberately not AntialiasingMode itself. What is stored is a player setting that has to keep its meaning across Unity upgrades, and persisting a framework enum means a reordering there silently changes what an existing saved file says. This order is ours. Post-process antialiasing rather than MSAA. MSAA lives on the render pipeline asset and has its own option (ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption), written onto whichever asset the quality level uses; the two stack rather than fight: MSAA for geometry and leaf edges, this over the finished image.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientCastNamep.summary: Class ClientCastNameplateDisplay Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Shows what an observed character is casting on its nameplate. public sealed class ClientCastNameplateDisplay Inheritance object ClientCastNameplateDisplay Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why observers needed this. The only thing that reached an observer about another character's activation was the spawned ability object, so a self-buff, a pet summon or any consumable happened in complete silence: a character stood still, a bar somewhere changed, and nothing on screen connected the two. CharacterCastBroadcast is sent from the activation state machine, so it covers every activation whether or not anything spawns. Not for the owner. The server excludes the owner from the broadcast, and this ignores the local character if one ever arrives: the owner's own cast is predicted and already drawn by its cast bar, which is ahead of anything the server can say. Drawing a second, later version of it on the owner's own nameplate is exactly the desync the message is meant to avoid. Fields ExpiryGraceSeconds Extra time past a cast's own duration before it is dropped without a stop message. public const float ExpiryGraceSeconds = 1.5 Field Value float Remarks Not a loss allowance. The stop rides Channel.Reliable, and that is a correctness requirement rather than a comfort: the receiver keys a stop on the caster, so an unreliable stop from cast N reordering behind the start of cast N+1 clears the wrong row — reachable at instant-attack cadence, and pinned by CastVisibilityTests.TheCastMessageIsReliableAndAStopNamesWhatItEnds. (This used to say the stop was unreliable and could be lost; it cannot.) What the grace is for is a stop that never EXISTS: a caster that disconnects or is despawned mid-cast, and a cast that finishes slower than this peer computed because a speed debuff landed on the caster after the row was opened. Without it such a plate would read "Casting" until that character left view. MinimumDwellSeconds The shortest time a cast stays on a nameplate. public const float MinimumDwellSeconds = 0.6 Field Value float Remarks An instant ability starts and ends inside one tick, so start and stop arrive together and a plate written and cleared in the same frame shows nothing at all. Holding the row briefly is what makes an instant cast readable as an event. Methods Clear() Drops every row without unregistering. For a world change, where the network manager survives but every object id in FishMMO.Client.ClientCastNameplateDisplay.active is about to mean something else. public void Clear() Initialize(NetworkManager) Registers the broadcast handler. public void Initialize(NetworkManager networkManager) Parameters networkManager NetworkManager The client's network manager. ResolveExpiry(float, float, bool, float, float) When a row is dropped if no stop message ever arrives for it. public static float ResolveExpiry(float now, float duration, bool durationKnown, float remaining, float heldAllowance) Parameters now float Unscaled time the row is being opened at. duration float The activation's computed duration in seconds. durationKnown bool False when the ability could not be resolved at all. remaining float Seconds of the activation still to run, which may be negative. heldAllowance float Extra seconds a held activation may legitimately run for. Returns float The unscaled time to drop the row at. Remarks A zero-duration cast expires on the DWELL, not on the grace. The server no longer sends a stop for an activation that began and ended on one server tick (see AbilityController.SuppressesRedundantCastStop) — 17 of the 37 authored abilities are instant, the default attack among them — so for those this is the only thing that ever clears the row. An ability this peer cannot resolve — one learned after it started observing, or an NPC's set it never received — also reports zero, and that one may well be a five second cast whose stop is coming. Those keep the grace, which is why ResolveDuration(CharacterCastBroadcast, AbilityController, out bool) reports whether it resolved anything rather than leaving the caller to read zero two ways. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientChatSetti.summary: Class ClientChatSettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll How large the text in the chat log is drawn, so that a player who cannot comfortably read the default can make it larger without moving every other panel on the screen. public static class ClientChatSettings Inheritance object ClientChatSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why this is not the interface scale. The UI tab already offers one, and it is the wrong control for this. It works by dividing the panel asset's authored reference resolution, so it resizes every panel and every word in every one of them, and it stops at 1.5x. A player who can read the rest of the HUD and not the chat log gets nothing from it: turning it up pushes panels off the screen to fix one list of text, and 1.5x of a 12px line is 18px whether or not 18px is the size they needed. Points, not a multiplier. The control names the size it sets, so "16 pt" means sixteen points the way it would in any other application. A multiplier over the default was the other option and it reads worse: the number a player wants to see is the size they are choosing, not the ratio between it and a default they are not thinking about. What it deliberately does not cover. The chat tabs and the channel selector stay at their authored sizes. Both sit in containers of fixed height — the tab strip is 24 units and the selector 20 — so a font that grew inside either would clip rather than enlarge, and a setting that visibly breaks the panel is worse than one with a boundary. They are chrome; the message log and the input field are the text a player reads and writes, and those are what this covers. Why the range stops where it does. The panel is a fixed 222 units tall, a number chosen against the bands above and below it that UIChat.uss documents at length. At twenty points the log shows roughly eight lines, and past that it stops being a log and becomes a window onto one. The ceiling is a property of the panel's height rather than of legibility, which is why it is here and not at some larger round number.
