api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientConnectio.title: Class ClientConnectionManager | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientConnectio.summary: Class ClientConnectionManager Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Manages client connection lifecycle: connect, disconnect, reconnect with exponential backoff, and connection state tracking. Extracted from Client.cs. public class ClientConnectionManager Inheritance object ClientConnectionManager Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Constructors ClientConnectionManager(NetworkManager) Creates a ClientConnectionManager and subscribes to NetworkManager connection events. public ClientConnectionManager(NetworkManager networkManager) Parameters networkManager NetworkManager The FishNet NetworkManager to manage. Fields EnsureConnectionToken Optional coroutine run immediately before every StartConnection, used to obtain the one-time connection token the game server needs to recover this client's real IP. Every game server — Login, World and Scene — sits behind the same L4 UDP proxy and binds to loopback, so all of them see 127.0.0.1 as the source address and all of them reject a handshake that arrives without a token. Hooking the fetch here rather than at the individual call sites means world/scene routing and automatic reconnects get a token too, not just the login screen. public Func<IEnumerator> EnsureConnectionToken Field Value Func<IEnumerator> Properties CanReconnect Returns true if the current connection type supports reconnection (World, Scene, or an in-flight world connect). public bool CanReconnect { get; } Property Value bool Remarks ConnectingToWorld counts. ConnectToServer(string, ushort, bool) sets it for every world connect — including the reconnects TryReconnect() issues — and FishMMO.Client.ClientConnectionManager.OnClientConnectionState(FishNet.Transporting.ClientConnectionStateArgs) clears CurrentConnectionType to None on the drop that arms the retry, so by the time an attempt fails ConnectingToWorld is the only type left describing it. Without it here, a failed reconnect read as a non-reconnectable failure: no further retry was armed, so MaxReconnectAttempts never counted past one, OnReconnectFailed (and its quit-to-login forward) never fired, and the client sat disconnected with no path forward. lastWorldAddress is assigned before StartConnection on that same path, so a retry always has an address to dial — and TryReconnect no-ops when it does not. ClientState The current local connection state (Stopped, Starting, Started, Stopping). public LocalConnectionState ClientState { get; } Property Value LocalConnectionState ConnectionEstablishTimeoutSeconds Timeout in seconds waiting for a new connection to reach Started state. Default 20. public float ConnectionEstablishTimeoutSeconds { get; set; } Property Value float ConnectionStopTimeoutSeconds Timeout in seconds waiting for a connection to fully stop. Default 10. public float ConnectionStopTimeoutSeconds { get; set; } Property Value float CurrentConnectionType The type of server currently connecting to (None, Login, World, Scene). public ServerConnectionType CurrentConnectionType { get; set; } Property Value ServerConnectionType IsSceneHandoffReconnect True when the reconnect currently armed or in progress was caused by a scene server deliberately handing the client back, rather than by a lost connection. public bool IsSceneHandoffReconnect { get; } Property Value bool Remarks A zone change, a channel switch and a cross-scene bind-point respawn are all implemented as a deliberate drop, so from the outside they are the same event as an outage: OnReconnectPending and OnReconnectAttempt fire for both. Anything that explains the wait to the player needs to tell them apart — labelling a routine teleport "connection lost" is worse than saying nothing at all. Set alongside the shortened handoff backoff in FishMMO.Client.ClientConnectionManager.OnClientConnectionState(FishNet.Transporting.ClientConnectionStateArgs) and cleared once a connection is established, so it describes the wait that is actually running. MaxReconnectAttempts Maximum reconnect attempts before giving up. Range [1, 255]. Default 10. public int MaxReconnectAttempts { get; set; } Property Value int MaxReconnectDelay Maximum delay in seconds for exponential backoff. Default 60. public float MaxReconnectDelay { get; set; } Property Value float NetworkManager The FishNet NetworkManager managing this client connection. public NetworkManager NetworkManager { get; } Property Value NetworkManager ReconnectAttemptWaitTime Base wait time in seconds between reconnect attempts. Default 5. public float ReconnectAttemptWaitTime { get; set; } Property Value float ReconnectsAttempted Number of reconnect attempts made since the last successful connection. public int ReconnectsAttempted { get; } Property Value int SceneHandoffReconnectDelay Delay used for the first retry after a scene server hands the client back, instead of the full backoff. Jittered so a scene-wide event does not send every client at once. public float SceneHandoffReconnectDelay { get; set; } Property Value float Remarks A scene-to-scene transfer is implemented as a deliberate drop: the scene server releases the character and disconnects, and the client is expected to return to the world server to be re-routed. That return went through the ordinary reconnect backoff, so every teleport and channel switch cost a full ReconnectAttemptWaitTime (5s) of dead time — during which the scene has already unloaded and the loading overlay has already been dismissed by OnSceneEndUnload, leaving the player looking at an empty world. Only the first attempt is fast-pathed, and only from a Scene connection. If that attempt fails the normal exponential backoff resumes from attempt 1, so a genuinely unreachable world server is still not hammered. Methods CancelReconnect() Cancels pending reconnect and fires OnReconnectFailed immediately. public void CancelReconnect() ConnectToServer(string, ushort, bool) Initiates a connection. Guards against concurrent calls via CAS. public void ConnectToServer(string address, ushort port, bool isWorldServer = false) Parameters address string Server IP or hostname. port ushort Server port. isWorldServer bool If true, stores address for reconnection logic. ForceDisconnect() Forces the connection closed and prevents auto-reconnect until reset. public void ForceDisconnect() Remarks The suppression flag is only latched when there is a connection left to tear down. FishMMO.Client.ClientConnectionManager.OnClientConnectionState(FishNet.Transporting.ClientConnectionStateArgs) is what consumes it, so latching it against a connection that is already Stopped strands it: no further Stopped transition is raised to clear it, and the next ConnectToServer(string, ushort, bool) aborts inside OnAwaitingConnectionReady(string, ushort, bool) — silently, with the guard released and no connection started. The login screen reaches that state routinely, because every auth-error dialog calls this whether or not the transport is still up. IsConnectionReady(bool) Returns true if connected and optionally authenticated. public bool IsConnectionReady(bool requireAuthentication = true) Parameters requireAuthentication bool If true, also checks connection is authenticated. Returns bool True if the connection is ready for use. ResetReconnectState() Resets all reconnect state: attempt count, connection type, stored address. public void ResetReconnectState() Shutdown() Unsubscribes from NetworkManager events. Call during client teardown. public void Shutdown() TryReconnect() Attempts a reconnect with exponential backoff. The backoff delay is set in FishMMO.Client.ClientConnectionManager.OnClientConnectionState(FishNet.Transporting.ClientConnectionStateArgs) when the connection stops and counted down in Update(). This method is called by Update() when the timer expires — it must NOT reset the delay or the reconnect will never fire. public void TryReconnect() Update() Drives reconnect timer. Called every frame from the owning client. public void Update() Events OnConnectionAttemptFailed Fired when a non-reconnectable connection attempt fails (e.g. login server unreachable). public event Action OnConnectionAttemptFailed Event Type Action OnConnectionSuccessful Fired when a connection to the server is successfully established. public event Action OnConnectionSuccessful Event Type Action OnReconnectAttempt Fired on each reconnect attempt with current and max attempt counts. public event Action<int, int> OnReconnectAttempt Event Type Action<int, int> OnReconnectFailed Fired when all reconnect attempts are exhausted without success. public event Action OnReconnectFailed Event Type Action OnReconnectPending Fired the moment a reconnect is armed, before the backoff delay begins. public event Action OnReconnectPending Event Type Action Remarks OnReconnectAttempt fires when the retry actually starts, which leaves the whole backoff window unreported. That window is not idle time during a scene transfer: the scene server has already unloaded the client's scene, so the loading overlay has been dismissed by the unload-end event and the player is looking at an empty world until the retry fires. Shortening the delay for a deliberate hop reduces that to a flicker; this event closes it, by letting the overlay treat "a reconnect is coming" as a transition in progress rather than waiting for it to begin.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientDisplaySe.summary: Class ClientDisplaySettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Everything the client knows about display modes: which ones the hardware offers, which one the player saved, and how to put one into effect. public static class ClientDisplaySettings Inheritance object ClientDisplaySettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Split out of the options panel so the two callers that need it can share one implementation. The panel needs the option lists to build its dropdowns; the boot phase needs the resolve-and-apply half and nothing else. While this logic lived inside the panel, the boot phase had no way to reach it — which is why a saved resolution was never applied at start-up, only ever by pressing Apply in a panel the player had to open first. Brightness is re-applied on every scene load. UnityEngine.RenderSettings.ambientLight is per-scene state baked into the lighting settings of whichever scene is active, so loading a scene discards it. The client loads several — launcher, login, world, and one per world scene transfer — so a brightness set once at boot survived only until the first load. Brightness drives two properties, because which one is read depends on the scene. UnityEngine.RenderSettings.ambientLight is consulted only under AmbientMode.Flat. Every world scene in this project is authored AmbientMode.Skybox, where ambient comes from the skybox's spherical harmonics scaled by UnityEngine.RenderSettings.ambientIntensity and ambientLight is ignored outright — so a slider that wrote only ambientLight did nothing at all anywhere the player actually plays. It appeared to work while testing, because the login and preboot scenes are authored Flat. Both are written, so the setting has an effect whichever mode a scene uses and stays correct if one is re-authored. This is an ambient control and not an exposure control: it scales indirect light, leaving direct lights and the skybox itself alone. A true gamma control would need a URP Volume carrying a Color Adjustments override, which is a rendering asset rather than a setting. Fields DefaultAnisotropicFiltering Texture filtering when nothing has been chosen. public const ClientDisplaySettings.AnisotropicOption DefaultAnisotropicFiltering = PerTexture Field Value ClientDisplaySettings.AnisotropicOption Remarks Per-texture, which respects what the art was imported with rather than overriding it. Forcing it on costs little on any modern GPU but is still a decision about someone else's art, so it is offered rather than imposed. DefaultBrightness Brightness used when the player has never chosen one. public const float DefaultBrightness = 0.5 Field Value float Remarks Mid-scale rather than maximum. This scales indirect light (see the class remarks), so 1.0 is the top of the slider with no headroom left to raise it — a player who finds the world too bright can only go down, and one who finds it too dark has nowhere to go. Half way leaves adjustment in both directions. Only applies to a player who has never set a brightness; an existing saved value is read in preference to this and is not overwritten. MaximumBrightness Highest brightness the slider offers. public const float MaximumBrightness = 1 Field Value float MinimumBrightness Lowest brightness the slider offers. public const float MinimumBrightness = 0 Field Value float Methods ApplyAnisotropicFiltering(AnisotropicOption) Writes an anisotropic filtering mode into the quality settings. public static void ApplyAnisotropicFiltering(ClientDisplaySettings.AnisotropicOption option) Parameters option ClientDisplaySettings.AnisotropicOption The mode to apply. An unrecognised value falls back to per-texture. ApplyBrightness(float) Writes a brightness level into the scene's ambient lighting and remembers it. public static void ApplyBrightness(float value) Parameters value float Brightness in the range 0..1. Clamped. ApplyMsaa(MsaaOption) Writes a multisampling choice onto the active quality level's pipeline asset. MSAA lives there and nowhere else in URP; the vegetation follows it on its own (VegetationDistanceFade reads the asset every frame for the leaves' alpha-to-coverage). public static void ApplyMsaa(ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption option) Parameters option ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption ApplyQualityLevel(int, bool) Switches to a quality level and puts the player's VSync preference back on top of it. public static void ApplyQualityLevel(int index, bool applyExpensiveChanges) Parameters index int Index into UnityEngine.QualitySettings.names. applyExpensiveChanges bool True to let Unity re-create render targets and reload textures. Worth it when the player is watching and waiting for the result; not during boot, where the stall reads as a hang. Remarks SetQualityLevel installs that level's own authored vSyncCount, which is a property of the level and has nothing to do with what the player chose — so the preference is re-applied afterwards. Doing that here rather than at each call site is what stops the two from being forgotten separately. ApplySaved() Applies every saved display setting: mode, VSync, frame-rate cap and brightness. public static void ApplySaved() Remarks Order matters in one place only. VSync is written before the frame-rate cap because UnityEngine.Application.targetFrameRate is ignored outright whenever the active quality level has vSync enabled — so a cap applied first is silently discarded by a VSync value applied second. ApplySavedAnisotropicFiltering() Applies the stored anisotropic filtering mode. public static void ApplySavedAnisotropicFiltering() ApplySavedBrightness() Applies the saved brightness to the scene's ambient light. public static void ApplySavedBrightness() ApplySavedDisplayMode() Puts the saved resolution, refresh rate and fullscreen mode into effect. public static void ApplySavedDisplayMode() Remarks Nothing happens when no complete display mode has been saved. That distinction matters: a fresh install must keep whatever mode the player launched in — forcing one of the enumerated modes on first run would resize a window the player had already sized, and on a multi-monitor setup can move it to a different screen. ApplySavedFrameRate() Applies the saved render frame-rate cap. public static void ApplySavedFrameRate() Remarks Deliberately runs after the bootstrap system has installed its own menu-time cap. That cap is the default for a client with no preference — and ResolveSavedFrameRate(List<int>) resolves to the same number, so running afterwards re-applies it rather than replacing it. A player who has chosen a cap gets theirs, and getting the order backwards is indistinguishable from the setting not being saved at all. ApplySavedMsaa() Applies the stored multisampling choice to the active pipeline asset; with none, leaves the quality level's own (2026-11-05: 4× on High Fidelity at native scale, off on Balanced and Performant). The leaves' and the grass's soft edges are alpha-to-coverage, which only MSAA can draw; 4× cost about 0.3 ms at 2560×1440 in Flo Monolith (msaa1). public static void ApplySavedMsaa() ApplySavedQualityLevel() Applies the saved quality level, matched by name. public static void ApplySavedQualityLevel() ApplySavedVSync() Applies the saved VSync preference. public static void ApplySavedVSync() ApplyVSync(bool) Writes a VSync preference into the active quality level. public static void ApplyVSync(bool enabled) Parameters enabled bool True to wait for the display's refresh. Remarks Every VSync write goes through here so it cannot happen without the editor safeguard in FishMMO.Client.ClientDisplaySettings.CaptureAuthoredQuality() having run first. AvailableMsaa() The multisampling choices this device can draw, in dropdown order. WebGPU allows a sample count of 1 or 4 only (its spec), so 2× is not offered there: asked for, it measured exactly as 4× did in the browser (2026-11-04). public static ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption[] AvailableMsaa() Returns MsaaOption[] BuildFrameRateChoices() The selectable frame-rate caps for this machine, ascending. public static List<int> BuildFrameRateChoices() Returns List<int> Remarks The floor is the network tick rate. FishNet derives ticks from the update loop, so a frame rate below the tick rate cannot deliver them on schedule and the client falls behind the server's timeline — offering such a value lets a player break their own connection from a settings menu. The ceiling is ResolveMaximumFrameRate(): no longer the display's fastest mode, which the platform can misreport (60 Hz for a 480 Hz panel under KDE Wayland), and which VSync matches when that is what the player wants. BuildFullscreenOptions() The fullscreen modes this platform offers, in the order they are presented. public static List<FullScreenMode> BuildFullscreenOptions() Returns List<FullScreenMode> Remarks The list is built conditionally, so an index into it is not the UnityEngine.FullScreenMode value — on a build without exclusive fullscreen the second entry is MaximizedWindow. The stored key is always the enum value. BuildRefreshRateOptions(Vector2Int) The refresh rates this display offers at a given resolution, slowest first. public static List<RefreshRate> BuildRefreshRateOptions(Vector2Int size) Parameters size Vector2Int Returns List<RefreshRate> BuildResolutionOptions() The distinct width/height pairs this display supports, smallest first. public static List<Vector2Int> BuildResolutionOptions() Returns List<Vector2Int> Remarks Deduplicated. Screen.resolutions returns one entry per width/height/refresh-rate combination, so a monitor offering three refresh rates lists every resolution three times. CurrentMsaa() What the options show: the player's choice, or with none the active quality level's own MSAA. public static ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption CurrentMsaa() Returns ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption MatchOcclusionToMsaa(UniversalRenderPipelineAsset) The GPU Resident Drawer's occlusion culling on exactly when multisampling is off. Under MSAA on Vulkan URP resolves the depth attachment in hardware and allocates it without multisampled binding (bindTextureMS false), but the drawer's depth pyramid (core InstanceOcclusionCuller) picks its Texture2DMS variant from isMSAAEnabled alone: Unity refuses the bind every frame ("A non-multisampled texture being bound to a multisampled sampler… enable the bindMS flag") and the pyramid reads no depth, so nothing was occluded under MSAA anyway. A Unity bug in a package we do not embed; switching it off where it cannot work loses nothing and stops the error. public static void MatchOcclusionToMsaa(UniversalRenderPipelineAsset pipeline) Parameters pipeline UniversalRenderPipelineAsset ResolveSavedFrameRate(List<int>) The frame-rate cap to apply, given the caps this machine offers. public static int ResolveSavedFrameRate(List<int> choices) Parameters choices List<int> Returns int Remarks Three cases, and they are deliberately different from one another. No preference at all — a fresh install — keeps the boot-time menu cap of BootstrapTargetFrameRate. This used to return the display's fastest mode instead, which made the bootstrap cap dead on arrival: it was installed before the first frame and replaced microseconds later by the settings apply, so a fresh install rendered its launcher and login screens as fast as the panel allowed and pegged a core drawing a static menu. Somebody with no opinion about frame rate should get the modest default, not the maximum. A saved value this machine offers is honoured exactly. A saved value it does not offer falls back to the fastest available, and not to the default: that is the player who moved the game to a different monitor, and they did express a preference — the old number is just meaningless on the new hardware, so the closest thing to "as fast as I asked for" is the most this display can do. SupportedMsaa(MsaaOption) The nearest choice this device can draw (a 2× saved elsewhere is 4× on WebGPU). public static ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption SupportedMsaa(ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption option) Parameters option ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption Returns ClientDisplaySettings.MsaaOption ToHz(RefreshRate) Converts a refresh-rate ratio to hertz. public static float ToHz(RefreshRate rate) Parameters rate RefreshRate Returns float TryResolveSavedDisplayMode(out Vector2Int, out RefreshRate, out FullScreenMode) Reads the saved display mode, rejecting anything this display cannot present. public static bool TryResolveSavedDisplayMode(out Vector2Int size, out RefreshRate rate, out FullScreenMode mode) Parameters size Vector2Int The saved resolution. rate RefreshRate The saved refresh rate, or the display's own when none was saved. mode FullScreenMode The saved fullscreen mode. Returns bool True when a complete, supported mode was found. Remarks A saved resolution the display no longer offers is refused rather than approximated. The most common way to get one is moving the install to a different machine, and forcing an unsupported mode there is exactly the failure the options panel's confirmation countdown exists to protect against — except at boot, where there is no countdown and no panel.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientGrassSett.summary: Class ClientGrassSettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll How far the terrain's grass and small details are drawn: the player's choice, in metres. public static class ClientGrassSettings Inheritance object ClientGrassSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks It replaces the scene's own detail distance on the GPU-driven path. Unity's terrain caps a detail distance at 250 m and draws every instance to it at full density, so scenes were authored short (Cov Viaduct: 120 m). The GPU renderers (the blade grass and the detail scatter, on the terrains TerrainDetailInstancing takes) generate and cull on the GPU and thin with distance (full density near, a dithered fraction toward the edge), so they draw much further for little cost. There is no CPU path (2026-10-27). A performance control. Resident instances, chunk builds and memory grow with the square of the distance; the thinning bounds what is drawn, not what is kept. Fields DefaultDistance Grass distance a fresh install uses, in metres. public const float DefaultDistance = 200 Field Value float Remarks The blade grass covers the ground in full to 50 m and thins into the far field's ground colour beyond (its rings run to 600 m for a player who sets it further). 500 m was tried as the default (2026-10-07) and judged excessive. MaximumDistance Longest grass distance offered, in metres. public const float MaximumDistance = 1000 Field Value float Remarks The blade grass and the GPU detail scatter hold nothing per blade, so their cost past a few hundred metres is the far field's thin share. The scatter's mesh details (ferns, pebbles; not bushes, whose reach is their own) stop at TerrainDetailInstancing.MaxChunkDistance whatever this is: the instances it generates grow with its square. MinimumDistance Shortest grass distance offered, in metres. public const float MinimumDistance = 50 Field Value float Properties Distance The chosen grass distance, in metres. public static float Distance { get; } Property Value float Methods SetDistance(float) Writes the grass distance and notifies the renderer. public static void SetDistance(float value) Parameters value float Events OnChanged Raised when the grass distance changes. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientHotbarSet.summary: Class ClientHotbarSettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll How a game with more than one hotkey bar shows them: every bar at once, stacked above the first, or one bar at a time with pages. public static class ClientHotbarSettings Inheritance object ClientHotbarSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Whose choice is what. How MANY bars there are is the game's decision (HotkeyBarCount), because the server stores and validates every slot on every bar. How they are LAID OUT is the player's: both layouts drive the same slots with the same keys, so nothing about the choice reaches the server. Why both layouts. Stacked shows everything and costs screen: each extra row pushes the resource bars, the buff strips, the cast bar and the chat log's lower edge up by a row (see UITKHudLayout). Paged costs nothing on screen and shows one bar at a time; holding a bar's modifier shows that bar for as long as it is held, so what a key is about to fire is always what is on screen. With a single bar neither layout changes anything, which is why the Options row is hidden then rather than offered as a choice between two identical results. Fields DefaultLayout The layout a fresh install uses. public const ClientHotbarSettings.HotbarLayout DefaultLayout = Stacked Field Value ClientHotbarSettings.HotbarLayout Remarks Stacked, because a game that ships several bars has presumably done so in order that they be seen; paging is the opt-in for a player who wants the screen back. LayoutLabels Player-facing names of ClientHotbarSettings.HotbarLayout, indexed by ordinal. public static readonly string[] LayoutLabels Field Value string[] Properties BarCount Number of bars the game gives every character. public static int BarCount { get; } Property Value int Layout The chosen layout. public static ClientHotbarSettings.HotbarLayout Layout { get; } Property Value ClientHotbarSettings.HotbarLayout Page The bar a paged hotbar shows while no modifier is held, as a zero-based bar index. public static int Page { get; } Property Value int Remarks Remembered across sessions, like a window position: a player who keeps their gathering tools on the third page should not have to page back to it at every login. Clamped on read, so a count lowered by the game since it was saved lands on a bar that exists. VisibleRows How many bars are on screen at once: all of them when stacked, one when paged. public static int VisibleRows { get; } Property Value int Methods SetLayout(HotbarLayout) Writes the layout and notifies every panel that depends on it. public static void SetLayout(ClientHotbarSettings.HotbarLayout value) Parameters value ClientHotbarSettings.HotbarLayout SetPage(int) Writes the resting page of a paged hotbar. public static void SetPage(int page) Parameters page int Remarks Raises nothing. The only writer is the hotkey bar itself, which repaints as it pages, and nothing else on screen depends on which bar a paged hotbar is showing — every row is the same height, so the panels above it stay where they are. Events OnChanged Raised when the layout changes. public static event Action OnChanged Event Type Action Remarks The hotkey bar rebuilds its rows on it, and every panel that sits above the bar moves on it: the Options panel is a separate document, and a layout change that waited for the next scene load would leave the stacked rows drawn under the resource bars until then.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientInteracta.summary: Class ClientInteractableStateSystem Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Applies server-authoritative world state for interactables that change the scene rather than opening a window. public static class ClientInteractableStateSystem Inheritance object ClientInteractableStateSystem Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A switch throwing and a capture point flipping are world state: the server decides, and every client that can see the object has to be shown the result. Both already had a broadcast defined and sent — SwitchStateBroadcast to the observers of the switch, CapturePointUpdateBroadcast to the observers of the point — and neither had a single handler on the client, so a door opened on the server and stayed shut on every screen. This lives outside the UI because neither message belongs to a panel. It resolves the object the message names through Objects, which the client populates from each interactable's spawn payload, and writes the state onto the component. Anything that wants to draw it — a target frame, a world label, an objective HUD — reads it from there. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientMapSystem.summary: Class ClientMapSystem Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll The state both map panels share: which scene is being mapped, how much of it the character has explored, what they have pinned to it, and the overhead camera that photographs it. public static class ClientMapSystem Inheritance object ClientMapSystem Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why the panels do not each own this. The minimap and the world map draw the same world, and almost everything they need is expensive to have twice: a second fog grid is a second quarter-megabyte that has to be revealed in step with the first or the two maps disagree about where the player has been; a second overhead camera is a second full scene render every frame; a second note list is a second writer to the same file. Both panels are views onto this. Lifetime. Driven entirely from SetCharacter(IPlayerCharacter) and Tick(), which the minimap calls — it is the panel that is always present. The world map reads the same state and works whether or not the minimap is open, but a build that removes the minimap panel entirely has to drive this from somewhere else. Holds the authored waypoints the map draws once they are discovered. public static WorldSceneDetails SceneDetails { get; } Property Value WorldSceneDetails SceneDisplayName The scene's player-facing name. public static string SceneDisplayName { get; } Property Value string SceneName The scene the loaded state belongs to. public static string SceneName { get; } Property Value string Methods AddNote(Vector3, string, string, int) Adds a note at a world position. public static MapNote AddNote(Vector3 position, string title, string text, int colorIndex) Parameters position Vector3 Where to pin it. title string The note's title. text string The note's body. colorIndex int Which palette colour to draw the pin in. Returns MapNote The note, or null when the character's note allowance is full. ExploreArea(Rect) Explores every chunk a world-space rectangle touches. public static int ExploreArea(Rect worldArea) Parameters worldArea Rect The rectangle, on the XZ plane, in world metres. Returns int How many chunks this explored that were not explored already. ExploreAround(Vector3, float) Explores every chunk within a radius of a world position. public static int ExploreAround(Vector3 worldCenter, float radius) Parameters worldCenter Vector3 Centre of the area, in world space. radius float Radius in world metres. Returns int How many chunks this explored that were not explored already. Remarks The shape a consumable usually wants: "reveals the land within five hundred metres". A chunk counts when the circle reaches any part of it. ExploreChunk(int, int) Explores one chunk by its grid coordinates. public static bool ExploreChunk(int chunkX, int chunkZ) Parameters chunkX int The chunk's X index. chunkZ int The chunk's Z index. Returns bool True when that chunk had not been explored before. Remarks For content that names chunks directly. Grid coordinates are only meaningful alongside the scene's bounds and chunk size, both of which change when a level designer moves a boundary volume — so anything authored against them should be re-checked when that happens. Naming a world position through ExploreAround(Vector3, float) does not have that problem and is the better choice unless the grid is genuinely what is being described. ExploreEverything() Explores the whole of the current scene. public static void ExploreEverything() Remarks For the map that hands a player an entire zone. A scene whose definition disables fog is already fully explored and has nothing to save, so this does nothing there. Flush() Writes anything outstanding immediately. public static void Flush() Remarks Called on scene change, character change and application quit. The debounce is a throughput optimisation, not a durability policy — every path that ends the current map's life has to close it out, or the last stretch of walking before a zone change is silently lost. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientNameplate.summary: Class ClientNameplateDisplay Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Decides which overhead nameplates are up without being targeted: every NPC and every other player inside their own chosen ranges, and the player's own. Driven from Client.Update. public sealed class ClientNameplateDisplay Inheritance object ClientNameplateDisplay Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why this is not part of the nameplate layer. UITKNameplateLayer answers rendering questions — how far, how many, is it behind a wall. Whether a character deserves a nameplate at all is a gameplay question about who the viewer is and who they are looking at, and it has to be asked of every character in view, including the ones whose plates are currently hidden. That is this class, walking BaseCharacter.ClientCharacters. Ownership of a plate's visibility is split three ways, and the split is what keeps the three from fighting: UITKTarget turns the current target's plate on, and asks ShouldStayVisible(ICharacter) before turning it off again on clear. Without that ask, untargeting an NPC standing next to the player blinked its nameplate off for one sweep interval before this class put it back. UITKPetControl turns the player's own pet's plate on; the rule here agrees (an owned character that is not the player is always kept), so a sweep never undoes it. This class owns everything else: NPCs and other players by their two ranges, the local player by the own-name toggle. Any further "keep this name up" rule — party members, guild mates — belongs in Decide(bool, bool, bool, bool, float, float, float, bool) rather than in a second writer that would have to be reconciled with it. Cost. One dictionary walk every SweepIntervalSeconds, a squared distance per NPC, a standing colour per visible plate, and a visibility flip only on a transition. The walk is deliberately not per frame: a nameplate appearing a fifth of a second after the player crosses the range is invisible, and the walk touches every character in view. Distances use a small hysteresis (ExitRangeMultiplier) so a character idling exactly on the boundary does not toggle every sweep. Fields ExitRangeMultiplier A nameplate that is already up stays up until the character is this many times the range away. Five percent: a metre and a half at the default range, enough to absorb the jitter of two characters standing on the line and small enough to be unnoticed. public const float ExitRangeMultiplier = 1.05 Field Value float SweepIntervalSeconds Seconds between sweeps of the client character registry. public const float SweepIntervalSeconds = 0.2 Field Value float Methods ApplyGuildRowColor(ICharacter) Colours a player's guild row: the friendly colour when they are in the local player's guild (the local player's own row included), the style's grey otherwise. public static void ApplyGuildRowColor(ICharacter character) Parameters character ICharacter The player whose plate to colour; pets are left alone, their row names an owner. Remarks Rewriting a row with the values it already has is a no-op on the plate, so the sweep can call this freely. Decide(bool, bool, bool, bool, float, float, float, bool) The visibility rule, as arithmetic on facts about one character. public static bool Decide(bool isPlayer, bool isOwner, bool isTargeted, bool wasVisible, float sqrDistance, float npcRange, float playerRange, bool showOwnName) Parameters isPlayer bool Whether the character is a player character. isOwner bool Whether this client owns the character: the local player, or their pet. isTargeted bool Whether the character is the local player's current target — hovered, or pinned to the target frame. wasVisible bool Whether the plate is currently up, which selects the exit distance. sqrDistance float Squared distance from the local player, in metres squared. npcRange float The NPC nameplate range, in metres; zero or less means target only. playerRange float The other-player nameplate range, in metres; zero or less means target only. showOwnName bool Whether the player's own nameplate stays up. Returns bool True when the nameplate should be up. Remarks Static and free of Unity types so the truth table can be pinned by a plain unit test. Initialize() Subscribes to world entry and settings changes. Call during client startup. public void Initialize() MarkFor(FactionAllianceLevel) The mark for a displayed standing. public static NameplateMark MarkFor(FactionAllianceLevel level) Parameters level FactionAllianceLevel Returns NameplateMark SameGuild(ICharacter, ICharacter) Whether two characters belong to the same guild; no guild (ID 0) is nobody's guild. public static bool SameGuild(ICharacter a, ICharacter b) Parameters a ICharacter b ICharacter Returns bool ShouldStayVisible(ICharacter) Whether a character's nameplate should stay up when the target frame stops framing it. public static bool ShouldStayVisible(ICharacter character) Parameters character ICharacter The character being untargeted. Returns bool True to leave the plate up; false to let the target frame take it down. Remarks Answered from the same rule the sweep applies, so the target frame and the sweep can never disagree about a character that is both untargeted and in range. Without a live display the answer falls back to the pre-range behaviour: the player's own plate stays, everything else goes. Shutdown() Unsubscribes. Call during client teardown. public void Shutdown() Standing(ICharacter, ICharacter, out Color) The standing colour and mark a viewer gives a character: one rule for the overhead plate and both target cards. public static NameplateMark Standing(ICharacter viewer, ICharacter character, out Color tint) Parameters viewer ICharacter The local player. character ICharacter The character being drawn. tint Color The standing colour; white when either side has no faction. Returns NameplateMark The mark to draw, or None. Remarks The player's OWN standing is how a stranger sees them: red with crossed swords while their aggression is on (anyone outside their party and guild may fight them), the neutral colour and no mark while it is off. Their own PET acts under them (HarmRule.Principal), so it is red with crossed swords while their aggression is on — it may be fought too — and otherwise carries the friendly shield: it is on their side. Everyone else is the viewer's displayed standing toward them. Tick() Runs one sweep when the interval has elapsed. Call once per frame. public void Tick()

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientNameplate.summary: Class ClientNameplateSettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll How overhead nameplates look: how large, how strongly, how solid a background, which rows are worth reading, whether icons are drawn, and how many may be on screen at once. public static class ClientNameplateSettings Inheritance object ClientNameplateSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Separate from ClientWorldLabelSettings on purpose. The two are drawn by different layers with separate budgets, and they answer different questions for a player: damage numbers are feedback you read for a second, and a nameplate is furniture you look past all day. Wanting one loud and the other faint is an ordinary preference that a single shared opacity could not express. What is deliberately still shared is the draw distance and the hide-behind- geometry toggle. Both are statements about projected world UI as a whole rather than about nameplates, and a second copy of each would let a player set two answers to one question and then wonder which won. The three rules that decide WHICH nameplates are up — the two ranges and the own-name toggle — stay in ClientWorldLabelSettings with their original configuration keys. They are read by ClientNameplateDisplay rather than by the layer, and moving their keys would silently reset the choice of every existing install for nothing but tidiness. Every default here is what the layer draws with no configuration at all, so a fresh install looks exactly as it did before these controls existed and only a player who moves something changes anything. Fields DefaultBackgroundOpacity Background strength a fresh install uses: the style's own opacity, unmodified. public const float DefaultBackgroundOpacity = 1 Field Value float DefaultMaxVisible How many nameplates a fresh install draws at once. public const int DefaultMaxVisible = 64 Field Value int Remarks Sixty-four, matching UITKNameplateLayer.MaxVisiblePlates as authored. DefaultOpacity Nameplate opacity a fresh install uses. public const float DefaultOpacity = 1 Field Value float DefaultScale Nameplate size multiplier a fresh install uses. public const float DefaultScale = 0.5 Field Value float DefaultShowGuild Whether a fresh install shows the guild row. public const bool DefaultShowGuild = true Field Value bool DefaultShowIcons Whether a fresh install draws nameplate icons. public const bool DefaultShowIcons = true Field Value bool Remarks On: an icon is only ever drawn because a developer authored one, so the default is to show what they authored. No plate carries one out of the box. DefaultShowTitles Whether a fresh install shows the title row. public const bool DefaultShowTitles = true Field Value bool MaximumBackgroundOpacity Strongest background offered. public const float MaximumBackgroundOpacity = 1 Field Value float MaximumMaxVisible Most nameplates offered. public const int MaximumMaxVisible = 256 Field Value int MaximumOpacity Strongest nameplates offered. public const float MaximumOpacity = 1 Field Value float MaximumScale Largest nameplate size multiplier offered. public const float MaximumScale = 2 Field Value float MinimumBackgroundOpacity Faintest background offered. public const float MinimumBackgroundOpacity = 0 Field Value float Remarks Zero IS a setting here, unlike the plate opacity above: it means no background at all, text straight over the world, which is a look people ask for by name. The text stays, so nothing disappears and the effect of the slider is visible all the way down. MinimumMaxVisible Fewest nameplates offered. public const int MinimumMaxVisible = 8 Field Value int Remarks Eight rather than the world labels' sixteen. A nameplate budget is spent on the nearest plates first, so a low setting is a legitimate "only the few things around me" choice rather than the failure a low label budget would be mid-fight. MinimumOpacity Faintest nameplates offered. public const float MinimumOpacity = 0.2 Field Value float Remarks A fifth, not zero: an invisible nameplate is what the two ranges and the own-name toggle are for, and a slider that reached zero would give a player a second, much less discoverable way to turn nameplates off — one they cannot see the effect of while dragging it. MinimumScale Smallest nameplate size multiplier offered. public const float MinimumScale = 0.5 Field Value float Properties BackgroundOpacity The chosen background strength, as a multiplier on each style's own opacity. public static float BackgroundOpacity { get; } Property Value float MaxVisible The chosen nameplate budget. public static int MaxVisible { get; } Property Value int Opacity The chosen nameplate opacity. public static float Opacity { get; } Property Value float Scale The chosen nameplate size multiplier. public static float Scale { get; } Property Value float ShowGuild Whether the guild row is drawn. public static bool ShowGuild { get; } Property Value bool ShowIcons Whether nameplate icons are drawn. public static bool ShowIcons { get; } Property Value bool ShowTitles Whether the title row is drawn. public static bool ShowTitles { get; } Property Value bool Methods IsRowVisible(NameplateSlot) Whether a row of a given kind is drawn at all. public static bool IsRowVisible(NameplateSlot slot) Parameters slot NameplateSlot The row's slot. Returns bool False when the player has turned that kind of row off. Remarks Answered here rather than in the renderer so "which rows does the player want" has one home, and so the rule can be read without a panel. Only the two optional rows are refusable: a nameplate with its name row turned off is not a nameplate, and a status row is transient enough that hiding it would mostly hide nothing. IsRowVisible(NameplateSlot, bool, bool) Whether a row of a given kind is drawn, against settings the caller has already read. public static bool IsRowVisible(NameplateSlot slot, bool showGuild, bool showTitles) Parameters slot NameplateSlot The row's slot. showGuild bool Whether guild rows are wanted. showTitles bool Whether title rows are wanted. Returns bool False when that kind of row is turned off. Remarks The renderer asks the question for every row of every plate it draws, and reading the configuration store that often would undo the caching the rest of that loop is built around. It caches the two answers and calls this; the overload above is the same rule for anyone who is not in a hot loop, so there is still only one definition of it. SetBackgroundOpacity(float) Writes the background strength and notifies the layer. public static void SetBackgroundOpacity(float value) Parameters value float SetMaxVisible(int) Writes the nameplate budget and notifies the layer. public static void SetMaxVisible(int value) Parameters value int SetOpacity(float) Writes the nameplate opacity and notifies the layer. public static void SetOpacity(float value) Parameters value float SetScale(float) Writes the nameplate size multiplier and notifies the layer. public static void SetScale(float value) Parameters value float SetShowGuild(bool) Writes the guild row setting and notifies the layer. public static void SetShowGuild(bool value) Parameters value bool SetShowIcons(bool) Writes the icon setting and notifies the layer. public static void SetShowIcons(bool value) Parameters value bool SetShowTitles(bool) Writes the title row setting and notifies the layer. public static void SetShowTitles(bool value) Parameters value bool Events OnChanged Raised when any of these change, so the layer can re-read them. public static event Action OnChanged Event Type Action Remarks Its own event rather than OnChanged: the layer listens to both — it still takes the draw distance and the occlusion toggle from there — and two events cost one more subscription while keeping "who owns this setting" a question with one answer.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientNetworkSt.summary: Class ClientNetworkStatsSettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Whether the network statistics overlay is drawn, and whether it draws its traffic graph. public static class ClientNetworkStatsSettings Inheritance object ClientNetworkStatsSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Off by default. The overlay is a diagnostic: a player who has never asked how much the game sends has no use for a table of byte counts in the corner of the screen, and a fresh install should look the way it did before the overlay existed. Why the settings live here rather than on the panel. For the reason ClientCrosshairSettings gives: UITKNetworkStats is a panel whose OnStarting can re-run, and the options panel must be able to read and write the choice in a scene where the overlay has not started yet. These are plain reads off ClientSettings, so neither side has to wait for the other. Visibility is the only thing the setting owns. Sampling follows it: the overlay reads the transport's counters only while it is shown, so turning it off also stops the once-a-second connection statistics read the transport makes on its behalf (see TransportTraffic.Capture). It is a separate choice for the player who wants the numbers in less screen space. Properties Enabled Whether the overlay is drawn at all. public static bool Enabled { get; } Property Value bool ShowGraph Whether the overlay draws its traffic graph. public static bool ShowGraph { get; } Property Value bool Methods SetEnabled(bool) Writes whether the overlay is drawn and notifies it. public static void SetEnabled(bool value) Parameters value bool SetShowGraph(bool) Writes whether the traffic graph is drawn and notifies the overlay. public static void SetShowGraph(bool value) Parameters value bool Events OnChanged Raised when either setting changes. public static event Action OnChanged Event Type Action Remarks The overlay subscribes; the options panel raises. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientSettings..summary: Class ClientSettings Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll The client's single owner of GlobalSettings: it creates the store, names every key exactly once, clamps everything read out of it, and owns the one debounced write that puts it back on disk. public static class ClientSettings Inheritance object ClientSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why one owner. The store used to be created lazily by whichever of two unrelated places asked for it first — LauncherSettings.EnsureLoaded in the launcher scene, and UITKOptions.EnsureConfigurationLoaded the first time the player opened the settings panel. In a client started past the launcher, neither ran, so Configuration.GlobalSettings stayed null through the whole of boot: keybinding overrides were skipped without a word (PlayerInputController.LoadBindingOverrides returns early on a null store), panel positions were never restored, and the theme loaded from nothing. Every one of those failures looked like a setting that had not been saved rather than one that had never been read. Why the keys live here. A configuration key is a string shared between the control that writes it and the code that applies it, and the two are usually in different files. Naming them in one place is what makes it impossible for a panel to write "Brightness" while the applier reads "brightness" — and lets a setting be applied at boot by code that has never heard of the options panel. Why every read clamps. Configuration.cfg is a plain text file: a player can edit it, a crash can truncate it mid-write, and a build from a different machine can leave values this one cannot honour. Values reach RenderSettings.ambientLight, Screen.fullScreenMode and AudioListener.volume, none of which validate what they are given. Clamping on the way in is the only place it can be done once. Why writes are debounced. Save() serialises and rewrites the entire file. A slider bound straight to it rewrites the file once per frame for as long as it is held. Everything here coalesces onto a short quiet period and is flushed on panel close, on quit, and on demand. And why there is exactly one of them. UITKPanelPositions used to keep a second pending flag and a second deadline over the same file. Both wrote the whole of it, so a player who dragged a window and changed a setting in the same breath got two full serialisations of identical content — and each timer could fire inside the other's quiet period, which is the case a debounce exists to prevent. The two intervals also disagreed, a second against three quarters of one, so which of two simultaneous changes reached the disk first depended on which subsystem had last been touched. Panel positions now request and flush through here like every other setting. Fields AnisotropicFilteringKey Texture filtering. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientSettingsB.title: Class ClientSettingsBootstrap | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientSettingsB.summary: Class ClientSettingsBootstrap Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Loads the client's configuration and applies the player's settings during boot. public static class ClientSettingsBootstrap Inheritance object ClientSettingsBootstrap Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The problem this solves. Nothing loaded the settings file at client start-up. Configuration.GlobalSettings was created lazily by whichever of two places asked for it first — the launcher, or the options panel — and the options panel ships closed, so in a client launched past the launcher neither ran. Every setting that is only ever applied by the options panel's OnStarting was therefore not in effect until the player opened the menu, and every setting read from the store by something else came back as a default: keybinding overrides were skipped (LoadBindingOverrides returns early on a null store), panel positions were not restored, and the theme was built from nothing. Two phases, and why. The store is loaded at UnityEngine.RuntimeInitializeLoadType.BeforeSceneLoad, which precedes every scene's Awake — so the first panel to register already has settings to read. The settings are applied from a hook the bootstrap system raises, immediately after it installs the boot-time frame rate and VSync defaults. Applying them earlier than that would work exactly once and then be overwritten by those two lines. Input is created here too. PlayerControls used to be constructed only on world entry, which meant the Key Bindings tab could not show a single binding until the player was in the world, and a saved override was not loaded until then either. Creating the asset at boot costs nothing — it is data until an action map is enabled — and makes the bindings inspectable and editable from the login screen, which is where a player who has just installed the game will look for them.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.ClientWorldCloc.summary: Class ClientWorldClock Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll The client's mirror of the world clock: adopts the scene server's anchor and reads it at FishNet's tick. public sealed class ClientWorldClock Inheritance object ClientWorldClock Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Core, so the world's time exists on the client whatever world content is installed: the sky and the weather run on it, and so do the sea, a mill's sails and the modules' own clocks. Nothing here predicts or decides anything. The anchor belongs to one server. It names a tick of the server it came from, and FishNet restarts the tick at 0 on a disconnect and counts the next server's ticks after — so a scene hop or a reconnect read the old server's anchor against the new server's tick, and the sky (and everything on the world's clock) was off by the two servers' difference in uptime, often days, until the new anchor came with the character. It is forgotten the moment the connection stops (Reset()); without one the clock is this machine's UTC, a fraction of a second out at most, and the next server's anchor arrives on spawn. UITKWorldLabelLayer already carried every one of them as a serialized field tuned in ClientPreboot.unity. Each default below is the value authored there, so a fresh install draws exactly what it drew before this existed and only a player who moves a control changes anything. Two of them are performance controls, not taste. The draw distance and the visible-label cap bound the cost of the client's hottest UI loop — one projection, one style diff and one sort entry per label per frame. A machine that struggles in a crowded hub gets a real frame back by dropping either, which is the same reason the minimap's refresh rate is exposed. Scale multiplies rather than replaces. A label's font size is computed from its world-unit size and its distance from the camera, so a fixed point size would throw away the perspective behaviour that makes a distant nameplate small. One full-screen pass into a new colour texture that then becomes the camera's colour, so nothing is copied back. With Normal vision, the filter off or its strength at 0, no pass is added. The correction is the usual daltonisation: simulate what the dichromat sees (Machado et al. 2009, severity 1), take the difference from the original, and move it into the channels that eye does distinguish. It cannot add information, only move it, so it is a supplement to the safe colours (ColorVision), not a replacement for them. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.DownloadRateTra.summary: Class DownloadRateTracker Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Measures transfer rate over a trailing time window and estimates remaining time. public class DownloadRateTracker Inheritance object DownloadRateTracker Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A sliding window rather than a cumulative average. Dividing total bytes by total elapsed time keeps reporting a healthy rate for minutes after a transfer has actually stalled, because the historical average drags the number up — which is exactly when the player most needs to be told something is wrong. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.DripSounds.html.title: Class DripSounds | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Client.DripSounds.html.summary: Class DripSounds Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll A cave's drips, synthesised (2026-10-20, caves livened): a drop into its puddle, a drop on wet rock or on the stalagmite it has built. Each is a recipe over SoundSynth run from a seed, so a variant is the same sound on every client. public static class DripSounds Inheritance object DripSounds Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Into water: the plink. What is heard of a drop falling into still water is barely its impact (a faint tick of a few milliseconds) and mostly the small bubble it pinches off a millisecond or two later: the bubble rings at its Minnaert frequency (about 3.3 kHz over its radius in millimetres, so 1–3 kHz for a drop's 1–3 mm bubble) and its pitch climbs as it rises and shrinks against the surface, dying within a tenth of a second. Not every drop traps one: some only plop, a duller knock and a low short ring of the water's surface. On rock: the splat. A drop on wet rock is a short bright burst of a water film breaking (2–6 kHz, under a hundredth of a second) and its spatter landing round it a few tens of milliseconds after, softer. The cave's ring is not in the clip: the drips play through the world's sound (WorldAudio's Effects), where the cave's reverb round the listener and the echoes off its far walls (AcousticEnvironment) give each its tail. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.FishDepthPyrami.summary: Class FishDepthPyramid Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Each game camera's depth as a pyramid of farthest depths, built after its opaques, for the GPU culling of the instanced props, trees and details to drop what was hidden behind what was drawn (FishTerrainInstancing.compute FishOccluded, main view only). public static class FishDepthPyramid Inheritance object FishDepthPyramid Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Unity's own occlusion culling works only for static scene renderers; the props are data drawn indirectly (CliffRockInstancing), so nothing culled them behind a hill. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.FogOfWarDefault.summary: Class FogOfWarDefaults Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Defaults for the exploration grid, in one place so the store, the map and the definition's override all agree. public static class FogOfWarDefaults Inheritance object FogOfWarDefaults Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Fields ChunkSize Length of one exploration chunk's side, in world metres. public const float ChunkSize = 40 Field Value float Remarks Forty metres, which divides a shipped thousand-metre scene into a grid of twenty-eight chunks — each one an eighth of a percent of the scene. This was 128 metres, and the reversal is worth keeping. The chunk model replaced a per-cell reveal whose percentage crept by a point per sixty metres walked, and the answer at the time was a grain coarse enough that entering a chunk was a visible step: a little over one percent each. That swapped one failure for another. On a nine-chunk grid the displayed value only ever moves in whole numbers, so a step of a bit over one percent reads as a fixed increment — the readout looks like a count of blocks rather than a measurement of ground, which is how it was reported. Both failures have the same root: a whole-number percentage over a coarse grid. So the grid is fine enough to be worth measuring and the readout shows the fraction — UITKMap.FormatExplored prints as many decimals as one chunk is worth (tenths here, hundredths on a generated 4.6 km world). At this size one chunk is 0.13% and a hundred metres of straight walking crosses two and a half of them, so the number climbs as the player travels instead of lurching once a block. A scene that wants a different grain sets FogChunkSize on its map definition. A small interior wants a smaller number still: a two-hundred-metre scene at the default is five chunks across. Going much below this is self-defeating for the same reason the 128-metre grain was wrong in the other direction — a scene of ten thousand chunks moves the tenths digit once per twenty metres, which is a readout that appears to flicker rather than to measure.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.FogOfWarMap.htm.title: Class FogOfWarMap | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Client.FogOfWarMap.htm.summary: Class FogOfWarMap Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll The part of a scene a character has explored, as a grid of chunks over the scene's bounds. public sealed class FogOfWarMap Inheritance object FogOfWarMap Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A chunk is either explored or it is not, and walking into one explores the whole of it. That is the entire model: there is no coverage value, no radius, and no falloff. What the player gets is a map that opens up a block at a time as they travel, and a percentage that means exactly what it says — chunks visited out of chunks in the scene. This replaced a per-cell radial reveal that stored a coverage byte for every four metres of ground: a thousand-metre scene was a 277 by 277 grid, seventy-seven thousand bytes held in memory, gzipped on every save, and uploaded to a texture through a dirty-rectangle tracker. The percentage it produced moved by about one point per sixty metres walked, which read as a readout that never changed. The same scene is twenty-eight chunks square here: seven hundred and eighty-four bytes, no compression, and no dirty rectangle. Chunk size is a scene's own business. It comes from the map definition, falling back to FogOfWarDefaults.ChunkSize, so a cramped dungeon can be divided more finely than open country without anything else changing. It is baked into the saved file and a change discards the old one — a chunk index means a different piece of ground at a different size, so changing either starts every character again in that scene. The default is finer than it once was, and the world map's readout prints tenths of a percent; both halves of that decision, and the reason neither works on its own, live on FogOfWarDefaults.ChunkSize. Constructors FogOfWarMap(Rect, float) Builds an entirely unexplored map over a world rectangle. public FogOfWarMap(Rect worldRect, float chunkSize) Parameters worldRect Rect The world rectangle to cover, on the XZ plane. chunkSize float Length of one chunk's side in world metres. Fields Explored Chunk state meaning the character has entered this chunk. public const byte Explored = 1 Field Value byte Unexplored Chunk state meaning the character has never been here. public const byte Unexplored = 0 Field Value byte Properties ChunkCount Total number of chunks in the scene. public int ChunkCount { get; } Property Value int ChunkSize The length of one chunk's side, in world metres. public float ChunkSize { get; } Property Value float Chunks The chunk grid, row-major from the rectangle's minimum corner. public byte[] Chunks { get; } Property Value byte[] Remarks Exposed because the store writes it verbatim — one byte per chunk, which for any real scene is smaller than the header describing it. ChunksX Number of chunks along the X axis. public int ChunksX { get; } Property Value int ChunksZ Number of chunks along the Z axis. public int ChunksZ { get; } Property Value int ExploredChunkCount How many chunks have been explored. public int ExploredChunkCount { get; } Property Value int Remarks Kept as the grid is written rather than counted on demand. That is what lets ExploredFraction() be a division instead of a walk, and it is why this class no longer needs a cached fraction and a dirty flag to guard it. GridRect The world rectangle the chunk grid actually spans. public Rect GridRect { get; } Property Value Rect Remarks Not WorldRect, and the difference is visible. The grid rounds up to whole chunks, so it always covers the scene's rectangle and usually overhangs it — by up to one chunk short of a full one on each axis. Anything mapping the chunk grid onto screen space has to use this rectangle: treating the texture as covering WorldRect stretches it by the overhang, which at four-metre cells was a rounding error nobody could see and at chunk sizes is a third of a chunk of drift by the far edge — the fog visibly out of step with the ground it describes. IsDirty True when the map has changed since it was last written to disk. public bool IsDirty { get; } Property Value bool WorldRect The world rectangle, on the XZ plane, this map covers. public Rect WorldRect { get; } Property Value Rect Methods ClearDirty() Clears the dirty flag after the map has been written to disk. public void ClearDirty() ExploredFraction() The fraction of the scene that has been explored. public float ExploredFraction() Returns float Zero to one: explored chunks over total chunks. FromChunks(Rect, float, byte[]) Rebuilds a map from chunks loaded off disk. public static FogOfWarMap FromChunks(Rect worldRect, float chunkSize, byte[] chunks) Parameters worldRect Rect The world rectangle the chunks cover. chunkSize float Length of one chunk's side in world metres. chunks byte[] The chunk data. Must be exactly the grid's size. Returns FogOfWarMap The loaded map, or null when the data does not match the grid. Remarks Returns null rather than resizing. A chunk array of the wrong length means the scene's bounds or chunk size changed since the file was written, and stretching old data across new bounds would put the player's explored ground in the wrong place — worse than starting again, because it looks plausible. Every byte is normalised to one of the two states rather than trusted. The file is signed, so this is not defending against tampering; it is making sure a future writer that stores something else in this array cannot leave a chunk that is neither explored nor unexplored, which nothing downstream has a meaning for. GetTexture() The fog as a texture, alpha carrying the fog, rebuilt only when a chunk has changed. public Texture2D GetTexture() Returns Texture2D The fog texture. Never null once the map exists. Remarks RGBA rather than a single-channel format because UI Toolkit multiplies the sampled texel by the vertex colour: leaving the colour channels at white lets the fog be tinted to whatever suits the theme, where a single-channel texture would force it to be black. Point sampling, and that matters. A chunk either has been visited or has not, and the edge between the two is a real boundary the player can walk across — so it is drawn as one. Interpolating would smear each chunk into its neighbours and produce a soft blob that no longer lines up with the ground it describes. The whole grid is uploaded on any change. At the default grain that is under a thousand texels for a shipped scene — four kilobytes — so the dirty-rectangle bookkeeping the per-cell version needed still buys nothing here. IsDiscovered(Vector3) Whether a world position has been explored. public bool IsDiscovered(Vector3 worldPosition) Parameters worldPosition Vector3 The position to test. Returns bool True when the chunk holding the position has been entered. Remarks A position outside the grid reads as explored. Off-map is not a place the player can discover, and reporting it as fogged would hide every marker that sits just outside a scene's derived bounds — which, since those bounds are a boundary volume plus padding, includes things a level designer legitimately put at the edge. ReleaseTexture() Destroys the texture. public void ReleaseTexture() Reveal(Vector3) Explores the chunk containing a world position. public bool Reveal(Vector3 worldPosition) Parameters worldPosition Vector3 Where the character is, in world space. Returns bool True when this entered a chunk that had not been explored before. Remarks Returning false is the ordinary case and says nothing is wrong: a character standing still, or crossing ground it has already walked, re-enters the same explored chunk several times a second. A position outside the grid also returns false — see ClientMapSystem, which reports that case rather than letting it pass unnoticed. RevealAll() Explores the entire map. public void RevealAll() Remarks For scenes whose definition turns fog off, and for the map baker's preview. Cheaper and clearer than special-casing "no fog" at every draw site. RevealArea(Rect) Explores every chunk that a world-space rectangle touches. public int RevealArea(Rect worldArea) Parameters worldArea Rect The rectangle, on the XZ plane, in world metres. Returns int How many chunks this explored that were not explored already. Remarks Touching, not covering. A rectangle that clips the corner of a chunk explores that whole chunk, because a chunk is the smallest thing this map can describe — asking for half of one is not a question it can answer, and rounding the other way would let an area smaller than a chunk reveal nothing at all. RevealAround(Vector3, float) Explores every chunk within a radius of a world position. public int RevealAround(Vector3 worldCenter, float radius) Parameters worldCenter Vector3 Centre of the area, in world space. radius float Radius in world metres. Zero or less explores nothing. Returns int How many chunks this explored that were not explored already. Remarks The shape a consumable naturally wants — "reveals the land within five hundred metres". A chunk counts when the circle reaches any part of it, so the result is a disc rounded outwards to the chunk grid rather than a square. RevealChunk(int, int) Explores one chunk by its grid coordinates. public bool RevealChunk(int chunkX, int chunkZ) Parameters chunkX int The chunk's X index. chunkZ int The chunk's Z index. Returns bool True when that chunk had not been explored before. Remarks The grain everything else here is built on, and the one to reach for when something other than a character's feet decides a chunk is known — a map fragment that names the chunks it fills in, a quest that opens up the valley it sends you to, a trigger volume at a vista. Out-of-range coordinates are ignored rather than throwing: a scene's grid changes size when its bounds are re-derived, and content that named a chunk beyond the edge should be inert, not fatal. TryGetChunk(Vector3, out int, out int) The chunk containing a world position. public bool TryGetChunk(Vector3 worldPosition, out int x, out int z) Parameters worldPosition Vector3 The position to convert. x int The chunk's X index. z int The chunk's Z index. Returns bool True when the position is inside the grid.

api/unity/FishMMO.Client.FogOfWarStore.h.summary: Class FogOfWarStore Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Reads and writes a character's explored-territory maps on the local machine. public static class FogOfWarStore Inheritance object FogOfWarStore Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why it never goes to the server. Exploration is a per-character convenience that changes several times a second and is worth nothing to anybody else. Sending it would mean a write path, a table, a migration and a sync broadcast for data whose entire purpose is to decide which pixels are dark. A player who reinstalls loses their revealed map and re-walks it, which is a fair trade for a subsystem that costs the server nothing. What the signature is for, and what it is not. Each file carries an HMAC over its contents, keyed from the character and a build constant. That detects a file edited by hand or copied from another character, and it makes the failure loud instead of silent — a mismatched file is discarded and exploration starts again rather than being trusted. It is explicitly not a defence against a determined player: the key is in the binary, so anybody willing to extract it can forge a fully-revealed map. That is acceptable because of where the value lives. Revealing the map early gains a player nothing the game rewards — the Cartography skill this feeds must be advanced by the server, from the positions it already receives, and never from anything read out of this file. Keep it that way and forging the file buys a nicer-looking minimap and no progression at all. api/unity/FishMMO.Client.GuildMessageOfT.summary: Class GuildMessageOfTheDayGate Namespace FishMMO.Client Assembly FishMMO.Client.dll Decides when the guild's message of the day is written into chat. public sealed class GuildMessageOfTheDayGate Inheritance object GuildMessageOfTheDayGate Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The server sends the guild's text to a member every time they connect to a scene server, which is every zone change as well as the login, and again to the whole guild whenever an officer edits it. Printing every copy would repeat the same line at each zone line. So the rule is: once per login, and again only when the text is different from what was last shown — an edit, a new guild, or a different character. An empty message is remembered but never printed, so a guild that sets one later while the player is online still has it announced.
