api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class AIRetreatDecision Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll Decides whether a fleeing NPC keeps running, turns around, or disengages. public static class AIRetreatDecision Inheritance object AIRetreatDecision Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why this exists as a solver and not as distance tests inside the state. The reported behaviour — an NPC that runs away forever the moment a player chases it — is not a bug in any one comparison. It is the absence of any state that survives a tick: the old state compared the target's distance against SafeDistance and nothing else, so the same inputs always produced the same answer, and a pursuer faster than the NPC meant the inputs never changed. A decision that can see how long this has been going on, and how many times it has already happened, is what makes a chase end. Pure and Unity-free, matching AICombatDecision: every input arrives in the context and the roll is supplied by the caller, so the whole ladder is assertable. Fields PURSUIT_CLOSING_SPEED Closing speed above which a target counts as pursuing. public const float PURSUIT_CLOSING_SPEED = 0.5 Field Value float Remarks Not zero: two bodies shuffling around each other inside a NavMesh agent's avoidance radius produce a small positive closing speed in any direction, and treating that as a pursuit would stop every retreat from ever disengaging. Ground speed is several units a second, so half a unit cleanly separates "walking me down" from "standing nearby". Methods Decide(in AIRetreatContext) Reaches the outcome for this tick. public static AIRetreatOutcome Decide(in AIRetreatContext context) Parameters context AIRetreatContext The inputs for this tick. Returns AIRetreatOutcome The outcome for this tick. Remarks The order of these tests is the design. The two hard stops come first, because a chase that cannot end is worse than a chase that ends too early: an NPC that keeps fleeing is unkillable by a melee player, while one that turns too soon merely loses a fight it was going to lose anyway. A pursuer turns Disengage into KeepRetreating. That single rule is the reported issue. Reaching SafeDistance used to be sufficient on its own, so an NPC that outran nothing in particular stopped and went idle while the player was still running at it — and then the out-of-combat sweep re-acquired the player and the NPC fled again, forever. Being far away only means the NPC is done running if nobody is following.

api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class AISeparation Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll Keeps NPCs from standing inside one another without Unity's crowd avoidance. public static class AISeparation Inheritance object AISeparation Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Unity's NavMesh crowd is one global simulation. A scene server stacks several instances of the same world scene at the same coordinates, so with obstacle avoidance on, an NPC in one instance steered around NPCs in every other — invisible shoves, tripped stuck timers, spawner-mates in two instances pushing each other off their paths. Avoidance is therefore off on every NPC agent (AIController.InitializeOnce) and this takes its place. It is scene-scoped by construction: neighbours come from the NPC's own UnityEngine.PhysicsScene's AIBodyGrid, which is separate for every stacked instance. Attackers around one target are spaced by AICombatSlots; this only stops bodies overlapping in the wander, idle and approach cases the ring does not cover. Methods CoincidentPushDirection(uint, uint) The horizontal direction selfKey pushes in when its body coincides with otherKey's. public static Vector3 CoincidentPushDirection(uint selfKey, uint otherKey) Parameters selfKey uint The pushing body's key. otherKey uint The coincident body's key. Returns Vector3 A unit horizontal direction. Remarks The pair's axis depends only on the unordered pair, and the lower key pushes along it while the higher pushes against it, so the two answers are exact opposites. Equal keys — which distinct NPCs never have, see IdentityKey — fall back to a fixed direction. Resolve(Vector3, uint, IReadOnlyList<Vector3>, IReadOnlyList<uint>, float, float) The velocity that moves self out of its neighbours' bodies. public static Vector3 Resolve(Vector3 self, uint selfKey, IReadOnlyList<Vector3> neighbours, IReadOnlyList<uint> neighbourKeys, float radius, float maxSpeed) Parameters self Vector3 This NPC's position. selfKey uint This NPC's identity key; breaks the tie when two bodies coincide. neighbours IReadOnlyList<Vector3> Positions of nearby NPC bodies. neighbourKeys IReadOnlyList<uint> Each neighbour's identity key, in the same order. radius float Distance at which a neighbour starts to push, in metres. maxSpeed float Push speed when fully overlapped, in metres per second. Returns Vector3 A horizontal velocity, zero when nothing is inside the radius.

api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class AIShelterSettings Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll Whether, and in what, an archetype's NPCs go and stand out of the weather. [Serializable] public class AIShelterSettings Inheritance object AIShelterSettings Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Off by default, deliberately (Q15). Every existing archetype in the project gets this struct at its defaults, and at its defaults it does nothing at all. Weather arrives across a whole region at once, so a default of "on" would have every NPC on the continent abandon its post the first time a front came through — patrols leaving their routes, merchants leaving their stalls, and quest targets nowhere to be found. Sheltering is something an archetype opts into because it makes sense for that creature. It reads the same weather the player's exposure does. A WeatherReading taken at the NPC's own position, so an NPC already under a canopy has nothing to walk away from and an NPC in the open does — from the same numbers that are soaking the player standing next to it. Severity is read from the kinds actually chosen, not from one fixed channel. An archetype that shelters from lightning and nothing else must not be driven out by heavy rain it does not care about, and would be if this measured precipitation regardless. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Struct AIStateClock Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll Schedules a state's updates and reports how much time each one covers. public struct AIStateClock Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks A state asks to be updated every updateRate seconds, and the brain ticks far more often than that. The clock now accumulates the ticks between updates and hands the state the real interval. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class AggressionDispatcher Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll Routes combat events to the one NPC that cares about them, instead of broadcasting every event to every NPC in the scene. public static class AggressionDispatcher Inheritance object AggressionDispatcher Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The problem this replaces. Each AggressionState used to subscribe individually to the global damage, heal and kill events. That meant a single sword swing invoked one delegate per NPC in the scene — a thousand NPCs, a thousand calls, of which exactly one was for the NPC actually being hit and 999 returned immediately from a reference comparison. At a busy raid boss with a few hundred hits per second the wasted work is measured in hundreds of thousands of calls per second, all to deliver a handful of events. What it does instead. One subscription for the whole process. Damage is the hot path and is dispatched by dictionary lookup on the defender — O(1) regardless of how many NPCs exist. Heal and kill have to consider several NPCs (a heal matters to anyone tracking either party), and they are dispatched through a reverse index — character ID to the NPCs whose tables track it — so they cost the number of NPCs actually involved, not the number registered. The index replaced a walk over every registered state. That list spans every scene instance on the process and every pooled, inactive NPC, and heal events are frequent — every heal-over-time tick, heal action and consumable raises one — so two thousand registered NPCs and a hundred HoT ticks a second was two hundred thousand iterations a second to find the handful of NPCs that cared. The tables themselves keep the index exact through FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI.AggressionController.EntryAdded and FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI.AggressionController.EntryRemoved. Server-side only. Registration happens when an NPC's aggression state is built and is released when it is destroyed. Remarks A pet and its owner are one target as far as hate is concerned. Hit the owner and the pet answers; hit the pet and the owner answers — an NPC with a brain by engaging the aggressor through its own aggression state, a player through whatever it chooses to do. Without this a pet's attackers were invisible to its owner and an owner's attackers invisible to the pet, so an NPC with a summon stood and watched it being killed. Any owner, not only a player: the link is keyed on characters, so an NPC that is ever given a pet gets the same behaviour with no further wiring. Kept here rather than on Pet because the dispatcher is where a damage event is turned into threat, and the lookup has to be one dictionary read on the hot path. Returns bool True when one was found. Remarks "Whatever is attacking me and hates me most." An NPC's threat toward a character accumulates from that character's hits on it — and, since a pet's hits are credited to its owner, from the pet's hits too — so the highest entry is the thing the subject and its pet have attacked the most. That is the pet attack command's third choice, after the owner's pinned and hovered targets. Reads the reverse index, so it considers only the NPCs actually tracking the subject. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class AggressionState Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll Manages the aggression (threat) system for a single NPC. Owns the AggressionController instance, subscribes to global damage/heal/kill events, and tracks the per-NPC target re-evaluation timer. Extracted from AIController to keep the controller focused on navigation and state management. One instance per NPC — plain C# class. Event-driven combat entry: every hit this NPC takes is reported through OnHitRecorded, and the brain decides from its own state whether that hit starts a fight (OnThreatReceived(ICharacter)). It used to fire only when the table went from empty to non-empty, and nothing but a kill ever emptied it: a fight that ended any other way — the target out of reach, zoned, leashed away — left entries behind, so every later hit from beyond the detection radius was recorded and ignored, and each one refreshed the entry that kept it from ever going stale. Deciding per hit from the brain's state has no edge to consume. Replay safety: Event handlers are guarded to ignore damage/heal/kill events fired during prediction replay. Global combat events are not replay-suppressed by the damage controller, so we suppress them here. public class AggressionState Inheritance object AggressionState Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Constructors AggressionState(ICharacter) Creates a new aggression state with a threat table at the default weights, and subscribes to global damage/heal/kill events. Remarks A target that stands somewhere the NPC cannot path to — on a rock, across a gap, behind a door — produces a partial path. The NPC walks to the closest reachable point and stops, still "in combat", still holding threat, and never attacks or disengages. That is the melee equivalent of the stuck pet, and it is how players kite mobs into a permanent no-op. Recovery first tries to walk around; failing that, the NPC gives up on the target so a leash or a fresh sweep can take over. Remarks The classifier reads what an ability does out of its ECA actions, so this needs no list of ability IDs on the state: an ability whose graph only heals or only buffs is filtered out of the attack rotation wherever it came from, and one added tomorrow is filtered out too. Deliberately permissive at the edges. An ability that both damages and buffs stays in — the damage is the point. A self-cast shield stays in, because the NPC aims it at itself rather than at the enemy and casting it mid-fight is exactly right. Only an ability that is purely supportive and aimed at someone else is excluded, which is the case that produced the actual absurdity: an NPC healing the player it was trying to kill. [Tooltip("Most of this boss's adds alive at once before timed mechanics stop calling more. Phase adds always arrive, and count towards it.")] [Min(1)] public int MaxLiveAdds Field Value int Remarks A timed mechanic fires every Interval for as long as the fight lasts, so a party that tanks the boss and ignores its adds used to meet one more every interval without end: a 30-second summon left forty NPCs in the instance after twenty minutes, each on the AI tick and each a spawn every observer is sent. A mechanic that fires with the boss at its cap calls in nothing, and tops the adds back up to the cap as they die. A phase's SpawnOnEnter adds always arrive: a phase is entered at most once per pull, so they are bounded by what was authored, and a phase that silently came up short of the adds it names would be a different encounter. They count towards the cap all the same, so the timed mechanics hold off while they live. Twelve because it is the most attackers AICombatSlots seats on one ring around a target, which makes it about the largest crowd a timed summon can mean: past it, adds stand on an outer ring waiting for a place. No shipped boss script exists yet (every catalogue entry's is empty), so no authored encounter changes; one written against the old behaviour reaches the cap only if its adds are left alive for twelve intervals. two reasons: taunts have to be prioritised over raw damage regardless of what the scoring picker thinks, and body-blocking means walking to a position derived from a third character rather than from the target. As a pet this is the "defender" stance made concrete — the pet plants itself between its owner and whatever is trying to reach them. Fields BlockRepositionTolerance The defender only bothers repositioning when it is further than this from its ideal blocking spot. Prevents jitter. [Tooltip("Only reposition when further than this from the ideal blocking spot.")] public float BlockRepositionTolerance Field Value float BlockStandoffDistance How far in front of the protected character the defender plants itself, in world units. [Tooltip("Distance in front of the protected character to hold the line.")] public float BlockStandoffDistance Field Value float BodyBlock When true the defender positions itself on the line between the enemy and the character it is protecting, rather than simply closing on the enemy. [Tooltip("Stand between the enemy and the protected character.")] public bool BodyBlock Field Value bool TauntAbilityTemplateIDs Optional escape hatch: template IDs to treat as taunts in addition to whatever AIAbilityClassifier identifies. [Header("Defender Behavior")] [Tooltip("Optional. Extra AbilityTemplate IDs to force-treat as taunts. Normally empty — taunts are detected from the ability's ECA actions.")] public List<int> TauntAbilityTemplateIDs Field Value List<int> Remarks Normally empty. A taunt is recognised by the threat-manipulating action in its own ECA graph — ApplyTauntAction or ApplyThreatAction — so a defender asset works for any creature whose spellbook contains one, and picks up a taunt added later without being edited. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Enum NPCCombatStyle Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll Combat style archetype that broadly describes how the NPC approaches combat. Designers pick a style per personality asset; the AICombatPersonality weights then fine-tune the behaviour. public enum NPCCombatStyle Fields Aggressive = 1 Prefers closing to melee range and high-pressure attacks. Balanced = 0 Default balanced approach — no strong bias. Berserker = 4 All-out damage, ignores self-preservation. Never retreats. Cautious = 3 Avoids risk, retreats earlier, favours safe abilities. Defensive = 2 Prefers keeping distance, kiting, and control abilities. Determined = 6 Never breaks. Fights to the last point of health and holds its threat target. Functionally "Berserker without the target chaos". Pathetic = 5 Cowardly. Breaks and runs as soon as it is meaningfully hurt, and keeps running. A Pathetic personality is guaranteed to have a retreat threshold even if the designer left the field at zero — see EffectiveRetreatHealthThreshold. Rampaging = 7 Berserk and unfocused: never retreats, ignores the threat table, and re-picks a random living enemy at RampageRetargetChance on every re-evaluation.

api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class NPCGroup Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll A pack of NPCs that fight together: a shared focus target, group alerts, roles, and a tactic that arranges members around the enemy while they orbit it. public sealed class NPCGroup Inheritance object NPCGroup Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A plain runtime object, owned by whatever founded it. A spawner whose pack is enabled (Enabled) founds one when its first NPC spawns and adds every NPC it spawns after that, with the role its entry names; a boss founds one for the adds it calls in. It used to be a scene MonoBehaviour with inspector-assigned members and its own Update, and nothing ever created one: NPC brains are added to pooled instances at runtime on the server, so there was never a brain in a scene for an inspector to point at, and Group was never set. Membership is the living members. A brain leaves on death (SuspendForCorpse()), on despawn and pool reset (FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI.AIController.ResetForPool()) and when it is destroyed with its scene. A pack whose last member leaves is Released: it stops ticking, refuses members, and its founder makes a new one for the next spawn. So a respawn rejoins its spawner's pack while any member of it still stands, and founds the next one after a wipe. Ticked by the brain host, inside the AI contract. AIBrainHost calls Tick(float, int) on every network tick; the pack thinks only on AI ticks (the same whole divisor of the network tick the brains use), only while a member is in a tier that fights (TierEvaluates(AILodTier)), and every EVALUATE_INTERVAL seconds scaled by that member's LOD interval. A pack with nobody near it costs a tier read per member per AI tick and does nothing else. Constructors NPCGroup(NPCPackSettings) Founds a pack with authored tuning. public NPCGroup(NPCPackSettings settings) Parameters settings NPCPackSettings The spawner's pack block; null founds an untuned pack. NPCGroup(PackTactic, bool, float, float) Founds a pack. public NPCGroup(PackTactic tactic, bool focusTargeting, float tacticOrbitRadius, float kiteRotationSpeed) Parameters tactic PackTactic How members arrange themselves while orbiting the focus. focusTargeting bool Whether the focus follows the tank's target. tacticOrbitRadius float The tactic ring's radius, in metres. kiteRotationSpeed float Degrees per second the Kite ring turns. Fields CLUSTER_SPREAD Total arc, in radians, a FocusFire cluster is spread over (about 30°). public const float CLUSTER_SPREAD = 0.52 Field Value float DEFAULT_KITE_ROTATION_SPEED Default KiteRotationSpeed for a pack founded without authored settings. public const float DEFAULT_KITE_ROTATION_SPEED = 30 Field Value float DEFAULT_ORBIT_RADIUS Default TacticOrbitRadius for a pack founded without authored settings. public const float DEFAULT_ORBIT_RADIUS = 5 Field Value float EVALUATE_INTERVAL Seconds of AI time between evaluations for a pack whose most active member is in the Active tier. Other tiers multiply it by their LOD interval. public const float EVALUATE_INTERVAL = 0.5 Field Value float Properties AliveMemberCount Living members at the last evaluation. public int AliveMemberCount { get; } Property Value int FocusTargeting When true, the pack's focus follows the target of its living, fighting tank. public bool FocusTargeting { get; } Property Value bool GroupTarget The focused enemy's transform, or null. See GroupTargetCharacter. public Transform GroupTarget { get; } Property Value Transform GroupTargetCharacter The enemy the pack is focusing, or null. public ICharacter GroupTargetCharacter { get; } Property Value ICharacter Remarks Set by AlertGroup(ICharacter) and, with FocusTargeting, by the tank's target at each evaluation; dropped when the pack is no longer fighting. Held with the ID it had, for the reason TargetCharacter is: a pooled character's object is re-issued to somebody else after a despawn, and a bare reference would hand the pack's DPS the pool's next occupant as their focus. IsInCombat True when a member was fighting (in any combat state) at the last evaluation. public bool IsInCombat { get; } Property Value bool KiteRotationSpeed Degrees per second the Kite ring turns. public float KiteRotationSpeed { get; } Property Value float LowestHealthMember The most wounded living member, or null when every living member is at full health. public AIController LowestHealthMember { get; } Property Value AIController Remarks Null rather than "whoever happened to be first" when nobody is hurt: a defender reads this to decide whom to body-block for, and shielding a healthy packmate took it out of the fight for nothing. LowestHealthPercent Health fraction (0-1) of LowestHealthMember; 1 when nobody is wounded. public float LowestHealthPercent { get; } Property Value float MemberCount Members, living or not yet pruned. public int MemberCount { get; } Property Value int Members The members, in joining order. public IReadOnlyList<NPCGroupMember> Members { get; } Property Value IReadOnlyList<NPCGroupMember> Released True once the last member has left. A released pack never takes a member again. public bool Released { get; } Property Value bool Tactic How the pack arranges itself around the enemy it focuses. public PackTactic Tactic { get; } Property Value PackTactic TacticOrbitRadius Radius of the ring an orbiting member takes its tactic slot on, in metres. public float TacticOrbitRadius { get; } Property Value float Methods AddMember(AIController, NPCGroupRole) Adds a brain with a role, taking it out of any other pack first. Adding a member again updates its role. public bool AddMember(AIController controller, NPCGroupRole role) Parameters controller AIController The brain joining. role NPCGroupRole The role it plays here. Returns bool False when the brain is null or this pack has been released. Remarks The first member hands the pack to its brain's host, which ticks it from then on. AlertGroup(ICharacter) Tells the pack that one of its members has engaged enemy: the pack focuses it, and every member free to fight joins in. public void AlertGroup(ICharacter enemy) Parameters enemy ICharacter The character a member has engaged. Remarks Called by ChangeState(BaseAIState, List<ICharacter>) whenever a member enters an attacking state with a target. Who answers is decided by the member, with the same rule a hit is asked (MayAnswerPackAlert(bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool)): not a member already fighting, evading on a leash, immortal, dead or without a brain that runs. AssignFormation(PackTactic, IReadOnlyList<NPCGroupRole>, IReadOnlyList<float>, float, float, List<int>, List<float>) Assigns each formation member a bearing around the focus for a tactic. public static void AssignFormation(PackTactic tactic, IReadOnlyList<NPCGroupRole> roles, IReadOnlyList<float> bearings, float flankFront, float kiteAdvance, List<int> order, List<float> angles) Parameters tactic PackTactic The tactic. roles IReadOnlyList<NPCGroupRole> Each formation member's role. bearings IReadOnlyList<float> Each member's current bearing from the focus, in radians. flankFront float The Flank tactic's front bearing: the tank's, or the direction the enemy faces. kiteAdvance float Radians the Kite ring turns this evaluation. order List<int> Scratch list, overwritten. angles List<float> Receives each member's assigned bearing, index for index; a member's current bearing when the tactic is None. Remarks Fitted to where the members already stand, never to the world axes. The slots used to be absolute angles from world +X, so a Flank's "front" was east whatever the enemy faced and a FocusFire cluster formed on the east side even when the pack had come from the west. Now: Surround — an even ring, rotated to the angle that moves the members least (the circular mean of each member's bearing less its ring step), members kept in the order they stand around the enemy. Kite — the same ring advanced by kiteAdvance, so the ring turns from wherever the members are rather than from a stored angle they have drifted away from. FocusFire — a CLUSTER_SPREAD arc centred on the members' mean bearing: they converge from the side they are already on. Flank — tanks at flankFront, everyone else across the rear half-circle in the order they stand; a single flanker directly behind. (It used to put a lone flanker at the side, 90° from the front.) Pure, so every tactic's geometry can be pinned without a scene. BearingOf(Vector3) The bearing of a horizontal offset, in the convention OrbitState places by: (cos a, 0, sin a). public static float BearingOf(Vector3 offset) Parameters offset Vector3 The offset. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..title: Enum PackTactic | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Enum PackTactic Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll How an NPCGroup arranges the members fighting its focus. Each such member is given a bearing around the focus (PackSlotAngle), which OrbitState steers to on the pack's TacticOrbitRadius. public enum PackTactic Fields Flank = 2 The tank holds the front and everyone else spreads across the rear half-circle; a lone flanker goes directly behind. The front is the tank's side, or, with no tank fighting the focus, the direction the enemy faces. FocusFire = 3 Members close in from the side they are already on, in a tight arc. Combined with FocusTargeting for maximum single-target pressure. Kite = 4 A Surround ring that keeps turning, at KiteRotationSpeed. Best for ranged/caster groups that want to avoid melee contact. None = 0 No coordinated positioning — members act independently. Surround = 1 Members spread evenly around the focus, the ring rotated to move them least. Best for mixed groups that want to prevent the enemy from fleeing. Remarks Bearings are fitted to where the members already stand (see AssignFormation(PackTactic, IReadOnlyList<NPCGroupRole>, IReadOnlyList<float>, float, float, List<int>, List<float>)), not measured from the world axes. A tactic shapes the orbit manoeuvre only: an archetype whose attacking state has no Orbit variety state never orbits, and its approach is spaced by the combat-slot ring as any attacker's is.

It is deliberately not driven off Target — that means "the thing I am fighting" everywhere else in the AI, and the two meanings cannot share one field. They used to, and the result was a pet that stopped following its owner permanently the moment a fight ended, because ending a fight clears the target. Not getting stuck is the other half of this state's job. A pet chases a player who runs through doorways, off ledges and around props, so it meets every NavMesh failure mode there is. Three layers handle it: a follow band so the pet is not repathing every tick, a stuck detector that walks it out of geometry, and a distance leash that teleports it when the owner has simply gone somewhere the pet cannot walk. Fields AggressiveSweepRate How often (seconds) an aggressive pet sweeps for something to attack. [Header("Engagement")] [Tooltip("Seconds between hostile sweeps while in the Aggressive stance.")] public float AggressiveSweepRate Field Value float FollowDistance How far the pet is allowed to drift from its owner before it moves back. [Header("Following")] [Tooltip("Distance from the owner at which the pet starts catching up.")] public float FollowDistance Field Value float FollowHysteresis How far inside FollowDistance the pet closes before it stops again. [Tooltip("Extra distance the pet closes past the follow distance before stopping.")] public float FollowHysteresis Field Value float Remarks Without a band, a pet sitting exactly at the follow distance flickers between "close enough, stop" and "too far, move" on alternating ticks, which reads as a stutter and repaths constantly. StuckTeleportSeconds Seconds the pet may be wedged before it teleports to its owner. [Tooltip("Seconds wedged on geometry before the pet teleports to its owner. 0 disables.")] public float StuckTeleportSeconds Field Value float Remarks The distance leash alone is not enough: a pet jammed behind a crate five metres from its owner is stuck indefinitely without ever exceeding TeleportDistance. This is the escape hatch for that case, and it only fires after the generic recovery has already tried to walk the pet out. TeleportDistance If the pet ends up further than this from its owner, it teleports rather than walking. [Tooltip("Distance from the owner beyond which the pet teleports instead of walking. 0 disables.")] public float TeleportDistance Field Value float Remarks Covers what pathing cannot: the owner mounting and riding away, a teleport, a zone transition, or a pet left on the wrong side of a chasm. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class PetSupport Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll How a pet uses the heals and buffs it knows: on its owner first, always, then on itself and the friends around it. public static class PetSupport Inheritance object PetSupport Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Driven by what the pet knows, not by its archetype. A pet's spells can come from its summon spell (AbilityOnSummonEvent), so a melee pet may well know a heal. The heals and buffs are found the way HealerAttackingState finds its heals — from the ability's own ECA actions (AIAbilityClassifier) — and a pet that knows none finds nothing to do here. Run in combat by BaseAttackingState before the attack, and out of combat by PetIdleState, so a pet patches its owner up after a fight as well as during one. The order is fixed. The owner is looked after first, at any distance: an owner below the heal threshold is healed, and an owner missing a buff the pet can give is buffed, before anyone else is considered — the pet walks back to its owner to do it. Then the most wounded of the pet itself and its friends, then their buffs. AIPetSupportSettings tunes the threshold and the reach; it cannot reorder this. A friend is someone the pet's owner may not harm and is on the same side as: the owner's party, guild and other pets, and anyone the owner is allied with (IsFriend(Pet, ICharacter)). Static and single-threaded, like the healer's ally sweep: every call runs to completion inside one synchronous AI tick, which is what lets the filters below share one scratch recipient instead of allocating a closure per pick. The leash sends a fighting NPC home through this state, and it is also one of the calm movement states TransitionToRandomMovementState() drifts between. Only the first is an evade: while a leash that ended a fight has the NPC walking home it takes no damage, threat, taunt, debuff or knockback (IsEvading, CharacterEvade). api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..title: Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer.AI Classes AIAbilityClassifier Works out what an ability does by reading the ECA action graph the designer already built, so archetypes never have to name specific abilities. AIAbilityCondition Abstract base class for AI ability conditions. Each condition evaluates a boolean predicate that determines whether an ability rotation entry should be selected. Conditions are ScriptableObject assets that can be shared across multiple rotations. Subclasses override Evaluate(AIController, ICharacter, ICharacter) to implement specific checks such as health thresholds, buff presence, distance comparisons, etc. AIAbilityReach How far an ability can actually hit something from, as the AI should reason about it. AIAbilityRotation ScriptableObject that defines an ordered list of ability entries with conditions. Attach to an AIController to give NPCs intelligent, designer-driven ability selection instead of (or in addition to) the default scoring-based picker. In Priority mode, entries are evaluated top-to-bottom and the first match wins — ideal for conditional behaviour such as "use Heal when health ≤ 40%, else use Fireball". In Sequence mode, the NPC advances through the list in order, trying the next entry each evaluation — ideal for structured rotations such as "Fireball → Frost Bolt → Pyroblast → repeat". AIAbilityRotationEntry A single entry in an AI ability rotation. Pairs an ability template with a set of conditions that must all be satisfied for the ability to be selected. AIAdoptGroupTargetNode Behavior tree leaf that adopts the pack's focus. If the NPC belongs to an NPCGroup whose GroupTargetCharacter is a living target, this node sets the NPC's Target to it and returns Success. Use case: "Focus the tank's target" → place this before a StateTransition to AttackState. AIAimProfile How well an NPC aims: which point on a target it shoots at, how long it needs to settle, and how far it misses by while it has not. AIAimSolver The pure arithmetic behind an NPC's aim: which point to aim at, how accurately, and with how much error. AIArchetypeTemplate A complete, reusable AI brain in one asset: which states an NPC uses, how it picks abilities, how it behaves in combat, how it accrues threat, and how it is throttled at distance. AIBehaviorNode Abstract base class for all behavior tree nodes. Nodes are ScriptableObject assets so designers can build trees entirely in the Unity inspector without code. Behavior trees sit above the state machine layer and decide which BaseAIState the NPC should transition to. The state machine then handles the actual movement, combat, and animation logic. Node types: AISelector — Tries children left-to-right, returns first success. AISequence — Runs children left-to-right, fails on first failure. AIInverter — Inverts the child's result. AIRepeater — Repeats the child a configurable number of times. AIConditionNode — Leaf that checks an AIAbilityCondition. AIStateTransitionNode — Leaf that transitions to a BaseAIState. AIBehaviorTree Root container for a behavior tree. Assign to BehaviorTree to give an NPC high-level decision-making above the state machine. The tree is evaluated once per AI tick (governed by AI LOD). If the root node returns Success, the tree produced a state transition and the current state's UpdateState is skipped for that tick. If it returns Failure, the current state continues normally. Example tree: AIBehaviorTree (root = Selector) ├─ Sequence: [Condition: IsDead] → [StateTransition: DeadState] ├─ Sequence: [Condition: HP ≤ 30%] → [StateTransition: RetreatState] ├─ Sequence: [Condition: EnemyNearby] → [StateTransition: AttackState] └─ StateTransition: WanderState AIBodyGrid Where every NPC body in one physics scene stands, bucketed into a uniform grid so a separation query reads a handful of cells instead of running a physics overlap. AIBrainCatalogue Which brain each NPC prefab runs. AIBrainCatalogue.Entry One NPC prefab's brain. AIBrainHost Attaches, drives and detaches the server-side brain of every NPC spawned under one FishNet.Managing.NetworkManager. AIBuffCondition Condition that checks whether a character has (or doesn't have) a specific buff or debuff. Examples: - "Self has buff 42" → target already has a HoT, skip re-applying. - "Target missing debuff 7" → apply the DoT. AICombatDecision The single combat decision shared by every attacking state. AICombatPersonality Data-driven combat personality asset that makes two NPCs with the same ability set behave differently in combat. Assign to Personality. The personality provides per-AbilityCategory score multipliers that PickBestAbility(float) applies on top of the default scoring. Two warriors sharing the same ability list but with different personalities will favour different abilities and positioning. Range thresholds control how abilities are classified. Abilities whose Range falls below MeleeRangeThreshold are considered melee; those above are ranged. Abilities with HitCount greater than 1 or grounded spawn targets are classified as AOE. Self-targeted abilities are classified as Support. AICombatSlots Hands each attacker its own standing spot in a ring around a shared target, so a pack surrounds its victim instead of piling onto one point. AICompositeNode Composite node that wraps a list of children. Base class for AISelector and AISequence. AIConditionNode Leaf node that evaluates an AIAbilityCondition and returns Success or Failure. Use case: "Is the NPC's health below 30%?" The existing AIAbilityCondition system is reused so designers don't need to create duplicate condition assets. Any condition that works in an ability rotation also works as a behavior tree guard. AIController Controls AI navigation, state transitions, and behavior for NPCs using NavMeshAgent. Handles movement, enemy detection, leash logic, waypoints, state management, and provides a virtual camera for aiming abilities at targets during combat. AIDistanceCondition Condition that evaluates based on the distance between the NPC and its current target. Examples: - "Distance ≤ 3" → in melee range, use a cleave ability. - "Distance ≥ 15" → far away, use a snipe ability. AIGroupInCombatNode Behavior tree leaf that checks if the NPC belongs to an NPCGroup and whether the group is currently in combat. Returns Success when the group is fighting. Use case: "If my pack is in combat → join the fight (even if I haven't been attacked)." AIHasTargetNode Behavior tree leaf that checks if the NPC currently has a combat target. Returns Success if Target is not null, Failure otherwise. Use case: "If has target → stay in combat" in a behavior tree selector. AIHealthCondition Condition that evaluates based on a character's health percentage. Can check either the NPC's own health or the current target's health. Examples: - "Self health ≤ 40%" → use a defensive or healing ability. - "Target health ≤ 20%" → use an execute ability. - "Self health ≥ 80%" → use an offensive stance ability. AIInverter Decorator that inverts the child's result. Success becomes Failure and vice versa. Running passes through unchanged. Use case: "If NOT low health → continue attacking." AIIsDeadNode Behavior tree leaf that checks if the NPC is alive. Returns Success when alive, Failure when dead or missing damage controller. Use case: First check in a selector — "If dead → DeadState". Combine with AIInverter to get "IsAlive". AILodSettings Distance thresholds and per-tier update intervals for AI level-of-detail. Assign to LodSettings. AIPetSupportSettings How a pet uses the heals and buffs it knows: who it looks after, and when. See PetSupport. AIRandomCondition Condition that passes with a configurable random probability each evaluation. Useful for introducing variety — e.g., "30% chance to use a special attack". AIRepeater Decorator that repeats its child a configurable number of times per evaluation. Returns Success after all repetitions succeed. Returns Failure if any repetition fails. When RepeatCount is 0, repeats indefinitely (always returns Running). AIRetreatDecision Decides whether a fleeing NPC keeps running, turns around, or disengages. AISelector Selector (OR) node. Tries each child left-to-right and returns Success as soon as one child succeeds. Returns Failure only if every child fails. Returns Running if any child is running. Use case: "Try heal → if that fails, try attack → if that fails, wander." AISeparation Keeps NPCs from standing inside one another without Unity's crowd avoidance. AISequence Sequence (AND) node. Runs each child left-to-right and returns Success only if every child succeeds. Returns Failure on the first child that fails. Returns Running if any child is running. Use case: "Check health condition AND then transition to retreat state." AIShelterSettings Whether, and in what, an archetype's NPCs go and stand out of the weather. AIStateTransitionNode Leaf node that transitions the NPC's state machine to a specific BaseAIState. Always returns Success after triggering the transition. This is the bridge between the behavior tree (decision layer) and the state machine (execution layer). The tree decides "attack", and this node calls ChangeState(BaseAIState, List<ICharacter>) to make it happen. AISwimRisk The decision an NPC makes when the way to its target is through deep water: scored, never scripted. The risk is how long it would be in the water against how good a swimmer it is, with its breath on top for one that swims under; its appetite for risk is its courage, scaled by how much it wants this target. In if the appetite covers the risk; otherwise it waits on the shore; and past its leash, it lets the target go. AISwimSettings Whether, and how, an archetype's NPCs swim (2026-10-05: not all NPCs can swim; swimming NPCs will probably drown, and an AI decides whether to chase into the water or stay on land). AISystem The scene server's NPC brain system: runs one AIBrainHost for the process. AITargetSelection Target-picking strategies shared by the attacking states and the behaviour tree. AIUtility Shared utility methods for the AI subsystem. Provides common operations used across ability rotations, boss scripts, and attacking states to eliminate duplication (DRY). AggressionController Manages an aggression (threat) table for a single NPC. Tracks threat from damage, healing, resource expenditure, and arbitrary point adjustments. Threat decays over time. Target selection uses both raw threat points and a vulnerability multiplier based on the target's current health and mana percentages. Plain C# class — one instance per NPC, owned by AggressionState. AggressionDispatcher Routes combat events to the one NPC that cares about them, instead of broadcasting every event to every NPC in the scene. AggressionEntry Tracks accumulated aggression (threat) from a single character toward an NPC. Points are gained when the character damages the NPC, heals an enemy, spends resources, or takes other aggressive actions. Points decay over time so stale threats fade. AggressionState Manages the aggression (threat) system for a single NPC. Owns the AggressionController instance, subscribes to global damage/heal/kill events, and tracks the per-NPC target re-evaluation timer. Extracted from AIController to keep the controller focused on navigation and state management. One instance per NPC — plain C# class. Event-driven combat entry: every hit this NPC takes is reported through OnHitRecorded, and the brain decides from its own state whether that hit starts a fight (OnThreatReceived(ICharacter)). It used to fire only when the table went from empty to non-empty, and nothing but a kill ever emptied it: a fight that ended any other way — the target out of reach, zoned, leashed away — left entries behind, so every later hit from beyond the detection radius was recorded and ignored, and each one refreshed the entry that kept it from ever going stale. Deciding per hit from the brain's state has no edge to consume. Replay safety: Event handlers are guarded to ignore damage/heal/kill events fired during prediction replay. Global combat events are not replay-suppressed by the damage controller, so we suppress them here. BaseAIState Abstract base class for all AI states. Defines common parameters and logic for state transitions, leash checks, enemy detection, and line of sight. BaseAttackingState The one attacking state. Handles target selection, spacing, ability activation and mid-combat re-targeting for every NPC archetype. BossPhase Defines a single phase of a boss encounter. A boss transitions to the next phase when its health drops below HealthThreshold. Each phase can override the boss's behavior tree, attacking state, and spawn adds. BossScript ScriptableObject that defines a boss encounter's phases and timed mechanics. Assign to BossScript to make an NPC a scripted boss. The AIController evaluates the boss script every tick: Checks health against phase thresholds. On phase change, applies overrides (behavior tree, attacking state, ability rotation) and spawns adds. Ticks all active timed mechanics and force-activates abilities or spawns when timers fire. Example setup: Phases: [0] HP ≥ 70% — default behavior [1] HP < 70% — spawn 2 adds, switch to Phase2 behavior tree [2] HP < 40% — enrage: switch to melee attacking state Timed Mechanics: Meteor — every 30s, force-cast AbilityTemplate #5 Summon — every 60s, spawn skeleton prefab (only in phase 1) BossScriptState Per-NPC runtime state for a BossScript. Tracks the current phase index, timed mechanic timers, and handles phase transitions and mechanic activations. This is a plain C# class (not a ScriptableObject) because it holds mutable state that differs per NPC instance — the same BossScript asset may be shared across multiple boss spawns. BossTimedMechanic Defines a timed mechanic that fires at regular intervals during a boss encounter. E.g., "Every 30 seconds, cast Meteor." CasterAttackingState Caster archetype preset (mages, warlocks, crowd controllers). Sits at the far edge of its spell range, refuses to be meleed, and interrupts its own cast to escape when something gets inside the panic radius. DefenderAttackingState Defender / tank archetype. Fights in melee, keeps its taunts on cooldown to hold threat, and physically interposes itself between the enemy and whoever it is protecting. GetBehindState Combat sub-state that circles the NPC around to the back of its current target. HealerAttackingState Healer archetype. Keeps caster spacing from the enemy, but interrupts its damage rotation to top up the most wounded nearby ally. IdleState AI state for idle behavior. Handles update rate, entering, exiting, and transition logic for NPCs. MeleeAttackingState Melee archetype preset. Closes to weapon reach, never backs away, and occasionally steps into a flanking or orbiting sub-state for variety. NPCGroup A pack of NPCs that fight together: a shared focus target, group alerts, roles, and a tactic that arranges members around the enemy while they orbit it. NPCPackSettings How a spawner's NPCs fight as a pack: whether they are one at all, and the tactic, focus and ring they share. Authored on an ObjectSpawner, baked into its SpawnerDefinition, and read by the running spawner when it founds an NPCGroup. OrbitState Combat sub-state that strafes the NPC in a circle around its current target. PatrolState Waypoint patrol. Walks the spawner-supplied waypoint ring in order. PetAttackingState Pet combat preset. A plain melee-tuned attacking state with pet-appropriate defaults. PetIdleState A pet's out-of-combat state: heel near its owner, hold position on a Stay order, and enter combat when the pet's PetStance says it should. PetSupport How a pet uses the heals and buffs it knows: on its owner first, always, then on itself and the friends around it. RangedAttackingState Ranged archetype preset (archers, hunters, gunners). Holds a working distance, kites when the target closes, and breaks away hard once the target is inside the panic radius. RetreatState Moves the NPC away from its target until a safe distance is reached, then disengages. ReturnHomeState AI State for returning the NPC to its home position. Handles healing and movement speed adjustments. RogueAttackingState Rogue archetype. Melee, but refuses to trade blows face-to-face: it circles into the target's rear arc before opening, and drifts back around whenever the target turns on it. SeekShelterState Walks to the nearest cover and waits there until the weather passes. WanderState Wandering behaviour. The NPC drifts to random points around its home, pausing at idle now and then. WildlifeFleeState Prey's "attacking" state: it never attacks, it runs. Slotted as a prey archetype's AttackingState, so everything that sends an NPC into a fight sends prey into flight instead: being hit (OnThreatReceived), a herd-mate's alarm (the spawner's pack, NPCGroup.AlertGroup) and its own search noticing a threat (WildlifeRules.Notices). Structs AICombatContext Everything the shared combat decision needs, as plain numbers. AICombatPlan The decision produced from an AICombatContext. AIKiteBudget Limits how long an NPC may keep backing away from its target before it has to stand and fight. AIRetreatBudget The memory a retreating NPC needs to stop retreating: how long it has been running, how many times it has run during this fight, and whether it has committed to fighting instead. AIRetreatContext Everything Decide(in AIRetreatContext) needs to reach an outcome. AIStateClock Schedules a state's updates and reports how much time each one covers. AISwimRiskInput The facts a chase across water is decided on. NPCGroupMember One brain in an NPCGroup, and the role it plays there. PetSupport.Choice One support cast a pet has decided on. Enums AIAimPoint The point on a target's body an NPC aims at. AICombatIntent What an NPC has decided to do about its current target this combat tick. Produced by Plan(in AICombatContext) and executed by BaseAttackingState. AILodTier AI Level-of-Detail tiers. Determines how frequently an NPC's brain ticks based on its proximity to the nearest player observer. AIMovementProgress How an NPC is faring against its current destination. AIMovementResult Outcome of asking an NPC to move somewhere. AINodeResult Result of a behavior tree node evaluation. AIRetreatOutcome What a retreating NPC should do next. AIRotationMode Determines how the rotation evaluates its entries. AISwimMode How a swimming NPC goes through water. AITargetingMode How an NPC picks which enemy to hit when several are available. Supplied by TargetingMode and consumed by PickTarget(AIController, List<ICharacter>). AbilityCategory Ability category inferred at runtime from an ability's template data. Used by AICombatPersonality to apply personality weights. AgentAvoidancePriority Defines avoidance priority levels for AI agents. Higher values cause agents to avoid others more aggressively. Used to control how strongly an agent tries to avoid collisions with other agents in the navigation system. ComparisonOperator Comparison operators for numeric condition evaluation. ConditionSubject Determines which character a condition evaluates against. NPCCombatStyle Combat style archetype that broadly describes how the NPC approaches combat. Designers pick a style per personality asset; the AICombatPersonality weights then fine-tune the behaviour. NPCGroupRole Roles that NPCs can play within an NPCGroup, authored per spawner entry (NPCSpawnableSettings.PackRole). PackTactic How an NPCGroup arranges the members fighting its focus. Each such member is given a bearing around the focus (PackSlotAngle), which OrbitState steers to on the pack's TacticOrbitRadius. PetSupport.Kind What a support choice does. PetSupport.Step What Plan(AIController, LayerMask, bool, out Choice) decided to do this tick. WaterVerdict What an NPC chasing something across water decides to do.

Three paths hand out abilities — the ability crafter, the merchant selling a premade, and (in principle) anything a content author adds next — and all three had their own copy of "construct, learn, persist". Only the item layer had worked out what the copies were missing, which is why InteractableSystem.SendNewItemBroadcast was emptied into CharacterInventorySystem.TryGrantItem and its doc says so. This is the same move for abilities, and it is the fix for the same class of bug. The bug. Ability(template, events) sets ID = -1 by design — its own doc comment says the database assigns the real id — and nothing ever put that id back. PersistAbilityAsync read IsSuccess and threw away the long the upsert returned, so AbilityController.LearnAbility filed every crafted ability under -1: crafting a second ability from a different template silently replaced the first, and because HotkeyData.UnsetReferenceID is also -1 a hotkey bound to either of them validated against the sentinel. The identity is applied here, before the learn, so the window in which a crafted ability has no key does not exist. Why the learn is deferred rather than corrected afterwards. The item layer can hand an item a provisional identity and correct it on the wire because an item lives in a slot: it can be locked while unidentified, and the slot re-sent (CharacterInventorySystem.ApplyAssignedIdentities). An ability has no slot — the instance id is its key on the server, in the client's known-ability table, in AbilityActivatedBroadcast, and in every persisted hotkey row. Deferring the grant costs one database round trip inside a request that already waits for its result broadcast, and removes the window entirely. Methods InitializeOnce() Initializes the ability system, registering the forget request handler. public override ServerComponentInitializationStatus InitializeOnce() Returns ServerComponentInitializationStatus OnDeinitialize() Cleans up the ability system, unregistering broadcast handlers. public override void OnDeinitialize() OnServerAbilityForgetBroadcastReceived(NetworkConnection, AbilityForgetBroadcast, Channel) Handles a request to forget one crafted ability. public void OnServerAbilityForgetBroadcastReceived(NetworkConnection conn, AbilityForgetBroadcast msg, Channel channel) Parameters conn NetworkConnection Network connection of the requesting client. msg AbilityForgetBroadcast Forget request naming the ability. channel Channel Network channel used for the broadcast. Remarks Addressed by the ability's row identity, never by its template. The service's statement matches WHERE id = ?, and a template id would either match nothing — reporting success for a delete that removed no row — or, on a table with several rows per template, remove the wrong one. The guard is held until the delete lands, not until this handler returns. A second forget arriving in that window would otherwise read the same live ability and delete the same row twice, and a re-craft arriving in it would see a character that still knows the ability. OnUpdate(float) Drains stale ingress entries with bounded cleanup each frame, and applies database-minted ability identities that arrived during the frame. protected override void OnUpdate(float deltaTime) Parameters deltaTime float TryGrantAbility(IPlayerCharacter, AbilityTemplate, IReadOnlyList<int>, Func<IPlayerCharacter, bool>, Action, Action<IPlayerCharacter, Ability>, Action<IPlayerCharacter>) Builds and grants a new crafted ability to character. public bool TryGrantAbility(IPlayerCharacter character, AbilityTemplate template, IReadOnlyList<int> events, Func<IPlayerCharacter, bool> settle, Action releaseGuard, Action<IPlayerCharacter, Ability> onGranted, Action<IPlayerCharacter> onFailed) Parameters character IPlayerCharacter The character receiving the ability. template AbilityTemplate The ability template the crafted ability is built from. events IReadOnlyList<int> The crafted event template ids to attach, or null for none. settle Func<IPlayerCharacter, bool> Takes the caller's charge on the main thread once the row exists. Null when the grant is free. Returns false, having answered the player, to have the row revoked. releaseGuard Action Releases the caller's in-flight guard. Always invoked, exactly once, by this system. onGranted Action<IPlayerCharacter, Ability> Runs on the main thread once the ability is settled, learned and broadcast. onFailed Action<IPlayerCharacter> Runs on the main thread when the ability could not be recorded. Returns bool true when the grant was admitted; false when it was refused outright. Remarks Asynchronous by contract. A true return means the request was admitted, not that the ability exists yet. Exactly one of onGranted or onFailed runs later, on the main thread, once the database has answered. This method takes ownership of releaseGuard. It is invoked exactly once on whichever path finishes the request — a synchronous refusal, a refused enqueue, or the persist's continuation — so a caller must NOT also release it, and a caller that holds a request-open guard across this call passes the release in here instead of running it in its own finally. A refusal is synchronous and already reports itself through the return value, so onFailed is reserved for a persist that was attempted and did not land. Callers answer a false return themselves. Payment is settled on completion, not before the call. A caller that charges for the ability passes the charge as settle; it runs on the main thread once the row exists and only if the character is still resident, and the ability is learned strictly after it returns true. If the character has left, or settle returns false, the row is revoked and nothing is learned, announced or owed. Charging before the call was how a persist that failed after the player left became an unrefundable loss. A false from settle means the caller has already answered the player; neither onGranted nor onFailed runs for it.

AllowsUnclaimedItemWrite(CharacterSessionLeaseData) Whether an item write may land on a character whose row holds no claim at all. Pure. public static bool AllowsUnclaimedItemWrite(CharacterSessionLeaseData lease) Parameters lease CharacterSessionLeaseData The claim the write was captured under. Returns bool True only when the write carries no usable claim. Remarks Only a write that has no claim to quote. Every assertion used to pass allowUnclaimed: true, and a character this server has just released is exactly that — Offline, owned by nobody — so a batch captured under the released claim and run a moment late was accepted: it landed after the release, over the rows the next load reads and over anything written to the offline character since. That made the item gate weaker than the one every other character write now passes (CharacterWriteGate): a write that carries a claim must find that claim, and one that finds the character released is refused as Forbidden, reported as NotOwned, and not reconciled. A batch with no triple at all (ResolveSessionLease(long) found none, which a resident character does not produce) keeps the old fallback: refused over a live claim by anyone, accepted on an unclaimed row. It cannot prove anything either way, and refusing it outright would lose the write of a resident whose claim bookkeeping had gone missing. CaptureDespawnFlush(IPlayerCharacter, CharacterSessionInfo?) Captures a full snapshot of a departing character's containers, to be awaited by the character system before it releases the session. public Func<Task<ItemWriteOutcome>> CaptureDespawnFlush(IPlayerCharacter character, CharacterSessionInfo? lease) Parameters character IPlayerCharacter The departing character. lease CharacterSessionInfo? The session this server still holds for it, already taken out of the live token map. Returns Func<Task<ItemWriteOutcome>> The flush to await, or null. Remarks Main thread only, while the character is still resident. The returned work writes the snapshot in one transaction under lease; the caller awaits it before the release so the next owner reads it. Returns null when there is nothing to capture. The caller must look at the outcome. Retry means the items are not in the database: the claim must be kept and the same work run again before it is released, because once another server claims and loads the character nothing can deliver them. The work may be run any number of times — a rerun of a flush that did land re-states the same rows, and one overtaken by a later write reports Superseded. ClassifyOwnershipRefusal(DatabaseResult) Says what an ownership refusal means for an item write. public static ItemWriteOutcome ClassifyOwnershipRefusal(DatabaseResult refusal) Parameters refusal DatabaseResult The failed assertion. Returns ItemWriteOutcome The outcome to report. Remarks Forbidden is a claim that belongs to someone else (or a deleted character): final, and the one outcome that must never be retried over the owner's state. A transient failure of the assertion itself proved nothing either way and is worth another attempt. Anything else — a missing character, a malformed triple — will fail the same way next time. Returns bool True if swap succeeded, false otherwise. Remarks The vacated slot is the whole reason this overload exists. Item rows are keyed (character_id, slot), so a move onto an EMPTY slot writes the item at its new index and leaves the row at the old index untouched — the same item persisted twice. Only the write side was emitted here before, because affectedItems collects non-null items and a move-to-empty produces exactly one of them, which reads like a complete description of the change and is not. The 60-second snapshot prunes the stale row, so this never survived a clean shutdown — but "duplicated until the next snapshot, permanently if the scene server dies first" is not a guarantee worth relying on when the delete costs one list entry. TryGrantItem(IPlayerCharacter, Item, InventoryType) Grants an item to one of a character's containers: places it, tells the owning client, persists it, and hands it the identity the database assigns. public bool TryGrantItem(IPlayerCharacter character, Item item, InventoryType container) Parameters character IPlayerCharacter The character receiving the item. item Item The item. May be merged into stacks the character already holds. container InventoryType Which container receives it. Returns bool True when the whole item was placed. Remarks THE grant path. Every server-side source of a new item — pickups, corpse and chest loot, merchant purchases, mail, quest and achievement rewards, the ECA give action — comes through here, because it is the only path that completes an item: a fresh item has no database identity, and until its first write returns one it cannot be equipped (the attribute ledger declines an id of zero), used, moved, or safely written a second time. The slot it lands in stays locked until that identity arrives; see TryPersistGrantedItems(IPlayerCharacter, List<Item>, InventoryType, string). All-or-nothing on the container: the whole stack fits or nothing is placed, so a caller that reserved the item elsewhere (took it off a corpse, charged for it) can put it back on a false return. TryPersistGrantedItems(IPlayerCharacter, List<Item>, InventoryType, string) Persists a grant of items — freshly created items and the existing stacks they merged into — through the atomic item-batch machinery, so an item the database has never seen (ID 0) gets the identity the write returns assigned onto the live Item and the owning client is told the final instance id and seed. public bool TryPersistGrantedItems(IPlayerCharacter character, List<Item> modifiedItems, InventoryType container, string operation) Parameters character IPlayerCharacter The character the items were granted to. modifiedItems List<Item> The items the grant touched, as returned by the container add. container InventoryType The container the items are in. operation string Short operation name used in persistence log lines. Returns bool True when the batch was enqueued within the worker's threshold; false when it was admitted over it and waits behind the backlog (or, the worker not running, went to the bounded fallback). The write runs either way. Never a rollback signal — memory is already authoritative. Remarks An item with no identity has its slot LOCKED from here until the identity lands, so nothing can move, merge, consume or equip it in between. That window is one database round trip. Without the lock a second write captured in that window inserted a second row for the same item, which the load path then handed back as two items. TryRunExchange(IPlayerCharacter, IPlayerCharacter, Func<ItemExchangeLeg[]>, Action<bool>, string) Runs a two-character exchange — a completed player trade — as ONE database transaction whose commit is the point of truth, so a crash at any instant leaves the database holding either the whole trade or none of it, and memory never diverges from that in a direction that duplicates anything. public bool TryRunExchange(IPlayerCharacter first, IPlayerCharacter second, Func<ItemExchangeLeg[]> applyOnMainThread, Action<bool> onFinished, string operation) Parameters first IPlayerCharacter One party. second IPlayerCharacter The other party. applyOnMainThread Func<ItemExchangeLeg[]> Called on the main thread while both row locks are held. Returns the two legs (first's then second's) after mutating memory, or null to abort before anything was mutated. onFinished Action<bool> Called on the main thread once, with true when the transaction committed and false when it was aborted or rolled back. Only called with false after a null apply, or with the memory mutation still in place and every touched slot already unlocked, so the caller can undo it. operation string Short operation name used in persistence log lines. Returns bool True when the exchange was accepted for execution. False means nothing will run and nothing was changed. Remarks THE PROTOCOL, in order, because the order is the guarantee: Worker: open the transaction and take BOTH characters' session row locks, in ascending id order. From here no other write for either character can commit until this transaction ends: every write takes the same lock. Main thread, while the locks are held: applyOnMainThread re-validates and mutates memory (or returns null to abort with nothing changed), and the resulting rows are captured with their journal sequences and versions stamped NOW. Every write captured before this instant therefore carries a lower sequence and lower versions than the trade; every write captured after carries the trade's content. The slots in TouchedSlots are locked until the outcome is known. Worker: write both characters' rows and the ledger, commit. Main thread: unlock, then onFinished(true). On any refusal: roll back, unlock, onFinished(false) — the caller undoes its memory mutation exactly, which the locks make possible — then every write captured from memory while the exchange was applied is VOIDED in the journal, because its content described a trade that never happened, and both characters are reconciled from the restored memory. Crash analysis: before the commit, memory is lost and the database rolls back — the trade never happened for either side. After the commit, the database holds the whole trade for both. A write captured before the apply that lands after the commit is older by sequence and version and is refused. There is no interleaving in which one character's half is durable and the other's is not.

A character found below DeathAltitude is killed through Kill(ICharacter) with no killer, which is the whole death path every other death takes: the dead flag, the death pose for observers, the OnKilled subscribers (this system's own, which sends a player its death dialog; the pet, arena and aggression systems), the ECA triggers and the cooldown reset. Nobody is credited, the same as an operator's kill: there is no one to give the standing, quests or achievements to. The player then respawns from the death dialog as from any death. A walk, not a trigger. One height comparison per character a few times a second, and none at all while no cloud world is loaded. A trigger volume under the islands would need a collider as wide as the scene in every cloud world and would fire only on entry, so a body that arrived below the line any other way (a load, a teleport, a revive) would never be told. The body stays where the deck took it. KCCController holds a character that nobody is steering once it is below the line, so a corpse does not fall for as long as its player sits at the death dialog (at terminal velocity it would leave the range network positions are written in within minutes). Nothing is left in the void. An NPC lost to the deck goes straight back to its spawner instead of becoming a corpse nobody can reach, and a revive of a body the deck holds (a resurrect accepted, an operator's revive) puts the character on the nearest island ground that will hold it (CloudWorldLanding). A bind point that is open air in a cloud world is passed over the same way, so a respawn cannot drop the character straight back in. Remarks The ordering this performs is the whole point of the method, and it is why callers must not simply rewrite SceneHandle and disconnect. Scene population is credited and debited by handle, and the disconnect pipeline debits the handle the character carries at that moment — so a handle rewritten first debits the destination instance, which this server may not even host, while the source instance keeps a resident it no longer has. Neither error self-corrects: the source's phantom population makes it advertise capacity it does not have, keeps it from ever being recognised as empty and unloaded, and eventually makes it look full, at which point players queue for a scene instance that is in fact deserted. The character is released promptly (no combat-logout linger) because the destination scene server has to be able to claim it, exactly as for a teleport. Remarks Combat-logout linger exists to stop a player escaping a losing fight by closing the client, so it triggers on a dropped connection — and the server itself drops connections for reasons that have nothing to do with the player quitting. A hand-off to another scene server is implemented as a dropped connection. One that lingered would leave the body — and its session claim — on the source server while the client arrives at the destination, which then cannot claim the character and kicks it, repeatedly, until the linger expires. An administrative kick is the operator removing the player, so there is no escape to deny. Lingering there keeps the kicked player's body in the world and holds their character claim for the length of the linger — which makes a kick the opposite of a remedy for a character that is stuck. The teleport and bind-point-respawn paths avoid this by releasing the character themselves before disconnecting. Callers that instead rely on the ordinary disconnect pipeline must announce the intent here first. The marker is consumed by that disconnect, so it cannot leak onto a later session on a recycled connection id. This is the ordinary end of a linger, not a special teardown: the body is persisted and despawned and the claim released, exactly as when its timer runs out. A command is listed only when TryParseCommand(string, IPlayerCharacter, ChatBroadcast) would run it for this caller: above Banned and at or above the command's registered level. The level is the caller's server-loaded AccessLevel; nothing the client sends reaches this. A player therefore never sees /gm or /admin, and a game master never sees /admin. Sub-commands are not listed here. /gm and /admin are one entry each whose summary points at their own help, which is derived from their tables and is itself behind their access gate. Nothing in this listing could leak a sub-command name. No oracle. /help <command> answers a command the caller may not use with exactly the line it answers a command that does not exist, and echoes nothing typed. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class ChatFloodMute Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll The escalation from refused chat lines to a temporary mute: a sender whose lines the rate gate refuses too often within a short window is muted for a few minutes. public static class ChatFloodMute Inheritance object ChatFloodMute Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks ChatRateGate already bounds what any sender can put through, so a flood costs nobody else anything. It was silent, though: a flooding client kept hammering the gate for as long as it liked and was never told, and the lines it did get through — one a second at the default refill — kept arriving in everybody's chat. Past a threshold the sender is muted and told why, with a system line. Counted from refusals, not from lines. An honest player is refused now and then: two short lines typed inside the minimum gap, or several delivered at once after a network stall — a few, once. The threshold sits well above that: at the defaults, ten refusals within ten seconds takes a client sending twice the sustained rate for ten seconds once its burst is spent, or anything much faster for about a second. The window opens at the first refusal and closes a fixed time later; a refusal after it has closed opens a new one. Reaching the threshold mutes the sender and empties the window, so a sender who goes on flooding while muted reaches it again and the mute is pushed out from then: the mute ends a full term after the flooding stops. Monotonic seconds. A duration measured on the wall clock ends early or late when the host clock is stepped (see FishMMO.Server.Core.MonotonicClock). This is never compared with anything outside the process, so the process clock is the right one. Pure, so the rule can be pinned by a test without a character, a connection or a server. ChatSystem holds one ChatFloodMute.State per character that has been refused. Returns string The line; well inside ChatBroadcast.MaxTextLength. Remarks Says why and for how long, and that commands still work: a player refused with no reason types the line again, and one who is not told they can still file a ticket has no way to ask. The remaining time is rounded up, so the first line of a three-minute mute says three minutes and not two. api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..title: Class ChatRateGate | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Server.Implementation..summary: Class ChatRateGate Namespace FishMMO.Server.Implementation.World.SceneServer Assembly FishMMO.Server.dll The per-sender chat rate rule: a token bucket, then a minimum gap between messages. public static class ChatRateGate Inheritance object ChatRateGate Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A pure function over the sender's four rate fields, so the rule can be pinned by a test without a character, a connection or a server. ChatSystem copies the fields off the character, charges, and copies them back. On the monotonic clock. The ticks are MonotonicClock.NowTicks, not the message's legal receipt stamp: a bucket and a gap are local durations, and on the wall clock a host stepped back refused every sender for the size of the step. A character's fields start at zero, which reads as "never", whatever the clock. Charged when a message is queued, not when it is processed. The incoming queue used to take everything a client sent and charge the bucket only as the queue drained, so the queue's size bounded nothing any one sender did. Its global cap then kicked whichever connection happened to push it over — after a one-second main-thread hitch with a hundred busy players, the next honest player to type (hot-path audit L2). Charged at the door, a sender can occupy the queue only at the rate the bucket allows, so the cap is reached by many honest senders at once or not at all, and nobody is kicked for it. Methods TryCharge(ref State, long, int, double, double) Charges one message against state. public static bool TryCharge(ref ChatRateGate.State state, long nowTicks, int capacity, double refillPerSecond, double minimumGapMilliseconds) Parameters state ChatRateGate.State The sender's rate state; updated in place. nowTicks long Monotonic ticks as the message was received. capacity int Bucket capacity: the burst a sender may send. Zero or less disables the bucket. refillPerSecond double Tokens returned per second. Zero or less disables the bucket. minimumGapMilliseconds double Minimum gap between messages. Zero or less disables it. Returns bool True if the message may be sent. Remarks The token is spent before the gap is tested, as it always was: a message refused by the gap still cost its token. A bucket marked full is filled on the first message whatever the elapsed time; it used to be filled only when some time had passed since the last refill, which in the same tick left a new character's first message refused against an empty bucket it had been told was full.
