Every spatial selector now gates on ResolvesTargetsLocally(EventData) instead, so the caster's own client predicts its selections. This is kept for a future selector whose consumer is genuinely server-authoritative and has nothing to predict — one that resolves loot rights, or picks a persistence target. Reach for it only when you can say why a client must see NOTHING; if the answer is "the effect is authoritative", that is already handled a level down by the action's own IsServer(ICharacter, EventData) gate, and this one would merely also delete the caster's feedback. Server only, and not "not a replicate tick". Every physics selector used to open with if (tickData.IsReplicateTick) yield break;, on the theory that a replicate tick means a client replay. It does not. AbilityObject's self-target dispatch and its OnPreSpawn/OnSpawn dispatches, and AbilityController's activation triggers, all attach a TickEventData built from the replicate PredictionTick — on the server as well. So the guard fired on the server too, and a point-blank area ability selected nothing and dealt no damage on any peer. AbilityApplyAreaAction was corrected for exactly this and gates on the peer instead; this is the same rule, applied at the selector. The tick payload is left on the event untouched. It still carries real information for the tick-domain consumers downstream (buff stamping, cooldowns) — it just never meant what the old guard read it as. QueryBufferSize(int) Query buffer size for a selector whose authored cap is maxHits. protected static int QueryBufferSize(int maxHits) Parameters maxHits int Returns int Remarks Deliberately larger than the cap. Sizing the buffer at exactly MaxHits makes the physics broadphase perform the truncation, in its own order, before the selector ever sees the candidates — so a cap of 5 in a crowd of 20 picked five arbitrary characters and the deterministic sort that follows had nothing to work with. Querying wide and capping after the sort is what makes the cap mean "the first five in a defined order". A starting size, not a limit. It only moves the truncation point from MaxHits up to MaxHits * 4; every caller must still grow the buffer through TryGrowQueryBuffer<T>(ref T[], int) when a query comes back full. The rule itself lives on TargetOrdering now, because the ability actions resolve hits without a selector and need the identical arithmetic — it was duplicated inline in AbilityApplyAreaAction for exactly as long as it lived somewhere only selectors could reach. This forwarder stays so the selectors read naturally. ResolvesSelectionsLocally(EventData) ResolvesTargetsLocally(EventData), reachable from outside the selector hierarchy. public static bool ResolvesSelectionsLocally(EventData eventData) Parameters eventData EventData The event driving the selection. Returns bool True when this peer may resolve a spatial selection for itself. Remarks The fan-out in TriggerExecution has to ask the same question the selectors ask, for the opposite reason: a selector asks it to decide whether to resolve, and the fan-out asks it to tell an EMPTY SELECTION apart from a DECLINED one. Those two had the same shape and very different meanings — "nobody was standing there" must run nothing, while "this peer is not allowed to look" must still let the authored presentation play, or a chain, area, cone or line ability is silent on every screen but the caster's. One implementation, because two copies of this predicate drifting apart is how an observer starts resolving somebody else's hits. Public rather than internal: the answer is a peer fact, not a selector implementation detail, and the fan-out lives in a different namespace. ResolvesTargetsLocally(EventData) True when this peer may resolve a spatial selection for ITSELF — the server, or the client that owns the initiator. protected static bool ResolvesTargetsLocally(EventData eventData) Parameters eventData EventData Returns bool Remarks This is the gate every spatial selector uses, and it is deliberately wider than IsAuthoritativePeer(EventData). Selection used to be server-only, which made the cap trivially agreed — the client computed nothing, so it could not compute something different. The cost was that an area, cone, line or chain ability produced NO client-side prediction at all: the selector yielded an empty set on the caster's own machine, so no action downstream ever ran, and the entire "hit what you see" path (predicted numbers, immediate resource movement, impact FX at the predicted tick) applied only to projectiles, whose hits are resolved by AbilityObject's sweep rather than by a selector. Why widening it is safe: selection is not authority. A selector answers "which bodies are in this volume", never "what may be done to them". Every action re-asks that question for itself one level down — ApplyDamageAction, ApplyHealAction and ApplyBuffAction gate on MayPredict(ICharacter, EventData) and predict feedback, while ApplyThreatAction, ApplyTauntAction, ApplyReviveAction, ApplyDispelAction, the equip actions and the achievement action gate on IsServer(ICharacter, EventData) and stay server-only. So opening the selector grants a client exactly the predictions it was already trusted to make for a projectile hit, and nothing else: no kill, no combat report, no loot rights, no threat. What makes the two peers agree. The same thing that already makes the projectile sweep agree, and it is not reproducible float arithmetic. The server runs its gather inside GatherRewound(EventData, GameObject, List<GameObject>, GatherTargets), rewound to the caster's view; the client runs the identical gather against its live world, which IS that view — this is precisely why LagCompensationTick.TryResolve answers false off-server rather than trying to rewind a second time. Both therefore query the same world, rank it with the same distance-then-identity order, and cap the same list. The residual disagreement is interpolation error at the volume boundary, exactly the bound a swept projectile hit has always carried. And when they do disagree, it self-corrects. A body the client picked and the server did not gets its predicted damage undone by the next authoritative resource push, and its predicted number greys out unconfirmed (PredictedCombatEvents); a predicted buff the server never applies is dropped by the confirmation deadline in BuffController. A body the server picked and the client did not simply arrives as an ordinary combat report. Both are bounded to about a round trip and neither can accumulate. An OBSERVER still answers false, and that part has not moved. It holds every character interpolated against its own latency, has no input stream for the caster, and is going to be told what happened — a third party resolving somebody else's area ability for itself is the failure this whole gate exists to prevent. The DETACHED-object case is why this is not simply MayPredict(ICharacter, EventData). When a caster despawns — including merely leaving an observer's streaming range — its in-flight ability objects are detached and their caster replaced by a SnapshotCharacter phantom, which has no NetworkObject. Both MayPredict and IsServer treat "nothing networked to ask" as permission (the undecidable case that keeps scene-authored triggers and edit-mode tests working), so a phantom's OnTick trigger would pass the peer gate on EVERY client and let a third party resolve selections — and, one level down, run the server-only actions too. Deferring to the ability object closes it: ResolvesHitsLocally reads the caster's NetworkObject and so answers server-only for a phantom, which is exactly the treatment AbilityApplyAreaAction, AbilityApplyHitscanAction and AbilityApplyTargetAction already take. Selections with no ability object in the event (a buff tick, a region trigger) keep the plain MayPredict answer. [Serializable] public class TargetedEntitySelector : TargetSelector Inheritance object TargetSelector TargetedEntitySelector Inherited Members TargetSelector.Conditions TargetSelector.IsAuthoritativePeer(EventData) TargetSelector.ResolvesTargetsLocally(EventData) TargetSelector.ResolvesSelectionsLocally(EventData) TargetSelector.GatherRewound(EventData, GameObject, List<GameObject>, TargetSelector.GatherTargets) TargetSelector.QueryBufferSize(int) TargetSelector.GetContext(EventData) TargetSelector.AreConditionsMet(GameObject, EventData) object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why this exists. Every other selector answers "what is in this volume", so its outcome is a function of where characters are at the moment the query runs. That makes it sensitive to the gap between where a client renders its peers and where the server holds them — measured at 0.45 m on a same-city connection and 2.2 m at 300 ms. A raycast is the worst case, having no width to absorb any of it. This selector asks a different question: "who did the server decide the caster is aiming at". The answer is an entity reference, and the only positional test left is a range check with metres of tolerance. The outcome stops being a function of peer position, so it is correct at 8 ms and at 300 ms alike, with no rewinding and no history buffer. That is exactly how instant ranged attacks have always worked in EverQuest and WoW, and it is why those games never needed lag compensation for them. Server authority. The target is whatever Current holds, and on the server that was written by the server's own raycast from the replicated aim in AbilityController.ResolveTargetAndSpawn. The client supplies a direction; the server decides what is under it. A client cannot name its victim through this path. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TeleportCasterA.summary: Class TeleportCasterAction Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll Blinks the caster up to MaxDistance metres the way it faces, stopping short of whatever is in the way, and plays ArriveFX where it lands. [Serializable] public class TeleportCasterAction : BaseAction, IAction Inheritance object BaseAction TeleportCasterAction Implements IAction Inherited Members BaseAction.TargetSelector BaseAction.StopChainOnFailure BaseAction.IsPresentation BaseAction.IsServer(ICharacter) BaseAction.IsReplayTick(EventData) BaseAction.IsClientPeer(ICharacter, EventData) BaseAction.SendToOwner<T>(ICharacter, T) BaseAction.TryResolveTarget(EventData, out ICharacter) BaseAction.TryResolveTargetOrInitiator(ICharacter, EventData, out ICharacter) BaseAction.GetTooltipContribution() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Wire it to the OnSpawn of a PointBlank ability (an invisible object at the caster's feet). The departure effect is an ordinary PlayFXAction before this one in the same event, played at the object, which stays where the caster stood. Because the object is what observers are sent, every client sees both ends of the blink. One destination on every peer. It is measured from the cast's spawn pose (the caster's feet and facing on the tick it cast, which the server sends observers exactly), or from the caster's own pose on a replayed tick, where the object is not made again and the pose is the same one. A capsule the size of the caster's is swept along the ground a step high, so a blink stops at a wall rather than passing it, and then dropped onto the ground there. The move runs on the server and the owner (TeleportTo(Vector3)) and again on a replayed tick (ReappliesOnReplay): the caster's position is motor state, so a correction for an earlier tick takes the blink back and the replay of the cast's tick must put it back. FindObjectsInactive) Object.ToString() Object.name Object.hideFlags object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Why a component at all. Unity's terrain engine binds four splat textures per pass and knows nothing of arrays, so something has to give every tile the rest through UnityEngine.Terrain.SetSplatMaterialPropertyBlock(UnityEngine.MaterialPropertyBlock). A property block is not serialized, so it is pushed whenever this enables — on scene load, after every domain reload, in edit mode as in play mode (ExecuteAlways) — and again when a tile's alphamaps are replaced (a layer added in the terrain inspector) or the scene's arrays are rebaked. Painting stays live. The alphamaps are still the weights everything edits; each tile's index map is baked from them on the GPU (TerrainIndexMapBaker) when it is bound and, in the editor, again whenever they change (a brush stroke, a repaint, an undo), so a stroke is on screen the same frame. A scene may carry up to MaximumLayers layers and a pixel still reads four index texels. Stored for play. In play (the editor's and a player's) a tile takes the index map the cut stored with the scene (IndexOf(TerrainData)) instead of baking one, while it is still the alphamaps' own — the same texels, so the ground looks the same either way — and a client build may then leave the alphamaps out (ClientTerrainLayerStripper). A tile with no usable stored map is baked from its alphamaps as before. The arrays are found by the scene's name (TerrainArraySet): off disk in the editor, by address in a player. Nothing here holds a reference to them, because they are build output that each machine regenerates. Client only. The object carries ClientOnlyObject, so server builds strip it with everything it references (and it destroys itself on a server that was built some other way), and in a server player this compiles to nothing but its serialized fields — a headless server has no use for a texture. Fields BackdropShaderName The shader of the ground past the scene's edge (SceneBackdrop), which draws with this scene's arrays too: its renderers are bound like the tiles, with their own control maps. public const string BackdropShaderName = "FishMMO/Backdrop Ground" Field Value string EditorBakeIfStale Set by the editor's array baker (an editor assembly this one cannot reference): bakes a scene's arrays if they are missing or stale, synchronously. Null outside the editor. public static Func<Scene, int> EditorBakeIfStale Field Value Func<Scene, int> MaximumControlMaps The most control maps the backdrop's shader reads (SceneBackdropBuilder bakes its own); tiles read index maps. public const int MaximumControlMaps = 8 Field Value int ObjectName The binder object's name in a generated scene. public const string ObjectName = "Terrain Arrays" Field Value string ShaderName The shader every tile drawn by this binder uses. public const string ShaderName = "FishMMO/Weather Terrain Array" Field Value string Properties BoundSet The set currently bound, or null. public TerrainArraySet BoundSet { get; } Property Value TerrainArraySet Provenance The provenance on the EditorOnly child, or null. public TerrainArrayProvenance Provenance { get; } Property Value TerrainArrayProvenance SceneKey The scene name the arrays are baked under. public string SceneKey { get; } Property Value string Terrains The tiles as assigned. See EffectiveTerrains() for the ones bound. public List<Terrain> Terrains { get; } Property Value List<Terrain> TilePushes Counts every push to a tile and every unbind: what a tile's block holds may have changed when it moves. The client's own heightmap draw (TerrainHeightmapSystem) copies the tiles' bindings into arrays and takes them again when it changes. public static int TilePushes { get; } Property Value int Methods BackdropRenderers() The renderers of this scene's backdrop that draw with BackdropShaderName. public List<Renderer> BackdropRenderers() Returns List<Renderer> Remarks A backdrop baked before it had control maps still uses URP/Lit and is left alone. Looked up on every push rather than kept, because a rebake swaps the material's shader under the same renderers. While the scene is still loading (OnEnable runs then) its roots cannot be listed, so the backdrops are found among the loaded objects instead; they are all deserialized before any OnEnable. Bind() Finds this scene's arrays and pushes everything to every tile, now. public void Bind() Remarks Synchronous in the editor (the set is read straight off disk), so a caller about to render — the world map's overhead capture — sees the arrays on that very render. In a player the set arrives by address a frame or two later; the tiles draw plain grey ground until it does. Bind(TerrainArraySet) Supplies an already loaded scene bake (for local rendering tools that do not run client boot). public void Bind(TerrainArraySet loadedSet) Parameters loadedSet TerrainArraySet BindAll(Scene, bool) Binds every binder in a scene, now, and returns how many it bound. In the editor it first bakes the scene's arrays if they are missing or stale (bakeIfStale). public static int BindAll(Scene scene, bool bakeIfStale = true) Parameters scene Scene bakeIfStale bool Returns int Remarks For anything that renders a scene it has just opened without waiting a frame — the world map's overhead capture. OnEnable has already pushed by then, but only what was on disk at that moment: a scene whose arrays were never baked on this machine would be photographed grey. Everything here is synchronous in the editor, so the very next Camera.Render sees the arrays. BindAllLoaded() public static void BindAllLoaded() EffectiveTerrains() The tiles bound: the assigned list, or every terrain in this scene when it is empty, so a tile added by hand to a scene whose list was never filled is still drawn. public List<Terrain> EffectiveTerrains() Returns List<Terrain> IndexMapOf(Terrain) The index map bound to a terrain by any enabled binder (baked here, or the scene's stored one), or null: for whatever else reads the ground's layers (the contact blend copies it into its own array). public static Texture IndexMapOf(Terrain terrain) Parameters terrain Terrain Returns Texture Push() Pushes the current set (or none) to every tile without looking for it again. public void Push() RepushScene(Scene) Re-binds every enabled binder in every loaded scene; the baker calls it after writing sets. public static void RepushScene(Scene scene) Parameters scene Scene SetFor(Terrain) The set bound to a terrain tile by whichever binder drew it last, or null: what names its layers. public static TerrainArraySet SetFor(Terrain terrain) Parameters terrain Terrain Returns TerrainArraySet

api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TerrainArrayLay.summary: Struct TerrainArrayLayerParams Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll The numbers one terrain layer contributes to the array terrain shader, besides its textures. public struct TerrainArrayLayerParams Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks A plain value rather than a UnityEngine.TerrainLayer because the layer whose numbers the ground draws with is not always one a scene may reference: when LOCAL art overrides a layer, its tiling and remaps come from an asset under Assets/LOCAL. These values are therefore copied into the baked TerrainArraySet (build output) and never into the scene. The packing mirrors what Unity's terrain engine hands URP's TerrainLit, so a layer looks the same in both shaders: the diffuse remap's maximum is a tint (URP ignores the minimum), the mask remap becomes an offset (the minimum) and a scale (maximum minus minimum), and a layer whose albedo carries smoothness in its alpha uses a smoothness multiplier of one. The two flags describe the textures the arrays end up holding, which may not be the layer's own. public static TerrainArrayLayerParams From(TerrainLayer layer, bool hasMask, bool albedoHasAlpha) Parameters layer TerrainLayer hasMask bool albedoHasAlpha bool Returns TerrainArrayLayerParams Pack(int, Vector4[], Vector4[], Vector4[], Vector4[], Vector4[]) Writes this layer into slot index of the five shader arrays. public void Pack(int index, Vector4[] st, Vector4[] tint, Vector4[] maskOffset, Vector4[] maskScale, Vector4[] surface) Parameters index int st Vector4[] tint Vector4[] maskOffset Vector4[] maskScale Vector4[] surface Vector4[] Remarks st: 1/tile size, offset/tile size — applied to WORLD x/z, so a texture runs straight across tile seams. tint: diffuse remap max rgb, normal scale in w. maskOffset, maskScale: the mask remap as sample * scale + offset. surface: metallic, smoothness multiplier, has-mask flag, 0. TerrainArrayBaker writes one of these per world scene into BakedDirectory, which is gitignored, from art that may live under Assets/LOCAL and must never be referenced by anything committed. Every machine bakes its own: opening a scene whose set is missing or stale rebakes it, and a client build bakes every world scene before it builds. Found by convention, never by reference. No scene points at a set: a committed scene holding the GUID of a file each machine regenerates would dangle on every other clone. The binder finds its scene's set by the scene's name — straight off disk in the editor, by AddressOf(string) in a player (the build puts the sets in a client-only addressable group). and noise seed, not its index: the scatter seeds every prototype from its rule (a distinct seed per rule and prefab), both survive any copy of the prototype, and a prototype added afterwards (a point of interest's wheat, a hand-painted one) simply has no entry. By name rather than by reference so the record pulls no prefab into a build the terrain's own prototypes do not (the server strips those). A biome is its cached-object id (Biomes.BiomeRegistry.IDOf), as the scene's biome map stores it, never a reference: a scene reference to a template would pull its art into the scene's bundle. A point of interest's prototypes (a herb grove's herbs and flowers, a cave mouth's growth, a field's wheat: prototypes a site adds to a tile after the scatter) are recorded too since 2026-10-16, for the biome the site stands in, marked Site: they take that biome's look of the prefab (or the old look where it has none), and keep their material's tints, as they had before, since no rule of the biome chose them. A site paints its own biome's prototype (2026-10-16, I4b): it reuses a tile's prototype of the plant only when that prototype is its own biome's (a rule's or an earlier site's, SiteLayer(string, int, IReadOnlyList<string>, IReadOnlyList<int>, IReadOnlyList<Entry>, out int)); where the tile's prototype of the plant is another biome's, the site adds one of its own (a copy of that one, with a noise seed of its own, SiteSeed(int, int, string, IReadOnlyList<string>, IReadOnlyList<int>, IReadOnlyList<Entry>)), so the plant takes the look of the biome the site stands in rather than whichever biome's prototype came first. Its cover goes on as before, measured against the plant's prototype it used to paint into (SiteCover(int, int, bool, int)), so a plant is no thicker for being split between two prototypes. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TerrainIndexMap.summary: Class TerrainIndexMap Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll The terrain's index map: for every texel of a tile's alphamaps, its four strongest layers and their weights, packed into eight bytes. What the array terrain shader reads in place of the alphamaps themselves, so a scene may carry up to MaximumLayers layers at the cost of four texel reads a pixel, however many it has. public static class TerrainIndexMap Inheritance object TerrainIndexMap Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why. The shader used to read every control map of a tile (four layers each) per pixel and keep the four strongest: 32 layers were eight maps and eight samples a pixel, and every layer more another map (2026-10-16: "every biome has unique textures for everything" needs far more than 32 layers a scene). The four strongest are found once per texel instead, here, and the pixel blends the four texels around it. A texel is two 32-bit words (R32G32_UInt): x the four layer ids, a byte each, strongest first; y their weights in bytes, each LESS the texel's fifth-strongest weight. That is the shader's seam-free rule (FishTopLayers) applied at the texel: a layer that drops out of the four does so at zero, so neither the bake nor the blend jumps where a fifth layer overtakes the fourth. Ground with four layers or fewer at a texel is stored exactly as painted. Ties go to the lower layer index, as the old per-pixel loop met them (it took the layers in index order and only a strictly greater weight moved one). Slots a texel has no layer for hold zero-weight layers, the lowest indices first, so the four ids of a texel are always distinct — the filter merges the four texels' entries by id. The filter (Filter(uint[], int, int, float, float, int[], float[]), FishTerrainIndexMap.hlsl): ids cannot be filtered by the hardware, so the four texels a bilinear sample would read are loaded, each texel's weights scaled by its bilinear share, entries of the same layer summed, and the four strongest kept less the fifth, normalised — the old rule on the merged weights. Where every texel of the four has four layers or fewer, the merged weights ARE the bilinear weights of every layer, so the result is the old shader's exactly. Where a texel had a fifth layer, the blend there is the old one at that texel's centre and stays continuous between centres; it differs from the old per-pixel choice by at most the texels' own fifth weights. Baked on the GPU from the live alphamaps (TerrainIndexMapBaker, FishTerrainIndexBake.shader) while the ground is edited, so a brush stroke is on screen the same frame. This class is the same bake on the CPU — the reference the GPU bake is checked against, the bake the cut STORES with the scene's terrain (TerrainDetailBake.IndexMap, what a player binds, so client builds need not ship the alphamaps), and the tests' — and the shader's filter, line for line. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TerrainIndexMap.summary: Class TerrainIndexMapBaker Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll Bakes a terrain tile's index map (TerrainIndexMap) on the GPU, from the tile's own alphamaps, into an R32G32_UInt render texture the array terrain shader loads. public static class TerrainIndexMapBaker Inheritance object TerrainIndexMapBaker Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks From the GPU's alphamaps, because a terrain paint stroke writes them there first and synchronises the CPU copy only when the stroke ends: baking from them keeps painting live (the binder rebakes a tile on every alphamap change), as reading the alphamaps per pixel did. Each map is copied into one slice of a scratch array, and one full-screen triangle (FishTerrainIndexBake.shader) writes every texel's four strongest layers. A 512² tile of eight maps is eight copies and one small draw; nothing is read back. Baked live while the ground is edited, stored for play (2026-10-16: "store index maps with the terrain at cut/repaint, still re-baked live while painting in the editor"). In edit mode every tile is baked here from its alphamaps, on every change. The cut also stores each tile's map, baked on the CPU by the same rule (Bake(float[,,])), in the scene's TerrainDetailBake; in play (the editor's and a player's) the binder uploads that (Upload(IndexMap, string, Shader)) when it is still the alphamaps' own, and bakes here only when it is not. A client build then leaves the alphamaps out of every tile whose stored map it has checked against them (ClientTerrainLayerStripper), and the CPU readers that used them (GroundColourMap, the grass's surface layers) read the stored map on such a tile. Integer arithmetic on bytes, so the GPU bake is BakeTexel(byte[], int, int, out uint, out uint) exactly; the editor checks a sample of texels against it once per tile and session (Check(Terrain, RenderTexture, int, int)). api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TerrainLayerTab.summary: Class TerrainLayerTable Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll A scene's per-layer numbers as one small float texture the array terrain shader loads by layer: column = layer, row = which number. Replaces the per-layer uniform arrays (_FishLayerST[32] and the rest). public static class TerrainLayerTable Inheritance object TerrainLayerTable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why a texture. At 256 layers the six arrays and the three path tables would be 27 KB of constants, pushed per terrain tile through its property block — more than the 16 KB uniform block OpenGL ES and WebGL guarantee, and exactly the pattern that broke the grass on OpenGL (large constant arrays varied per draw: unity-gl-indirect-args-barrier-bug). A structured buffer is not readable in a WebGL 2 fragment shader. A texture is one binding everywhere, read with Load (no sampler, exact floats). Rows, Width columns each (Pack(int, Vector4[], Vector4[], Vector4[], Vector4[], Vector4[]) for the first five): RowST: 1 / tile size and offset / tile size, applied to world x/z. RowTint: the diffuse remap maximum (a tint), normal scale in w. RowMaskOffset, RowMaskScale: the mask remap as sample × scale + offset. RowSurface: metallic, smoothness multiplier, has-mask flag. RowFlora: what the layer is made of for the planet's looks (LayerFlora()). RowPaths: the slices of the layer's own biome's path ground, road ground and cobbles (−1 none). RowBackdrop: not a layer's but a backdrop channel's: the scene layer channel c of the backdrop's control maps holds (ControlLayers), c itself when the backdrop names none. RowGlow: the layer's glow (2026-10-25, phase I2r; Biomes.BiomeGroundGlow.Pack), zero for none. RowClock: how the layer follows the shared clock (2026-10-26, phase GROUND-BANDS; Biomes.BiomeGroundClock.Pack): x kind, y from, z to, w falloff; zero for none. RowClockShare: x the share a clocked layer keeps outside its window, y the layer that takes the rest (−1 none), w 1 in every column when any layer of the scene follows a clock (the shader's one test before it reads more). Columns past the scene's layers hold a neutral layer, no flora and no paths, as the arrays' unused slots did. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TerrainSnowHole.summary: Class TerrainSnowHoleFade Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll How much of its deep-snow lift each heightmap vertex of a terrain tile keeps near a hole in the terrain: none at a hole's edge, all of it FadeMetres away, eased between. One byte a vertex in an R8 map the array terrain shader loads at the vertex (FishTerrainSnowHoles.hlsl), handed to each tile by TerrainArrayBinder. public static class TerrainSnowHoleFade Inheritance object TerrainSnowHoleFade Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why. A hole is cut where rock is the ground (a cave's mouth, a canyon wall), and that rock meets the hole's edge flush. The terrain's vertices rise under deep snow and the rock does not, so lifted to the snow's full depth the terrain's edge stood that far over the rock with nothing under it. The rock stays where it is; the snow comes down onto it over the last metres. Why a map. Scanning the holes from the vertex (2026-10-19) reached three cells and was read only at the vertices drawn: a far patch's vertices stand several cells apart, so its fade collapsed into a flat square plate that moved with the level of detail. Here every vertex's own value is the exact distance to the nearest hole quad, its own tile's or a neighbour's, so a vertex shared by two patches or two tiles is lifted alike whichever draws it. Every tile of a cut used to carry the scene's whole palette: Moron 2's 210 layers are 53 control maps of 512² RGBA with mips, 74 MB a tile, when no tile paints more than 62 of them (measured over the saved tiles, 2026-10-27). A tile now keeps exactly the layers it paints: those with a non-zero weight byte anywhere on it. No weight changes, so every texel — the ones on a seam too — holds the bytes it held, and two tiles meeting at a seam agree there as before, whatever either keeps. Dropping light layers by a threshold as well was measured and refused: 1–5% fewer maps for a visible change. The scene's numbering stays the truth. The texture arrays, the layer table, the index maps, the backdrop's channels and the path slices all count the scene's layers (the binder's provenance, one entry per array slice). A tile's channel c is scene layer SceneLayers[c], its channels kept in scene order, so ties between equal weights still go to the lower scene layer as they did. Null means a tile that carries the whole palette in scene order (every scene cut before this): channel and scene layer are the same number. Remarks The preferred form for any dispatch reached from a replicate. IsReplay is then a fact about the execution rather than a claim the caller had to remember to make, which is the whole difference between a guard that protects something and one that reads as though it does. See IsReplay. TickEventData(ICharacter, PredictionTick, bool) Creates tick event data from a replicate input tick. public TickEventData(ICharacter character, PredictionTick tick, bool isReplay = false) Parameters character ICharacter The event initiator. tick PredictionTick The replicate-domain tick. isReplay bool True when this execution is a reconcile replay of the tick. Properties IsReplay True when this execution is a reconcile REPLAY of a tick that already ran once. public bool IsReplay { get; } Property Value bool Remarks Deliberately separate from IsReplicateTick, which says which CLOCK the tick is counted on and nothing about how many times it has been executed. Conflating the two was a real defect: every ability spawn and every self-target dispatch carries a replicate-domain tick, on the server as much as on the owner, and each of them is skipped outright on a replayed tick — so a guard that read the domain flag as "this is a replay" answered true for exactly the dispatches that are never replays. The visible cost was that PlayFXAction refused every self-buff and self-heal impact effect on every peer, permanently; the quieter one was that the owner drew no predicted number for a self-heal. Set it only where a dispatch genuinely re-runs during a reconcile. Every current dispatch site gates replays before it builds this payload — ResolveTargetAndSpawn returns before it spawns, BuffController tests its own isReplayingTick, the activation triggers test state.ContainsReplayed(), and the hit, tick and destroy dispatches run off TimeManager.OnTick, which is not replayed — so nothing sets it today. That is the right place for the gate, not a gap to be plugged here: skipping the whole dispatch also skips the RNG draws and the selector fan-out inside it, which a flag read by four actions cannot. How a site that CANNOT gate says so. By handing over the FishNet.Object.Prediction.ReplicateState it is running under, not a hand-written bool. The bool overload exists for the sites that have no replicate state to offer and can therefore prove they are not replays; a prediction dispatch that has one has no excuse to answer the question from memory, and the state overload is what makes the answer follow the dispatch instead of being remembered. BaseAction.IsReplayTick is the consumer. IsReplicateTick True when Tick was sourced from a replicate input tick and may be used directly with prediction-domain state such as buff expiry or cooldown start ticks. False when the tick is a raw authoritative wall-clock tick such as TimeManager.LocalTick. public bool IsReplicateTick { get; } Property Value bool ReapplyOnly True for an event dispatched a second time on a REPLAYED tick only so that what the correction took back is put back (a self-cast heal, buff or cost): only actions that answer ReappliesOnReplay run. public bool ReapplyOnly { get; set; } Property Value bool Tick The tick carried by this event. public PredictionTick Tick { get; } Property Value PredictionTick Methods IsForCharacter(ICharacter) Returns true when this tick was sourced from the same character whose prediction-domain state is about to consume it. public bool IsForCharacter(ICharacter character) Parameters character ICharacter The character whose prediction-domain state will consume the tick. Returns bool True when the tick belongs to character.

api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.ToastBroadcast..summary: Struct ToastBroadcast Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll A short, transient message shown to one player. public struct ToastBroadcast : IBroadcast Implements IBroadcast Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Deliberately general rather than bindstone-shaped: any server system that refuses an action for a reason the player could otherwise not see can send one, and several already have that problem. BindstoneAction computed a precise rejection — wrong scene, inside an instance, not enough clearance — and wrote every one of them to a server-side debug log, so binding either worked or did nothing and the player could not tell which. Text is sent rather than a message id. A message id would be the right answer for a localised client, and this should become one when localisation exists; sending text now keeps the failure mode "the wrong words appear" rather than "a system cannot report at all". The client truncates, so a caller cannot use this as an unbounded channel. Fields Severity How prominently it reads. public ToastSeverity Severity Field Value ToastSeverity Text What to show. Truncated by the client at UITKToast.MaximumLength. public string Text Field Value string

api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TooltipContent..summary: Class TooltipContent Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll A tooltip as structured data: an icon, a title, and typed rows. public sealed class TooltipContent Inheritance object TooltipContent Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Tooltips used to exist only as one rich-text string, assembled by every template type in its own BuildTooltip and handed to a single Label. That made the content impossible to work with anywhere else: the crafting panel could not lay stats out in columns, could not show what an added effect changed, and could not mark a requirement the character fails, because by the time it had the tooltip everything was already <color> tags in a sentence. Two systems produced tooltips this way — items and abilities — and neither could reuse a line of the other's. The rows carry meaning instead, and every producer in the game builds one of these. ToRichText() flattens them for anything that genuinely needs a string, and the client renders them as real elements. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TooltipStyle.ht.summary: Enum TooltipStyle Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll Character styling a row asks for, on top of its tone. [Flags] public enum TooltipStyle : byte Fields Bold = 1 Bold. Italic = 2 Italic. Large = 16 Larger than the surrounding text. None = 0 No extra styling. Small = 32 Smaller than the surrounding text. Strikethrough = 8 Struck through — used for a value something else has replaced. Underline = 4 Underlined. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TooltipTone.htm.title: Enum TooltipTone | FishMMO Documentation
api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TooltipTone.htm.summary: Enum TooltipTone Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll How a row should read: neutral fact, an improvement, a penalty, or background detail. public enum TooltipTone : byte Fields Accent = 5 Worth noticing, without being good or bad. Bad = 2 Worse for the player. Good = 1 Better for the player. Muted = 3 Secondary detail. Neutral = 0 An ordinary fact. Unmet = 4 Something the player cannot currently satisfy. Remarks Deliberately not a colour. The renderer owns the palette — the same content is drawn into a hover tooltip, an inline details pane and a crafting preview, and those do not agree on what "good" looks like. A tone survives that; a hex string baked into a sentence does not, which is exactly what the string-concatenating tooltip system this replaces produced.

api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.TwoFactorSetupB.summary: Struct TwoFactorSetupBroadcast Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll Broadcast sent by the server after account creation containing encrypted TOTP setup data (otpauth URI and recovery codes) for two-factor authentication. WARNING: The nonce-derivation scheme on both client and server depends on C# struct field declaration order matching FishNet serialization order. The server sends OtpauthUri first, then RecoveryCodes, and the client consumes them in that exact sequence via receiveNonceCtx.NextNonce(). If these fields are reordered, the nonce streams desynchronize and TOTP silently breaks. DO NOT reorder OtpauthUri and RecoveryCodes. public struct TwoFactorSetupBroadcast : IBroadcast Implements IBroadcast Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Fields OtpauthUri Encrypted otpauth:// URI for authenticator app setup (AES-GCM, server->client). WARNING: FIELD ORDER IS WIRE PROTOCOL -- DO NOT REORDER. The nonce-derivation scheme depends on field declaration order matching FishNet serialization order. See struct remarks. WARNING: Declaration order IS the wire protocol (see struct remarks). This field MUST remain declared before RecoveryCodes. public byte[] OtpauthUri Field Value byte[] RecoveryCodes Encrypted newline-delimited plaintext recovery codes (AES-GCM, server->client). WARNING: Declaration order IS the wire protocol (see struct remarks). This field MUST remain declared after OtpauthUri. public byte[] RecoveryCodes Field Value byte[] Seq Explicit message sequence number (server->client). NOTE: Seq is declared LAST. The nonce derivation calls NextNonce() for byte-array fields first, then uses Seq for replay tracking. Reordering fields will desynchronize the nonce stream. The client does NOT use Seq-1 / Seq derivation for these two fields. Instead, it calls receiveNonceCtx.NextNonce() twice sequentially — first for the OtpauthUri, then for the RecoveryCodes. Consequently, the server MUST send the URI before the recovery codes (i.e. the order of the fields in the struct defines the nonce order on the wire). The Seq value itself is only used for replay-window tracking, not for computing per-field nonces. public uint Seq Field Value uint

GetNearestPositionOnSphere(Vector3, Vector3, float) Gets the nearest position on the surface of a sphere centered at pointB, from pointA. public static Vector3 GetNearestPositionOnSphere(Vector3 pointA, Vector3 pointB, float radius) Parameters pointA Vector3 The point to project from. pointB Vector3 The center of the sphere. radius float The radius of the sphere. Returns Vector3 The nearest position on the sphere surface. GetRandomConicalDirection(Vector3, float, DeterministicRNG) A rotation looking along a direction drawn uniformly from inside a cone opening along forward. public static Quaternion GetRandomConicalDirection(this Vector3 forward, float coneAngleDegrees, DeterministicRNG random) Parameters forward Vector3 Axis the cone opens along. A degenerate vector yields the identity rotation. coneAngleDegrees float TOTAL spread of the cone. Zero or less means no deviation; 360 or more is the whole sphere. random DeterministicRNG Deterministic generator. Required — a shared or per-process stream would desynchronise peers. Returns Quaternion A rotation whose forward axis is the sampled direction. Remarks This used to read Quaternion.Euler(startPosition - ((distance * forward) + (RandomOnUnitSphere(random) * coneRadius))), which fed a WORLD POSITION into Euler(float, float, float) as if it were Euler angles in degrees. The result was a function of the object's absolute map coordinates rather than of its heading, the arc was applied as a sphere radius, and the same ability produced unrelated rotations at different places in the world. The start position and distance are gone because a direction does not depend on either. Sampling is uniform over the spherical cap, not over the polar angle: drawing cos(theta) flat keeps the density even across the cap, where drawing theta flat would bunch results towards the axis. Every draw comes from random so two peers running the same ability with the same generator state produce the same direction. Returns Vector3 A random Vector3 inside the flat toroid (z = 0). Returns Vector3 A random Vector3 inside the toroid. Returns Vector3 A random Vector3 inside the bounding box. Place one in a world scene and give it a WaypointIndex that no other waypoint in that scene uses — the index is the bit the character's unlock record stores, so it must never change once the scene ships; a renumbered waypoint is a waypoint every existing character loses. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.WaypointRegistr.summary: Class WaypointRegistry Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll Server-side index of the live waypoints in every loaded scene, by Unity scene handle and authored waypoint index. public static class WaypointRegistry Inheritance object WaypointRegistry Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A fast-travel request names a waypoint by (scene, index), not by scene-object ID: the waypoint may be on the far side of the zone, outside the requesting client's observer range, so the client has no object ID to send. The server resolves the pair here against the objects actually loaded, which also means the destination position comes from the live transform rather than from a cache that could be stale. Keyed by scene handle rather than name because scene stacking loads several copies of one scene (instances) into one process, and a character in one instance must land at the waypoint in that instance. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.WaypointTravelP.summary: Struct WaypointTravelPolicy Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll The game-wide rule for where a player may fast travel from: when RequireNearbyWaypoint is on, only from within NearbyRange of a waypoint they have discovered in the same scene instance (issue #253). Off, the map's travel button works from anywhere. public readonly struct WaypointTravelPolicy Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Where it is set. The server's InteractableSystem asset owns the values and installs them in Server when it initialises; the travel request reads them from there. The owner client is told the server's values in the WaypointController spawn payload, so the map can grey out its button and say why rather than send a request that will be refused. The client's copy is a hint only — the server re-checks every request. What counts as the origin. Any live waypoint in the traveller's scene instance, including the destination itself, measured from the waypoint's own transform (the position the map cache bakes). It must be one the traveller has discovered whenever the request also requires the destination to be discovered: a player standing at a stone they never activated has not "used" it. Interacting with a waypoint discovers it, so in play this costs nothing. Who it binds. The player's own map request. Designer-authored moves (TeleportToWaypointAction — a town-portal item, a quest return) are exempt: being usable away from a waypoint is their point. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.WaypointUnlockM.summary: Class WaypointUnlockMask Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll The waypoints a character has discovered in one scene, as a growable bit set: bit N of page N / 64 is set when waypoint N is unlocked. public sealed class WaypointUnlockMask Inheritance object WaypointUnlockMask Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why a bit set. A scene has tens of waypoints, every character eventually unlocks most of them, and the whole set is read and written together: on login, in the spawn payload, and on save. One row per (character, waypoint) would be a forty-byte row for a single bit; the set stores those bits as bits. The same shape is on the wire and in the database (character_waypoints, one row per non-empty page), so nothing translates between representations — see CharacterDialogueChoiceData for the precedent. Why pages. A single 64-bit word would cap a scene at 64 waypoints, and the day that cap is hit is the day a designer's sixty-fifth waypoint silently fails to persist. Pages make the set unbounded (to MaxIndex, a sanity cap on authoring rather than on storage) at the cost of one extra small integer per row. Persistence without a version. Bits are only ever set, and the database merge is an OR. So "what still needs writing" is exactly unlocked & ~persisted, and confirming a write is persisted |= written; a bit set while a write was in flight is not in written and stays dirty. No counter to bump and no stale-confirmation hazard — the trap the versioned tables fell into (see the attribute/ability persistence notes). Fields BitsPerPage Bits per page. A page is one ulong and one database row. public const int BitsPerPage = 64 Field Value int MaxIndex Highest waypoint index a scene may author. Sixteen pages. A bound on authoring mistakes and on what a payload may ask the controller to allocate, not a design limit anyone is expected to reach. public const int MaxIndex = 1023 Field Value int MaxPages Most pages a scene can have, derived from MaxIndex. public const int MaxPages = 16 Field Value int Properties IsDirty Whether any page is dirty. public bool IsDirty { get; } Property Value bool IsEmpty Whether no waypoint is unlocked. public bool IsEmpty { get; } Property Value bool PageCount Number of pages allocated. Trailing pages may be empty. public int PageCount { get; } Property Value int Methods Add(int) Unlocks a waypoint. public bool Add(int waypointIndex) Parameters waypointIndex int Returns bool True when the bit was newly set; false when it was already set or the index is invalid. Contains(int) Whether a waypoint is unlocked. public bool Contains(int waypointIndex) Parameters waypointIndex int Returns bool GetPage(int) The unlocked bits of a page. Zero for a page beyond the allocated range. public ulong GetPage(int page) Parameters page int Returns ulong IsPageDirty(int) Whether any bit of a page has not been confirmed by the database. public bool IsPageDirty(int page) Parameters page int Returns bool IsValidIndex(int) Whether an index is within [0, MaxIndex]. public static bool IsValidIndex(int waypointIndex) Parameters waypointIndex int Returns bool MarkPersisted(int, ulong) Records that the database holds these bits of a page. public void MarkPersisted(int page, ulong writtenMask) Parameters page int writtenMask ulong PageOf(int) Which page an index lives on. public static int PageOf(int waypointIndex) Parameters waypointIndex int Returns int Restore(int, ulong) Installs persisted bits: unlocked and already confirmed, so they are not dirty. public void Restore(int page, ulong mask) Parameters page int mask ulong Remarks OR-ed in, never assigned. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.Weather.Surface.summary: Class SurfaceWater Namespace FishMMO.Shared.Weather Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll The open water in the loaded scene — a sea, its lakes and rivers: where anything falling out of the sky stops, whether a point is under a surface, and how high the water stands at a place. public static class SurfaceWater Inheritance object SurfaceWater Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A sea has nothing to hit. The weather finds the highest surface around the camera by casting rays down, and a ray goes straight through water to the sea bed. So rain and snow fell through the sea and landed on the sand under it, splashes burst on the bottom, and the lens kept its raindrops with the camera three metres down. Wherever the ground is lower than the water, the water is the highest surface. Published by the water, read by the weather. The water depends on the game and never the other way round, so the weather cannot ask it — each body of water registers itself here, the way the server registers its weather host into WeatherTimelines.Commands. One sea, any number of inland waters. The sea stands at one level everywhere its ground is lower (TryGetLevel(out float)). A lake or a river stands only where it is (SurfaceWater.IAreaSource), so the question that covers both is the water at a place: TryGetSurfaceAt(float, float, out float). api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.Weather.Weather.summary: Enum WeatherExposureInput Namespace FishMMO.Shared.Weather Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll What one term of an exposure state reads: a channel of the blended weather, or one of the driver's physical air properties. public enum WeatherExposureInput : byte Fields AirHumidity = 2 0 dry air … 1 saturated. Present without any rain: this is what muggy is. AirInstability = 3 0 … 1: how willing this air is to build a storm, before it has built one. AirLowPressure = 1 0 a settled high … 1 the middle of a deep low. AirPolarNight = 6 0 … 1: how far the sun has stopped rising here. A polar winter, by itself. AirTower = 4 0 … 1: how strongly a storm tower stands over this spot. AirWindSpeed = 5 0 calm … 1 at 30 m/s. The driver's real wind, not the channel's blended one. Channel = 0 A channel of the blended weather. The default, and what most states want. Remarks The channels are the weather as it looks — how much is falling, how hard the wind blows, how thick the fog is. The air properties are the physics underneath it: the pressure field, how much water the air can hold, how willing it is to build a storm. They are not the same thing, and some states are only expressible in the second. "Soaked" is rain, a channel. "Clammy" is saturated air, which is present with no rain at all. "Ears popping" is a deep low, which is invisible in every channel there is. All of them are normalised to 0..1 so Onset and Full mean the same thing whichever is chosen — including AirLowPressure, which is the driver's signed pressure read as depth-of-low so that, like every other input here, more of it drives harder.

A recipe's ingredients are always WeatherExposureTemplate levels, so the whole set can be evaluated in one pass with no ordering to get right and no way to write a cycle. Two recipes can name the same ingredient, and both hold. Nothing of it rides the wire. A recipe is a pure function of the levels, and the levels already reconcile — so both peers reach the same verdict from the same numbers, and the reconcile payload does not grow by a byte for any number of recipes. What is NOT derivable is which side of the hysteresis band a recipe was on, and that is re-derived after a reconcile exactly the way a single state's hold is: see WeatherExposureController. Static content only. Like every template, this holds no runtime state; which recipes a given character currently satisfies lives on that character's controller. object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks It reads the weather, not the layer that caused it. A template names inputs and a temperature response, and is evaluated against the blended WeatherReading where the character is standing. So a state does not care whether the rain came from the biome's background, a storm cell overhead or a GM's preset — only that rain is falling on this spot. And it can read the physics, not only the look of it. A term reads either a channel of the blended weather or one of the driver's air properties — the pressure field, the humidity, the instability, the real wind (see WeatherExposureInput). The second kind is what lets a state exist that has no visible weather at all: saturated air with nothing falling out of it, or a deep low that can only be felt. The temperature it reads is the physical one. Temperature carries the biome's climate, the body's distance from its suns, its atmosphere's greenhouse, the latitude and the season — so Chilled comes on by itself on a world far from its star, at a high latitude, in its winter, without anybody authoring a cold region. Shelter protects. The drive is scaled by how exposed the character is, so standing under a roof stops the rain wetting them, while ShelterProtection at 0 marks a state a roof is no defence against — cold air is still cold indoors. Everything a term can read — the blended channels, the driver's air, the physical temperature, how sheltered the spot is — comes from one sample, taken at one place and one tick. Hand the pieces in separately and it becomes possible to pass a frame from here with an air from somewhere else, and the state would be driven by weather that never existed. Pure: the same sample gives the same answer on the server and on the owner, which is what lets the level be predicted at all. api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.Weather.Weather.summary: Class WeatherExposureTick Namespace FishMMO.Shared.Weather Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll Converts a prediction replicate's tick into the tick the weather timeline is evaluated at. public static class WeatherExposureTick Inheritance object WeatherExposureTick Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Two clocks, and they are not the same one. The weather timeline is anchored in the SYNCHRONISED tick (TimeManager.Tick): WeatherTimeline.WorldSecondsAt measures from WorldSecondsTick, which the scene server stamps from its own TimeManager.Tick and broadcasts. A replicate's input.GetTick(), however, is the OWNING CLIENT's unsynchronised LocalTick — a counter that restarts at zero on every connect — so on the server the two differ by an arbitrary per-connection constant. Feeding an input tick straight to the weather would read the forecast for some other hour entirely, and would read a DIFFERENT wrong hour on the client than on the server, so the reconcile would fight the prediction for ever. The mapping. FishNet hands us the pairing it reconciled on: ClientStateTick is the local tick of the last reconcile and ServerStateTick is the server tick of that same reconcile. The difference between them is the constant, so FishNet 4.7 publishes that pairing only WHILE it reconciles — PredictionManager resets both to UNSET_TICK after every reconcile, where 4.6 left them standing until the next. Read raw, live prediction would then fall back to the client's synchronised estimate while replay used the pairing, and the two would disagree by however far the estimate is off. So WeatherExposureTick.ReconcilePairing remembers the pairing of the last reconcile per PredictionManager (from OnPreReconcile), and live prediction and replay read the same numbers again. It is forgotten when the client connection stops, because LocalTick restarts. weatherTick = ServerStateTick + (inputTick − ClientStateTick) and this one line is correct both live and in replay. In replay it is provably so: FishNet walks ClientReplayTick and ServerReplayTick forward together from ClientStateTick + 1 and ServerStateTick + 1 (PredictionManager, the while (ClientReplayTick < localTick) loop), so for the replicate being replayed at client tick t the server's tick is exactly what the formula returns. That identity is what Resolve(bool, uint, uint, uint, uint, uint) asserts against when a replay tick is supplied, and what the closed-loop tests pin. On the server the input tick is not used at all. The server IS the authority on when "now" is; its own TimeManager.Tick is the weather's tick, and the client's counter is only a label for matching inputs to reconciles. Pure arithmetic on purpose: everything here takes plain numbers, so the whole mapping can be tested without a NetworkManager, a connection or a running scene. Fields Unset FishNet's "no tick" sentinel, repeated so callers need not reference TimeManager. public const uint Unset = 0 Field Value uint Methods FromReplayCounters(uint) What Resolve(bool, uint, uint, uint, uint, uint) must return while FishNet is replaying, from FishNet's own replay counters. Equal to the formula by construction — see the remarks on this class — so it exists to be asserted against rather than to be used in its place. public static uint FromReplayCounters(uint serverReplayTick) Parameters serverReplayTick uint Returns uint Remarks Not used by the controller. Taking the replay counter directly would work, but it is only valid inside a replay, so the controller would need two code paths where one will do — and a second path is a second thing to get wrong. ReplayAgrees(uint, uint, uint, uint) True when the formula and FishNet's replay counter agree for one replayed step. The closed-loop check, in one place, for tests and for a debug assertion. public static bool ReplayAgrees(uint clientStateTick, uint serverStateTick, uint clientReplayTick, uint serverReplayTick) Parameters clientStateTick uint serverStateTick uint clientReplayTick uint serverReplayTick uint Returns bool Resolve(NetworkBehaviour, uint) Resolve(bool, uint, uint, uint, uint, uint) for a behaviour on a predicted object, reading the clocks off its own managers. Every predicted thing that reads the weather goes through this, so there is one place the two tick domains are reconciled and one place to get it wrong. public static uint Resolve(NetworkBehaviour behaviour, uint inputTick) Parameters behaviour NetworkBehaviour The behaviour being replicated. inputTick uint The replicate's own tick, in the owning client's domain. Returns uint Resolve(bool, uint, uint, uint, uint, uint) The synchronised tick to evaluate the weather at for one replicate step. public static uint Resolve(bool isServer, uint serverTick, uint clientSyncTick, uint clientStateTick, uint serverStateTick, uint inputTick) Parameters isServer bool True when this peer is the server, which owns the clock. serverTick uint The server's own TimeManager.Tick. Used only when isServer. clientSyncTick uint The client's estimate of the synchronised tick (TimeManager.Tick), used only before a first reconcile has established the pairing. clientStateTick uint The last reconcile's client tick (WeatherExposureTick.ReconcilePairing), or Unset. serverStateTick uint The last reconcile's server tick (WeatherExposureTick.ReconcilePairing), or Unset. inputTick uint The replicate's own tick, in the owning client's domain. Returns uint A tick in the weather timeline's (synchronised) domain. Zero is a real answer — it is the first tick of the timeline, which is where a mapping that would fall below it is clamped — and is also what Unset happens to be, since FishNet's sentinel is literally zero. Nothing downstream needs to tell the two apart: both mean "read the oldest weather".

api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.Weather.html.summary: Namespace FishMMO.Shared.Weather Classes ShelterQuery Where an NPC can get out of the weather (Phase 4 of the core and modules plan, 2026-11-18): the nearest shelter volume's bounds. The World Simulation module installs Source from its weather volumes; with none installed there is no shelter anywhere, and an NPC that would seek one stays where it is. SurfaceWater The open water in the loaded scene — a sea, its lakes and rivers: where anything falling out of the sky stops, whether a point is under a surface, and how high the water stands at a place. WaterQuery The water of a scene, for the simulation: where a character swims, how deep an agent would have to go, what drowns or burns. Keyed by scene, as WeatherQuery is, and answered at a synced server tick, so the server and a predicting client get the identical answer. WeatherChannels The channel table: counts, blend rules and helpers. WeatherExposureIngredient One exposure state a recipe needs, and how far into it the character has to be. WeatherExposureRecipe A state that exists only where two or more others do at once: soaked AND chilled is frozen, which is not what either one alone means. WeatherExposureTemplate A state the weather can put a character into — wet, chilled, wind-burnt — and the buff that goes with it. Static content: what the weather has to be doing, how long it takes to build and to wear off, and what it applies. Never any runtime state; the levels live on WeatherExposureController, one set per character. WeatherExposureTerm One input's contribution to an exposure state. WeatherExposureTick Converts a prediction replicate's tick into the tick the weather timeline is evaluated at. WeatherQuery The weather at a place and tick, for gameplay: the core's question, answered by whichever weather is installed. Structs WaterSample The water over a place at a tick. WeatherAir What the air is doing at a place and a moment: the synoptic state the weather driver computes. WeatherFrame One value per WeatherChannel. A value type with named fields so sampling weather for every player every second allocates nothing. WeatherReading The weather at a place and tick, as gameplay reads it: the frame of channels, the air, the temperature and the shelter. Core vocabulary (Phase 4 of the core and modules plan, 2026-11-17). Interfaces ISeaLevel A scene's sea as the water contract needs it: its level at a tick. SeaTide (the tide driven by the world's moons) implements it; a game without that module can register a flat sea. SurfaceWater.IAreaSource Water that stands only in some places: lakes and rivers. SurfaceWater.IDaylightSource A sea that dims the daylight on its way down to its floor (2026-10-25, phase I2m, decision 36 (c)): how much per metre, the scene cut's (BiomeSeaFloors.DaylightExtinction); 0 for none. SurfaceWater.IFlowingAreaSource Area water some of which may be molten lava (a lava tube's river, a pit in its chamber): which the highest surface over a place is, so what lives, wades, splashes or floats in water can leave lava alone. SurfaceWater.ILavaAreaSource SurfaceWater.ISource What a body of open water tells the weather about itself. SurfaceWater.IStackedAreaSource Area water that stands at more than one level over a place (2026-10-21: a cave's stream under a lava tube's river on the level over it, a lake on the hill over both): which surface a height is in or over, not only the highest. SurfaceWater.IWaveSource Water whose drawn surface moves (the sea's waves): what a floating body is set on to ride them. Enums PrecipitationKind What mostly falls. WaterBody What a body of water is, to anything that swims, wades or drowns in it. WeatherBlendRule How a channel combines when several layers write to it. WeatherChannel Everything a weather layer can say about the world. A frame is one value per channel, each 0..1 unless noted, and blending layers means combining these channels. WeatherExposureInput What one term of an exposure state reads: a channel of the blended weather, or one of the driver's physical air properties. WeatherExposureTemperatureResponse How a state answers to how cold or hot it is where the character stands. WeatherKindMask A set of kinds of weather, for what a volume shelters from or suppresses. WeatherSceneMode How a scene gets its weather. Delegates ShelterQuery.NearestSource The nearest shelter of at least the strength within reach of a point; installed by the module.

FindObjectsInactive) Object.name Object.hideFlags object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Who simulates. The server and the owning client, driven from CharacterPredictionController's single [Replicate] like every other controller. An observer never runs it: state forwarding is off on every prefab, and the buffs it applies reach observers the way all buffs do. Why it can be predicted at all. Everything it reads is a pure function of the tick and the position. The weather timeline is deterministic from its seed and clock anchor, both of which the client already holds; shelter is a point-in-collider test (WeatherVolume.Contains, and so RegionGeometry.ContainsPoint) rather than a physics trigger, which matters because triggers poll in OnPostPhysicsSimulation, outside the replicate, are not rolled back, and re-fire their Enter/Exit on every replay (N12). So the owner can work out the same answer the server will, and a replay of the same tick gives the same answer again. Which clock. The weather is evaluated at a SYNCHRONISED tick, and the replicate's tick is the owner's unsynchronised counter: see WeatherExposureTick, which is where that conversion lives and is tested. No new field in the input. Nothing is sent up from the client; the whole step is derived from the tick, the character's own position and the timeline both sides already have (N12). What does ride the reconcile is the levels, because they are timers — see Exposure. Called once per tick before OnReplicate(ref CharacterReplicateData, ReplicateState, Channel). public void PopulateInput(ref CharacterReplicateData input) Parameters input CharacterReplicateData ResetState(bool) Resets this NetworkBehaviour so that it may be added to an object pool. public override void ResetState(bool asServer) Parameters asServer bool RestoreFromReconcile(ExposureReconcileEntry[]) Takes the server's levels as the truth, and re-derives which buffs are held. public void RestoreFromReconcile(ExposureReconcileEntry[] entries) Parameters entries ExposureReconcileEntry[] Remarks The held set is rebuilt from the restored levels rather than carried across the reconcile, because the levels have just been overwritten: a buff whose level the server says never reached the threshold must not still be marked as held, or it would never be applied again. Dequantising here — the same function the server quantised with — leaves both peers on bit-identical levels, so the replay that follows starts from the server's state exactly. RestoreFromReconcile(ExposureReconcileEntry[], BuffReconcileEntry[]) RestoreFromReconcile(ExposureReconcileEntry[]), with the server's buffs for the same tick: they say which side of a hysteresis band a state or a recipe was on, which the levels alone cannot. public void RestoreFromReconcile(ExposureReconcileEntry[] entries, BuffReconcileEntry[] serverBuffs) Parameters entries ExposureReconcileEntry[] serverBuffs BuffReconcileEntry[] Remarks Inside the band (between release and apply) "held" depends on which way the level was travelling. The server's answer is in the same correction: the buff is on its list or it is not. Without it a state in the band kept whatever this client last believed, and every recipe was read as NOT held, so a buff the server was holding by its release margin was taken off by the owner at its next sample, put back by the next correction, and taken off again by the replay: an icon and an effect flickering once a second.

api/unity/FishMMO.Shared.WithinRangeCond.summary: Class WithinRangeCondition Namespace FishMMO.Shared Assembly FishMMO.Shared.dll Passes when the evaluated character is within a distance of the initiator. [Serializable] public class WithinRangeCondition : BaseCondition, ICondition Inheritance object BaseCondition WithinRangeCondition Implements ICondition Inherited Members BaseCondition.TargetSelector BaseCondition.Combine BaseCondition.Invert BaseCondition.Check(ICharacter, EventData) BaseCondition.GetTooltipContribution() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Position-sensitive, and that has consequences. This is the first shipped condition whose answer depends on where characters ARE rather than on what state they hold, so it is the first that can disagree with the query that produced its candidate. Every selector that queries space evaluates its conditions inside the same lag-compensation scope as the query (see TargetSelector.GatherRewound), so used there this measures the same world the candidate came from. Used anywhere else — attached to a Trigger's top-level conditions, or to a condition's own TargetSelector — it measures live server positions instead. That is not wrong, but it is a different question, and at 300 ms of latency the two answers differ by a couple of metres. Prefer a generous radius over a tight one for exactly that reason: this is a gate, not a hit test. A hit test belongs in a selector. Distance is measured between transform origins and compared squared, so no square root runs per candidate. IgnoreVerticalDistance makes it a cylinder rather than a sphere, which is usually what an authored "within 10 metres" means on terrain with any relief. Fields IgnoreVerticalDistance When true, distance is measured on the horizontal plane only. [Tooltip("Measure horizontal distance only, ignoring height difference.")] public bool IgnoreVerticalDistance Field Value bool Remarks A sphere centred on a caster reaches less far along the ground as the height difference grows, so a target on a ledge one metre up is out of a ten metre sphere at 9.95 metres horizontally. Authors almost always mean the cylinder. MaximumRange Maximum distance, in metres, between the initiator and the evaluated character. [Tooltip("Maximum distance in metres. [TemplateReference(typeof(AchievementTemplate))] public int AchievementTemplateID Field Value int Amount public uint Amount Field Value uint Seed The attribute-generation seed the granted Item is built from. public int Seed Field Value int Remarks Rolled by ItemSpawnableSettings at spawn so this drop has an identity of its own. Without one, pickup built the item through the template-only constructor, whose seed derives from a database id that is still zero — so every generated ground drop of a template rolled IDENTICAL attributes from RNG(0), and rolled a DIFFERENT set after a relog once a real row id existed to derive from. Zero means "no seed was rolled" and pickup keeps the old derive-from-id behavior. Properties Template The item template defining the type of item this world object represents. public BaseItemTemplate Template { get; set; } Property Value BaseItemTemplate Title The display title for this interactable, shown in the UI. public override string Title { get; } Property Value string Methods ReadPayload(NetworkConnection, Reader) Reads network payload data for this interactable, setting its ID and registering it in the scene. public override void ReadPayload(NetworkConnection connection, Reader reader) Parameters connection NetworkConnection The network connection. reader Reader The network reader. ResetState(bool) Clears the rolled stack and seed when this instance returns to the pool. public override void ResetState(bool asServer) Parameters asServer bool Remarks Per-life state. A pooled world item that is not reset comes back out of the pool still carrying the amount and seed its previous life was spawned with, and ItemSpawnableSettings only overwrites them when the object is respawned through a spawner — an item dropped by script would keep the old number, and a stale seed would silently hand a new drop the previous drop's attribute roll. The template is deliberately left alone: templateID is a serialized field a designer may have authored on the prefab, and zeroing it here would strip that on the first despawn. Amount is the half that is always injected at spawn. WritePayload(NetworkConnection, Writer) Writes the scene object ID, then the template, stack size and generation seed. public override void WritePayload(NetworkConnection connection, Writer writer) Parameters connection NetworkConnection writer Writer Remarks WritePayload(NetworkConnection, Writer) is what sends the scene object ID, and this override used to skip it. The consequence was total: a client's copy of a world item kept ID 0 and was never entered into Objects, so the interact key sent InteractableID = 0 — an ID the server never issues, because scene object IDs count down from zero and are always negative. Every ground drop in the game was therefore impossible to pick up, and the refusal path is silent, so it looked like a dead keypress rather than a bug.
