See AccountRegistrationService. Constructors AccountController(AccountRegistrationService, SelfServiceService, PasswordResetService, SrpLoginService, TwoFactorService, PanelRegistrationOptions, IAccountService, IWebSessionService, PanelSessionManager, IWebHostEnvironment, RegistrationFormTokenService, IBetaCodeService, VerificationOptions, BetaOptions, ILogger<AccountController>) public AccountController(AccountRegistrationService registration, SelfServiceService selfService, PasswordResetService passwordReset, SrpLoginService srp, TwoFactorService twoFactor, PanelRegistrationOptions options, IAccountService accounts, IWebSessionService webSessions, PanelSessionManager sessions, IWebHostEnvironment environment, RegistrationFormTokenService formTokens, IBetaCodeService betaCodes, VerificationOptions verification, BetaOptions beta, ILogger<AccountController> log) Parameters registration AccountRegistrationService selfService SelfServiceService passwordReset PasswordResetService srp SrpLoginService twoFactor TwoFactorService options PanelRegistrationOptions accounts IAccountService webSessions IWebSessionService sessions PanelSessionManager environment IWebHostEnvironment formTokens RegistrationFormTokenService betaCodes IBetaCodeService verification VerificationOptions beta BetaOptions log ILogger<AccountController> Methods BeginTwoFactorSetup() Starts two-factor enrolment. Does not enable it. [HttpPost("2fa/setup")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> BeginTwoFactorSetup() Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks For an account whose two-factor is already ON this is a re-enrolment, and it replaces the live authenticator and every recovery code the moment it runs: the secret it writes is the one sign-in reads. That is the same weight as disabling two-factor or regenerating the codes, so it takes the same fresh step-up those do. Without it, a borrowed signed-in browser could swap the owner's authenticator for one of its own. A first enrolment needs no step-up — there is no authenticator to prove, and nothing is enabled until 2fa/confirm. ChangeEmail(ChangeEmailRequest) Changes the contact email and restarts verification. [HttpPost("email")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> ChangeEmail(AccountController.ChangeEmailRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.ChangeEmailRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> ChangePassword(ChangePasswordRequest) Changes the account password. [HttpPost("password")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> ChangePassword(AccountController.ChangePasswordRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.ChangePasswordRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks The current password is proved by a full SRP exchange, not by sending it: the browser asks for a challenge, derives a proof from the password the user typed, and submits that alongside the new salt and verifier it derived locally. Neither password is ever transmitted, so there is nothing here that could leak one. Every game token and every OTHER panel session is revoked on success. The session making the change survives, because signing the user out of the page they are looking at to tell them it worked is not an improvement. Character(long, ICharacterService) One of the signed-in account's characters. [HttpGet("/api/characters/{id:long}")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> Character(long id, ICharacterService characters) Parameters id long characters ICharacterService Returns Task<IActionResult> Characters(ICharacterService) The signed-in account's characters. [HttpGet("/api/characters")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> Characters(ICharacterService characters) Parameters characters ICharacterService Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks Read-only, and deliberately so. Creating and deleting a character are in-game only — deletion spans fourteen sub-entity tables inside one unit of work in the login server, and a second implementation of that is how a shard loses data. CompletePasswordReset(PasswordResetCompleteRequest) Completes a reset with a browser-derived salt and verifier. [HttpPost("password-reset/complete")] [AllowAnonymous] [EnableRateLimiting("Register")] public Task<IActionResult> CompletePasswordReset(AccountController.PasswordResetCompleteRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.PasswordResetCompleteRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks There is no password parameter here either. The browser generates a fresh salt and derives the verifier locally from the username this code resolved to, so the shard never holds anything a password could be recovered from. ConfirmTwoFactorSetup(CodeRequest) Enables two-factor once a code from the new authenticator verifies. [HttpPost("2fa/confirm")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> ConfirmTwoFactorSetup(AuthController.CodeRequest request) Parameters request AuthController.CodeRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> DisableTwoFactor() Turns two-factor off, invalidating every recovery code with it. [HttpDelete("2fa")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> DisableTwoFactor() Returns Task<IActionResult> LookupPasswordReset(PasswordResetCodeRequest) Returns the account name a reset code belongs to. [HttpPost("password-reset/lookup")] [AllowAnonymous] [EnableRateLimiting("Register")] public Task<IActionResult> LookupPasswordReset(AccountController.PasswordResetCodeRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.PasswordResetCodeRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks The browser cannot derive an SRP verifier without the username, because the username is an input to the key derivation. Holding the code already proves control of the mailbox the code was sent to, and the mail names the account, so answering this adds nothing an attacker did not already have. The code travels in the BODY, never in the path or the query string: URLs end up in access logs, proxy logs, Referer headers and browser history, and a reset code in any of those is a reset code somebody else can use. Me() The signed-in account's own profile. [HttpGet] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> Me() Returns Task<IActionResult> MyBetaCodes() The beta codes the signed-in account has redeemed. [HttpGet("beta")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> MyBetaCodes() Returns Task<IActionResult> Policy() Returns the account rules, so the browser can apply exactly the server's validation. [HttpGet("policy")] [AllowAnonymous] public IActionResult Policy() Returns IActionResult Remarks It deliberately takes no input. An endpoint that answered "is this password allowed?" would require the password to be transmitted — which is the one thing this whole design exists to prevent. The rules come from Authentication, which the LoginServer uses too, so the browser, the game client and the server cannot drift. RedeemBetaCode(RedeemBetaCodeRequest) Redeems a beta code for the signed-in account. [HttpPost("beta/redeem")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] [EnableRateLimiting("Auth")] public Task<IActionResult> RedeemBetaCode(AccountController.RedeemBetaCodeRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.RedeemBetaCodeRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks For an account made before the gate went up, or whose redemption at registration lost a race for a code's last use. The service's refusal is passed through unaltered: it deliberately gives one message for every kind of bad code. RegenerateRecoveryCodes() Issues a fresh set of recovery codes, discarding the previous ones. [HttpPost("2fa/recovery-codes")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> RegenerateRecoveryCodes() Returns Task<IActionResult> Register(RegisterRequest) Creates an account from a browser-computed SRP salt and verifier. [HttpPost("register")] [AllowAnonymous] [EnableRateLimiting("Register")] public Task<IActionResult> Register(AccountController.RegisterRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.RegisterRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks There is no password parameter. The browser derives the salt and verifier locally with the same SRP rules the game client uses, so the shard never holds anything a password could be recovered from — the same property the in-game path has. RegistrationForm() Issues a registration form: a signed token and the randomised decoy fields to render. [HttpGet("register/form")] [AllowAnonymous] [EnableRateLimiting("Register")] public IActionResult RegistrationForm() Returns IActionResult Remarks Rate-limited under the registration bucket, because a token is only ever wanted by somebody about to register. The in-game client gets nothing like it — bots there speak the protocol, not the page — see the README. RequestPasswordReset(PasswordResetRequest) Starts password recovery for the account at an email address. [HttpPost("password-reset/request")] [AllowAnonymous] [EnableRateLimiting("Register")] public Task<IActionResult> RequestPasswordReset(AccountController.PasswordResetRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.PasswordResetRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks Always 200, always the same body. It says nothing about whether the address is registered, whether the account is banned, or whether the per-account resend cooldown suppressed the mail — a reset form that answered differently for a registered address would be an account enumeration oracle, and that is exactly what they are probed for. ResendVerification(ResendVerificationRequest) Sends a fresh verification code for one channel, if the account is owed one. [HttpPost("verify/resend")] [AllowAnonymous] [EnableRateLimiting("Register")] public Task<IActionResult> ResendVerification(AccountController.ResendVerificationRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.ResendVerificationRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks Always the same 200 and the same words: unknown account, verified account, a channel it never chose, or a cooldown still running. Anything else would say which names exist. Discord is refused with a 400, for every account alike: its code is sent once, as one DM, and is never re-sent. Because the refusal does not depend on the account, it says nothing about one. RevokeSession(long) Revokes one of the signed-in account's other sessions. [HttpDelete("sessions/{id:long}")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> RevokeSession(long id) Parameters id long Returns Task<IActionResult> Sessions() The signed-in account's live panel sessions. [HttpGet("sessions")] [Authorize(Policy = "Self")] public Task<IActionResult> Sessions() Returns Task<IActionResult> Verify(VerifyRequest) Redeems a verification code from any channel. [HttpPost("verify")] [AllowAnonymous] [EnableRateLimiting("Register")] public Task<IActionResult> Verify(AccountController.VerifyRequest request) Parameters request AccountController.VerifyRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks One endpoint for every channel, because any one correct code verifies the account: the player types whichever code reached them first, and the database finds which channel it belongs to. There used to be a verify-phone twin; it is gone with the every-channel rule. Every failure — wrong code, unknown account, verified account, the third wrong code opening a support ticket — is one 400 with InvalidCodeError.

The browser runs SRP-6a against the same parameters the game client uses and sends a public ephemeral and a proof; the challenge endpoint takes a username and nothing else. Nothing here is audited: it is a player (or an operator) authenticating as themselves, on anonymous or TwoFactorPending endpoints the audit filter excludes. Constructors AuthController(SrpLoginService, TwoFactorService, TwoFactorResetFlow, TwoFactorResetOptions, PanelSessionManager, IWebHostEnvironment, ILogger<AuthController>) public AuthController(SrpLoginService srp, TwoFactorService twoFactor, TwoFactorResetFlow reset, TwoFactorResetOptions resetOptions, PanelSessionManager sessions, IWebHostEnvironment environment, ILogger<AuthController> log) Parameters srp SrpLoginService twoFactor TwoFactorService reset TwoFactorResetFlow resetOptions TwoFactorResetOptions sessions PanelSessionManager environment IWebHostEnvironment log ILogger<AuthController> Methods Challenge(ChallengeRequest) SRP message one. [HttpPost("srp/challenge")] [AllowAnonymous] public Task<IActionResult> Challenge(AuthController.ChallengeRequest request) Parameters request AuthController.ChallengeRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> CompleteTwoFactorReset() Uses an effective reset: the old factor is replaced and the new one handed over. Does NOT sign in. [HttpPost("2fa/reset/complete")] [Authorize(Policy = "TwoFactorPending")] public Task<IActionResult> CompleteTwoFactorReset() Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks Every panel session on the account is revoked, this one included, and this browser is given a fresh session that has proven the password only. It becomes a signed-in session through 2fa/reset/confirm with a code from the new authenticator, and not before. ConfirmTwoFactorReset(CodeRequest) Finishes a completed reset with a code from the NEW authenticator, and only then signs in. [HttpPost("2fa/reset/confirm")] [Authorize(Policy = "TwoFactorPending")] public Task<IActionResult> ConfirmTwoFactorReset(AuthController.CodeRequest request) Parameters request AuthController.CodeRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks Recovery codes are refused here: the point of this step is proving the new authenticator was actually saved, and a recovery code shown on the same screen proves nothing about that. GetTwoFactorReset() The pending reset for this signed-in-by-password session's account, if any. [HttpGet("2fa/reset")] [Authorize(Policy = "TwoFactorPending")] public Task<IActionResult> GetTwoFactorReset() Returns Task<IActionResult> Logout() Ends this session. [HttpPost("logout")] [AllowAnonymous] public Task<IActionResult> Logout() Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks The cookie is deleted whatever happens, but "signed out" is only answered once the session row is revoked. Deleting the cookie ends this browser's copy; the row is what ends every other copy of it, and a logout that reported success while the row lived on left a copied cookie working until the idle timeout. Proof(ProofRequest) SRP message two. [HttpPost("srp/proof")] [AllowAnonymous] public Task<IActionResult> Proof(AuthController.ProofRequest request) Parameters request AuthController.ProofRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks A locked account, a wrong password, an unknown account and a banned one all answer 401 with GenericFailure. The one different answer — 403, stage verification-required — is given only after a CORRECT proof, so it reveals nothing to anyone who does not already hold the password. RequestTwoFactorReset() Asks for a delayed two-factor reset. Asking again returns the same request; the clock never restarts. [HttpPost("2fa/verify")] [Authorize(Policy = "TwoFactorPending")] public Task<IActionResult> VerifyTwoFactor(AuthController.CodeRequest request) Parameters request AuthController.CodeRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks Counted and locked under AuthLockoutOptions. A good code also cancels any pending self-service two-factor reset, and the holder is emailed that it was.

an account: it is the only one that can cause a process to run on another machine. Everything about it is shaped by containing that. A command carries a verb from a closed enumeration and the name of an application some daemon already reported supervising. It carries no path, no arguments and no shell. The daemon then looks that name up in its own configuration file on disk and refuses anything it does not recognise. So the worst an attacker with this endpoint — or with the database password — can do is restart a FishMMO process that was already configured to run. They cannot make a game host run something new. Queued, not executed. The panel writes a row; the daemon collects it on its next poll. Every acknowledgement here says so, for the same reason the server board does: an operator who believes a process has restarted, when the row has not been collected, will press the button again. Operator plus a step-up, and every command is audited. A queued command that nobody can attribute is the one thing worse than not having the capability at all. Constructors DaemonController(IDaemonService, AuditScope, ILogger<DaemonController>) public DaemonController(IDaemonService daemon, AuditScope audit, ILogger<DaemonController> log) Parameters daemon IDaemonService audit AuditScope log ILogger<DaemonController> Methods AppEvents(string, string, int?, DateTime?, DateTime?, int, int) The supervision history: what the daemons observed changing, newest first. That route lists what operators asked this panel for. This lists what the supervisors saw happen by themselves — a process that died overnight, the restarts that followed, and whether it came back — which nobody asked for and which nothing else records. The row in daemon_apps behind the hosts page is overwritten on every heartbeat, so a fault that has already been recovered from is otherwise invisible in every view there is. It is not process output, and it must never become it. Nothing a supervised process wrote reaches here: every row is derived in the database service by comparing one heartbeat against the stored one, from two status values and two integers, and the sentence describing the transition is composed from those. Server logs carry connection strings, tokens and paths inside exception messages, so a route that relayed them would turn this read-only view into a way of reading secrets out of a game host — and would let a compromised daemon put text of its choosing in front of an administrator. A read, at the same policy as the other two reads here, and deliberately not audited — looking at a history is not an action taken on anything. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Cont.summary: Class DatabaseReplies Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Controllers Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Turns a failed DatabaseResult into the reply the panel gives for it. public static class DatabaseReplies Inheritance object DatabaseReplies Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A failed result is one of three different things, and the panel used to answer all three the same way — a 400 carrying ErrorMessage: Not found. The row the request named does not exist. A 404, with the caller's own wording, because "no such account" is a sentence the page already knows how to say. A refusal. The service said no: a value out of range, a ticket above the actor's tier, a stale version, a code that does not redeem. The message was written by the service to be read, and it is passed through as a 400 exactly as before. A fault. The database failed: a dropped connection, a timeout, a statement that threw. Its message is built from the underlying exception (BaseService.MapFinalException) and can carry a host, a port or a column name, which is nobody's business in a browser — and a 400 told the browser the request was wrong, when trying it again was the right thing to do. A 503 with the caller's own wording, and the real message goes to the log, where it is useful. A controller that treats a particular code specially (a 409 for a stale edit, a named collision) still does so before calling this. This is the answer for everything else. A window is the two controls on the server board — lock, and schedule a shutdown — applied to a set of servers under one record, because doing that by hand across a dozen servers is where one gets missed. Starting a window writes each server's own row through the same service the per-server buttons use. The plan is rows, so the operator can close their laptop. The shutdown deadline is an absolute instant written onto each server; the server counts down to it inside its own process, warns its players as it passes each mark, and stops. A twenty minute drain does not need this panel, this browser or this process to be running for the shard to go down on time. What the panel does afterwards is observe: the status on these responses is derived from what the servers' rows say now, and is brought up to date by each read. Cancelling does not unlock anything, and this controller says so every time. Scheduling a shutdown sets locked = true in the same statement, and cancelling clears the deadline alone. A cancelled window therefore leaves every target closed to new arrivals until somebody unlocks it on the board. Getting that wrong strands a shard with nobody able to log in and the cause nowhere near where anyone will look, so the acknowledgement names the servers that are still locked rather than merely warning in general terms. Operator to read, Operator plus a step-up to write, matching the per-server controls: a window is those controls applied twelve times, and the weaker of two faces of one capability is the way around the stronger. Three other screens already answer "is the shard up": the server board owns game server processes, their pulse and their population; daemon hosts owns supervised OS processes and the daemons watching them; the queues page owns email queue depth. Repeating any of those here would produce a second number for the same fact, and two screens that disagree by one poll interval is worse than one screen. What is left over — and what nothing else in the panel can tell you — is the state of this process and of the database every other page reads through. That is all this endpoint returns. The pool figures belong to this process alone. ConnectionPoolMetrics is a field on the singleton factory this host built at startup, fed by an EF connection interceptor. It counts connections the Control Panel opened. Each game server runs its own pool against the same PostgreSQL and is invisible here, and so is PostgreSQL's own max_connections ceiling. Saying "the pool" without saying whose would invite an operator to read a healthy panel as a healthy shard. No secret, connection string or password can leave this endpoint. That is enforced by what is fetched, not by care at the point of serialization. This controller never takes a dependency on NpgsqlDbConfiguration, which is the only type here that holds a connection string. Two diagnostic strings that could carry credential material — the driver's own connect-failure message from TryConnectAsync, and the exception text behind an unavailable schema check — are deliberately not projected at all: they are arbitrary exception text from a database driver, and no amount of reading them today guarantees what a future Npgsql release puts in one. Both are written to the application log instead, and the payload says so, so an operator knows the detail exists and where it is rather than believing there was none. Every other string sent from here is either a literal authored in this repository or a name from a closed set (a migration identifier, a {Service}.{Method} operation name, an audit action id). Reads here are not audited. Glancing at a health page is not an operator action, and a page polled every ten seconds by every open tab would write more audit rows than every real action combined — burying the log this same endpoint reports on. It is gated at Operator and logged to the application log, exactly as the audit log's own reader is. This endpoint measures by acting. The round trip is a real connection, so the page contributes to the very counters below it: each poll adds one to connections opened and closed. That is worth the honesty of a latency figure that was actually observed rather than one cached from somebody else's query. [HttpPost("email/{id:long}/retry")] [Authorize(Policy = "Operator.StepUp")] [Audited("platform.email-retry", TargetType = "email", TargetRouteValue = "id")] public Task<IActionResult> RetryEmail(long id, PlatformQueuesController.ReasonRequest request) Parameters id long request PlatformQueuesController.ReasonRequest Returns Task<IActionResult> Remarks This does not send anything. Delivery belongs to the login server; all this does is make the row eligible to be claimed again, which is why the acknowledgement says the message was re-queued rather than sent. If nothing is claiming — the case this page exists to reveal — the retry will appear to do nothing, and the honest thing is to say so rather than let a green toast imply mail went out. Step-up, not plain Operator, because it touches the account verification path: a borrowed unlocked session should not be able to re-queue a verification email for an account somebody is trying to take over. The reason is mandatory for the same reason it is on every other write in this panel — the audit row is only as useful as what it says about why. A row reading as failed is one the drain gave up on after its attempt limit, so a release grants exactly one more attempt. The audit row names the account and nothing else personal. Neither the phone number nor the message body is put in Details or the log line; the service does not even return the number. Both omissions are deliberate and neither is an oversight. On values: the panel has no use for the material that would justify putting every key the shard depends on one serialization mistake away from a browser. The read goes through FetchInventoryAsync, whose projection does not name the value column, so the material never enters this process at all — as opposed to being fetched and then carefully not sent. On rotation: these three keys do not rotate alike, and the machinery that knows how lives in the LoginServer and the installer rather than here. totp_master_kek encrypts every enrolled TOTP secret; replacing it without re-encrypting them locks every player out of two-factor permanently, and no undo exists because the old key is gone. signing_key_kek has an atomic swap path in the LoginServer that coordinates with a running server, which a web request cannot join. A button here would be a one-click, irreversible shard outage, and its presence would imply somebody had made it safe. What this page is for is the question an operator actually has at three in the morning: is the key there, and is it the right shape. A missing or truncated key has no other symptom until something tries to use it and fails somewhere unrelated. The application bytes and the UDP payload are MEASURED by each server's own transport (the managed WebTransport socket and msquic). The bytes on the wire are ESTIMATED — payload plus 28 bytes of IPv4 and UDP header per datagram — because no user-space counter sees an IP header; the estimate is computed as this reads, never stored, and is an upper bound because msquic over-counts the datagrams of a burst it sends in several batches. The field names carry Estimated so no client can present one as the other. No data is null, never zero. A server with no rows in a window has no figure for it; the page prints "no data". A server that ran and moved nothing has zeros, which is a different fact. At Operator, beside the server board it belongs with. Nothing reaches into a process. Each server adopts its own row on its next pulse, which is what lets a command issued here reach a machine the panel cannot address — and it is why every acknowledgement says what was written rather than claiming the server has already done it. An operator who believes a world is locked when the row has not been read yet will let the next player in and not understand why. There is no start, stop or restart, and there cannot be one here. A stopped process polls nothing, so no row will ever reach it. Those need a supervising daemon on each host, which is a separate component with its own trust boundary; pretending otherwise with a button that writes a row nobody reads would be the worst kind of control panel lie. The same capability exists in-game as /admin lockserver and /admin shutdown, at Admin. These sit at Operator plus a step-up so the two surfaces agree about who may use them: two faces of one capability that disagree means the weaker is the way around the stronger. is a game master's daily work, and requiring an administrator for it means the person actually handling the report cannot act. The step-up is what makes that safe — a borrowed unlocked session cannot ban anybody without the authenticator. Every action here is recorded by AuditActionFilter. Nothing in this file calls an audit method; it assigns to AuditScope only where it knows something the filter cannot. What is deliberately absent. anywhere in the panel. Guild and party membership is game state: it is changed by players in the world, held in the memory of the scene server that owns the characters, and replicated to the database through the update tables. A row edited here would be overwritten by that server's next save, or — worse — would not be, leaving the roster on screen and the roster in the game permanently disagreeing. Support looks; the game decides. Nothing here is audited, deliberately. The audit log records privileged actions, and reads are not actions: a log in which "looked at a guild" outnumbers every ban and every rename by a thousand to one is a log nobody can read. Every route that changes something carries [Audited]; none of these change anything. and every scene server adopts it on its next pulse, a couple of seconds later, and jumps its players' clocks to it. Nothing here reaches into a process — so every acknowledgement says what was written, never that the world has changed. If no scene server is running, the row is read by nobody. All clock arithmetic happens in the database. The world time a write replaces, the anchor it writes and the instant it stamps come from one reading of the database clock inside the statement (see WorldClockControlService), so this host's clock skew cannot move the world. This controller only parses and formats: a world timestamp is the row's epoch plus world milliseconds, written Format; a change is +1h30m, -90s, +2d3h4m5.25s. Both forms are parsed by WorldClockText, the same code available to the in-game /admin time commands, so the two surfaces agree about what a typed value means. The row is created by the first scene server to start, which knows the calendar's epoch. Until then there is nothing to write and the page says so; every write answers 404 with the service's sentence. Writes sit at Operator plus step-up, as server control does: the in-game commands are Admin, and two faces of one capability that disagree about who may use it make the weaker one the way around the stronger. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class AccountRegistrationService Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Creates accounts from the browser, performing exactly the same steps, in the same order, as the LoginServer's AccountCreationSystem. public sealed class AccountRegistrationService Inheritance object AccountRegistrationService Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The two paths must not drift: an account created on the web and an account created in the game client have to be indistinguishable afterwards, or a player who registered on one and signed in on the other would find their 2FA missing, their verification never sent, or their salt and verifier shaped differently. The sequence mirrored from AccountCreationSystem.ProcessAccountCreationAsync, with the panel's additions marked: Validate the username against IsAllowedUsername(string). Bound the salt and verifier lengths (256 / 1024). (panel) Validate the optional profile with TryValidate(AccountProfileData, out AccountProfileData, out string). (panel) With the beta gate on, or a code given, check the code is redeemable — BEFORE the account exists. Persist the account with IAccountService.PersistAsync. (panel) Persist the profile and chosen channels, then redeem the beta code. Auto-verify when the development policy says so or the server verifies nothing; otherwise send a code on every channel Effective(AccountVerificationChannels, AccountVerificationChannels, AccountVerificationChannels) names, or verify without one when it names none. Only when the player opted in to two-factor: generate a TOTP secret, encrypt it under the deployment master KEK, persist it, then enable TOTP. With it, generate recovery codes, hash them, persist them. (panel) The secret, the enable and the codes are one transaction — see EnrolAsync(string, bool, CancellationToken). Return the otpauth URI and the plaintext recovery codes once (none without the opt-in). Everything after the account row exists is best effort, as it is in game: a follow-on step that fails is logged, and the account is kept rather than a half-made registration being reported as a failure the player then retries into "that name is taken". Constructors AccountRegistrationService(IAccountService, IEmailQueueService, ISmsQueueService, IBetaCodeService, ISupportTicketService, PanelRegistrationOptions, VerificationOptions, BetaOptions, VerificationResendThrottle, SelfServiceService, ILogger<AccountRegistrationService>) public AccountRegistrationService(IAccountService accounts, IEmailQueueService emailQueue, ISmsQueueService smsQueue, IBetaCodeService betaCodes, ISupportTicketService supportTickets, PanelRegistrationOptions options, VerificationOptions verification, BetaOptions beta, VerificationResendThrottle throttle, SelfServiceService selfService, ILogger<AccountRegistrationService> log) Parameters accounts IAccountService emailQueue IEmailQueueService smsQueue ISmsQueueService betaCodes IBetaCodeService supportTickets ISupportTicketService options PanelRegistrationOptions verification VerificationOptions beta BetaOptions throttle VerificationResendThrottle selfService SelfServiceService log ILogger<AccountRegistrationService> Fields CouldNotCreateError The one refusal for a registration that could not be created, whatever the reason. public const string CouldNotCreateError = "That account could not be created." Field Value string InvalidBetaCodeError The one refusal for any beta code problem. Passed through from the service's own wording. public const string InvalidBetaCodeError = "That beta code is not valid." Field Value string InvalidCodeError The one answer to every code that does not verify: a wrong one, an expired one, an unknown account, an account already verified, and the third wrong code that opens a ticket. public const string InvalidCodeError = "That verification code is not valid. After three incorrect codes a support ticket is opened for the account, and staff will contact you by email." Field Value string Remarks The verify endpoint is anonymous, so anything that differed between those cases would say which names exist, which are verified, and how many guesses an account has had. Saying up front what three wrong codes do costs nothing, because it is true of every account. TwoFactorNotSetUpWarning What a new account is told when it was created without two-factor. public const string TwoFactorNotSetUpWarning = "Your account was created, but two-factor could not be set up on it. Sign in and set it up from My account." Field Value string Methods ChannelNames(AccountVerificationChannels) Wire names for a set of channels: "email", "sms", "discord". public static string[] ChannelNames(AccountVerificationChannels channels) Parameters channels AccountVerificationChannels Returns string[] ParseChannel(string) Parses a wire channel name, or None. public static AccountVerificationChannels ParseChannel(string name) Parameters name string Returns AccountVerificationChannels RegisterAsync(RegistrationInput, CancellationToken) Creates an account from a browser-computed salt and verifier. public Task<AccountRegistrationService.RegistrationResult> RegisterAsync(AccountRegistrationService.RegistrationInput input, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters input AccountRegistrationService.RegistrationInput cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<AccountRegistrationService.RegistrationResult> Remarks The password is never a parameter here, and there is nowhere for it to arrive: the browser derives the salt and verifier with the same SRP rules the game client uses and sends only those, so this service could not log or leak a password if it tried. ResendAsync(string, AccountVerificationChannels, CancellationToken) Sends a fresh code for one channel, when the account is owed one. public Task ResendAsync(string username, AccountVerificationChannels channel, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters username string channel AccountVerificationChannels cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task Remarks Returns nothing, deliberately. The endpoint is anonymous and answers identically whatever happens here — unknown account, verified account, a channel it never chose, a cooldown still running — or it would say which names exist and what they chose. A code still waiting in the queue is not replaced: generating a new one would invalidate the code in the message that is about to arrive. Email and SMS only. The Discord code is delivered once, as one DM, and is never replaced — a second code would strand the first DM, and the bot never sends another — so the endpoint refuses a Discord resend before it gets here. VerifyAsync(string, int, CancellationToken) Redeems a verification code from any channel. public Task<(bool Ok, string Error, bool Retry)> VerifyAsync(string username, int code, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters username string code int cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<(bool Ok, string Error, bool Retry)> Remarks PersistVerifiedByCodeAsync matches the code against every code the account holds — email, SMS and Discord — and checks the expiry, in one statement. Any one match verifies the account outright; there is no second code to ask for afterwards. Every wrong code is counted through RecordAsync(IAccountService, ISupportTicketService?, string, CancellationToken), in the database the login server counts into, and the third in a row opens a support ticket. What that did is logged and never returned: the answer is InvalidCodeError whatever happened, so the endpoint cannot be used to learn anything about an account. A wrong code, an unknown account and a verified one all come back from the service as the same VALIDATION_ERROR, so counting only that keeps every one of them identical. A database fault is not a wrong code: it used to be counted as one, so a correct code typed during an outage was told it was invalid and moved the account towards an automatic ticket. It is answered with "try again" instead — the same for every account, so it says nothing either.

api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class AuditActionFilter Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Records every privileged request — reads as well as writes — whether or not its author remembered to. public sealed class AuditActionFilter : IAsyncActionFilter, IFilterMetadata Inheritance object AuditActionFilter Implements IAsyncActionFilter IFilterMetadata Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Every Game Master and Admin action must appear in the audit log. The in-game commands get that for free because they are audited at the single access gate where a command cannot be registered without declaring a level. HTTP endpoints had no equivalent: coverage depended on each author adding a call, which is exactly the kind of discipline that holds until the day somebody is in a hurry. This filter is that equivalent. It runs on every action, decides from the endpoint's own authorization policy whether the action is privileged, and writes a row if it is. An endpoint added tomorrow with no audit code in it is still recorded. Reads are recorded too (2026-09-14). Every Game Master and Admin action is tracked, with no exception, and looking at a player's account, tickets or chat is an action. A read with no AuditedAttribute is recorded under view.<controller>.<action> with its query string as the details, so what was searched for is part of the record. Player self-service and anonymous endpoints are still not recorded: those are not staff. It records refusals as well as successes, including the request that never reached the action because model binding rejected it — an operator repeatedly failing to reach something is the more interesting record. Automatic refreshes are not recorded (2026-09-14, the owner's decision "skip auto-refreshes"). The first load of a page and every refresh somebody asked for — a Refresh button, a filter change, a page click, the re-read after an action — are recorded. A page re-reading itself on a timer is not: the browser marks those requests with X-Panel-Refresh: auto (RefreshHeader), and a GET or HEAD carrying it is skipped here unless it was refused. A board polled every five seconds would otherwise bury every row that matters. The header is trusted for reads only. A write is recorded whatever it carries; nothing a client sends can make one skippable. For a read, the browser already decides whether to issue the request at all — the mark hides nothing the shipped page does not leave out by simply not polling — and the shipped page marks only its timers, so every page an operator opens still leaves its row. A refused read is recorded even when marked (here, and by PrivilegedRequestMiddleware for a refusal decided by policy): a refused poll is a probe, and refusals are rare. What the mark cannot defend against is an operator who edits the page's script to mark every read; those reads would go unrecorded. That is the cost of a client-side mark, accepted with the decision. Closing it would need a server-side rule, such as skipping only a repeat of a read the same session recorded recently. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class AuditCoverage Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Checks at startup that every privileged write endpoint declares what it records. public static class AuditCoverage Inheritance object AuditCoverage Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks AuditActionFilter already guarantees that a privileged write is recorded even with no attribute on it, so nothing goes unlogged. This check is about the quality of that record, and about when the mistake is found: a derived action name changes the day somebody renames a controller method, which silently breaks every saved query and every retention rule written against it. It runs once, over the endpoint table, at boot. Outside production it throws, so the omission is a failed first run rather than a hole discovered months later. In production it logs an error and starts anyway — refusing to serve a shard because an endpoint has a weak audit name would be a worse outage than the problem. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class EmailQueueDrainService Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Delivers the outbound email queue. This is the process that turns a queued row into a message in somebody's inbox. public sealed class EmailQueueDrainService : BackgroundService, IHostedService, IDisposable Inheritance object BackgroundService EmailQueueDrainService Implements IHostedService IDisposable Inherited Members BackgroundService.Dispose() BackgroundService.StartAsync(CancellationToken) BackgroundService.StopAsync(CancellationToken) BackgroundService.ExecuteTask object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This used to live in the LoginServer, driven from a Unity frame callback: a timer accumulated deltaTime, one message went out every ten seconds, the send was fire-and-forget with a flag to stop two overlapping, and the blocking network call to the relay happened on a game server's tick. It worked, and none of it belonged there — sending mail was paced by frame time, and a relay that took its time held up a loop whose job is players. This is an ASP.NET Core host with a thread pool, real asynchrony and an existing BackgroundService pattern, so the work moves here and the game server goes back to only enqueueing. The queue is the coordination, not this class. DequeueNextAsync claims a row with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so a panel and a login server — or two panels — racing for the same row is already handled: each gets a different row or nothing. Nothing here assumes it is the only drain, which is what makes the migration safe to do one process at a time. The verification stamp is conditional, and that condition is the reason EmailKind exists. After a successful send the old drain always called PersistVerificationEmailSentAsync, which stamps verification_email_sent_at. That column once ended the grace period an unverified account signed in under; there is no grace period any more, and it now records only when a verification code last reached the player — which staff read on the account page and in the ticket three wrong codes open. A stamp after a password reset would tell them a code arrived when none did. So the stamp still follows the row's kind, and the kind is a column rather than a guess at the subject line. Nothing here is audited. The audit log records what an operator did; a background loop delivering mail is not an operator action, and writing one audit row per verification email would bury the rows that record a person doing something. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class MaintenanceAdvanceService Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Advances maintenance windows on a timer, so their record does not depend on somebody having the page open. public sealed class MaintenanceAdvanceService : BackgroundService, IHostedService, IDisposable Inheritance object BackgroundService MaintenanceAdvanceService Implements IHostedService IDisposable Inherited Members BackgroundService.Dispose() BackgroundService.StartAsync(CancellationToken) BackgroundService.StopAsync(CancellationToken) BackgroundService.ExecuteTask object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Starting a window is already complete when it returns: each target's own row carries a lock and an absolute deadline, and the server counts down to it inside its own process. None of that needs this service, and nothing here is required for a shard to stop on time. What needs it is everything the panel knows afterwards. Two things go wrong without it. The smaller one is that statuses stay stale: every read advances the record, so with nobody looking, a window whose servers stopped an hour ago still reads "Draining" until the next person opens the page. The shard went down on time and only the bookkeeping is late — but an operator checking whether last night's maintenance finished is reading exactly that bookkeeping. The larger one is the retry. The plan is committed before any server is touched, so a panel that dies mid-actuation leaves a visible half-written window rather than a locked shard with no record — and AdvanceAsync(CancellationToken) is what finishes those writes. Left to a reader, a target whose deadline was never written sits unwritten until somebody happens to look, and a server the operator believes is draining is in fact still open and still taking players. A failed pass is logged and the timer continues. Refusing to serve the panel because one advance could not reach the database would turn a transient fault into an outage on the one surface an operator opens during an incident. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class PasswordResetService Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll "Forgot password" recovery: the path for an account holder who cannot sign in at all. public sealed class PasswordResetService Inheritance object PasswordResetService Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The server never sees a password here either. The browser generates a new SRP salt and derives a new verifier from the username and the password the user typed, and sends only those; ChangePasswordAsync(string, string, string, CancellationToken) — the one credential write in the panel — persists them. There is deliberately no second path that writes a verifier. A reset does not satisfy or weaken two-factor. Nothing here touches totp_enabled, totp_secret, totp_verified_at or the recovery codes, and nothing may be added that does. After a reset the account holder still has to pass TOTP or burn a recovery code at sign-in. That is the whole point of the split: the eight recovery codes are the answer to a lost authenticator and email is the answer to a lost password. If an emailed link could also clear the second factor, compromising a mailbox would be a complete account takeover and the second factor would protect nothing. The token is a secret. At least 32 bytes of RandomNumberGenerator output go to the mailbox; only its SHA-256 is stored, so a database read yields no working tokens. A plain hash rather than a slow KDF is right because the token is full-entropy random and not guessable — the hash exists to stop a leaked table being replayed, not to resist a dictionary. No account enumeration: RequestAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) reports nothing about whether the address is registered, whether the account is banned, or whether the resend cooldown suppressed the mail. The caller answers the same way regardless. Constructors PasswordResetService(IAccountService, IPasswordResetTokenService, IEmailQueueService, IWebSessionService, SelfServiceService, PanelRegistrationOptions, IWebHostEnvironment, ILogger<PasswordResetService>) public PasswordResetService(IAccountService accounts, IPasswordResetTokenService resetTokens, IEmailQueueService emailQueue, IWebSessionService webSessions, SelfServiceService selfService, PanelRegistrationOptions options, IWebHostEnvironment environment, ILogger<PasswordResetService> log) Parameters accounts IAccountService resetTokens IPasswordResetTokenService emailQueue IEmailQueueService webSessions IWebSessionService selfService SelfServiceService options PanelRegistrationOptions environment IWebHostEnvironment log ILogger<PasswordResetService> Fields InvalidCodeError The one answer for an unknown, malformed, expired or already-used code. public const string InvalidCodeError = "That reset code is not valid or has expired." Field Value string Remarks Distinguishing them would tell an attacker which of their guesses was structurally right, so every failure in this file uses this exact string. Methods CompleteAsync(string, string, string, CancellationToken) Spends a reset token and installs the browser-derived credentials. public Task<PasswordResetService.Outcome> CompleteAsync(string code, string salt, string verifier, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters code string salt string verifier string cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<PasswordResetService.Outcome> Remarks Order matters and is deliberate. The token is spent first, by one conditional UPDATE in the database, so a double submission cannot write twice; a credential write that then fails costs the account holder a second email, which is the cheap direction to fail in. Afterwards every panel session and every game token for the account is revoked and any other outstanding reset token is invalidated. The revocations are the point rather than housekeeping. A reset is what somebody does when they believe their account is compromised, so a session left alive would defeat it, and a reset token requested earlier by an attacker would still be live in their hands the moment the victim finished resetting. The game tokens are revoked inside ChangePasswordAsync(string, string, string, CancellationToken) rather than here, which is the one place in this sequence that differs from the obvious reading of "credentials, sessions, tokens": reusing the panel's single credential write is worth more than the interleaving, and all three are attempted before this method returns. A revocation that fails does not undo the reset; it is logged and comes back as SignedOutEverywhere false, so the reply can say so. LookupUsernameAsync(string, CancellationToken) Returns the account name a valid, unexpired, unused token belongs to, or null. public Task<string> LookupUsernameAsync(string code, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters code string cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<string> Remarks The browser needs the username before it can derive a verifier, because the username is an input to the SRP key derivation. Handing it to somebody holding the token gives away nothing: the token went to that account's mailbox, and the mail names the account already. This is a read — it does not spend the token, which only CompleteAsync(string, string, string, CancellationToken) does. RequestAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) Issues a reset token for the account at an email address and queues the mail. public Task<PasswordResetService.RequestOutcome> RequestAsync(string email, string requestedIp, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters email string requestedIp string cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<PasswordResetService.RequestOutcome> Remarks Every refusal returns the same empty outcome, and the caller answers identically in all of them: an unknown address, a malformed one, a banned account, a cooldown still running, or a database that is down. An endpoint that answered differently for a registered address would be an account enumeration oracle, which is exactly what a password reset form is probed for. Banned accounts are never mailed. A reset cannot help them — the access level, not the password, is what refuses the login — and sending would make the endpoint an abuse vector against whoever owns the address. FetchForLoginAsync already refuses a banned account, and refuses it with the same failure as a missing one.

api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.title: Class PrivilegedRequestMiddleware | FishMMO Documentation
api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class PrivilegedRequestMiddleware Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Wraps authorization: turns a step-up refusal into a 428, and records refusals the action filter never sees. public sealed class PrivilegedRequestMiddleware Inheritance object PrivilegedRequestMiddleware Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks It must be registered before UseAuthorization. Authorization short-circuits on failure and never calls its next, so anything registered downstream of it is simply not entered when it refuses. This middleware used to sit after it, which meant the 403-to-428 rewrite below never ran: an operator whose step-up window had lapsed got a dead-end "Forbidden" on every moderation action instead of being asked for a code, since the browser keys its step-up prompt on the 428. The second job exists because AuditActionFilter is an action filter, and an action filter does not run when authorization refuses the request — so a refusal decided by policy left no trace at all. That is the gap this closes: an account probing endpoints it may not reach is precisely the pattern the audit log exists to make visible, and it is already what the in-game command gate records. Reads as well as writes, since 2026-09-14: every Game Master and Admin action is tracked, and a refused look at something above one's level is as much a probe as a refused write. A refusal is recorded even when the browser marked the request as an automatic refresh (X-Panel-Refresh: auto, see RefreshHeader). The action filter skips a marked read that it answered, because a page polling itself every few seconds would bury the log; this middleware never consults the header. A refused poll is a probe like any other refused request, the mark is the client's word and so worth nothing as an excuse, and refusals are rare enough that recording every one costs nothing. The header is only ever trusted for a read that was allowed; a write is recorded whatever it carries. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class RegistrationFormTokenService Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll The registration form's anti-bot token and its randomised honeypot fields. public sealed class RegistrationFormTokenService Inheritance object RegistrationFormTokenService Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why a signed token rather than a fixed hidden field. A honeypot with a fixed name is defeated once, by whoever writes the bot, and then forever. Here every form gets two or three decoy names drawn at random from names a form-filling bot or an autofill heuristic fills in (website, company, fax...), and the token binds exactly which names this form carried, so a bot cannot learn a list to leave empty from one page load and replay it. Why it is signed. The server keeps no per-form state. The token is base64url(json).base64url(HMAC-SHA256) under a random per-process key: a forged or edited token fails the MAC, and a panel restart simply invalidates open forms (the browser fetches a fresh one if the submit is refused and the user tries again after reloading). Why an age window. A form submitted less than MinimumAge after it was issued was not filled in by a person: a human cannot type an account name, an address, two matching passwords and pick an age in three seconds, and a script does it in milliseconds. A token older than MaximumAge is refused so a harvested token is not good forever. None of this tells the caller why it refused: Check(string, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>) returns a reason for the log, and the controller answers with the same message a genuine failure gets. This used to write the live secret and replace the live codes here, so a re-enrolment the player did not finish — a scan that never happened, a closed tab — left them with an authenticator that no longer worked and codes they may never have saved (issue #267). A first enrolment is staged the same way; confirming it is what turns two-factor on. A re-enrolment still needs a fresh step-up to start: whoever confirms holds the new authenticator, so without it a borrowed signed-in browser could swap the owner's for its own. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class ServerBandwidthRollupService Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Rolls the servers' bandwidth minutes into hours and enforces the retention of both tables, on a timer, so the Bandwidth page's 30-day figures and a year of history exist whether or not anybody has the page open. public sealed class ServerBandwidthRollupService : BackgroundService, IHostedService, IDisposable Inheritance object BackgroundService ServerBandwidthRollupService Implements IHostedService IDisposable Inherited Members BackgroundService.Dispose() BackgroundService.StartAsync(CancellationToken) BackgroundService.StopAsync(CancellationToken) BackgroundService.ExecuteTask object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Why here. The game servers write their own minutes and nothing else; a rollup there would run once per server process and compete with the tick. Nothing in the repository prunes on a schedule, and PostgreSQL has no scheduler without an extension, so the panel — the one long-running host that reads these tables — owns it, as it owns the maintenance advance (MaintenanceAdvanceService, which this is modelled on). Safe to run twice, and safe in two panels at once. Every hour row is recomputed from its minutes and SET, never added to, so repeating a pass changes nothing. Each pass takes a transaction-level advisory lock first and the second panel skips; the lock is there to keep two panels' multi-row upserts from deadlocking each other and their retention batches from fighting over the same rows, not for correctness of the numbers. See IServerBandwidthReportService. The first pass after this panel starts is a catch-up: it rolls every hour that still has minutes, covering however long no panel was running. Later passes roll the last RollupWindowHours hours, which reaches past the latest a server's retried minute can arrive. Retention folds each hour into its row before deleting its minutes, so a pass that deletes can never lose traffic the rollup had not reached. A failed pass is logged and the timer continues, for the reason the maintenance service gives: a transient database fault must not become a panel outage. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class SmtpSender Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll The panel's SMTP sender, configured exactly the way the LoginServer's is. public sealed class SmtpSender : ISmtpSender Inheritance object SmtpSender Implements ISmtpSender Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Configuration is deliberately identical to FishMMO.Server.Implementation.Smtp.SmtpService. The same environment variables (FISHMMO_SMTP_HOST and friends) take precedence over the same configuration keys (Smtp:Host and friends), so one set of credentials configures whichever process happens to be draining the queue. Two processes that had to be configured differently to send the same mail would be a trap waiting for whoever migrates the drain again. System.Net.Mail, and no new package. SmtpClient is formally obsolete for new work and MailKit is the better library — it speaks modern authentication, reuses connections, and is what Microsoft's own obsoletion notice points at. Taking a dependency is not a decision this change is allowed to make, so this uses the framework client, the same one the LoginServer already used against the same relay. If the relay ever needs OAuth or connection reuse, that is the moment to revisit it. EnableSsl means STARTTLS, not implicit TLS. The client connects in the clear and upgrades, which is what port 587 expects and what the intended relay wants. Implicit TLS on port 465 is not supported by this client at all — pointing it at 465 hangs until the timeout rather than failing usefully — so a deployment that only offers 465 needs MailKit, not a configuration change. Every message goes out as multipart/alternative: plain text and HTML. The previous sender set IsBodyHtml = true for everything, and three of the four bodies this system sends are plain text written with \n line breaks. Delivered as HTML those newlines collapse, and the result is one run-on paragraph with the code buried in the middle of a sentence — including a 43-character password reset token, which is exactly the kind of thing a reader has to be able to pick out and copy. Sending both parts also scores better with spam filters than either part alone. The missing part is derived here rather than stored. The queue carries one body column and gains no second one: the LoginServer's own verification mail is already HTML and cannot be changed from this side, so the sender has to handle an HTML body correctly regardless — and once it does, deriving in the other direction costs nothing and fixes every message already sitting in the queue. See FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services.EmailBodyParts for how each direction is decided, and for why an already-HTML body is never escaped or wrapped twice. Nothing here logs a body. A verification body carries the six-digit code and a reset body carries the token; both are credentials, and a log file is not a mailbox. The recipient, the subject and the outcome are logged, and that is all. Constructors SmtpSender(IConfiguration, ILogger<SmtpSender>) Reads the SMTP settings once, at construction. public SmtpSender(IConfiguration configuration, ILogger<SmtpSender> log) Parameters configuration IConfiguration log ILogger<SmtpSender> Remarks Once, because a relay that changes underneath a running process is not a thing operators do and a half-applied credential change is worse than a restart. Properties ConfigurationSummary One line naming where mail goes, or why it goes nowhere. Safe to log: it never contains the username or the password. public string ConfigurationSummary { get; } Property Value string Remarks Built once, at construction, and never contains the credentials — so the drain can log it verbatim on the way up, whether it says where mail goes or why it does not go. IsConfigured Whether this deployment has a relay worth talking to. public bool IsConfigured { get; } Property Value bool Remarks False is a supported state, not a fault. A panel brought up for development, or one standing in front of a shard whose mail goes out elsewhere, has no relay and should not be spending a database round trip every couple of seconds claiming messages it cannot deliver. Methods SendAsync(string, string, string, CancellationToken) Sends one message, returning whether the relay accepted it. public Task<bool> SendAsync(string to, string subject, string body, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters to string Recipient address. subject string Subject line. body string The stored body, either plain text or HTML. Both parts are derived from it; see SmtpSender. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancellation token. Returns Task<bool> True when the relay accepted the message; false for every failure, which is what the queue records as an attempt.

api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class SrpLoginService Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll The server half of the panel's SRP-6a login, using the same ServerSrpData and the same 2048-bit SHA-512 parameters the LoginServer uses. public sealed class SrpLoginService Inheritance object SrpLoginService Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The panel never sees a password. It answers a challenge with the account's salt and a public ephemeral, then verifies the client's proof; only the proof crosses the wire. An in-flight exchange has to survive between the two requests, so it is held in memory keyed by an opaque handle the browser echoes back. Memory rather than the database because it is worthless after ten seconds and worthless to anyone but the one browser that started it; the trade is that a panel restart mid-login makes the browser start again. Lockout. The password step is counted in the database, in the same columns the LoginServer counts into, under AuthLockoutOptions. A locked account is refused before its proof is evaluated, and the refusal is GenericFailure — word for word the answer to a wrong password — so the lock never becomes a way to learn a name exists or a guess was right. The lookup and the count run for unknown and banned names too, so the two paths also cost the same round trips. Constructors SrpLoginService(IAccountService, PanelRegistrationOptions, VerificationOptions, AuthLockoutOptions, IServiceScopeFactory, ILogger<SrpLoginService>) public SrpLoginService(IAccountService accounts, PanelRegistrationOptions options, VerificationOptions verification, AuthLockoutOptions lockout, IServiceScopeFactory scopes, ILogger<SrpLoginService> log) Parameters accounts IAccountService options PanelRegistrationOptions verification VerificationOptions lockout AuthLockoutOptions scopes IServiceScopeFactory log ILogger<SrpLoginService> Fields GenericFailure The one answer to every failed password step: wrong password, unknown account, banned account, expired exchange, and a sign-in that is locked. public const string GenericFailure = "That username and password do not match an account, or sign-in is temporarily locked after repeated failures. Try again later." Field Value string Methods ChallengeAsync(string, CancellationToken) Message one: look the account up and answer with its salt and a server ephemeral. public Task<SrpLoginService.ChallengeResult> ChallengeAsync(string username, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters username string cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<SrpLoginService.ChallengeResult> Remarks An account that does not exist, or that is banned, gets a plausible fake salt and a fake verifier. The exchange proceeds normally and fails at the proof, so the two cases are indistinguishable in both timing shape and response shape. This is the same property SrpService.DerivePerUsernameFakeSalt gives the game path. An unverified account gets its REAL salt and verifier, and is marked. A wrong password still fails exactly as it would for anyone; a right one is told which verification codes it may enter instead of being handed a session. Before this, the unverified account was faked, and a player who had simply not typed their code was told their password was wrong. There is no grace period. An account used to be let in until its first code had been delivered, which made "the mail relay is down" and "verification is required" the same thing for as long as the relay stayed down. Now an account owes a code from the moment it exists, and a player who never receives one reaches staff through the ticket three wrong codes open. Proof(string, string, string) Message two, with no lockout and no verification gate: a proof of the CURRENT password by a session that is already signed in (the password change). public SrpLoginService.ProofResult Proof(string handle, string clientPublicEphemeral, string clientProof) Parameters handle string clientPublicEphemeral string clientProof string Returns SrpLoginService.ProofResult Remarks The exchange is removed before it is evaluated, so a handle is single-use and a wrong proof cannot be retried against the same server ephemeral. SignInProofAsync(string, string, string, CancellationToken) Message two for SIGN-IN: the lockout, the proof, the failure count, and the verification gate. public Task<SrpLoginService.ProofResult> SignInProofAsync(string handle, string clientPublicEphemeral, string clientProof, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters handle string clientPublicEphemeral string clientProof string cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<SrpLoginService.ProofResult> Remarks The exchange is removed before anything else, so a handle is single-use. A locked password step is refused WITHOUT evaluating the proof, with GenericFailure. A failed proof is counted; the failure that starts a lock queues one security notice. A good proof clears the count. A proven, unverified account is issued its Discord code if it is owed one and has none, and is told which codes it may enter. VerificationRequiredMessage(AccountVerificationChannels) The one message naming the codes an unverified account may enter. public static string VerificationRequiredMessage(AccountVerificationChannels outstanding) Parameters outstanding AccountVerificationChannels Returns string Remarks Names every outstanding channel, because any one of them verifies the account: a player told only about the email may not think to look in Discord, where the code already is.

api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.title: Class TwoFactorResetFlow | FishMMO Documentation
api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class TwoFactorResetFlow Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll The self-service two-factor reset, for an account holder who has lost the authenticator AND every recovery code. public sealed class TwoFactorResetFlow Inheritance object TwoFactorResetFlow Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The rules this exists to keep. Only a session that has already proven the password may ask, and asking starts a waiting period (DelayDays). The holder is emailed immediately; any successful sign-in with the real factor during the wait cancels it (VerifyForSignInAsync(string, string, bool, CancellationToken)). A stolen password alone therefore buys a week's notice to the real owner, not an account. Asking again returns the same request. The clock is never restarted (that would let an attacker keep the owner's cancellation window open forever) and never shortened. Completing a reset never satisfies two-factor. It replaces the factor and hands the new one over; the session is promoted only after a code from the NEW authenticator is typed. The account is never left with two-factor cleared. The new secret overwrites the old one while totp_enabled stays on, and the recovery codes are replaced in the same step, so the game login demands the new authenticator from the moment the reset completes. Clearing first and enrolling second would leave a window — or, on a failed write, an account — with the password as the only thing in front of it. Completion is one transaction: the request is spent together with the new factor, or not at all. A failure part-way leaves the request pending and the old factor in place. A password reset never satisfies two-factor and a recovery code never resets a password: nothing here touches the SRP credentials, and PasswordResetService touches nothing here. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class UtcDateTimeConverter Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Serializes every DateTime with an explicit UTC designator. public sealed class UtcDateTimeConverter : JsonConverter<DateTime> Inheritance object JsonConverter JsonConverter<DateTime> UtcDateTimeConverter Inherited Members JsonConverter<DateTime>.CanConvert(Type) JsonConverter<DateTime>.ReadAsPropertyName(ref Utf8JsonReader, Type, JsonSerializerOptions) JsonConverter<DateTime>.WriteAsPropertyName(Utf8JsonWriter, DateTime, JsonSerializerOptions) JsonConverter<DateTime>.HandleNull JsonConverter<DateTime>.Type object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Every timestamp column in this schema is timestamp without time zone holding a UTC value — the columns are even named for it, occurred_utc, last_saved, time_deleted. EF reads them back as Unspecified, and System.Text.Json then writes an unspecified kind with no designator at all: "2026-09-11T02:10:00". A browser parses that as local time. Not as UTC, and not as an error — every date in the panel was silently shifted by the operator's offset, which on this developer's machine is seven hours. The failure is invisible precisely where it matters: a character "last saved 7 hours ago" that was in fact saved a minute ago reads as a stale row, and an audit entry appears to have happened in the future. Stamping UTC on the way out is a statement of fact rather than a guess: the value in the column is UTC. Reading accepts either form, so a client that does send a designator is not broken by this. api/webservers/FishMMO.ControlPanel.Serv.summary: Class VerificationOptions Namespace FishMMO.ControlPanel.Services Assembly FishMMO-ControlPanel.dll Which verification channels this server actually verifies (Verification:*). public sealed class VerificationOptions Inheritance object VerificationOptions Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A player chooses the channels they verify with at registration — email, SMS, a Discord DM, or several — and a code goes out on each one this server switches on. Any one correct code verifies the account. More channels give the player more ways to receive a code, never more codes to enter. Which channels an account is actually sent and asked for is AccountVerificationRules, shared with the login server, not anything decided here: when nothing the player chose is switched on, the account falls back to one that is, so switching a channel off never lets an account in without a code. A server with every switch off verifies nothing, and registration takes the same auto-verify path the development AutoVerifyAccounts setting takes — one mechanism, not two. These switches must match the login server's VerifyEmail, VerifySms and VerifyDiscord, or an account could be let into the game and refused by the panel, or the other way round. Unlike the development bypass these are honoured in Production. They are a deliberate shard policy ("this shard does not verify phone numbers"), not a convenience that must not escape a laptop, and a shard that turns them all off is told so loudly at startup. api/webservers/FishMMO.WebServers.Signin.summary: Class ManifestJsonWriter Namespace FishMMO.WebServers.Signing Assembly Patcher.dll Emits the exact JSON bytes a signed manifest is made of. public sealed class ManifestJsonWriter Inheritance object ManifestJsonWriter Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks This exists instead of System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer because the signature is over the literal bytes the client receives, and ASP.NET's serialiser is not a stable part of that contract: its naming policy, escaping table and spacing are framework configuration, and a future AddJsonOptions call somewhere in Program.cs would change what goes on the wire without anyone connecting that to "patching stopped working". Owning the emitter makes the wire format a property of this file. The format is fixed and minimal: "key": value, pairs separated by ", ". The ": " spacing is one of the two the client verifier accepts (it tries ": " first), and it is the one the blanked-signature placeholder is written in, so the emitted document and the canonical message differ in exactly one place — the signature value — by construction. Insertion order is preserved and never sorted. The client does not care about key order (it substring-searches for one field), but a stable order keeps the ETag, the logs and a human diff meaningful.
